<image-desc>A portrait illustration of an individual, likely of Central African origin, depicted from the chest up against a plain, light-colored background. The person has dark skin and eyes directed toward the viewer. Their face is decorated with bold, circular painted patterns in shades of red, black, and white around the eyes and on the cheeks.

On their head sits an elaborate ceremonial headdress consisting of several large, white, fluffy pom-poms arranged in a row. Centered above the forehead is a golden metallic ornament with ornate scrollwork. Three feathers—two long dark ones and one shorter white one—are tucked into the back of the headdress, pointing upward.

The individual wears multiple strands of red beaded necklaces around the neck. Over their shoulders and chest is a complex red fiber or cloth ornament, featuring bulbous segments and ending in pinkish tassels at the shoulders and at the center of the chest. The person is otherwise bare-chested. The style of the illustration is a detailed watercolor or color lithograph, typical of 19th-century ethnographic studies.</image-desc>

# FOREWORD

...through accident or adventure of our own, and it is for this reason that some personal incidents have been included.

I wish to take this opportunity to thank the chief officials of my own Colony for their more than kind encouragement, and the authorities of the <term>Natural History Museum</term> for their unsparing kindness and generous help. Regarding the assistance given by my wife and her sister, I should like to say more, but I am prevented by the very conditions under which their help was given.

# CHAPTER I

## ON THE WAY TO OBAN

The <term>Ekoi</term> people are divided into two unequal parts by the boundary that separates the <term>Cameroons</term> from <term>Southern Nigeria</term>. Their land is most easily reached by way of the <term>Kwa River</term>, which flows into the <term>Cross River</term> a few miles from the latter’s mouth. For some distance before this junction, the <term>Kwa</term> is too wide to allow for a good photograph; it is not until nearing the beach where the main <term>Calabar</term>-<term>Oban</term> road runs that one can be taken.

The banks are fringed first with mangrove and screw pine, then, further on, by palm trees. When the part is reached that the <term>Ekoi</term> proudly call “our own water,” the river narrows and becomes more beautiful. At its edge grow giant arums, green on the outer sheath but cream splashed with purple inside. Behind these grow trees of every variety of shape and color, from mimosas with their delicate mauve or cream balls and feathery foliage, to the huge trumpet-shaped flowers of the *<term>Gardenia physophylla</term>*, the heavily scented, purple-splashed blooms of the *<term>Kalbreyeri</term>*, or the great *<term>Berlinia</term>*, whose white flowers shine with a pearl-like luster from among its dim, dark leaves.

Here and there, at a bend, one comes across beaches of clear white sand glistening with mica, where crocodiles lie sunning themselves. On the only occasion when I went down the river, after having spent all my ammunition during a long “bush tour,” the Fate that presides over such matters arranged an interesting scene. On the branch of a great tree, which hung directly over the water, lay a creature such as I have never seen before or since. In shape, it was like a medium-sized crocodile, but with a flat snout like that of a pig, and with

<summary>This chapter introduces the geography of the Ekoi people's territory, specifically describing the lush vegetation and wildlife found along the Kwa River as it approaches Oban.</summary>
<keywords>Ekoi people, Kwa River, Southern Nigeria, Cameroons, flora, Gardenia physophylla, Berlinia, crocodiles, Oban</keywords>

six to eight black rings around its tail. As if aware of its perfect security, it lay quite still until we were almost level, and then slid out of sight.

Sometimes a monitor lizard slips from a fallen tree trunk as one draws near, or a great snake ruffles the surface as it swims across with a bird, just caught, in its mouth. Huge butterflies of gorgeous coloring flutter here and there, and now and then a flash of turquoise hangs for a moment over the water as a kingfisher swoops down, to rise again with a tiny fish.

These fishes, called <term>Tatabonko</term> by the <term>Efik</term> and <term>Ekoi</term>, hold an important place in song and folklore. A little <term>Efik</term> ode to them begins—

> “ Enyenne nmonn asanga nben Tatabonko.”
> “ You are the lords of the water. You walk near the banks. O tiny <term>Tatabonko</term>.”

Every few minutes a grey heron rises, and over a small island, near the place where a <term>Sierra Leonean</term> has made a rice farm, circle flocks of mole-grey birds with breasts of vivid rose.

Now and again a space is passed where the coarse grass has been cropped short by that strange creature, the <term>manatee</term>. Except for an elephant, this is the most valuable prize which can fall to the lot of the <term>Ekoi</term> hunter. <term>Egbo Societies</term>—those powerful secret associations which, before the arrival of the white man, ruled the land—are known to give as much as £10 to £15 for a large one. This is not only because its flesh is thought to be a delicacy, but because they believe that it confers magical properties on those who eat it.

Magic is the keynote to which the lives of the <term>Ekoi</term> are attuned. The river itself is magical, and bold indeed would be 그 man or woman who should break an oath sworn on its name. For somewhere in its depths dwells <term>Nimm</term>—the terrible—who is always ready, at the call of her female worshippers, to send up her servants, the beasts that flock down to drink and bathe in her stream, to destroy the farms of those who have offended. <term>Nimm</term> is, above all, the object of the women’s devotion. She manifests herself sometimes as a huge snake, sometimes as a crocodile. Her priestesses have more power than those of any other cult, and the society which bears her name is strong enough to hold its own against the dreaded “<term>Egbo Club</term>.”

# ON THE WAY TO OBAN

itself. It is during the rainy season that she is most to be feared. In 1909, at the height of the rains, one of my best paddlers was coming up with a consignment of goods from Calabar. Several of his friends were in the canoe, and they were all talking and laughing. Suddenly, as his hand neared the water on the downstroke, the head of a crocodile appeared above the surface. The cruel jaws closed on the man’s wrist, and in a flash he was dragged under. “Nimm,” whispered the terrified survivors as they paddled on, “Who knows? Perhaps he had angered his wife, and she prayed to Nimm to avenge her.”

As one passes up the river, further and further from Calabar and all it represents, one leaves behind not only one’s own race, but one’s century as well, and glides backward through the ages, up the stream of time, to the childhood of the world—to a land full of mystery and terror, of magic plants, of rivers of good and ill fortune, of trees and rocks, ever looming to engulf unwary travelers; where the terror of witchcraft stalks abroad, and where, against this dread, the most devoted love or faithful service counts for nothing.

After a while the banks grow steeper, and one enters a deep gorge which the water has worn for itself in the course of centuries. Down this rolls the thunder of the falls, and seems to shut out all sounds from the world one has left, just as the wilderness, creeping down around one, curtains off familiar sights. This gorge forms the boundary between the sedimentary deposits below and the crystalline rocks of the hilly country, of which the greater part of the Oban district is formed. The line of demarcation lies along this parallel of latitude to the Calabar River on the one side and the Akwa Yafe on the other.

Beyond Obutong beach, navigation is impossible, for the great curve of the first falls reaches from side to side in one white horseshoe. Above this again comes a stretch of foaming water, and then in rapid succession the higher falls, which are very beautiful for their size.

After landing on the little beach, a climb of about two hundred steps, as steep as the staircase of many an old house at home, leads to a three-roomed Rest-house. On the first morning of my wife’s arrival here, she was dressing with her sister Bimba

My wife was sitting at the end of a bamboo bench, which runs along the wall, trying to tear off the long marching boot which she had pulled on without taking the precaution of first shaking it upside down to make sure that neither snake, lizard, nor millipede was hidden within. For the moment, the foot was stuck fast; beneath it, something writhed and squirmed. One jerk and the boot was in my hand. I ran with it to the open house door, followed by “boys” and carriers, who crowded around with anxious, frightened faces, each armed with a stick or machete to kill the reptile as it fell. A violent shake, and the cause of the commotion slid into view—a small oval bar of Roger and Gallet’s soap! Roar after roar of laughter burst from the delighted carriers at the sight, and for the rest of the day we heard frequent bursts of merriment, or saw one of them suddenly double up with mirth as the memory overcame him.

The fear of snakes is no idle one, for they literally swarm in the District. On another occasion, when we were staying in the same Rest-house, my wife and her sister had both gone to bed, while I was still working in the central room. This time it was Bimba who called, and, on running in, we found her huddled up under a rug. A long snake had lowered itself from the roof onto her mosquito net, the frail strings of which threatened to give way under its weight and collapse, reptile and all, onto the little, shrinking figure beneath.

When the unwelcome visitor had been disposed of, it struck me that it would be well to make a thorough search of the roof. As a result, seven cobras from 4 to 6 feet long were accounted for. The roof was low, and I shot at close range, so that each snake fell down in several sections through the close crisscross of palm stems which form the inner roof. Each part seemed endowed with a life of its own, so that before the little adventure was over, the floors of the three rooms were literally covered with a carpet of writhing snakes. # ON THE WAY TO OBAN

He found a puff adder sleeping beneath one of the benches. Later investigations proved the holes were entrances to the homes of an entire family of these beautifully marked, sluggish reptiles.

This rest-house lies close to the road that runs straight from Obutong to Oban. Roads like this—though naturally broader and better in older districts—are cut through the heart of the dense “bush.” They now cross the country in every direction, replacing the winding native tracks, often hardly distinguishable from those made by wild animals, which were the only means of communication over a great part of Southern Nigeria until 1902.

One hears from certain sources back home about the hardships imposed on the local people by the construction of these roads. In an insignificant, sparsely populated district like Oban, not only the construction but also the maintenance requires a considerable amount of labor from the small population. However, no one is quicker than the locals themselves to recognize the advantages gained from such improved means of communication, whether regarding personal safety or trade facilities. Whatever the people of the district have been called on to do in this regard has always met with a cheerful and willing response. On several occasions, towns have offered, of their own free will, to do more than was requested of them, and in some cases, they have even built new sections of road on their own initiative as a surprise for my next visit to their part of the country. It would perhaps be unnatural if they were not willing to comply with the single demand made of them by the government in return for all that it provides, and even for this work, they are well paid.

The local people quickly realize the importance of the change. Not long ago, a well-known black lawyer was discussing the matter with a local clergyman in my presence on board an Elder Dempster liner. His voice was so loud that it could be heard from one end of the deck to the other. “You should go to Sapele,” he said. “There you can walk for 200 miles, as safe as here. This Governor * makes good roads. We call him ‘the road maker.’ I am a black man myself, but I tell you truly. It is only white men who can make the way safe.”

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

Not far from Obutong stands a compound known as “Nwan's,” which is now rapidly falling into decay. Around it, plantain and breadfruit trees are heavy with their unharvested fruit, while coconut palms tower behind them, laden with great green globes. Calabash vines trail in all directions over the deserted homes, but those who planted them are afraid to return and gather the fruits of their labor, for no “Juju” <note>Traditional spiritual power or charms.</note> seems strong enough to keep the restless ghost in his grave. In the words of his family, “Nwan returned too much and made us afraid.” So they migrated to Esuk Aram and left the abandoned homestead and the small grave by the road.

The road from Obutong to Oban is made of sand and gravel, firm enough for a bicycle, but the bare feet of the carriers make no sound upon it. It leads under a continuous canopy of branches, so thick that sunlight only filters through to dapple the roadway or sparkle on the many streams that cross it. All along the way, one sees the tracks of wild animals that use the road as well as their human brothers. Antelope, buffalo, wild pig, leopard, and elephant all leave their traces—the latter too often in the form of broken bridges, which, unfortunately, were not built with such heavy traffic in mind. Here, as everywhere in the district, the streams are crystal clear and ripple over pebbly beds or between boulders of quartz or dark gneiss. The Ekoi people consider the former of these stones to be male and the latter female. White, star-shaped lilies rise above the water. These are often nearly 6 inches across, and usually four or five of them grow on a single stem. They have a faint, sweet scent and are in bloom for most of the year. Occasionally, the road passes through a village with its “Egbo” <note>A traditional secret society or administrative house.</note> house and “Juju” tree, or a small side path or farm track branches off from the main route, where offerings to gods or ancestors are hung on poles.

Near several of the towns are fragile little huts made of posts driven into the ground, supporting a palm-leaf roof. Around these are scattered various pieces of property, such as plates, dishes, etc.—all broken—and cloths which were once brightly colored but have faded in the sun and rain. These are small funeral shrines, built over the graves of distinguished people. The items scattered around are broken, so that their

astral forms may be set free, to be borne by the spirit of their owner into the spirit world.

At each end of the village of Ekong, as in most Ekoi towns, dried palm leaves about 30 feet long are raised high. These are stripped bare, except for a tuft at the top, and from them dangle small wooden objects, much like the shape of a Muslim prayer board. They form a charm to keep leopards away from the town, as do also the sections of palm trunk which are found half-buried across the pathway, flanked at either end with a small earthen pot containing “medicine.”

After a 15-mile march, Oban itself is reached. At the entrance, as in all Ekoi towns, ghost offerings can be found, hung on either side of the way or buried in the path. These are meant to appease the spirits and keep them from entering the town.

The Ekoi have a wonderful folklore and are never at a loss for a story or legend to explain their customs or beliefs. Many—of which the following is, perhaps, the best-known example—deal with the practice of ghost sacrifices at the entrance to the towns.

A dirt path runs between the dwellings where a few small figures are visible. A caption below the drawing reads: "Charm against Leopards. Ekong."</image-desc>

### WHY GHOST OFFERINGS ARE MADE BEFORE TOWNS.

Once a tortoise had two children who were born on the same day. When only two days old, they began to fight together, and they were so equal in strength that neither could overcome the other. Three days later, they went to clear the brush and make a farm for their father. While doing this, they heard a far-off drumming. They followed the sound, and it led them to the ghost town.

The ghosts were beating their drum for a wrestling match. “Let us try if we cannot conquer these tortoises,” said they.

<meta>This page continues the Ekoi folklore story explaining why ghost offerings are made at the entrances to towns, following the introduction of the two tortoise children who were equal in strength.</meta>

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

The first tortoise stepped forward and defeated twenty of the ghosts, one after the other, so that they fell down dead; for even though ghosts have died once, they can die a second time and thus become more dead than before.

In this town lived a ghost named Ne-Achi-Esam (the Man with Twenty Heads), who was a great wrestler. He was lying down in his house, sick with a very large boil, but when he heard the noise of the fight, he ran out and wished to take part in it. He said to himself, “My boil will hold me back; what can I do?” He placed his hand upon the boil and, through magic, transferred it to a nearby post.* So the post caught the boil, and he himself became well again. He went out and said, “Now I will see what I can do against Tortoise.” They clashed, and he fought so well that Tortoise retreated before him. A large box had been brought out and placed near the drum. Ne-Achi-Esam drove Tortoise against this with such force that he broke in two and fell to the ground dead. After this, the second tortoise tried to avenge his brother but met with a similar fate.

Then the ghosts went and fetched magic “medicine,” which they rubbed on all their companions who had been killed, so that they came back to life. Next, they cooked “chop” and ate it. Afterward, they all went back into the bush to collect firewood with which to roast the two tortoises.

Now one of the ghosts had a beautiful daughter who was in the fatting-house.† She felt pity for the tortoises, and when the other ghosts had gone, she slipped out and gathered magic leaves. She crushed these and laid them on the mouths and eyes of the tortoises. After a while, the tortoises came back to life. She pointed out the road to them and said, “Here is your path. Go home now before the others return.” So they thanked her and departed.

As the two hurried along, they heard the sound of the ghosts returning with the firewood, so they hid themselves in the bush until the way was clear. When one of the ghosts reached the spot, he stood for a long time and said, “I think the two tortoises have escaped and are hiding here.”

# ON THE WAY TO OBAN

Then the ghosts called to the black ants and sent them to search for the tortoises; they also called water from the river and commanded it to flow around and seek them. In their terror, the tortoises cried for help to Obassi Osaw.<note>The Sky God.</note> Consequently, neither the ants nor the water could find them. At last, everyone gave up the search and went home.

When the way was clear once more, the tortoises crept out and hurried onward. After a while, they saw a bunch of ripe plantains. They took seven of these and went on again until they came to a place where the road branched in two. There, they laid down the seven ripe plantains and continued onward.

When the ghosts returned to their town and found that their prey had escaped, they said, “Let us follow.” They ran very swiftly until they came to the place where the plantains lay.

The first ghost saw them and began to count—1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6—he counted, but could not add 7. The second ghost pushed him aside. “Go away,” he said, “you know nothing of addition.” He also counted up to six but could get no further. Then all the ghosts tried, but none of them could add the seventh number.

Meanwhile, Obassi Osaw had seen the danger the tortoises were in and determined to help them. He counseled them to use every effort to reach their town and there prepare to receive their pursuers. “There is one thing you can do,” he said, “to keep the ghosts from entering your town. Kill goats and cows, get palm oil and palm wine, and lay them before the entrance. When they see these sacrifices, they will eat and go back satisfied to their own place.”

The tortoises did this, and when the ghosts came before the town, they found a rich offering. All of them ate and were well content, except for Ne-Achi-Esam alone, who said, “Let us enter the town”; but the others answered, “No, we may not enter.”

Since then, when ghosts come to your house seeking something, you inquire by the charm<note>See Method of Divination, p. 174.</note> what sacrifice they are asking; having found out, you take it to the beginning of the road and offer it there.

This is the reason why, whenever you near a town, you see sacrifices set out for the ghosts so that they should no longer enter inside.

<meta>This page transitions from the folklore stories of the previous section to a detailed ethnographic description of the religious rituals and medical practices of the Ekoi people at Oban.</meta>

# 10 IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

At Oban, there are two circles of uncarved stones, each arranged around a "Juju"<note>A West African term referring to an object, belief, or ritual used as a charm or fetish.</note> tree. Here, mystic rites are performed when the moon is full and at the rising of the new moon. The latter ceremony takes place near the compound of Chief Itaokui, not far from the "Egbo"<note>A powerful secret society, also known as the Leopard Society, prevalent in the Cross River region.</note> house, and it is here that one of the most important of the women’s "Jujus" is held. At the new moon, the women and girls gather together. The head women sit on the stones of the circle and distribute "medicine" made of meat and plantains, mixed with Juju herbs and leaves. Even the very young girls partake of this. When everything has been consumed, they begin a dance that is only performed on this occasion.

The purpose of the ceremony is to ensure fertility when the time comes for marriage, and it is firmly believed that any neglect of it would be punished by barrenness. If a woman especially longs for a child, she brings a goat to be sacrificed; she then stands within the circle and prays that a baby may be born to her. Her forehead is smeared with the blood of the sacrifice, and it is considered certain that her prayer will be granted within the year.

Neither men nor boys are allowed to approach during these rites, although women are not prevented from watching when the men gather to perform theirs before the Juju "Nchibbi." This ceremony is performed at the smaller circle when the moon is full. The scene on bright moonlight nights is incredibly uncanny; it is difficult for any European who has suddenly come upon such a sight to believe that he is still in the twentieth century and has not instead stumbled upon some witches' sabbath from the Middle Ages.

Near the larger circle of stones stands the miniature house of the Juju "Ta Amat," where the "smallpox medicine" and the medicine used to ward off epidemics are kept. When the people fear the approach of an infectious disease, the head chief enters the little hut and prepares "medicine" compounded of magic herbs. The people drink this, and it is given to all strangers, especially to those who may have come from an infected area. In this way, it is hoped that disease may be warded off, while inoculation is practiced as a further safeguard. This is done by injecting into the arm the milky

<header>### ON THE WAY TO OBAN</header>

...juice from the leaves of a certain tree planted nearby for that purpose.

Oban was chosen as the seat of government for the District because it sits at a high elevation and is easily reached from all parts of the Ekoi country. Half a mile from the town stands the station on a hill, the top of which had to be leveled to make a flat space large enough for the necessary buildings. This cleared land forms the most extensive open space in the District, and the view from the house is beautiful enough to make up for the simplicity of the structure itself. In front, beyond the River Ataiyo, rises the rounded hill of Oban, covered to the summit by masses of flowering trees, some of which are always in bloom. Behind this, the sun sinks in a perfect wonder of color; and perhaps the sunsets and sunrises, beautiful everywhere, are the most gorgeous sights of all this magnificent land. On all sides the “bush” sweeps down and closes in the little clearing, while to the rear, beyond this green belt, tower the blue peaks of the Cameroons.

From the top of Oban hill, a good view can be seen. To the north lie clusters of peaks of every shape and form, 3,000 to 4,000 feet high, wooded to the summit and forming the watershed of the country between the Cross River and the sea. To the south flow those streams which unite to form the Calabar, the Kwa, and the Akwa Yafe Rivers; while to the north flow many of the main tributaries of the Cross River.

The rocks of the District are mostly metamorphic, and the hill on which the station is built is a good example of the geological formation of this part of the country. It is mainly composed of <term>gneiss</term>; but there is a large vein of <term>manganese</term>, and huge masses of <term>quartz</term> and <term>felspar</term>, with <term>pegmatite</term> dykes running through all. Traces of <term>ilmenite</term>, <term>columbite</term>, <term>magnetite</term>, tin, and <term>monazite</term> are also to be found.

There is always a slight breeze here, and even to the most careless glance, the difference in health between those children who live on the hill—in the new, well-ventilated houses built for the station people—and their peers in Oban itself, is very marked. The Ekoi are devoted parents, but it will take years of patient teaching before they grasp the...

### IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

...the importance of fresh air and simple sanitary measures for the health of their little ones. They are very particular about personal cleanliness, especially regarding bathing and washing their clothes, but the old habit of crowding together for safety in case of an attack from a hostile tribe still influences them to build their compounds with small, poorly ventilated rooms. They seem completely indifferent to the presence of foul smells, and the high death rate among their children is chiefly due to this cause. Indeed, the death rate is so high that it is barely offset by the birth rate.

One day, sixty-two married women were chosen at random in the town of Oban. It was found that 270 children had been born to them, of whom 163 had died. This results in an average of 4.3 children for each woman, of whom only 1.7 now survive. Of these sixty-two women, one had given birth to fifteen children, and seven others had ten or more, while only four were childless.

Oban gives its name to the district; because of this and its location, it is regarded as the central point of their race by all Ekoi under British rule, and even by many on the other side of the border.

Perhaps, therefore, before going further, it would be best to pause here and attempt to give some account of the influences that have shaped the character of the people.

# CHAPTER II

## RELIGION

THE religion of the Ekoi is an altogether fascinating study. Its principal features are the cult of ancestors and of nature forces. These dominate the lives of the people to such an extent, and have such numerous ramifications, that it becomes impossible to arrange them definitely under headings or to say where one begins and the other ends. Ancestor worship, nature <term>jujus</term>, secret societies, the major events of life, and the most common daily actions all blend inextricably into a complicated ritual.

Of actual deities, there are only two: Obassi Osaw,* the sky god, and the earth god, Obassi Nsi; but there are countless hordes of less powerful spirits of trees, lakes, rocks, and rivers. The entire bush is populated with these supernatural beings; its dim twilight is thick with terrible, half-human shapes, similar to the werewolves of our own northern lands. Here, even more truly than in ancient Greece, the terror of Pan reigns supreme.

The shadow of the bush lies heavy over everything; but beneath the thousand superstitions that have grown like fungus in its dark places, one can still find traces of an older, purer form of worship—possibly a relic of that forgotten time when the Ekoi were a people living in open lands, swept by fresh air and bounded by wide horizons.

Indeed, on every hand, beneath modern corruptions and disfigurements, indications can be found of a form of worship that carries us back to the oldest known Minoan civilization and links the beliefs of the present-day Ekoi with those of the ancient Phoenicians, Egyptians, Romans, and Greeks.

In some ways, the Ekoi form may indeed be called the most ancient of all; for while in the oldest representations...

<meta>This page continues the comparison between Ekoi religious practices and ancient Minoan, Egyptian, and Mediterranean civilizations, specifically focusing on the symbolism of birds and trees.</meta>

of Minoan bird and tree worship which have come to light, the tree is shown almost entirely conventionalized into a pillar shape, and later as a mere pedestal for the bird; among the Ekoi it still keeps its original form, that of the actual, living tree.

The smallest town has its "Juju" tree. There are many varieties of these, but each stands alone, usually in an open space before the Egbo house. They are generally bound around with <term>tie-tie</term> <note>A local term for strong, flexible vines or creepers used as rope.</note>, or surrounded by a little fence decorated with linked rings of the same. On the branches of these trees hang countless nests of one kind or another of the weaver bird. Even the smallest child knows that these are sacred, for on them depends the prosperity of the town. Should they be injured or driven away, the women would become barren and the cattle would cease to bear young. The birds know that they are safe and flit fearlessly back and forth, keeping up such a loud twittering and crying that it is almost impossible to hear oneself speak in their neighborhood.

Surely in this we have the oldest depiction of the marriage of earth and sky—Sky Father and Earth Mother—for of all created things, the bird is most akin to the air and sky, while the tree, with its roots in the dark ground, reaching even (as in many Northern sagas) to the underworld, is the best and oldest personification of Mother Earth.

Another possible depiction of this mystic marriage was found painted on the inner wall of the Egbo house at Mbeban. What first struck me was an apparent representation of the Cretan double-headed axe, lying horizontally across a knobbed scepter. Over these again, diagonally, lies an Egbo feather. Without any hint from me, these signs were explained in a way which matched exactly with my own interpretation.

...ascends from below when vegetation springs up, and, at the same early epoch, gives visible proof of her presence in the sacred tree. Where, as was the case with the sarcophagus from Hagia Triada, we see the axe embedded in the tree trunk, there we must recognize the union of the sky-father with the earth-mother—a union essential to the fertility of crops, and beasts, and men. The axe embedded in a tree is the prototype of the axe embedded in a wooden column or a stalactite pillar. Ultimately, a double-axe of the usual type is found serving as a symbol of the united deities, the axe head being the male element and the axe handle the female element in their union.”

In the Ekoi representation, the cleft base of the axe may well be a highly conventionalized remnant of a pillar or tree, while the feather—now that of the peacock sacred to Egbo societies—probably in earlier days was merely a bird symbol. The two circles may well be intended as eggs, and therefore as indications of fertility.

In the course of the ages, strangely enough, Mother Earth has become Father Earth in Ekoi legend. The two principal deities, as has been mentioned, are now Obassi Osaw, the Sky God, and the Earth God Obassi Nsi. Still, enough legends and fragments of ritual have been collected to show that the older idea has not yet quite died out. This may be seen from the following conversation with Ndum of Nsan, one of the most interesting of the Ekoi. He is as yet practically untouched by “White” influence, knows no word of English, and is a mine of folklore.

“Who is Obassi Nsi?” he was asked.

“He is the Obassi who is kind to us,” he answered.

“Where does he live?”

“Under the earth. There is a world beneath the earth whose king is Obassi Nsi.”

“Which do you think is the more powerful—Obassi Nsi or Obassi Osaw?”

“Both are powerful, but Osaw is cruel and Nsi is kind and good.”

“Why then do you pray to Obassi Osaw?”

“Obassi Nsi told us to do so, so that Osaw might spare our lives, for the latter always seeks to kill us.”

“How do you know that Osaw is fierce and cruel?”

> "How do you know that Obassi Nsi is good?"

> "He never shows us terrifying things as Osaw does, such as thunder or lightning, nor the sun which blazes so hot as to frighten us sometimes, and the rain which falls so heavily at others as to make us think there will be no more sunshine. > "What do you think happens to you when you are buried?"

> "You said that you were told to make offerings to Osaw, in order that he might spare your lives. How then can Nsi, who does not want you to die, partake of these?"

Surely Nsi must be a woman and our mother, for it is well known to all people that a woman has the tenderest heart."

Another story in which a female deity also appears was told by Itambo Isom of Niaji.

### HOW THE POOR BOY CAME TO THE LAND OF OBASSI OSAW.

Two great friends once lived in the same town. One was poor and the other very rich, and each of them had an only son.

One day, the poor man died, and not long after, his rich friend also fell ill. The rich man therefore called the two boys and said:

“I do not think that I can live much longer on earth. I have gathered together everything necessary for the funeral ceremonies of my dead friend. When I die, I would like you two boys to live together.” Next, he told them to go to the farm and fetch yams. When these were brought, he said:

“Cut them into pieces and boil them. Mix them with palm oil, and let me try if I can eat once more.”

When all was ready, the boys brought the dish before him. He put some of the food in his own mouth and threw some on the ground, calling at the same time on the name of his late friend. Soon after the offering had been made, he himself died.

The two children did not know that their protector was dead. They thought only that he was very ill, so they left him and went out weeping.

On their return, they saw the body lying there and the yams left almost untouched. They ate these, then licked up the palm oil, washed the calabash, and hung it up again in its place.

Now, since neither of the fathers had any brothers or sisters, one of the principal men in the town took the boys to his house and cared for them. They grew up very quickly, and one day they left their foster father and went back to the rich man’s old compound.

Not long after, their former guardian saw them roaming and said:

“Why will you not live with me as you used to do? Come, let us go back to my house. You are not yet old enough to live alone.”

They answered, “We will not live in any house but our own.”

So the man was angered and said, “From today, I am finished with you. Never come to me again.”

The boys replied, “We are in charge of our fathers’ property. We have neither brother nor sister to share it with us. We are strong and healthy and can take care of ourselves until we are fully grown.”

When they were alone, the son of the rich man said to the poor man’s son, “Come, we must perform the ceremonies for the deaths of our fathers. Let us hold both funeral performances at the same time.”

The poor man’s son said, “I do not agree. My father died first. Let us go step by step.” So they began the rites for the death of the poor man. They killed two cows and two goats, and when all the initial customs were finished, they began those for the rich boy’s father. For him, they killed twelve cows and twelve out of their remaining fifteen goats. From what was left, the poor boy took one goat and the rich boy took two for their own.

The next day they bought a chicken. In the course of time, it grew to be a hen and hatched ten eggs, of which they each took five. Both tended the chicks, but a hawk came and carried off all those which belonged to the poor man’s son. A leopard also came and ate his only goat.

Then Mkpaw-Ekett (the poor boy) went to Nsuma-Mbi (the rich boy) and said, “A hawk has taken away all my chickens and a leopard has eaten my goat. My father is dead; I have no relations to care for me. I cannot endure such continued misfortune, and I wish, therefore, to hang myself and die.” The rich boy comforted him for that time, but next day, very early in the morning, Mkpaw asked:

“Do you have any eggs to give me so that I may go and make a sacrifice?”

Nsuma gave what his friend wanted and then went to work on his farm.

As the sun rose, the poor boy stood with the eggs in his hand. He looked up at the sun and held them so that they pointed toward it. “Male God! Female God!” he cried, “Will you open the gate for me?” Then the eggs slipped from his hand, and out of each flew a small chick. These surrounded the boy and flew with him up to the sky, to the kingdom of Obassi Osaw.

As he said this, he went to the box and asked for a fine cloth to give to his friend. When the cloth fluttered out from under the lid, Mkpaw said:
“Here is a gift for you, so that you may know I have truly come from the home of my parents.” At this, they were both very happy and began to dance.
Now, the rich boy had recently married. Hearing the sound of dancing and singing, his wife ran in. Before they could stop her, she grabbed the box to see what it was.
So both sons died.

consisting usually of a growing tree, a carved post, and a sacrificial stone, sacred to one or the other of the Deities. By far the majority of these are dedicated to Obassi Nsi, as is shown by the <term>coco yams</term> planted, or laid in a small heap, close by. Those of Obassi Osaw can easily be distinguished by the clump of <term>epiphytic ferns</term> <note>ferns that grow on other plants but are not parasitic</note> growing upon the tree trunk.

Before beginning the day's work, each man or woman who still follows the old custom takes a <term>calabash</term> of water and goes into the central court to wash. With eyes lifted to the newly risen sun, they pray:

> “ Eyo ofu, eyo egu, ’me eyange eyange.”
> “Sun of the morning, sun of the evening, let me be free from danger today.”

This is done because the sun is supposed to be appointed by Obassi to receive all prayers offered on earth and carry them before him.

Next, water is taken in the right hand and held high, while the name of Obassi Osaw is invoked. Then a little is taken in the left hand and poured out on the ground to request the protection of Obassi Nsi.

In all ceremonies, whether connected with <term>Juju</term> or ancestor worship, the names of the two Deities must first be invoked.

When the new moon is seen in the sky, every man, woman, and child comes out and offers a prayer in the following words:

> "'Mi mfe, 'Mi mfe ka osaw, nkaiyen njum ebi."
> "New moon, new moon in the sky, let me not see anything bad."

Or

> "'Mi kpe, afanikǒng akajoi na 'me."
> "This moon, let trouble not come to me."

# CHAPTER III

## RELIGION (*continued*)

Not far from Nsan, a town of some importance to the west, the road passes near a small lake. This is supposed to be haunted by the ghosts of the departed Ekoi and is regarded as the dwelling place of a great nature <term>Juju</term>, on which the prosperity of the surrounding country depends.<note>A far more beautiful example of a Lake of the Dead is to be found in the old home of the Ekoi, across the German border. For a description, see Chapter XIV.</note> A rumor of this lake had reached my ears, but when first asking for its location, the question was met with expressions of the blandest and blankest ignorance regarding the existence of any such thing. When the line of march was altered to search for it, the carriers begged to be excused from accompanying us and were therefore left behind.

A struggle through dense bush, in what seemed the most probable direction, brought us suddenly into a broad belt of fern. Through this we waded knee-deep and finally emerged onto a smooth stretch of grass, which was obviously a lake bed during the rains. Across this, we could see the edge of the water, which shrinks in the dry season until it is scarcely bigger than a large pond. The surface was still; not a ripple stirred the grassy fringe. Nearby grew bushes about ten feet high, covered with what looked, from a distance, like tufts of creamy flowers, but proved on closer inspection to be the nests of that curious and little-known creature, the tree-nesting frog.<note>*Hylambatus rufus.*</note>

One or two of our people had followed us to the edge of the water. Among these was Eyiddimfonni (Hater-of-the-rich), the Priest of <term>Eja</term>, a cult for the protection of farms and cattle, in which certain forms of thunder worship are also mixed. Eyiddimfonni volunteered the information that he and his

companions were very brave men to venture there, as the place was haunted by devils, into whose power fell all those who dared to set foot beyond the belt of fern.

Later, we learned that nothing must be allowed to trouble the water, even so much as at its very edge; otherwise, the guardians of the lake would be enraged and bring disaster, in some dire form such as famine or disease, on the whole countryside. The place is a sanctuary for all wild things, for no hunter would dare to penetrate the belt of fern in search of a wounded bird or beast which had fled there.

In walking around, we came upon no less than five crocodiles’ holes, and the tracks on the soft mud showed the owners to be “at home” in each case. These crocodiles are regarded as manifestations of the guardian spirits of the place, and therefore as especially sacred. Here by night come the ghosts of long-dead Ekoi, to drift in sad companies, hopeless and wailing, over the surface of the water. Even in the bright sunlight, the place has an uncanny look, and one can easily imagine that at midnight, when the white mists shimmer ghost-like in the light of the moon, people with the terror and mystery of the “bush” in their blood would rather sit chatting around the fire or dance by torchlight in the open spaces of the towns, than seek out this uncanny spot on the chance of holding communion with the spirits of their long-dead kin.

As we stood at the edge, gazing out over the water, its quiet was suddenly broken by a broad ripple, and little fish were seen to spring agitatedly above the surface. A great python was crossing, and this, we learned, shared with the crocodiles the guardianship of the Sacred Lake.

Everywhere in Ekoi mythology, the cult of the snake is found to be closely connected with that of the crocodile. In many of the <term>Egbo</term> houses, a representation of the former is to be seen modeled in high relief on the wall at the farther end, while the crocodile is usually found carved on the principal pillar. Those families who are members of the Cult of <term>Nimm</term>*, never drive a snake from their houses, but take powdered chalk and strew it before the visitor very softly, so as not to frighten it in any way. Possibly the cult of the snake and crocodile has descended from very ancient times. It is well known that both were honored in Egypt as tutelary gods; and if the Ekoi have migrated, as seems likely, from East Africa, it is probable that the original reason for deifying the snake and cat—that is, that these creatures were the primary hunters of the plague-carrying rat—lies behind the powerful snake cult, while traces of cat worship are still to be found.* Rats are a great pest throughout the land, and every possible means is taken to control them, though with little success.

In Egypt, the snake was not only the guardian of the house and tomb, but a snake goddess also presided over the harvest festival, held in the month of Pharmuthi or April. Doubtless, among other attributes, she was regarded as the protector of the harvested grain, and her cult grew from the practice of introducing non-poisonous snakes into granaries in order to protect their contents from predatory rodents. Nimm is also looked upon as the guardian of farms and crops, and her great festival falls at the time of the gathering of the new yams.

ten ambassadors to Epidaurus to confer with the Aesculapian priests. Valerius Maximus tells us how the tribune Quintus Ogulnius, chief of the embassy, returned with the snake sacred to the god of healing, and how a temple to Aesculapius was subsequently built on Tiber Island. A beautiful medallion of Antoninus commemorates this event. A galley is represented passing beneath a bridge, and from its prow, a snake moves toward the figure of the Tiber god, who stretches out his right hand in a sign of welcome. This legend, I have no doubt, refers to the introduction of rat snakes in Rome for the purpose of destroying rats and thus stamping out the plague. In fact, Pliny clearly states that “the Aesculapian serpent was imported to Rome from Epidaurus; it was kept in the public <margin>|</margin>edifices, and also in private houses” <insert>/</insert> and we know from Aelian and other authors that the Egyptians kept domestic snakes in their houses and looked upon them as tutelary gods. <insert>/</insert> Indeed, from the remotest antiquity throughout the East, snakes were kept in houses for the purpose of destroying rats and preventing diseases carried by rats. Certainly, non-venomous rat snakes are a far better protection against plague than cats or dogs because they are not likely to harbor fleas. For years I have thought that the guardian snakes painted on the walls of Roman houses might be a vestige of the long-forgotten introduction of rat snakes to save Rome from the plague. Only a few days ago, in looking through Dyer’s book on Pompeii, published in 1871, I came across the figure of a painting found in a baker’s shop on the Via Consularis. In this fresco are represented the two guardian serpents moving, as usual, toward an altar placed between them, on which is placed the incense-yielding pine cone sacred to Aesculapius, but above each snake is a bird darting after a fly. The tail, which is considerably shorter than the wing, the peculiar markings, and the very action in which they are represented—catching flies on the wing—show that these birds are the common spotted flycatcher. The association of the snake with the flycatcher, a bird even at the present day kept in the houses of Southern Italy for the purpose of destroying flies, proves beyond doubt that the tutelary reptile is also depicted here as an emblem of a pest-destroying animal. Early in 1909, an official, who was passing through the District, mentioned that in the course of his tour he had visited a tribe where the snake cult seemed very strong.

One of the carriers happened to kill a small python. He carried it back to camp, cut it into several "lengths," and laid one or two of these on a dish in preparation for cooking. News of what he had done reached the chiefs of the town, and they came in a body, followed by an excited crowd, to ask that the man should be punished for his sacrilege. They also demanded the machete <note>machete; a large, heavy knife used as a tool or weapon</note> with which the snake was killed, the dish on which it had lain, and a considerable fine to appease its "manes" <note>the deified spirits of the dead</note>, so that it would not return to trouble them.

A superstition connected with this cult came to light in July 1911.

On our return to headquarters after a "bush" tour, the warder mentioned in his report that a python, some 22 feet long, had been killed close to the prison. He had ordered this to be skinned and had himself witnessed the extraction of the "bad parts," which he had intended to bury in a deep hole in a place known only to himself, so that they could not be used by witchcraft to harm anyone. Before these could be buried, one of the chief clerks had demanded that they should be given up to him. At first the warder refused, but afterwards, reflecting that, while the Commissioner was away from the station, this clerk was his representative, he gave up the parts in question on the distinct understanding that they were to be kept for my return. Needless to say, they disappeared.

<margin>vertical pencil line</margin>
Subsequent inquiries brought out the information that the most dreaded portion of these "bad parts" is the gall. This, used in a certain way, is capable of producing the most dire results. Of all animals, the snake and leopard are most feared for the magical properties of their gall. This will be seen from the following legend told by Ojong of Oban.

One of the slaves thought to himself, "I will ask my master why the gall is always taken away before the meat is shared." He did so, and the master explained that the gall was a strong "medicine" and would cause death if mixed with food or drink.

When the slave had learned this, he called together all his fellow slaves and explained to them how galls could be used as poison. Then they plotted among themselves and said, "Let us kill the free-born and become free ourselves."

Now, one of the slave girls loved her mistress and could not bear for any harm to come to her, so she said, "Tomorrow, touch no food and drink no water in the house; only come into the bush with me, and I will bring you all that you need."

The woman, however, paid no attention to what her slave had said, but drank what was offered to her by other servants and died soon after. She left a tiny baby girl, and when the slaves prepared to leave the town and called to the faithful maid to go with them, she said, "I cannot come; I will not leave my mistress's child." When they urged her, she took up the baby and carried it with her.

After they had gone a little way, her sweetheart came and said, "What are you doing? All the other free-born are now dead. Give me the child so that I may kill it too."

The girl saw that her charge could never be safe among the slaves, so she turned and ran back from where she had come. When she reached her late mistress's house, she laid the child down inside and shut the door. Then she went back again to rejoin her companions.

One day the son of Obassi Nsi went hunting in the bush. After a while he came to a ruined village, in which only one house was still standing unharmed, and smoke was rising from it. He went up to it and there saw a beautiful girl who had evidently just come out of the <term>fatting-house</term>. The room was empty except for herself and a great number of calabashes. She was so beautiful that he wished to have her as his sweetheart. She was willing, so he stayed with her for some time and then went back home.

Another day he went to visit her again and asked, “Do you live here alone, or is anyone with you?” She would not answer this. After a while he began to ask her to go with him to his father’s town, but in the end he had to go alone, because she was afraid to leave Calabash.

After the young man had gone, Calabash said to her foster child, “Next time your sweetheart comes, go home with him.” The girl answered, “Why should I go and leave you alone?”

That night, the son of Obassi said to his parents, “While I was hunting I found a town in the bush, and in it lived one very beautiful girl dwelling alone. I married her, but she will not leave her home and come with me.” His father answered, “Tomorrow I will send my people with you to bring her here.”

Next day, the Prince set out with a large procession, and when Calabash saw them coming, she said to her foster child, “Let us go now with your husband; only remember one thing. Pot and I take the place of your mother. Allow no one to borrow us from you.”

The woman came and sat down by the fireside. She turned around and saw Calabash. She recognized her at once and took her in her arms, weeping as she held her. The girl said, "Do you not recognize me as well? I am the child of your former mistress."

The slave went out and sought Obassi Nsi. "I am the foster mother of your son's wife," she said. "After me, Calabash came and took care of her. The slaves killed all the free-born people in the town with leopard gall. Among them, the girl's mother also perished."

When Obassi heard this, he called forth the Nsibidi * images and ordered them to go through the whole town and put to death all the slaves who had killed the free-born.

This was done. Then Obassi called the townspeople before him and said, "From now on, the free men must keep the gall themselves. It must never again be entrusted to the slaves."

That is the reason why we maintain the custom even to this day. For after a kill, when it is time to divide a leopard or a snake, no slave may go near until the leading men in the town have removed the gall.

---

By the side of the main road, at the point nearest to the Sacred Lake, stands a huge cotton tree draped with strips of cloth and other votive offerings. This is the special Juju tree for the town of Nsan. In this spot, therefore, the spirits of both the woods and the water may be worshipped in close proximity.

Giant trees grow everywhere in the bush, each with some special magical property, but perhaps the cotton trees are not only the tallest of all, but the most dreaded. It is difficult to obtain good photographs of such trees because of the density of the surrounding bush, which would take too long to clear for a sufficient distance. The one shown in the illustration is a relatively poor specimen that happened to stand at the edge of an open space.

Should a man or woman among the Efik or Ekoi wish to avenge themselves on an enemy, a certain way of bringing this about is to seek out one of these great trees in a lonely part of the bush.

# RELIGION

If the petitioner is rich and of the Efik race, a white bull should be offered in sacrifice, together with a dish of rice flour and a flagon of palm oil. For the poorer Ekoi, a white cock, or even a smaller offering, may suffice.

The name of the enemy is called aloud. The <term>Genius of the tree</term> hears, and from then on lies in wait to take revenge. Should a child be born to anyone so cursed, the tree takes possession of it. Such a child will see strange black shapes from its birth and be haunted by the demons of the bush. In time, the tree will seize and imprison the child, unless some powerful <term>Juju</term> man can be found to make strong “medicine” and so deliver it. There are two well-known ways of giving this “medicine.” It should either be poured upon a lump of brass, from which anklets are made for the child to wear, or the face must be cut and the medicine rubbed in. Either of these methods will prevent the Genius of the tree from obtaining possession of its victim, though it may trouble him through dreams and visions until about the age of eight years.

For those too poor to provide a bull, or any costly sacrifice, there remains another and more dreaded way of enlisting the services of the Genius of the tree. A man may buy vengeance, wealth, or power by offering himself. For a certain time, he will enjoy the fruits of his sacrifice, but at length the call comes, and he must go, to exist, imprisoned like Ariel within, as long as the tree lasts.

On December 5, 1908, a case came up in court against a man who killed his brother by forcing him to undergo the ordeal of eating <term>Esere bean</term>, in order to clear himself from the charge of trying to imprison their sister within a tree.

On another occasion, an accident revealed the fact that tree affinities are well known among the Ekoi.

One Sunday evening, cries were heard coming from the quarters occupied by the staff at Oban. Soon after, the Corporal was seen running toward the District House, with a torn tunic and a distracted air.

It seemed that one of the warders, named Oji, had suddenly become delirious and tried to run away into the bush. It was after the hour when station officials were supposed to be in

On my arrival, Oji stopped struggling and begged to be allowed to leave at once because his tree was calling.

In reply to questions as to what this might mean, he said:

> “I come, as the District Commissioner<note>The abbreviated form of District Commissioner used by the local people.</note> knows, from the country of the Ibos. There, the Oji trees grow and flourish—some in the water and some on dry land. To everyone who, like me, bears the name of the tree, a call comes at certain times of the year. When we hear our trees calling, no matter where we may be, we must set out at once, by night or day, and run until we reach the place where they grow. We cannot stop for anything until we reach them.
>
> “Tonight I was very tired and lay down on my bed. In my sleep, my tree began to call, ‘Oji, Oji!’ I woke up and still heard it calling. So I jumped up to run out into the night. It always calls around the time of the new yams—sometimes earlier, sometimes later. When they tried to stop me, it called louder and louder. So I fought them to get away and go to my tree. That is all.”

The torn uniforms and bruised limbs of the policemen seemed to prove that it was quite enough, indeed!

The policemen, mostly Yorubas, listened with an air of disdain to the “bushman’s” foolish story. Several of the Ekoi, on the other hand, who had come to find out the cause of the disturbance, eagerly claimed that such things happened in their country as well, and that once the call is heard, every man must follow it.

There are many stories about tree voices and the ceremonies necessary for invoking the help of the <term>Genius of the tree</term>. Perhaps the following is the best known of these stories.

One day they went together to the banks of the River of Good Fortune,<note>See page 90.</note> which flowed not far from their hut, and there prayed to <term>Obassi</term> to send them a child.

When they had prayed for a long time, the man asked his wife to help him back to their house. Some weeks later she told him that she thought their prayers were to be granted, and from this time on he prayed more and more fervently.

One day a son was born to them. He came into the world bearing a <term>Juju</term> knife in one hand and a small <term>calabash</term> full of <term>Juju</term> in the other.

When the father saw such an extraordinary child, he trembled and would have run away; but the infant said, “Do not be afraid, I am sent by <term>Obassi</term> to help you, because you have only one leg and one arm.”

His mother brought him the usual offering of rainwater—or <term>plantain</term> juice if no rainwater is to be had—which is always given to newborn children. This the infant refused and said in a strong voice, “Give me no water. Bring me food to eat.”<note>Compare this to the birth cry of Gargantua.</note>

Seven days after his birth, the child could walk alone. People said, “How is it possible for a week-old child to do such things?”

The boy answered, “It is because I am sent from <term>Obassi</term>. My younger brother will be coming soon.”

One day he took his <term>Juju</term> knife and held it out in his hand. The blade bent downwards of its own accord. He straightened it and held it out again in a different direction. A second time it bent. A third time he did as before, but this time the knife stayed straight and pointed into the bush. The boy followed the path which the knife showed. After a time, he came home and said to his mother, “Give me one single <term>plantain</term>.”

She did as he asked, and he took the fruit and went out. He plucked leaves in the bush, mixed them with the <term>plantain</term>,

The tree called out and he answered. It said to him, "Where are you going?" He answered, "I go where I choose, for the 'bush' is the town of my parents."

The cotton tree said, "Not so. This place belongs to me. Therefore, prepare a sacrifice of young palm leaves, palm oil, palm wine, meat, and twisted vines. Before you offer it to me, call on the name of your true father, <term>Obassi</term>."

The boy did as he was told and then went into the bush. Soon he heard the sound of a drum. At this, he returned and said to his foster father, "I think there must be a town in the bush, for I heard a drum being played."

The next day the boy set out again, and once more heard the sound of the drum, beaten as if for a wrestling match. He followed the sound and came eventually to a ghost town. In his hand, he carried the <term>calabash</term> of "<term>Juju</term>," which made him invisible. So he passed unseen through the town until he came to the <term>Egbo house</term>, near which the Lame Boy* lived. There he saw ghosts wrestling together. A <term>matchet</term> lay on the ground, and he noticed that if one ghost succeeded in throwing another against it, the latter died.

After a while, the newcomer wished to join in the wrestling, so he set aside his <term>calabash</term> of <term>Juju</term> and became visible to the ghosts. He started to wrestle. For a time, he was successful and defeated several of his opponents, but eventually, one of them forced him backward onto the <term>Juju</term> <term>matchet</term>. The boy died, and the wrestling continued until only one ghost was left alive. Afterward, this ghost made <term>Juju</term> medicine for the others, and they became as they were before. Only the boy was left lying dead.

All the ghosts then went into the bush to get firewood in order to roast their visitor so that they might have a great feast. But before leaving, they called the fowls and set them to guard the body. To one of the cocks they said:

"Watch well, and if you see the Lame Boy go near the dead body, crow loudly so that we may hear."

After they had all gone, the Lame Boy said to himself, "I am sorry for the boy."

He went and got corn and threw it on the ground before the fowls. They all ran to eat it and forgot their duty.

Now, when the ghost made the <term>Juju</term> medicine to revive his dead companions, he had made more than was necessary, and what was left he threw into the inner compartment of the <term>Egbo house</term>. While the fowls were busy pecking at the corn, the Lame Boy went there and got what remained of the magic medicine. He put this on the dead boy's eyes, and the boy stood up. When the Lame Boy saw that the stranger was alive once more, he said:

"Take your calabash of <term>Juju</term> and go home quickly."

The lad set out but had not gone very far before the fowls had pecked up the last grains of corn which the Lame Boy had thrown down for them. They therefore went back to keep watch over the corpse but found it gone. So the cocks crowed to call back the ghosts. These came hurrying in with their firewood but found that the visitor had been brought back to life and had fled from them.

Then the ghosts said among themselves, "Let us pursue him; perhaps we may yet overtake him."

When the boy reached the cotton tree, he told everything that had happened to him in the ghost town. Cotton Tree said, "When you reach home, cook <term>fufu</term> * and fresh plantains and offer them up in front of your father's house."

The boy had just enough time to do this before the ghosts arrived. They found the place spread with offerings, so they ate these and returned home. After that, he took a chicken and some palm oil and went and placed them before Cotton Tree. The tree accepted them and said:

# CHAPTER IV

## EGBO

The whole country is honeycombed with secret societies, among which the Egbo Club is the most powerful. Before the coming of the "white man," this institution ruled the land, and even now it has more influence in many ways than the Government itself, and has caused endless difficulty to administrators.

The Ekoi claim to have originated the whole idea of such clubs, which have existed among them for centuries, and are mentioned in some of their very old folklore tales. Later on, the Ododop and other tribes near Iffianga, Akwa, and Efut in the South Cameroons started a similar society, which gradually became more powerful than the original Ekoi one, and therefore more costly to join. The Efiks of Calabar were not slow to perceive the advantage of such institutions, and so founded the Ekkpe Club, which, with the growing importance of their town through the coming of white men, soon became the wealthiest of all Egbo Societies.

As the Efiks held the monopoly of the Calabar trade, they and their club obtained great influence over the Ekoi, who found it advisable to adopt many Efik customs and laws. This was especially the case with the Ekoi who live to the south of Oban, and therefore nearest to Calabar. Those to the north still keep their old Egbo practically unchanged, except for the inhabitants of Ndebbiji, who have adopted that of the Ododop people, which is almost the same as the Efik one.

Calabar was practically the only place where the Ekoi could obtain guns and gunpowder. To reach it, they had to pass through Efik territory. The roads were picketed by the latter people, and it was impossible to reach the factories except by their goodwill. Even if some men from the interior managed to reach a white official and attempted to lay their

It explains how the Ekoi originated these societies, but the Efiks of Calabar eventually developed the wealthiest version, using their trade monopoly to exert influence over neighboring tribes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the power dynamics between the Efik and Ekoi people, specifically how the Efik used their positions as interpreters and court officials to exploit the Ekoi, and transitions into the history and totemistic origins of the Egbo (Leopard) Society.</meta>

grievances before him, the Efik interpreter took care that the true state of affairs was not translated. If a case was tried in the Calabar Courts, the only chance a “bush man” had of winning was to enlist the help of some powerful Efik, and often the only way to do this was to promise to become his “member.” The methods by which Efik traders entrapped first one man and then his whole family into slavery were often extremely cruel. The only leverage the Ekoi held over their persecutors was that the Efiks feared their <term>Jujus</term> and wanted the dried meat killed and preserved by Ekoi hunters. The establishment of a Native Court at Oban did not improve matters much. Indeed, in some ways, it made them worse, as the clerk who ran it was always an Efik and ensured that judgment was given in favor of his own people.

It is natural that the most powerful society should be named after the most dreaded inhabitant of the bush, for “<term>Egbo</term>” is supposed to mean “<term>Ekkpe</term>” to the Efik and “<term>Ngbe</term>” to the Ekoi—that is, Leopard.*

Possibly among the Ekoi, where totemism is still an article of belief—though most of them will deny the existence of any such idea—the Leopard Society originally consisted only of those who belonged to this totem. On account of the animal's superior cunning and power, it would naturally attract the largest following. Later, as totemism began to lose its influence, first one and then another prominent individual who was not, strictly speaking, a “Leopard soul” might have been allowed to join, until it gradually became open to everyone.

There are many indications which seem to prove beyond doubt that some form of totemism still plays a part in the ritual of the Egbo Society. For instance, at some of the larger

On another occasion, a prominent member of the "<term>Egbo</term>," who had the reputation of knowing more "<term>Nsibidi</term>"—a primitive secret writing much used in this part of the world—than any man now alive, was asked to give me a little help in the study of this script. He refused to give any further information and soon after went away.

The importance of the society is obvious even to the most casual visitor to any land where it has gained a foothold, for the Club house is the main building in every town. Even the smallest village has its <term>Egbo</term> shed, and when a town decides to relocate, the first thing done—as soon as the new site is cleared, before even new farms are established or the land divided up—is to fix the position of the Club house. A small shed, called <term>Ekpa Ntan</term> (the house without walls), is built to mark the spot where the <term>Egbo</term> house is to stand.*

The multifaceted character of <term>Egbo</term> may be judged from the immense powers which it has claimed for itself in almost every direction. Under native rule, it took over practically all functions of government, made trade almost impossible for non-members, and exercised a deep influence on the religious and mystical side of the nation.

The ritual is certainly very ancient, and in it many <term>Juju</term> cults are mixed. The name of <term>Obassi</term> is called upon before every sacrifice, and an offering of food and drink is laid in front of the

<term>Etai Ngbe</term> (Leopard stone), the cut stone usually found before the second pillar of the Club house.*

It is difficult to discover more than the slightest fragments of the secrets of <term>Egbo</term>, as any known informant would face a swift death. Still, from what has been gathered—mostly, as in the case already mentioned, from fragments of song sung during various performances—there seems to be a close resemblance between these secrets and the Eleusinian and ancient Egyptian mysteries. Certainly, a considerable amount of hypnotism, clairvoyance, and spiritualism is taught, and far too many proofs have been given that some of the powers of nature are known and utilized by initiates in a way forgotten by or unknown to their white rulers.

For instance, some of the esoteric members seem to have the power of calling up shadow forms of absent people. Once, a display of this nature, given in the central courtyard of the compound of one of the head chiefs of Oban, was described to me.

It was midnight, and a bright moon was shining. In the open space at the center of the compound, a fire was burning. On this, "medicine" was thrown from time to time, which caused clouds of smoke to rise. These subsided, except for isolated "puffs," which after a time took on a definite shape.

The spectators sat on the ground in a semicircle behind the fire, facing a low mud wall. Beyond this, against the background of the moonlit sky, dark silhouettes began to pass, each clearly recognizable as that of some person known to be absent at the time. There was no sign of any artificial means of producing these shapes, which continued to pass for about fifteen minutes, at the end of which they grew faint and finally faded.

The chiefs claimed to have the power of calling up the shadow shapes of white men, but no case in which this had actually been done was cited.

There are seven grades which the aspirant must pass before he can be admitted to the deeper teaching or the revelation of any but the lesser mysteries. All may be entered by young boys, provided their fathers are wealthy enough to pay the necessary

1. <term>EKPIRI NGBE</term>. Small Egbo.

2. <term>EBU NKO</term> (an old word, the meaning of which is unknown). At a dance given by this grade, members must always wear their best clothes. Aspirants to each of these are marked with white chalk on both arms.

3. <term>MBAWKAW</term> (an old <term>Ekoi</term> word adopted by the <term>Efiks</term>). Aspirants to this grade are marked on the forehead with <term>Ekui</term> (cam-wood dye). These three grades are collectively called <term>Abonn Ogbe</term>, that is, children of the <term>Egbos</term>. They are neither important nor expensive to enter.

4. <term>NDIBU</term> (an old word of unknown meaning, equivalent to the <term>Efik</term> <term>Nyampke</term>). This is the second division, and it is considered a great honor to belong to it. It is often called “The Mother of the Grades.” Its president holds the second place in the entire society. If it were found necessary to expel a member who had reached this grade, death followed as a matter of course, so that none of its secrets would be revealed by the outcast.

When a man joins <term>Ndibu</term>, the head chiefs and officials stay in the <term>Egbo</term> house, while the young men dance and play around the town. The aspirant's best friend brings forward a calabash containing a leg of meat and two bottles of palm wine. The postulant then enters the clubhouse and sits down before the Chief, who puts powder on his head and recites all the names of the <term>Egbo</term>. The new member then rises and invokes the names in turn, while after each name, the chiefs call out “Owe,” that is, “our own.” He then goes out and dances with the young men. The performance is carried on for about eight days, during which time palm wine and meat are supplied to all.

At the present day at <term>Oban</term>, entrance to this grade costs about £30, which must be paid before full membership is allowed.

5. <term>OKU AKAMA</term> (the priest consents). This grade is not very expensive to enter, nor is it considered of much importance, but it must be passed before higher grades can be reached. The postulant is marked with yellow dye (<term>Ogokk</term>) on the abdomen and the back of his shoulders.

The old <term>Ekoi</term> grade was called <term>Asian</term>, but when <term>Oban</term> adopted the <term>Calabar</term> <term>Egbo</term>, the <term>Efiks</term> insisted on this being suppressed.

6. <term>ETURI</term> (metal or brass rod), <term>Efik</term> <term>Okpokgo</term>. In the old days during a ceremony, all fires had to be extinguished and no noise of any kind was allowed in the town. Formerly, very few men succeeded in reaching this grade, but now it is usually completed on the same day as

7. <term>NKANDA</term>, the highest and final grade. <term>Oban</term> took this from the <term>Efiks</term>, who again insisted on the destruction of the old <term>Ekoi</term> equivalent “Isong,” and of another old grade “Mutanda,” of slightly less importance.

<term>Nkanda</term> is more expensive than any other grade, and most men only enter it late in life. When a man has succeeded in joining this high grade, he is rubbed on his head and chest with yellow powder (<term>Ogokk</term>). Five rings are marked on his front and back. Two yellow ones, one around each breast, a white one in the center a few inches below, and, beneath this again, two more yellow ones, forming a square with those on the breasts.

On the back, the rings are arranged in the same way, but the central one is yellow and the four outer ones are white. The arms are decorated with alternating stripes of white and yellow, and until the last rite is finished, the man goes bare except for a long loincloth which reaches from his waist to his feet.

The chief of <term>Nkanda</term> is the president of the <term>Egbo Lodge</term>, and by far the most powerful man in the town. His office is sometimes hereditary, and only free-born chiefs can aspire to it. In the old days, a slave could not join <term>Egbo</term>, for fear that he might reveal its secrets to a new master. He could, however, be present at most of the ceremonies if his owner was a member of <term>Egbo</term> and permitted it.

One of the primary insignia of the <term>Nkanda</term> grade is called the <term>Ekabe</term> (<term>Efik</term> <term>Ekarra</term>) <term>Nkanda</term>. This is a type of hoop covered with bright-colored cloth. The attendant whose duty is to carry this performs many strange movements with it. He is required to hold back the <term>Okum</term> (or “image”) by its means if the latter, in a state of excitement, seems about to show himself to a non-member—particularly a woman—at a time when this is not permitted. Another symbol, used by both <term>Nkanda</term> and <term>Ebu Nko</term>, is the <term>Effrigi</term> (see drawing), a sort of wooden fan on which <term>Nsibidi</term> signs are inscribed.

The head priest of the whole <term>Egbo</term> Society is called <term>Iyamba</term>; the old <term>Ekoi</term> equivalent for this title was <term>Musungu</term>.

Other officials are the <term>Murua</term>, who carries the rattle during “plays,” and the <term>Isua</term>,<note>This is also the name given to a particular dance never performed except upon the death of one of the chief members, such as the <term>Iyamba</term>, or when fulfilling the latter’s “funeral rites.”</note> who is the master of ceremonies for the <term>Abonn Ogbe</term>. The head of each grade is called <term>Ntui</term> (chief) and acts as treasurer.

Those who belong to the four higher grades, and have paid their fees in full, may join in another ceremony called <term>Mariba</term>, or <term>Etem-I-Ngbe</term> (the bush leopard). This is performed in the depths of the forest with the greatest secrecy. It is during the “<term>Mariba</term>” that the successive mysteries are unveiled. The ceremony may also be performed at the funeral rites of very great chiefs.

The danger faced by non-members on such occasions, before the arrival of British rule, may perhaps be better understood by a case that happened not long before my arrival to establish the District.

During the “<term>Mariba</term>,” the sacred images, etc., are carried to a part of the forest where a little hut of green boughs has been built to receive them. Sentries are posted to keep all intruders from coming within a mile of this spot. On this occasion, however, two young girls, who were sisters, happened to have missed the patrol and trespassed unwittingly within the sacred precincts, probably in search of nuts or forest fruits, which abound everywhere. They were caught by the sentries and brought...
