...before the <term>Egbo</term>, condemned to death, and hanged almost immediately. Their brother, who was a member of the highest grade of the society, was allowed, as a great favor, to be present at their death and afterward to carry the bodies home to his family. In such a case, there could be neither hope nor thought of redress.

Sometimes rich and influential women are permitted to become honorary members of all grades, but they are never allowed to be full members, nor to know any of the mysteries.

Each grade has its particular dances and tunes, and each its own <term>Okum Ngbe</term> or <term>Egbo</term> “image,” which is never supposed to come out and show itself unless under direct inspiration to do so.

The so-called “image” is a figure robed from head to toe in a long garment, of the color appropriate for the grade, and pierced with eyeholes. It usually bears on its head a wooden framework covered with skin and shaped like a human head, often with two faces, one male and the other female. This represents the omniscience of the Deity looking both ways—into the future and back to the past—as well as the bisexual character shown in the oldest conceptions of <term>Obassi Osaw</term> (Sky Father) and <term>Obassi Nsi</term> (Earth Mother).

The <term>Okum</term> runs up and down accompanied by two attendants clothed in gorgeous, close-fitting, knitted garments, usually of red, yellow, and white. One of these carries a rod or whip, the symbol of the power of the society, which, under native law, had the right to flog to death any non-members who had seriously offended against its rules. The other bears the symbolic green boughs, which play so great a part in the lives of the <term>Ekoi</term>. At almost every important occurrence, from birth onward, green leaves of the kind appropriate for the event are used, and at the end they are gently drawn over the face of a dying man, so that his spirit may pass peacefully and without pain from this world to the next. Curiously enough, the scientific name of the tree used on this last occasion is *Croton amabilis*, though the small, dark leaves and inconspicuous flowers hardly suggest such a name.

There is great rivalry between the different towns as to which can produce the most gorgeous robes for “images.”

and members. The financial state of a place can be determined by a glance at one of the “plays,” as local resources are strained to the limit in the hope of outdoing neighboring towns. The chiefs of Oban shared the information that the play was much more impressive on the second New Year after my arrival than it had been previously, because the opening of a Government Station had brought them an increase in wealth.

The most interesting figure in last New Year’s dance, however, wore nothing that was either expensive or attractive. This was the <term>Ekuri Ibokk</term> (Efik for “axe-medicine”). It is a very old Ekoi <term>Juju</term>, but it was renamed a few years ago when the axe was placed between its jaws in addition to the other insignia.

The figure was dressed in a long gown of dark blue cloth, smeared with mud from the riverbed. This, to the Ekoi—just as it was previously to performers in the Greek Mysteries and to *Flamen Dialis*—is in itself a great “<term>Juju</term>.” Dark-spotted <term>Juju</term> leaves were fastened here and there over the robes of the figure. On its head it wore a crocodile mask carved in wood, perhaps a representation of *Nimm* herself. It was attended by two hunters armed with flintlock guns; a third carried a fishing net, and a fourth carried a strange clay trumpet covered with leopard skin. The “figure” was supposed to be deaf to human voices and to hear only those of the wild animals, except when awakened by the call of the trumpet. <term>Ekuri Ibokk</term> is the great “hunting <term>Juju</term>” of the Ekoi and had never before appeared to a European. It is the <term>Juju</term> that is supposed to have the power of “smelling out” all others, and the axe in its jaws is a sign of its particular ferocity. However, as powerful as it is, it is not immune to the very human weakness of wanting its photograph taken, and it appeared, lured by this offer, among its less exclusive brothers.

At such “plays,” all the principal characters carry wands or whips, the symbol of the society's power. As has already been mentioned, this society had the right to whip to death any non-members who ventured outside their houses during an <term>Egbo</term> performance or committed a serious offense in any way. Minor offenses were punished by fines, and the main revenue of the Club was derived from these.

One great advantage to be gained from membership in the old days was the ease provided for the recovery of debts.

A creditor brought his case before the <term>Egbo</term> Lodge in the debtor's town. The Council considered the matter, and if the claim was thought justified, the Club drum would be beaten through the streets, and the defaulter was ordered to pay. He was also required to provide a "<term>dash</term>" <note>a tip or gift</note> for the Egbo Society. Should he be unable to comply with both demands, his goods were seized, and, if other means failed, he or some of his family were reduced to the position of slaves in order to settle all liabilities.

There are many stories to account for the coming of <term>Egbo</term>, but perhaps the following is the best known.

### HOW THE FIRST EGBO IMAGE CAME.

One day Nki <note>The New Dormouse (*Graphiurus C. Dorotheæ*), discovered by the author in 1911.</note> went into the bush to gather palm kernels. He cut down a great cluster from which one kernel fell. This rolled down a crab's hole, right through to the ghost town, where the son of one of the chiefs found and ate it.

Nki climbed down from the palm tree and went in search of his kernel. He followed it until he came to the ghost town. There he saw the young chief and guessed what he had done. So he went before the head chief and said:

"Will you give me back the palm kernel which your son has eaten?"

The old chief answered:

"Here is a drum. Take it and beat upon it. It will repay you for what you have lost."

Nki did as he was told. Hardly had he struck the drum when a <term>calabash</term> full of fruit appeared. The chief said, "Take the drum with you," so Nki took it and went on his way.

When he reached home he called to his wives and said:

"Weep no more. I bring you food in plenty."

He beat the drum, and the <term>calabash</term> appeared as before. He ate of the fruit and gave some to all his family.

After this there was always much <term>chop</term> <note>food</note> in his house, for he needed only to strike the drum to obtain a fresh supply. He grew rich and hired people to work for him instead of working himself as he had done formerly.

<header>EGBO</header>

One day he hired the men of the town to go and clear a farm for him. All of them went except for Ngbe (Leopard) alone. Each day, Nki cooked twelve great calabashes of food for his workers.

When the farm was cleared, he hired the women to plant it and prepared food for them as he had done for the men. The wife of Ngbe took her portion home. Her husband seized it and ate it all, whereupon she said:

“When the others went to clear the farm for Nki, you refused to go with them. Why then do you eat my food?”

One day, Nki went to visit his farm. He put the magic drum into an inner room and locked the door. Then he gave the key to the Lame Boy and said, “If anyone should come and ask for this, do not give it to them.”

As soon as he was out of sight, Ngbe came and demanded the key. The boy refused to give it up, but Leopard said, “I will kill you if you do not give it to me.” So the boy gave it to him.

Ngbe opened the door, seized the drum, and bounded with it into the bush. There, he made a small clearing, set up the drum, and began to beat it. He struck it so strongly that almost at once several calabashes appeared, full of sweet things. There was too much for one person to eat alone, so Ngbe ate what he could and left the rest; he then broke the drum and threw away the pieces. Afterward, he went off to his house.

When Nki came home, he asked the Lame Boy for the key to the inner room, whereupon the boy told him everything that Ngbe had done.

Nki was sad over his loss. After a while, he went out into the bush as before. Again he cut palm kernels, but as none of them fell, he looked around for a crab hole, threw a kernel into it, and pushed it down with a long stick. He then followed it through the hole until he came again to the ghost town. Here he saw a chief and said:

“One of your sons has taken my palm kernel. Give it back to me.”

On this, the chief gave him an <term>Egyuk</term>, the long kind of drum which we now find in <term>Egbo</term> houses. Nki took it and went on his way.

Nki went on beating the drum, and after a while, the image went back into it. Then he took up the drum and went home.

The next day, Nki went out as if he were again going to his farm. No sooner was he out of sight than Ngbe came as before and demanded the key from the Lame Boy. This time, the latter gave it without difficulty, as his master had told him to do.

That is the reason why the "images" run up and down to this day and beat those who cross their path. It is because Ngbe broke the first long drum which was brought from the ghost town, and in which they used to dwell.

The reason we call them "Egbo" is because Nki gave that name to the first "image" which came out of the magic drum.

Beside the Egbo Club, there are almost innumerable societies,* secret and otherwise, some partially religious in character, some formed simply for amusement and entertainment, some for mutual protection, and various other purposes, such as to carry out special celebrations during the funeral customs of members. In many cases, such institutions grew from an "age class" which formed a club for its members; this became popular and outsiders were allowed to join.

## CHAPTER V

### Jujus

The term "<term>Njomm</term>," which can only be translated as "Juju," is so elusive that it defies definition. However, as far as can be gathered from the vague ideas of the Ekoi, it includes all the mysterious, misunderstood forces of Nature. These vary in importance from elementals, so powerful that they hold almost the position of demi-gods, to the "<term>Mana</term>" — to use a Melanesian term — found in herbs, stones, or metals. In another sense, the word also includes the means by which such forces may be controlled or influenced; secrets extracted from the deepest parts of Nature by men wiser than their peers, or mercifully granted to some favored mortal by one of the deities.

Jujus vary in importance in different towns according to local opinion, but a dominant one is found everywhere. Whatever other attributes may be claimed for it, protection against witchcraft always ranks first. Each of the lesser Jujus oversees its particular area, though in many cases their roles overlap. As an example of the various kinds usually found, those existing in 1907 at the small village of Ekong, on the Obutong-Oban road, can be mentioned.

1. OFIRI, thought at the time to be the most powerful of all Jujus for defending the town against witchcraft and theft. Its reputation for destroying wizards was so great that people came from hundreds of miles away to join the cult. Each member wears a metal collar or anklet on which some of the "medicine" has been poured, and carries back more "medicine" to be placed in a shrine at his own home.

2. NIMM ASAM (Nimm of the Spears). This is powerful against witchcraft and also helps hunters, but it is chiefly valued

...for its power of warning members against poison in food or drink, especially against that made from ground porcupine quills, which is called "the poison of *Nimm Asam*," and is the Ekoi equivalent for ground glass or ground palm stem. Certain members of this Juju are thought to have the power of producing the rainbow, and therefore causing the rain to cease for a time.<note>See p. 72.</note>

3. **EGPATIM**, against witchcraft and theft. This is of the same "family" as *Nimm Asam*.

4. **NKAJOKK**, the purpose of which is to ward off sickness from the town.

5. **EBUP** to ensure success in hunting and fishing.

6. **NGAPONG**, for protection against beasts of prey, especially leopards.

These six Jujus are common to the whole town, but most families have, in addition, others which have been handed down from father to son, and mother to daughter, for countless generations.

In Oban, the most powerful Jujus are the very old ones of *Okpata*, *Ejamet*<note>See p. 74.</note> and *Eja*—the first two against witchcraft and theft, and the latter to increase the crops, ward off wild animals from the herds, and give protection from thunder and lightning. The feast of *Eja* is the chief one of the year, and corresponds to the harvest festival,<note>See dances, p. 295.</note> as do those of *Mfuor* and *Animm* in some towns.

Among the lesser Jujus at Oban is that which takes the place of the *Ekong Ngapong*. It is called *Ngbe Abum Obbaw* (Leopard knocks his foot), and was brought from Mkpott about two years ago. Before its arrival, leopards had been a scourge. Five cows were once killed by them within twenty-four hours, while even in the middle of the town, compounds were entered and goats carried off.

One night, before the Station was built, when I was sleeping in the doorless Court House, I awoke to find a leopard sniffing around my mosquito net. It was after a long march, and I felt too tired to exert myself to repel the intruder except with a sleepy "sh—," but I was punished for this laziness by the loss of several of my best fowls, which it took in place of larger prey.

# JUJUS
E 2

The same thing happened again at the station before the doors had been hung.

Upon returning to Oban after being away on leave, a remarkable change was found. Since the installation of the new Juju, not a single leopard had shown itself within a mile of the houses, and not a sheep, goat, or cow had been lost. In fact, the cattle were wandering safely outside the town, eating my pineapples and damaging my rubber plantations.

The Juju is said to lose its effectiveness if certain rites are not observed. Since its arrival, palm kernels must be picked from the bunch before being brought into the town. If this is not done, a leopard will come before dawn and take a cow or sheep as a penalty. The same punishment is inflicted if any violent quarrel occurs in the town, or if a fire is lit outside a compound’s walls. The clear effectiveness of the Juju may perhaps be explained in part by the purgation ceremony described on page 220. It is possible that the strong-smelling pitch used to “renew the power” of the Juju might offend the nostrils of the keen-scented beasts of prey and cause them to avoid the town.

The four Jujus with the widest distribution are Mfam, Ofiri, Mfuor, and Akpambe. All of them protect against witchcraft and theft. The first is the oldest and was possessed by the Ekoi when they arrived in this part of the world. In some places, it is considered to be so powerful that it has had to be removed. For instance, in 1909, the people of Nsan came to beg that it might be taken away from their town, as many of the inhabitants were dying because of it. Mfam was said to kill anyone for theft, even if a man thoughtlessly ate a single plantain while passing through a farm without first obtaining the owner's permission. Wherever this Juju is dominant, the entrails of any animal killed in hunting must be brought before its priest.

To lift the taboo on entrails for the general public, an animal must be killed and brought into the town. Each man then takes his machete and scrapes his tongue, refusing to be bound by the “Ntubi” <note>Ntubi refers to a specific type of ritual prohibition or taboo.</note> (taboo). After this, the entrails are divided and eaten.

Early in 1909, the cult of Akpambe spread through the District and

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

It rapidly gained such a reputation that lodges were established in almost every town. The cult was started about a year earlier by a man named Obassi Abong, who was taught the necessary rites by his mother, a celebrated Juju woman of Okuri in the Cameroons, where its first shrine still exists (see photograph, p. 158). Many older cults were overthrown at the coming of Akpambe, but the shrine of Eburuk Pabi stands untouched. People even assert that the new Juju cannot enter a place unless Eburuk Pabi is there first; for the latter alone confers the power of “seeing” Akpambe. Certainly the “Okum” at each “play” bows before the shrine of Eburuk Pabi. It is somewhat significant that this last-named Juju is looked upon as female. Some claim that Eburuk Pabi is an old name for Obassi, in which case it may perhaps be taken as a further indication of the original femininity of Obassi Nsi. The sign of Eburuk Pabi is an earthen pot—always a female symbol.

Followers of Akpambe, Ekuri Ibokk, and Mfuor wear amulets of blue cloth containing “medicine,” the chief function of which is to ward off witchcraft.

The “images” of all three Jujus wear robes of dark blue native cloth, bordered with a fringe of palm-fibre and decorated with the silvery shells of a bivalve. From a certain resemblance in shape, these are supposed to represent the human ear and symbolize the all-hearing power of the spirit, like those pottery and enamel representations of the organ found in Egyptian temples. # JUJUS

When a man wishes to sacrifice, he must first call on Eyo (the sun) to carry his petition before Obassi. If the ceremony takes place in the morning, the title Eyo Ofu (sun of the morning) must be used, but if it is after noon, that of Eyo Egu (sun of the evening) is used.

The ceremonies specific to the various Jujus are long, complicated, and contain many fragments of old rituals whose meaning has long since been forgotten. An account of some of these may be of interest.

At Oban on February 2, 1908, a sacrifice was offered by a woman named Ogai Etab for the recovery of her health. When the townsfolk had assembled, the suppliant advanced holding a calabash of food, covered with a white cloth.

The priest received the offering, then took the cloth and held it up before the Juju, saying,
> “Here is the cloth brought by Ogai Etab. Through the charm, you told her that the sickness had fallen upon her because she had not offered a sacrifice for a very long time.”

Next, dried meat was taken from the calabash and offered with the same words, together with an earthen jar containing palm wine. After this, the priest called for water and filled his mouth; he then laid two Juju leaves on the back of his left hand. He blew the water out upon them and called aloud, 
> “Behold, here is food brought by Ogai Etab. Answer whether or not you will eat of it, Obassi-o-o! Obassi-o-o!”

The names of all deceased members of the cult were called, for ghosts have great power over the Juju which they served in life. This is particularly the case with the “Founder,” *i.e.*, the priest who first started the cult in a new town and is supposed to remain its guardian after death. Before any further step is taken, the Diviner (Mboni) assures the people that the ghost of the Founder is present.

When the long list of the dead was ended, the priest struck his right hand against the back of his left, on which the two leaves were lying. These fluttered down; one fell face upward, and the other downward. This showed that the sacrifice was accepted.

Next, the priest poured water into the earthenware pot where the <term>Juju</term> is supposed to live and said:

> "Here is fresh water. Make our bodies cool and fresh like water, so that fever may stay far from us!"

He then dropped in a little powdered white chalk, saying, "Here is chalk. Give us good fortune." Next, he added some palm wine and palm oil, saying, "Make our blood as rich and pure as oil and palm wine."

The meat was then cut into small pieces and divided among the worshippers, and dried corn mixed with palm wine was shared among them after it had been held before the <term>Juju</term>.

When everything had been eaten, the priest again laid two leaves upon his hand and said:

> "Now we have eaten and drunk. May we go home satisfied?"

He struck the leaves as before. If they had not fallen correctly, the woman on whose behalf the ceremony had been held would have had to go to the Diviner to find out why her petition had not been granted. The Diviner would then practice the charm and give a reason—for example, "The offering was not enough." In such a case, more food would have to be gathered and the entire ceremony repeated.

On the occasion described above, the woman was very ill and unable to collect everything that would usually have been considered necessary; however, the priest allowed the ceremony to take place on the understanding that the rest of the sacrifice should be offered later.

Another <term>Juju</term> for the recovery of health is called <term>Ntuanto</term>—that is, the Soul or Outbreathing. This ceremony was witnessed one day at Nsan. While we watched, Atop picked up an egg lying beside him and carefully broke it on the highest barb of the spear. The little dolls were then anointed in the same way, and the remaining shell was crushed in his hand and placed at the base of the <term>Juju</term>.

A delegation of chiefs was waiting at the Rest-house, so it was impossible to stay until the end of the ceremony; its purpose was to restore health to Atop himself, who was sick.

When I asked for the name of the <term>Juju</term>, I was told that it was called “<term>Monni Njomm</term>,” meaning Little <term>Juju</term>. However, when I shook my head and said I already knew it was one of the lesser <term>Jujus</term> and wanted to learn its real name, my informant looked confused, though somewhat amused, and answered that it was called *<term>Ntuanto</term>*, meaning the *Soul* or *Outbreathing*.

Cocks and tortoises are sacrificed not only on occasions like the one just described, but also to nearly all the greater <term>Jujus</term>, along with the blood of animals killed in the bush. During many ceremonies, pipes made from crabs’ claws are blown. The legendary reasons for these customs can be found in the following stories.

### WHY COCK AND TORTOISE ARE SACRIFICED TO THE JUJU.

Cock and Tortoise lived together in a town that was suffering from a great famine. No fruits ripened on the farms, and the yams and dried corn from the previous year’s harvest were all eaten. Consequently, the townspeople did not know how to satisfy their hunger.

Tortoise said to himself, “If I stay here, I will starve,” so he set out, determined not to turn back until he had found food.

After he had gone a long way, he came to a place where the ghosts had made their farm. They went here and there collecting plantains, yams, pumpkins, and other food. When they had gathered a great store, they divided it among themselves and returned home heavily burdened.

No sooner had they gone than Tortoise crept out from his hiding place, cut a great bunch of plantains, and hurried back with it. When he got home he began to cook, and, while he was busy preparing the food, Cock came in. Cock saw what his friend was doing and asked where the plantains came from.

Tortoise answered that he had seen them growing on a deserted farm. Cock asked if he might go with him there the next day, but Tortoise refused.

The next day he set out again for the ghost farm and came back at night with more plantains. Cock was waiting for him and said, “It is not right that you treat me this way.”

Tortoise replied, “The reason I will not let you come with me is that you cannot keep a secret.”

Cock asked, “What have I spoken about?” Tortoise only answered, “Be satisfied. I will give you a share of my food, but I cannot allow you to go with me.”

At dawn, therefore, he set out alone once more. This time, when he saw the ghosts preparing to go back to their town, he thought, “I should like to know where they come from.” So he followed behind them all the way.

Just before the entrance to the town, Tortoise hid himself in the bush, in a place from which he could see everything, but where no one could see him. He thought to himself, “I have never seen so fine a town before. Perhaps later I may enter and find out how the ghosts live.”

While he lay there hidden, some of the ghosts came by from the river. One of them said, “I smell the scent of fresh meat. What is it that can smell like that?” The other ghosts said, “Let us look around.”

They began to search up and down. When they came to the place where Tortoise lay, he hid himself inside his shell. The ghosts saw him but said, “This is only a stone.” After

Cock said, “Of two friends, it is not good that one should sit hungry in the town while the other goes out and feeds in plenty.”

Tortoise answered, “Everything you say is useless. You make too much noise to come with me.”

Cock said, “Good,” and spoke no more.

Shortly afterward, Tortoise went away. No sooner had he left the house than Cock flew inside. He found the bag which Tortoise usually carried, took out his knife, made a small hole, then scooped up some ashes from the hearth and put them at the bottom of the bag. He said to himself, “No matter how secretly you go tomorrow, I will know where you get all this food.”

Next morning, when Tortoise set out, the ashes fell along the road. Cock followed, and both arrived at the ghost farm.

After the ghosts had taken their food and gone away, Tortoise went to cut plantains as before. When he turned around to go back, he saw Cock. He was afraid and said, “Why did you come? Now we must hurry back. I fear that the owners of the farm may catch us.” Cock said, “Even if I make a noise, I do not think they will do me any harm.”

Tortoise replied, “If you make a noise, not you alone, but both of us will die.” In great fear, he hurried home, and for four days he did not leave his town.

At the end of that time, all the stolen plantains were finished, so he was forced to set out in search of more.

He said, “I will go back to the farm.” He went in front, and Cock walked behind. When they reached the farm, they saw the ghosts gathering their fruits.

Tortoise was called. He came shouting, “I had told Obassi about my daughter. It is he who has killed her!”

At daybreak, Obassi called a meeting of the townspeople and said to Tortoise, “Why did you do such a thing as to bring the dead body of my slave and say that it was your daughter?” Further, he said to all the townsfolk, “I cannot punish Tortoise because of the agreement he made with me before I saw the dead body, but from today, all sacrifices shall be made with Tortoise.”

That is the reason why the native people always offer a Tortoise to the Juju.

### WHY CRAB’S CLAW IS USED IN MANY JUJUS.

One year there was no fruit in the land, and all the people were hungry. Mbaw (Dormouse, *Graphiurus hueti*) went into the bush to cut <term>tie-tie</term> <note>Vines or creepers used as rope.</note>. He came to a river and walked along the bank. After a while, he saw a calabash floating on the water. He called, “Calabash, come here.” It came at his bidding, but inside, instead of food, he found a foul thing. He was so hungry that he tried to eat it, but could not; so he covered it up once more and sent it away. Next, he saw a log of wood floating down. Some plantains were lying on it. He called to the wood to come to him. It came. He ate some of the fruit, kept the rest, and sent the log away. When he got home, he gave some of the plantains to his friend Nki (Dormouse, *Graphiurus c. dorotheæ*).

Nki said, “Where did you get such sweet fruit? I should like to go with you tomorrow and find some for myself.” Mbaw said, “No.”

Very early in the morning, Nki woke up, filled a leaf with ashes from the hearth, then crept into Mbaw’s house, made a small hole in his bag, and put in the leaf full of ashes. Then he went back to his own home.

At daybreak, Nki went again and called for his friend, but the people said that Mbaw had already gone out to hunt. Nki searched until he found the marks of the ashes. He followed the trail until he met his friend down by the river. Another calabash had just come floating by. In it was the same thing as in the first. Mbaw asked Nki if he would taste it, but Nki said:

“No, I will not eat rubbish,” and threw it back in the water. Hardly was it out of sight before a second appeared full of plantains.

Nki called the calabash, and as it drew near the bank, he sprang upon it. It floated away with him down the river. They floated the whole day long, and at evening time, they came to the ghost town.

Nki hid in the bush and watched, for he was a curious man. The very first ghost he saw was his sister, who had died a year before. He called to her, and she took him to

Before Nki could reach the chief, all the ghosts came crowding in. They brought a small object like a trumpet, made from a crab's claw. They cried, "If a living person is here, let him die." Then they blew on the small instrument, and Nki died.

When the evening meal was finished, the ghosts played on the crab's claw once more. They had forgotten about Nki, but at the sound of the magic notes, he returned to life again. They hung up the trumpet on the wall of the house and went away, while Nki hid until morning.

At dawn, he saw children going to the spring to fetch water. He took the magic claw and followed them. Near a small stream, he saw a crab. He caught it and broke off a claw, which he hung up in place of the ghost trumpet, for he was very cunning.

When he was ready to escape, he blew on the magic pipe, and sleep overcame all the ghosts so that they could not follow. All day long he walked, and towards nightfall, he neared his home. Then he blew again on the crab's claw, and the ghosts woke up and found him gone.

They got another pipe to call him back. They played it for a long time. Nki heard them and shook the claw instead of answering, for ghosts can hear if you shake a crab's claw.

They blew again and again, and he always answered with his hand. Then he ran to Etuk (Bay Duiker) and said, "Will you please hold this for me?" but Etuk refused.

Nki ran a little further and came across He-goat. To him, he said the same thing. He-goat took the claw. Then Nki went back to his house.

When the ghosts blew again, the crab’s claw answered from the hand of He-goat. He-goat was frightened and shook his hand to get rid of the strange thing that made a noise by itself. The claw held tight, and he could not free himself. The ghosts followed wherever he went, because they heard the sound of the claw.

Then He-goat dug a hole and buried himself, but he left one foot above ground. When the ghosts reached the place, one of them tripped against the foot. Then they set to work and dug him up, and asked how he came to have their trumpet. When they heard the story, some of them said, “Let us kill him,” but others said, “No, only take away the crab’s claw.” This they did, and then they threw foul things upon his body, so that goats remain bad-smelling to this day.

It is because ghosts can hear when you play upon such claws that the crab is used in many <term>Jujus</term>.

## CHAPTER VI

### JUJUS (*continued*)

Several times it has come to my knowledge that <term>Jujus</term> have been used against me in Court, in hopes of securing a favorable decision, or of causing temporary dumbness and even sudden death, should an adverse judgment be considered. Probably something of the kind goes on every time a Court is held throughout the country, but knowledge of the fact seldom reaches the judge’s ears.

On one occasion, a man named Nsa Obassi brought a complaint against some members of the <term>Egbo Club</term> who had beaten him for being found outside his house during an <term>Egbo</term> performance. In the course of his evidence, he stated:

> "It was Inyan Ita and Oberi Oye who beat me most cruelly." The latter said, "You cannot bring an action for this, as almost all the town is involved in the matter. Besides, even if you should try to bring trouble upon us on account of it, you cannot succeed, for I have a strong <term>Juju</term> which I shall take into Court against you. When I stamp with my foot on the ground, the Judge will become dumb, and so will be unable to pronounce judgment for you."

It is useless to attempt to revoke any <term>Juju</term> without the proper offerings and full rites. In a case which came before the Native Court in 1907, Oyonmba, the head priest of <term>Nfam</term> at Ntebbashott, said in his evidence that the <term>Juju</term> had not been properly revoked, as it had been done without full ritual and empty-handed.

As an example of the revocation of a <term>Juju</term>, that of <term>Ofiri</term>, witnessed at Ekong in December 1907, may be quoted.<note>For revoking Juju Mfam, see page 139.</note>

“Do you receive the offering of my son?” The leaves fell as before, so I knew that all was well.

After this, I held up the mat, saying, “Here is the mat. Let no one sleep long upon it” <note>that is, fall ill</note>.

Lastly, I poured out the rest of the palm wine, crying, “Let all our goods remain safely in our houses.”

As has been said, the pot represents the female, and the three fetishes represent the male attribute of the <term>Juju</term>. When eggs are offered, one of them is usually broken and the forehead of the petitioner is marked with the yolk just above the junction of the eyebrows, over the pineal gland—which according to Descartes is the seat of the mind. This is done with the stated purpose of giving clear vision. Afterwards, the egg is crushed small and placed on the creepers around the <term>Juju</term> post.

It will be noticed that there is a very strong resemblance between the ritual described above and the daily service of the chief Egyptian temples, except that here actual food is offered to the Deity instead of incense.

It is somewhat curious that a lamb, regarded in most parts of the earth as an acceptable offering, should here be forbidden for sacrificial purposes. The mythical reason for this taboo is given in the following story.

"Go and hide yourself in the bush near my farm, and I will send Lamb to gather vegetables; then he will fall into your power."

Now Lamb knew, by the inner knowledge that was within him, how they had agreed together; so when he was sent to fetch yams from the farm, he went very cautiously and knew by the scent where Leopard was hiding. He went around by the other side, took the yams quickly, and ran back home. When <term>Obassi</term> saw him return in safety, he wondered how this had been done.

Some time later, Leopard went and said, "Will you send Lamb on an errand? Then I may catch him on the road."

Lamb said, "I thank you; she is one of my enemies." So he turned back and got a padlock and key, then went slowly on his way to the landing place. The box stood open. He crept around behind it, jumped on the lid, pressed it down, and then leaned over and locked it. After that, he pushed the box into the water and held it there until Leopard drowned. The latter looked at the body and saw that it was quite dead. He said, "Leopard made a fool of herself and ruined her own life." Therefore, he ordered his people to bury the body.

One day, Lamb went to his master’s room and found many rich clothes there. He made a bundle of the most splendid ones and carried them away with him. Then he took his gun and went out into the bush. He walked for some time until he came to a large cotton tree. There he unfolded the clothes and hung them all around the tree. When he had finished, he went home and said to his master:

"I have found the place where people used to get all their fine clothes in the old days. Yesterday I went into the bush and found a cotton tree from which colorful robes were hanging."

Obassi said, "I would like to see this. Can you lead me there?" and Lamb answered:

"If you are willing, you and I will go there together; but you must tell no one where we are going, for it is a great <term>Juju</term>. We must also take an axe with us."

When they got to the place, Lamb said, “Let us cut down the cotton tree, so that we may find out how it can produce such things as these.” To himself he thought, “Obassi tried to betray me to Leopard, so I myself will try to kill him today!” He took the axe and said further:

Lamb struck at the tree with such strength that after a time it was ready to fall. Obassi put out his hand to hold up the garments, but at that moment the great trunk came crashing down and buried him in its fall. At this, Lamb ran back to the town weeping, and said, “My master is lost; I do not know where he may be.”

The people all went out to search. They found the dead body and brought it home, but Lamb went to his mother’s house and told her all that had happened to him since he went to serve Obassi Nsi. He also said, “Earth is no longer safe for us. Let us flee to the sky.” He went outside and made a <term>Juju</term>; then he looked upward and prayed, and behold! A great rope began to come down from the sky.

When it reached the ground, he said to his mother, “Will you go first? I myself will come later.” He stood and watched while the rope drew her gently up, and then he went back to his place in the house of his master.

About a week later, while the townspeople were performing ceremonies for the death of Obassi, Lamb went outside and stood before them. He looked up into the sky and called, “My mother, my mother, send the rope down to me now.” She heard the voice of her son and threw down the rope. He laid his hand upon it and then said:

“I will confess about the death of my master. It was I who deceived and killed him in the bush, because he would have given me over to Leopard.” Then he quickly climbed up the rope and disappeared into the sky.

That is why we do not sacrifice a young sheep. After such behavior, he would not be an acceptable offering.

# JUJUS

...for a while they agreed to have different lands. Obassi Osaw fixed his dwelling place in the sky, while Obassi Nsi came down to earth and lived there.

After this separation, Nsi grew in power, “for when a child is born, it falls to the earth, and when a man dies, he returns to the earth, from which all things have sprung. Nsi is the governor of all crops that the earth ripens. The sky is bad, because sometimes it sends too much rain, and sometimes not enough.”

Often people who are <term>Efumi</term>* of crocodiles make rain for themselves, especially in midsummer, when the water grows too hot and low for their comfort.

When a farm has been cleared and prepared for sowing, the owner cannot plant yams until some rain has fallen; therefore, he goes to the priest of the great rain <term>Juju</term> and asks him to make the rain fall. Members of the cult of <term>Ekuri Ibokk</term> have special power in this regard. At the time of the new moon, they go out into the bush and gather magic leaves. They bring these home and dry them carefully in bundles. When rain is wanted, they cut them open and either pour water onto them from a calabash or lay them to soak in a bowl of water. Then it will surely rain.

Chief Ita Sakese of Oban was said to be able to produce rain by drinking water mixed with magic potions, or to stop the downpour by refraining from drinking water for two or three days at a time. During this period, he was not forbidden from drinking palm wine.

Early in 1909, a man near Obutong was shown a famous rain <term>Juju</term> and told that it was so powerful that rain would fall, even at the height of the dry season, if certain rites were performed before it. He was a skeptical soul, for as soon as he heard this, in a spirit of bravado, he seized the <term>Juju</term> and performed the rites. Unfortunately, the rest of the season was wet enough to strengthen belief even among the most doubting. In the words of the Ekoi—“*Njokk I mbuta eya nji*”—“an elephant of rain fell this year.” The man paid for his skepticism, probably at the hands of the owners of the ruined farms, for he disappeared, and no trace of him has ever been found.

--- Page 112 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on weather-related beliefs and rituals among the Ekoi, transitioning from rain-making ceremonies to the more contemporary practice of rain-stopping and the summoning of rainbows.</meta>

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

It is just another paradox, like those constantly appearing among the Ekoi, that importance is still attached to rain-making rites in a country where about 200 inches of rain fall annually; such customs are rarely found except where rainfall is unreliable. The ceremonies practiced for this purpose are likely another survival from the time when the Ekoi lived in parklands, but, as might be expected under current conditions, rain-stopping through magic arts has now become more important than the older ceremonies for producing rain.

Once, while visiting Effion Iyawe’s—a settlement near Ekkonnanakku—I noticed two bundles of thin roots wrapped in leaves hanging over a fire. The chief assured me that no rain could fall as long as the flame was kept burning.

A few hours later, on our way back, the rain poured down in torrents. Two or three days afterward, we met the weather prophet and asked why his <term>Juju</term> was not working. He eagerly began to explain that the failure should not be blamed on the <term>Juju</term>, but solely on the fact that he had been called away from home on urgent business, and the man assigned to tend the fire had neglected his duty and allowed it to go out.

Another way to stop a heavy downpour is to produce a rainbow. Certain <term>Juju</term> men claim to be able to do this without much difficulty. Ntui Itabon of Oban, for instance, is credited with this power. He only has to take powdered cam-wood, mix it with certain magic medicines in his palm, and then throw the red paste up toward the sky. He did this one day at three o’clock in the afternoon, and an hour later, a magnificent rainbow spanned the heavens.

Many members of the cult of Nimm Asam are supposed to have this power, though to varying degrees. Those of little importance can only produce a rainbow whose effects last for a few hours, but those more deeply initiated into the mysteries can guarantee fair weather for several days.

The bow itself is supposed to arch over the earth, with one end resting in one river and the other in another, far away.

Most winds are sent by Obassi Osaw, but those which

<meta>This page continues the description of various <term>Juju</term> cults among the Ekoi, shifting from rain-related magic to those associated with controlling wind, thunder, and lightning.</meta>

# JUJUS

...which cause the greatest damage to farms usually come from the great wind <term>Juju</term> “Mfepp.”

Members of this cult only use their power to harm others. They never acknowledge that they belong to the <term>Juju</term>, but use it against hostile towns, debtors who will not pay what they owe, or anyone against whom they have a grudge. They prove their power to aspirants by sending a sudden wind to blow down some giant forest tree, usually a cotton tree, which they have previously pointed out as an object on which to show their might.

Opinions differ as to the causes that produce Thunder (*Nsann*) and Lightning (*Nyanga Ainya*). Some think that the former is a giant who marches across the sky; others believe it is a great sheep that runs up and down in the house of Obassi Osaw. Some people, again, believe that Lightning is the servant of Thunder, while others believe they are enemies. Many Ekoi will put out all lamps during a storm, for fear that Thunder might notice their gleam and send his bolt to crush them. “When Thunder sees Lightning,” they say, “he is very angry, and growls ‘r-r-rong,’ ‘r-r-rong,’ to drive it away.”

“Nsann” is the name of a great <term>Juju</term> cult, whose members claim the power to produce storms and direct the lightning. Just as the initiates of the *Mfepp* <term>Juju</term> can show their power by overthrowing great cotton trees, those of *Nsann* demonstrate theirs by pointing out some tree, usually a coconut palm, and then causing it to be struck by lightning, for which these palms are thought to have a peculiar attraction. The Father Rector of the Catholic Mission at Calabar said that he considered them as great a protection as any lightning conductor for the houses near which they grew. In a storm, he had often watched the peculiar movement of the leaves, all of which swept upward to a point and only returned to their normal position when the storm was dying down.

Lightning is said to be attracted to rocks and peaks because of the fire within them; “For many stones contain fire, which a hunter can bring forth by striking them with his machete.”

whisper "A man will die today," for they think that all members of <term>Nsann</term> are powerful poisoners, and that the flash is a sign that a new victim has been singled out for death. The only <term>Juju</term> great enough to save a man from the power of <term>Nsann</term> is <term>Eja</term>, the festival of which is the chief one of the year and is celebrated at the time of the new yams. This cult, as already mentioned, is supposed not only to produce plentiful harvests but also to protect human beings, farms, and cattle from damage by lightning and thunderbolts.

No one who has attended the festival could fail to be struck by the resemblance between the present-day <term>Ekoi</term> ritual and those descriptions which have come down to us of the ancient <term>Adonis-Attis-Osiris</term> worship. The ecstatic frenzy of the dancers, the trances into which some of them fall, and the jealousy with which all strangers are excluded show that this ceremony holds a very special significance.

One day, while speaking to the chief of an important town about the local "<term>Eja</term>," he remarked that it had been brought from the interior many years before and was a most powerful <term>Juju</term>. To ensure its continued efficacy, however, sacrifices must be offered every two years. It struck me that this had not been done since my arrival in the District, and I asked the reason for the neglect. The old man grew confused and stammered that it had not been possible to confirm the <term>Juju</term> for three years because they had been unable to procure the most necessary ingredient for the "medicine." When questioned as to what was missing, and whether it would not be possible to help them in the matter, he grew more and more confused and at length answered that it was nothing that could be procured by a white man. None but a native could get it, and that only under certain circumstances. He further added that he dared disclose no more, or the <term>Juju</term> might kill him.

From later inquiries, it turned out that the ceremony had been performed with the utmost regularity before the coming of the "white man," and the fact that there had been difficulty in providing the necessary ingredients ever since his arrival seemed highly suspicious. Nothing more could be learned at the time; but some weeks later, a man came up to the house

This was interesting news, but I said, as casually as possible, "I thought that they did not possess the ingredients for confirming the <term>Juju</term>!" The man answered quite unsuspiciously, "In the past they did not, but now they have obtained all that is necessary."

Everyone knows that the easiest way to extract information from the local people is to assume more knowledge than one actually possesses. In this case, the man took for granted that I knew all about it; for in answer to the question, "Do they kill, or only mutilate their victim?" he answered, "They could not cut away so large a part without causing death." After this admission, it was comparatively easy—under the promise of not revealing the name of my informant—to get many further details.

As I had begun to suspect, the ingredient which had been so difficult to procure since the arrival of the "white man" was the same organ as that thrown to the symbolic tree in the <term>Osiris</term> ritual described by <term>Dr. Frazer</term>. Among the <term>Ekoi</term>, however, a woman is usually chosen as the victim. This is natural when one remembers that, until quite recent times among them, the woman, not the man, was the head of the house.

Somewhere in the bush, a poor woman had been put to death so that her mutilated body might bring prosperity to the <term>Ekoi</term> farms. It is useless, according to their belief, to use the required part of any corpse that had died by accident or from natural causes. The victim must be slain purposefully, or the ritual is of no use. None of the townspeople had disappeared on this occasion, so the murdered woman must have been some poor soul brought down from the interior or one kept prisoner in a lonely bush farm until it was thought that the time had come for her to be sacrificed without the knowledge of the "white man."

So jealously was the secret guarded that even the most anxious inquiries failed to find actual proof of the murder or bring to justice

On one occasion, during our visit to the Cameroons, after a long march through the beautiful pass of Okuri, we arrived at the village of Mbinda and settled down in the <term>Egbo</term> house. The day had been a good one from the point of view of the botany collection, and we were all in the highest of spirits.

<image-desc>A line drawing of an Eja fetish. It depicts a globular, bowl-like object hanging by a cord. The base of the bowl is supported by two open human lower jawbones which serve as a stand or feet.</image-desc>

Suddenly one of my companions, who was sitting opposite, stopped in the middle of a sentence, her eyes fixed in a stare of horror on something above my head.

An upward glance showed three gruesome objects dangling from the roof. They would not bear detailed description except in a strictly anthropological work, but as will be seen from the accompanying little sketch, each of the bowls that composed the body was set on a pair of widely opened human jaws which formed a foot or stand.

One glance was enough to show that these were <term>Eja</term> symbols. Later we learned that the fetish consists of two parts. The bowl, always the feminine sign, is called <term>Ekum Oke</term>, while the curved male symbol represents <term>Eja</term> himself. It has not been possible to learn anything concerning the origin of the names. We were only told vaguely that “<term>Eja</term>” always consists of the two personalities mentioned above. “<term>Eja</term>—he is a man, and the stronger of the two. <term>Ekum Oke</term> is a woman, less strong than <term>Eja</term>; nevertheless, without her, he can do nothing.”

At every great <term>Eja</term> festival, the following song is sung. It is perhaps worth noticing that <term>Ekum Oke</term> is first invoked:

The meaning of the last two lines, which is somewhat obscure, seems to be as follows:

If a poor man has nothing of sufficient value to offer to the <term>Juju</term>, his full brother or full sister must be sacrificed. The term “throat” includes all the children of the same father and mother.

At Obung, roots rubbed with charcoal are part of the composition of the <term>Eja</term> “medicine.” When an Obung man goes to another town to attend a “play” at which many people are expected to be present, he rubs some of the medicine on his forehead and some on the soles of his feet as a protection against any witch or wizard who may be among the crowd.

One of the chief ceremonies at the festival is the bringing in of the first fruits. Each family sends a representative bearing a basket of yams, the greater number of which are eaten during the feast, but a portion is reserved to be offered up at the entrance to the town.

Until the <term>Eja</term> festival comes round, neither <term>fu-fu</term> nor fresh yams may be eaten. Men may begin to eat these on the first and second days, but women may not touch any until the third. On the first day, neither food nor drink may be taken by either sex until the sun has reached its zenith.

At the actual offerings of yams, the following song is sung:

> “Achibong,    aba yi aiyu o-or-we.
> (Name of the original priest of the <term>Juju</term>), come eat yams o-or-we.
> Nta Asu,      aba yi aiyu o-or-we.
> Lord Asu, come eat yams o-or-we.”

On one occasion at which I was present, an old slave had been placed in a crouching position within a little fence by the <term>Juju</term>. He probably represented the human sacrifice formerly offered up at this time.

As a substitute for human sacrifice, however, the <term>Drill Ape</term> (*Papio leucophaeus*)—so rare in most places that the skulls I forwarded to the <term>British Museum</term> are said by the authorities to be the first they ever received—holds first place due to its close resemblance to man. They exist in vast quantities but are by no means easy prey, owing to their strength and fierceness.

The <term>Ekoi</term> firmly believe that <term>Drill Apes</term>, and indeed all anthropoids, are degenerate men. The story of their degradation is told in the following tale:

### WHY APE PEOPLE NO LONGER LIVE IN TOWNS.

->BY NTUI NENSHAW OF MFAMOSING.<-

Once, long ago, a man named <term>Nshum</term> (<term>Drill Ape</term>) lived in a town. The other men were building houses, but <term>Nshum</term> only ran around, ate their food, and would do nothing to help. One of the chiefs called to the idler and said, "Why do you not work like all the rest?" To this <term>Nshum</term> did not answer.

A few weeks later, all the townsfolk went to clear the farm, but <term>Nshum</term> refused to go with them and remained idle in the town.

Again the chief called and said, "Why do you not go and clear the farm like the others?"

At this, <term>Nshum</term> was angry, so he said, "I will live by myself; I will not stay in your town any longer." With that, he left them and went into the bush.

# JUJUS

The head chief ordered the people to take their nets and go out to catch him. They tried to do this, but he went too far and so escaped them.

At that time, men did not like to kill <term>Nshum</term> because he was a man like themselves, though a very bad one; but in the course of years, all the lazy people gathered together in the bush and not only drove away the good people who went near them but tried to do them harm.

One day, a hunter went into the bush. He saw some creature moving in the branches of a great tree and shot it. It was <term>Nshum</term>.

Then the hunter caught up the body and dragged it home to his town. He took it before the charm and said to the Diviner:

> “I have brought this creature who was once a man but has now become a bush-beast. You may practice on him on account of his laziness.”

The Diviner practiced the charm and said:

> “He is no longer a human being, but only a wild animal now. You may kill him and eat his flesh.”

This is the reason why it is no longer unlawful to eat <term>Nshum</term>. Before the charm was practiced, no one ate him. His name is still that of a person, and if a man is lazy, we sometimes call him “<term>Nshum</term>.”

# CHAPTER VII

## METAMORPHOSIS

The headdresses representing birds or beasts, worn by the "images" of the Egbo and other clubs, seem originally to have been connected with the common belief in metamorphosis. It is quite common to hear one of the Ekoi say of another, "he (or she) possesses" such and such an animal, meaning that the person alluded to has the power to assume the shape of that particular creature. To primitive people like the Ekoi, such cases seem to be on the same level as those recorded from other continents, where the souls of mystics or sick people are supposed to temporarily leave their bodies. It is a core belief that, by means of constant practice and hereditary secrets, a man can leave his human form and take on that of some wild creature. They say that every man has two souls: one which always animates the human shape, and a "bush soul," which at times is capable of being sent forth to enter the form of the animal "possessed." When a man wishes to send out his bush soul, he drinks a magic potion, the secret of which has been handed down in his family from time immemorial; some of this potion is always kept ready for use in an ancient earthen pot set apart for the purpose.

After drinking the potion, the bush soul is supposed to leave its human form and float invisibly through the town until it reaches the forest. There it begins to swell, and, safe in the shadows of the trees, it takes on the shape of its were-body. The most common animals "possessed" in this manner are the elephant, leopard, buffalo, wild boar, and crocodile. Different potions are naturally necessary for the assumption of each shape.

All totem animals were once the namesakes of the families that possess them. A man cannot belong to a totem to which neither his father nor mother belonged.

One advantage of being able to take on animal form is that an enemy's farms may be devoured during the night. That is why men with buffalo, elephant, or wild boar "bush souls" are usually found in the neighborhood of places where there are large, well-kept farms.

In Oban, where the farms are neither extensive nor particularly productive due to the unenterprising nature of the inhabitants, there are very few farm-devouring creatures, and the favorite were-beasts are leopards and crocodiles. Townsfolk claim that when crossing rivers—especially the Calabar and the Awa, which separate the British Ekoi from their kin in the Cameroons—men carrying loads have been attacked by a crocodile and terrified into dropping their possessions in their hurry to escape. Occasionally, goods have been returned by a friend who explained that it was only a trick he played as a joke while in crocodile form, but usually were-crocodiles have a particularly bad reputation, as they are supposed to overturn canoes in order to seize both goods and men.

Early in 1911, a delegation from Netim, one of the largest towns in the District, brought a chief and his son to the District Commissioner at Oban. These men were accused of having, in crocodile form, killed two women while the women were crossing the Calabar River. Some men stated that they had watched the women enter the water and, at about midstream, saw them dragged under by crocodiles. The chief and his son, who had long been suspected of such crimes, were immediately seized, and a meeting was held in the town. The dominant Juju was brought out, and the accused were asked to clear themselves by swearing their innocence upon it. This they refused to do and were therefore brought before the District Commissioner, who was administering the District at the time. He, quite naturally, said that it was not in his power to do anything in such a case, as more proof was necessary. The people returned to the town and held another meeting at which the accused were asked to swear their innocence on the "Broom Juju." This is held in considerable

The people swore that they went to the place indicated and found the body exactly as had been described. They then sent to Uyanga and found the other woman. After being confronted with the woman, the chief also confessed to the truth of the accusation, and within ten days both he and his son were dead—killed, as the townsfolk said, by the <term>Broom Juju</term>, but more probably by poison administered by avenging neighbors.

Should women strew fish poison in the water above the dwelling place of a <term>were-crocodile</term>, the <term>Efumi</term> of the crocodile dies within seven days.

Soon after my first arrival at Oban, information was brought that something of an unusual nature was happening. On investigation, it appeared that a certain chief had fallen under the suspicion of having, in the guise of a <term>were-leopard</term>, killed several cows and goats. Preparations were underway for ridding the town of him in a summary manner, when the arrival of the "white man" put an end to the proceedings of the impromptu tribunal.

A man of considerable intelligence, educated in England, and the brother of a member of the Legislative Council for one of the West African Colonies, offered to take an oath that he had seen Agbashan not only in his elephant form, but while actually undergoing the metamorphosis.

Those who have elephant affinities know at once if any beast that happens to be killed is “possessed” by a man’s soul. In the latter case, they would not eat it. Were-elephants are said to be seldom seen in the daytime, but there is a curious superstition regarding were-leopards. At noon or midnight, such creatures are supposed to rise on their hind legs and walk upright. Occasionally, when the people of a bush farm have left the compound and gone to work, one of these uncanny beings will creep up to the deserted dwelling and reconnoitre. If all seems safe, he will enter with the object of carrying off one of the domestic animals. In such a case, it is thought that he walks upright, holding his tail with his left hand and hiding his face behind a bunch of green boughs held in his right. Sick people, left behind while the rest of the family went to work, have repeatedly testified to having watched through door or wall chinks while their terrible visitor approached a lamb or kid in the manner described, then suddenly pounced upon its prey and carried it off to devour in the bush.

An old woman of Oban, named Awaw Ita, was suspected of having an even more sinister familiar. Her husband, beside whom she stands in the photograph, had a sore on his ankle. Somehow or other, the idea spread that this could not heal because a snake came out of her mouth every night to lick the wound while they slept. Curiously enough, as in similar cases in our own country during the Middle Ages, she herself firmly believed in the truth of the story and admitted to it when she thought that such a confession might cost her her life.

> “Last month I was in my house when the Juju Image entered the compound at night, with many companions. He called me, ‘Awaw Ita, Awaw Ita.’ I answered, and he said, ‘Come out.’ I followed him. He led me into Ntui Iterem’s compound, where all the Jujus are kept. Many people were gathered together. They said to me, ‘Do you possess a snake?’ I answered, ‘Yes,’ because I truly have one. In my country, Okorroba, which is a long way from here, both snakes and hippopotami are possessed by women. I left my snake in the bush of my land when I was brought from my home. When I sleep and dream, I sometimes see my snake, but not very often. In the daytime, I have not seen it since I was brought here as a slave many seasons ago.”

Fortunately for all parties, the wound was soon healed by means no more romantic or mysterious than the application of a little clean water and some ointment.

Cases of this kind are always being heard before the Native Court of the District. These Courts are mines of information regarding customs and beliefs, and the knowledge obtained from them can be relied upon; for, should one party to a lawsuit volunteer a false statement, it would be quickly corrected by the other. Three chiefs, unconnected with either side and from different towns, are always chosen to sit as an advisory committee and give information regarding native custom and law, which is followed except when it conflicts with British justice.

Another interesting case came to our notice lately. In 1909, while marching toward Ekkonnanakku—the new town built by a branch of the Ododop tribe, which came to settle in the District about five years ago—I noticed the skull of a great bush-cow <note>The African forest buffalo (Syncerus caffer nanus).</note>. It stood at the base of the Juju tree in the center of the settlement where the Head Chief, Awaw Anjanna, lived about twelve miles from his town. It was such an unusually fine specimen that I asked the chief if he were willing to sell it. He answered that he would rather not, as he liked to see it there and could not easily get another so large. He spoke naturally, even carelessly, and I attached no importance to the matter.

Between the settlement and the town, all along the way, lie huge boulders, water-worn and rounded like those on the sea—

shore. On our first visit, Awaw Anjanna took us along a hunters' track about a mile from his home, which led to the foot of a massive boulder. When we revisited Awaw Anjanna’s home two years later, we found it deserted. We thought the chief had finally yielded to the pleas of his people and gone to live among them.

Every day there is a fresh one at Awaw Anjanna's farm."

His tone was deeply sad, but my wife thought this was probably due to a fear that rations might be hard to obtain—as was the case in many places—because of the destruction caused by wild animals.

All along the road, we looked for the figure of the chief, who, in his spotless white linen coat and dark blue loincloth, used to come out a long way to greet us. There was no sign of him, and though the headmen of the town were assembled to meet us upon our arrival at Ekkonnanakku, we still looked in vain for his familiar figure. My first question was about his whereabouts. There was a moment of silence, and then one of the men answered:

> "He died a long time ago."

No other information was offered. Our condolences were received in silence, and the people clearly did not wish to be questioned on the matter.

There was obviously something wrong here, as, on the face of it, such a thing was impossible. After a while, the whole story came out.

It seems that the chiefs of the Ododop tribe are believed to be mysteriously linked with buffaloes. When one of them dies, his soul enters one of those animals. At night, too, the bush soul goes out in the form of his animal affinity. This explains the skull beneath the Juju tree.

All Ododop people are believed to have some totem or another, mostly wild boar or antelope, though some, like the chiefs, have buffalo souls.

Now Awaw Anjanna had, according to custom, attended court at Oban, for he was a particularly intelligent man and took a great interest in learning everything possible about the administration of justice. He returned home in excellent health, and two days later was sitting talking with several of his people when he suddenly struck his hand against his body and cried out:

> “They killed me at Oban.”

It was four o’clock in the afternoon. At that hour, a buffalo was seen coming down to drink at a stream that runs through the station garden. The Commissioner shot the beast, and it turned around and ran off, badly wounded. It was followed, but escaped for the time. In the excitement of the chase, two men were shot by mistake, one in the arm and the other in the body; fortunately, however, both recovered. Two days later, the buffalo was found dead in the bush, and about an hour before this discovery, Awaw Anjanna died at his small settlement over ten miles away. Just before his death, he sent a message to Ekkonnanakku to warn everyone who belonged to the buffalo totem to stay away from Oban, as it was too dangerous there.

Now his brother rules in his place. The old dwelling place stands lonely and deserted, with carefully padlocked doors; but the farms still seem to be tended, so that the soul of the dead

# METAMORPHOSIS

...chief, roaming up and down in buffalo form, may see that the space he reclaimed from the bush is kept in good order.

Whatever the case may have been in earlier times, there is now no restriction regarding marriage between the various totem peoples. For instance, a wild boar man may marry an antelope woman, or vice versa, and the children of such a marriage seem to be given the choice of totem. A <term>bush-cow</term> man will never shoot a beast of his own kind, though he may kill antelope or wild boar. However, after doing this, should he think that his kill is not an ordinary animal but one "possessed" by one of the townspeople, he must perform certain ceremonies over the body of the beast and then hurry back at top speed to bring a particular "medicine" to the man whose totem it was. Otherwise, the <term>Efumi</term> <note>A term referring to the individual or their "bush soul."</note> must die.

It was unfortunately impossible to obtain information regarding the nature of this medicine, but a few indications seemed to show that it was a part of the animal itself.

There are differences of opinion regarding the moment of death. Some assert that the man's death coincides with that of the animal; others believe that the possessor lives, though with decreasing strength, as long as the body of his animal relation remains whole. Should a man unknowingly eat a beast of the family to which he is mysteriously linked, he would fall sick. In this case, he must consult his <term>Juju</term> as to the cause of the illness and would recover after making the required sacrifice. However, should he eat it knowingly, he would surely die.

Amid these strange beliefs, one curious fact stands out. While nearly all other tribes in the District have been driven to despair by the destruction caused by boar, bush-cow, and other wild beasts, the <term>Ododop</term> farms remain untouched. Tracks are seen everywhere, but not a single plantain is trodden down, nor a yam uprooted. Here, strangely enough, the wild beasts seem to leave the farms alone and feed only on wild greenery.

The same man who had offered to swear that he had seen Chief <term>Agbashan</term> while he was changing into his elephant form wrote out and sent the following account of a ceremony at which he claimed to have been present. I provide it in his own words, for whatever it may be worth:—

"In the month of June, 1908, I was awakened from a peaceful"

# CHAPTER VIII

## OBAN TO NIAJI

To the northeast of Oban live those Ekoi of the purest blood. They show hardly a trace of having mixed with the Efifs <note>Likely referring to the Efik people of the Calabar region.</note> or any other people, and are of a more enterprising character than the rest of their race.

The way leads along a forest path, eight to ten feet wide and clear of trees, fringed with ferns and carpeted ankle-deep with a thousand little flowers. Amidst these, small Acanthaceæ raise their pure white or deep purple heads, recalling with curious vividness the violets of Worcestershire spinneys <note>A spinney is a small wood or thicket.</note>. Amid this wealth of flowers winds the foot-wide track, bare and smooth, which is all that the natives use.

The first river to be crossed is the Ojuk. On its banks, by the ford, a powerful Juju was formerly buried. So many people died after crossing that the “Okum” Ekuri Ibokk, described on page 45, was brought down to "smell out" the magic. He indicated a spot between the gnarled roots of a tree, and, after digging for a considerable depth at this point, a pot containing Juju medicine was discovered and removed. The path was then declared safe once more—but we did not find it so.

One evening we reached the river bank a little before sunset. I was ahead with my gun, next came Bimba, and then my wife, followed by our botanical collector. Suddenly I heard a warning cry, and looking back saw my wife pointing to a small cobra which had crossed the path between herself and her sister. Bimba at once passed me, so as to be out of the way, and our positions then formed a triangle, with the snake, between my wife and myself, for its apex. I shot, and thought that the reptile had been blown to pieces, as it disappeared. Next moment our collector sprang into the air with a yell of terror. The cobra had been “lofted” by the

After leaving this town, the next stopping place is Ako, where a specimen of that rare and wonderful creature, the Goliath beetle, was found. Up to this point, the road from Oban, though hilly, is one of the most level in the District, but from now onward it grows steep and rocky.

# OBAN TO NIAJI

...to venture on reproducing two of the more striking positions depicted.

After leaving Ntebbashott, the path leads down a steep, rocky slope into a charming little dell, through the center of which flows a stream of the clearest water. The carriers always set down their loads and run forward to drink from it; then, after plucking leaves from the banks, they form into an irregular procession and proceed to a heap of leaves which lies a few yards away. Here they rub the leaves they have gathered across their foreheads, saying:

> “ ‘Me nfonn ofa!
> (May) I have luck!’ ”

and then drop them on the heap.

The reason for this little ceremony is that the stream is called the River of Good Fortune, and anyone who conforms to the rite described above is supposed to have good luck throughout the current year. It is especially practiced by traders who travel up to the German Cameroons.

Another heap of leaves, with which a similar ceremony is connected for the prevention of misfortune, is to be found on the bank of the Calabar River (see p. 242).

Smaller mounds may occasionally be seen on the roadside. If these are pushed aside, they will usually be found to cover a dead chameleon. According to the tradition of the elders, if one of these creatures is killed on the road, it must not be thrown into the bush but left by the wayside. Each passerby then takes a few leaves, spits upon them, and drops them on the dead animal, saying, “Look! Here is your mat.”

> “ Enn! mkpa eya.
> Behold! Your mat.”

The reason is that when a chameleon has been killed, its spirit is supposed to go before Obassi Nsi and pray for revenge on the race of those who caused its death.

The rite is intended to placate the “manes” <gloss>spirits of the dead</gloss> of the dead creature and avert punishment.

When a poisonous snake is killed, this is also left lying across the road so that all who pass by may step over its body. It is thought that by doing so, the danger of snakebites will be averted until a new moon shines in the sky.

Niaji, the first town reached beyond the River of Good Fortune, lies at the base of Osaw Ifogi (High hill with holes—*that is*, caves). This is a conical peak, over 3,000 feet high, covered with flowering trees. During a single visit, six varieties new to science were discovered.

In 1909, the summit had been cleared for <term>theodolite</term> <note>A precision instrument used by surveyors to measure horizontal and vertical angles.</note> observations, except for one tree which stood among its fallen brothers as a lonely sentinel, visible for miles around. The top of the hill was too narrow to allow the tents to be pitched there with any degree of safety, so camp was made on the slope, about 50 yards below.

I began to take measurements, but storm clouds gathered, and the sky became overcast. At four o’clock, Itamfum, our second "boy" <note>In this colonial context, "boy" refers to a male domestic servant or personal assistant.</note>, who naturally determined the time by the sun, brought the lamps under the impression that it was 6:00 p.m. A strong wind arose, branches began to crash in every direction, and a few minutes later the storm burst upon us in all its fury.

We took refuge in one of the tents. For a while, the wind tore at the frail structure as if to carry it away. Then suddenly, we were enveloped in a blaze of light. At the same moment, a deafening crash occurred, and we were thrown to the ground by an irresistible force.

When consciousness returned, I found both of my companions unconscious and apparently dead beside me. I dragged them outside into the downpour, where pandemonium reigned. The carriers and "boys" were screaming at the highest pitch of terror, rushing helplessly back and forth, too frightened to think what to do. Meanwhile, the cook, the cook-mate, the interpreter, and one of my "boys" still lay in a helpless heap where they had been flung downhill by the force of the lightning strike.

When my wife regained consciousness, she explained that when she first felt the blow that struck her down, the thought flashed through her mind, *“This is death.”* There was no time for fear, only a feeling of interest that the experience, which must eventually come to everyone in some form, had arrived so swiftly. Afterward, she knew nothing until—she claims—a voice, very thin and far away, as if over a distant telephone, reached her ears. “Are you killed?” it piped. “Are you killed?” and then, “Oh, you’re both dead!” She

The next hour or so was the most unpleasant of our lives. We all suffered intense pain, and it was a long time before I could stand upright, while my wife bore for weeks the marks of scarlet zigzags, and Bimba's left arm became white and crinkled almost like tissue paper.

Niaji Peak is the center of a huge amphitheater of hills. As we sat in our sodden deck chairs amid a solid downpour, the storm receded from us, only to rumble around and return again and again, breaking overhead in deafening crashes and flashes which seemed to make closed eyelids and sheltering hands transparent.

The actual blow which had knocked us down had come so suddenly that there was no time for fear. Sitting there, counting the time between flash and crash to see whether the storm was receding or returning—with the expectation that next time it broke above us it must surely finish its work of destruction—would, I think, have tried the strongest nerves. The peaks are needle-pointed, there is much ironstone, and the storms here are among the worst in the world. Later we heard that one of the carriers, employed by a surveying party while delimiting the Nigerian Cameroons Boundary, had been struck and killed on a hill not many miles away.

When the storm had at length rumbled away in the direction of Calabar, we walked along the topmost ridge of the peak. As far as the eye could reach, chaos reigned. No sign of human habitation was in sight, and pacing from end to end of the long narrow summit gave one the curious sensation of being on shipboard, the sole survivors of a world overwhelmed in some mighty convulsion of Nature.

All around lay white mists, billowing and breaking like the crests of angry waves, which stretched, sweep upon sweep, to the great dark hills beyond. Above loomed a sky of somber gray, broken here and there by splashes of stormy orange, while in the distance, over Calabar, the mutter of the dying storm might still be heard.
