# CHAPTER IX

## WOMAN—POSITION, ETC.

Just outside Niaji, one can find the only attempt at a portrait statue known in the Oban District, though others existed until lately on the farther side of the boundary.

The figure represents Maia, a priestess of Nimm. It is modeled, rather crudely, in mud on a framework of sticks, and is placed above the grave of the woman it commemorates. A little hut has been built over it, and around this are hung most of the things the dead woman once used. These are all broken according to custom.

As has already been stated on page 2, Nimm is the special object of devotion for Ekoi women. Her cult—founded, according to tradition, by a divine woman who came down to earth for that purpose—seems to provide a satisfying expression for the religious feelings of her human sisters. Every eighth day is sacred to her and is called "the women's day"—

->"Ofu ane akai.<-
->Day of persons female."<-

On this day, women have even more power than usual, and no work must be done. Should anyone break the law and go to work upon their farm, Nimm would be angered and send up her servants, the animals, to destroy it.

Those newly initiated into the mysteries of Nimm are rubbed with red camwood dye. Afterward, they have the right to wear special ornaments around their necks and arms and to carry the "feathers of Nimm" in their right hands and in their hair, while in their left hands they carry a <term>juju</term> knife.

Each "Nimm woman" has a small shrine built in the corner of her room. On this stands a pot, usually an ancient earthenware one, containing "medicine" specific to the cult,

# CHAPTER IX

## WOMAN—POSITION, ETC.

Just outside Niaji, one can find the only attempt at a portrait statue known in the Oban District, though others existed until recently on the farther side of the boundary.

The figure represents Maia, a priestess of Nimm. It is modeled, somewhat crudely, in mud on a framework of sticks, and is placed over the grave of the woman it commemorates. A small hut has been built over it, and around this are hung most of the things the dead woman once used. These are all broken according to custom.

As has already been stated on page 2, Nimm is the special object of devotion for Ekoi women. Her cult—founded, according to tradition, by a divine woman who came down to earth for that purpose—seems to provide a satisfying expression for the religious feelings of her human sisters. Every eighth day is sacred to her and is called "the women's day"—

->"Ofu ane akai.<-
->Day of the female persons."<-

On this day, women have even more power than usual, and no work must be done. If anyone breaks the law and goes to work on their farm, Nimm would be angered and send her servants, the animals, to destroy it.

Those newly initiated into the mysteries of Nimm are rubbed with red camwood dye. Afterward, they have the right to wear special ornaments around their necks and arms and to carry the "feathers of Nimm" in their right hands and in their hair, while in their left hands they carry a <term>juju</term> knife.

Each "Nimm woman" has a small shrine built in the corner of her room. On this stands a pot, usually an ancient earthenware one, containing "medicine" specific to the cult,

At Niaji, in one of the compounds, the Juju Enyere is to be seen. This consists of a growing “Egakk” tree, to which an earthen pot is attached by a coil of thick bronze wire that continues down the trunk. The pot is closed by a flat earthenware lid and decorated with a fringe of split palm leaves and two Nimm feathers.

The Ekoi are a polygamous people, but until several years after my arrival, the chief wife, not the husband, was regarded as the head of the house. This is still true to a great extent, but there are indications that native customs in this, as with children, property, etc., are beginning to be influenced by those of white men; especially in places near European centers, such as Calabar. At Niaji, and the more northern towns, the change has hardly had time to make itself felt, and old customs still prevail. Each wife has complete control over her children, and the children almost always go with her if she leaves her husband.

<header>IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH</header>

Women's rights are so strictly guarded by native law that even now it is not at all unusual for a wife to summon her husband before the Court on the serious charge of having used some of her property—perhaps a pot or pan—without permission.
The following stories give some idea of the status of the sexes:

### WHY MEN MUST SERVE WOMEN.

Long ago, Obassi Osaw and Obassi Nsi decided to build two towns; the former for men, and the latter for women. Each was to be separate from the other. When both were inhabited, the people of the two towns began to exchange visits. Sometimes men visited the women's town, and sometimes women went to the men's. In the course of time, disputes arose over the ownership of the surrounding wilderness <note>the bush</note>, and the men began to fight their neighbors.
Obassi Nsi and Obassi Osaw said to one another, “What can we do to prevent this? Let us hold a meeting.”
When they had considered the question, they decided that it would be better for men and women to live together in one town. The women refused, saying, “The men began to kill us. Why should we go to live in their town? If the men want to live with us, let them come and live in ours.”
To this the men agreed, and that is the reason why, when we marry a woman, we must serve her as long as she lives with us.

---

The next story goes even further.

### HOW MEN CAME ON EARTH.

At the beginning of things, the world was inhabited by women only.
One day, Obassi Nsi happened to kill a woman by accident.
On hearing this, the rest gathered together and prayed to him, asking that if he intended to slay them, he should bring destruction on them all together rather than kill them slowly one by one.
Obassi Nsi was sorry for the grief that he had caused. So he offered to give them anything they should choose out of all

They asked him to list what he had to offer and said that they would all cry "Yes" when he named the thing they desired.

Obassi began and mentioned, one by one, all his fruits, birds, and animals, but at the name of each, they shouted "No."

At last, the list was nearly finished. Only one thing remained to offer. "Will you then take man?" Obassi asked at last.

"Yes!" they roared with a great shout, and catching hold of one another, they began dancing for joy at the thought of the gift Obassi was sending.

They accepted man, therefore, as compensation for the fellow woman whom they had lost. Thus, men became the servants of women and have to work for them to this day. For, although a woman comes under the influence of her husband upon marriage, she is still his owner and has a right to ask any service and expect him to do whatever she chooses.

---

It is not unusual in these stories for a man to lose his life rather than fail to satisfy some whim of his wife's, as, for example, in the following story:

### THE MAN WHO UNDERSTOOD ANIMALS' SPEECH.

Once, long ago, a man went into the bush to hunt. He saw an antelope and tried to kill it, but could not. The beast escaped and ran down a large hole in the ground. The hunter followed and found himself in a ghost town.

When he arrived, the antelope's mistress was questioning it about why it had returned so hurriedly. It replied that a hunter had tried to kill it in the world above. While speaking, it turned around and saw the man himself standing there aghast. It pointed him out to the ghost woman and said:
"That is the man."

Now, the hunter heard the sound of voices but could not understand what was being said.

The ghost woman called her ghost friends and told them what

The man noticed that the little ones looked sad and dirty, and that their hair was long, matted, and full of lice. So he called them to come and sit around him.

Before the ghosts left the town, they had loosened his bonds a little and put “medicine” in his ears, so that he might understand their speech. He then began, in order, from the first child to the last, to cut the hair from their heads and wash them all properly with water.

When the ghost people came back, they found their ugly children had been made neat and very clean. They embraced the hunter and thanked him heartily for what he had done. Those who had older children with matted and dirty hair brought them to him, so that he might care for them as he had done for the others. He worked so well that the ghosts said he should not be killed, but, on the contrary, should be free to go home. When his work was done, they gave him as a reward the power to understand the language of all animals; but they warned him that he must not reveal this to any living being, or he would die at once.

The hunter thanked them and returned home. His fellow villagers were glad to see him again, and he told them where he had been and how he got back, but he kept the secret of the language of the animals.

One day his mother-in-law heard of his return and went to visit him. She sat on the veranda of the house and ate corn which her daughter brought her. As she bit the grains from the cob, a few of them fell down, and a hen who was nearby saw this and began to call her chicks.

“Agbaw Okpok, Agbaw Okpok,” she cried—for that is the way a hen calls her brood—“If you want to pick up the fallen grains, do not go near the woman’s right hand, but go as close as you please to her left eye, because she is blind on that side and cannot see you.”

Upon hearing this, the man burst into a loud laugh, for indeed, his mother-in-law had lost her left eye. His wife thought that he was laughing at her mother and became annoyed with him. The husband explained that he was not laughing at what she thought, but only because he had just remembered a story which had once amused him. His wife asked to be told what it was and would not be satisfied until he granted her request. When he found out how much she wished to know, he told her what the hen had said and how he came to understand her speech. He then fell dead on the spot, just as the ghosts had warned him would happen if he revealed the secret.

This man was the only living being who ever understood the speech of animals. He told his wife what the hen had said simply to please her, fully knowing that his death would follow.

### WHY CHILDREN BELONG TO THE MOTHER.

There was once a beast called <term>Ejimm</term>,* who had two <term>Ejimm</term> sons named Obegud and Igwe. They lived in the bush near the home of a poor couple who had twelve children.

One day the parents left their little ones at home and went to the farm. While they were away, the children sang and played happily together, but the wicked beast <term>Ejimm</term> heard their voices. She told her son Obegud to go to their house and say that he had something to sell. This the beast did, and the children asked him to show his wares.

As soon as he had succeeded this far in his errand, he went back singing:—

> “ Obegud Obegud ayaya-ay
> Bia koko ayaya-ay
> Ajima anwa nwa ayaya-ay.”

(The narrator repeated this song very carefully, but had no idea of its meaning. It has apparently come down from very ancient times.)

When <term>Ejimm</term> knew from the sound of her son’s voice that all

At first, the woman would not go, but after a while, her husband persuaded her, so she left him.

On hearing this, <term>Ejimm</term> again set out in search of prey and came to the threshold as before. The man was well-armed, but at the horrible sight of the beast, his courage failed him. He ran for his life through the back doorway, leaving his children helpless before the greedy monster.

Again <term>Ejimm</term> seized a child and carried it off, rejoicing greatly over the prey she had found.

When the mother came back and heard that a second child had been taken, her grief knew no bounds. She turned fiercely on her husband and asked why he had not saved his child. To excuse his cowardice, he told her that he had been very ill and had been forced to leave the little ones for a while, during which time the monster had come.

The children, however, all cried, “No, mother. Our father fled in terror at the sight of the beast and left us to face the danger alone.”

Filled with fury at this, the woman ordered her husband to leave. He did not need to be told twice but went out and hid himself in the bush nearby.

The mother determined to risk her life to save her little ones.

# CHAPTER X

## WOMAN—POSITION, ETC. (*continued*)

By native custom, a man who wishes to marry an Ekoi maiden must serve her people for a considerable time, usually from two to three years. His work mostly consists of helping to clear the bush for the next season's farms, but other services may be required of him.

During this time, he is expected to give presents to the relatives of his future wife, the value of which varies according to his means. A very usual list of gifts offered to the father and mother, or guardians, is the following:

1 demijohn of palm oil.
1 head of plantains.
1 piece of dried meat.
2 bottles of rum.
2, or more, heads of tobacco.

Virginity in a bride is not considered of primary importance, though parents usually watch over their daughters with great care, and in some cases, girls are not allowed to go out alone.

Even if young girls are allowed considerable freedom before marriage, they may be regarded as fairly faithful once the ceremony has been performed. This is partly due to fear of the Jujus invoked by the husband, and partly because considerable damages may be claimed from the co-respondent, and also from the woman, should the husband consider the affair serious enough to demand a divorce.

The wedding ceremony is not regarded as having any religious character, and there is no trace of ritual symbolizing former marriage to a deity.

The actual marriage, according to native law, consists of the acceptance by the bride from the groom of at least one wedding

Acceptance must be followed by a public proclamation of the marriage before chiefs and people, after the bell has been rung around the town for that purpose. The actual words used in most towns are "Oho Oho Owe," but in some places "Ora Ho, Ora Ho" is called instead. The expressions are practically identical and mean "Our own." After these words, the names of the couple are usually added.

The proclamation is mostly a precautionary measure on the part of the husband. Ekoi women are unfortunately all too fond of persuading suitors to give them offerings as wedding gifts, which they afterwards declare they only regarded as "sweetheart" presents, therefore not binding them to marriage.

If an Ekoi mother does not approve of the man her daughter has chosen, she can sometimes persuade her to give him up by the threat of not providing her with a good "fatting-house"—<gloss>that is, not letting her have as much, or as rich, food during the time of her seclusion as she would have if she had chosen a suitor whom the mother favored.</gloss>

A case of this kind came before the native Court on March 3, 1909, when Mane Okon claimed damages for breach of promise to marry from Itakui Mbing Atan. The latter stated:

> "I promised to marry him, but said I did not want to take his present yet, as, if I accepted it, my mother, who did not approve of him as a husband for me, would not give me a good 'fatting-house' like the others. After two months spent in the 'fatting-house' I looked at him again, and said to myself, 'He does not seem to be a clever man. I do not think he would make a good husband.' I therefore chose another, and pointed him out to my father as the one I would have."

The period spent in the fatting-house varies, according to the wealth of the parents, from a few weeks up to two years. It is very common for a girl confined in this way to amuse herself by

# WOMAN—POSITION, ETC.

The little row of circles at the left-hand corner represents the first tally kept. This was later elaborated in the manner shown above.

Usually before leaving the fatting-house, the girl undergoes <term>clitoridectomy</term>, but this operation is sometimes performed in infancy, and sometimes not until after the birth of the first child.

When a girl leaves the fatting-house, it is an occasion of much rejoicing. A great feast is made and dances are held. The girl herself is smeared from the waist downward with a red dye made from the <term>cam-wood</term> tree. Fatting-house ornaments, consisting of tassels and chains made of dried palm-leaf fibre also dyed red, are hung around her neck, while a cross-piece of the same material is usually passed beneath the breasts. Her girdle of beads, cowries, and palm is also rubbed over with the same dye. Her face is painted in various patterns and colours, and her hair dressed in a very elaborate way and decorated with combs and large "pompoms" of white feathers, while over all nods a plume of the dark green and creamy feathers of the <term>Nkundak</term> (Greater Plantain-eater).

Unless my memory misleads me, some such custom also exists among the <term>Bavili</term> of the French Congo, where a girl is secluded for a time in the "Paint House," so called because, after being carefully fed and tended there in enforced seclusion, she is painted red before being led to the dwelling of her future husband.

At a wedding, besides the gifts presented to the bride and her people, offerings must also be sent to the chiefs of the town. A feast is made for the <term>Nkan</term>, or "age classes," of bride and groom. By this expression is meant those townspeople born within two or three years of one another. The men of roughly the same age form a sort of club among themselves, and the girls and women do likewise.<note>See p. 283.</note>

Immediately after marriage, if the husband is wise, he will try to persuade his wife to swear with him before the <term>Juju Njomm Ekatt</term> (the Foot Juju), which is supposed to keep wives faithful to their husbands.

...has been mentioned and is supposed to possess magic properties. Hens' eggs and a quantity of Mfu leaves are collected, and the leaves are placed in a vessel of fresh water; the woman then holds an egg in each hand, while the man pours water over them. Next, she lays the eggs on the ground and places two leaves beside them. The husband steps forward with his left foot and, while standing in this position, crushes the leaves in the vessel of water. Into this, the woman carefully stirs the mud brought for the purpose. After a while, when it is well mixed, she dips in her hand and makes a mark with the liquid on her husband’s forehead. He, in turn, does the same for her.

The object of this ceremony is to prevent women from having lovers after marriage. If they do so after the rite described above, it is thought that <term>Njomm Ekatt</term> will “catch” them and cause an illness from which they can only recover after confessing to their husbands and persuading them to revoke the <term>Juju</term>.

Another way of ensuring a wife's fidelity is to swear an oath with her before <term>Njomm Aiyung</term> (the <term>Blood Juju</term>).

Each of the contracting parties sucks a little blood from the other's wrist, as in the ancient marriage rite. Certain death is thought to follow any violation of this oath. The husband's blood that has entered the woman’s body is said to rebel at the first sign of unfaithfulness and flow so furiously through her veins that it causes a speedy death.

A third way is described on page 224.

Upon marriage, the wife becomes a member of her husband’s family and goes to live in his compound. A man’s first wife is always the head of the house. The younger wives obey her and defer to her in everything. Therefore, a wife likes her husband to marry many other women. The chief complaint of cruelty brought by the wife of <term>Njabong of Oban</term> before the Native Court was that her husband refused to marry anyone but herself.

Should a wife’s father die after marriage, it is customary for the husband to support his mother-in-law, though this is not mandatory. Each wife is given one side of the central <term>atrium</term>, and two fireplaces are made for her: one for her own use and one for her children. When the number of wives...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Ekoi domestic life, specifically focusing on the living arrangements within compounds and the legal and social definitions of marriage and labor obligations among wives.</meta>

IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

If the number of people exceeds the housing provided by one compound, another is built, and so on until there is enough room for everyone. The husband has his own private room where he entertains his male friends.

As a rule, the only objection a man's wives offer to him visiting other women is that if the latter receive his attentions, they should do their share of the house and farm work for his family. This was demonstrated during a case which came before the Court on May 17th, 1907. A man named Akari Ntui claimed a certain woman named Atim Okon as his wife. She denied the claim, and in her sworn evidence she stated:

> “I was never a legal wife of the plaintiff, nor was I his proper ‘friend.’ Okon Asibong was my real ‘friend,’ but the plaintiff used to visit me until his wife warned me that if her husband came to my house again, she would count me as one of his wives. I then sued the plaintiff to prove that I was not married to him. This happened at Obutong about five years ago.”

<margin>A pencil bracket appears in the left margin spanning the next two paragraphs.</margin>
There are almost no marriage restrictions among these people. A man may marry a woman of the same name and tribe, or of another. It is not even forbidden by native law for half-brothers and half-sisters to marry, although cases of this kind are extremely rare. One such case came before the Native Court on October 4th, 1909, between Ma Mfon Ita and Ntui Obassi.

In her sworn evidence, the former stated, “When I was a small girl, my father Itu gave me as a child-wife to Ntui Obassi. When I grew old enough for motherhood, the latter gave me in marriage to Ita Nken. I was not willing. I was never willing to live as a wife with either of them. I am Ntui’s half-sister.”

She was declared free by native law because her consent had never been given.

<margin>A pencil bracket appears in the left margin spanning the rest of the page.</margin>

> “My father told me that I was the wife of Njok Abang, but that when I grew up I would not have to continue the marriage con-”

The claim was disallowed by native law, on the same grounds as the previous one.

From the last case, it can be seen that parents occasionally promise their daughters in marriage without the daughters' consent. Such an arrangement could never become binding, however, unless the girl herself agreed to it when she reached marriageable age and accepted the wedding gift.

Very small children are sometimes persuaded to take presents and are afterwards claimed as wives, on the ground that these gifts, accepted years before, bound them to marriage. Little Ekoi girls are therefore very cautious about accepting gifts from their boy companions. That they have need to be wary is shown by the following case, heard on January 3, 1908, in which Ma Obassi of Ayabam claimed the return of her daughter from Chief Nenkui. She declared on oath:

"I sent my daughter Baii to Mfamosing. She went out to play with the children. Etim, the son of Nenkui, gave this ring to her, saying, 'Here is a present.' Baii asked, 'Are you giving this as a marriage proposal?' Etim answered, 'No, I am only giving it as a <term>dash</term>.' When Baii had taken the ring, the boy's relatives grabbed her and took her to their compound. There they kept her. She was about eight years old at the time.

"I went to Nenkui and begged him to give Baii back. He said 'No,' not unless I ransomed her by paying many pieces of cloth.

"Afterwards, I went to Obutong. My daughter escaped and ran away to me there. Nenkui sent after her and had her..."

If a man claims a girl as his sweetheart, and she wishes to show that his suit is hopeless, she calls for water and washes her hands before him.

This was done by Ikwo Okon, who stated on oath:
“Once Ntui Akam sent a messenger to ask me to go to his house. I did so, thinking that something good would happen. He asked me, ‘Why will you not accept my love? Are you afraid of your mother?’ I said, ‘I am too young for marriage.’ Next morning he brought palm oil to my mother. My older brother Usimebin took some of this, and my father took some also. A little while after, the defendant asked me to go and eat food with him. I went, and after we had eaten he rose up and said, ‘Now you are my “friend,” and we will continue like this until we become permanent husband and wife.’ At once I washed my hands and went away, telling him not to come to my mother’s house, and saying that I would never be his ‘friend.’”

When more than one man loves the same girl, magic rites are practiced by the suitors in order to secure her affection, or to keep another from winning her. Two well-known ways of bringing this about came up in Court on February 3, 1908. Obiri Awaw (sworn) stated:
“Two years ago my sister Ekpo Awaw gave Usin to me as a ‘friend.’ Obassi Ndo tried to take the girl away from me. So I took my company <note>Age class.</note> ‘Ekpe Kusua,’ and crossed two sticks before her door, so that the defendant should not visit there any more.
“Some time after I saw Usin sitting by Obassi on his veranda. I told her to go away, and he ran up to me, and said very angrily, ‘I know that you want to kill me.’ I raised my hands on high and said: ‘God knows my father knew nothing of poison, nor do I.’
“One morning I went to greet the mother of the girl, and saw the defendant tying up her food with a piece of native rope. This was a <term>Juju</term> to prevent the food from nourishing her if she carried on a friendship with anyone but himself.”

On March 3rd, 1909, Ekoli charged her husband before the Native Court with trying to bring about her death in this manner. She stated:

> “A month and a half ago I quarreled with my husband Itui Ita. While he was away my child died. On his return he asked me where it was. > “He took his Juju named Eburuk Pabi, held a machete in his right hand and the Juju in his left, and called ‘Eburuk Pabi! Eburuk Pabi! If Ekoli will not come to me, may you catch her! If she comes, may you not catch her.’ Soon afterward a fever took me, and I sent and told Effion Archibong.”

The latter stated on oath:

> “When the woman was ill, I sent for the accused and told him to gather meat for the sacrifice so that he might revoke the Juju. He did not deny that he had sworn Juju against her, nor make any objection to gathering the meat for the sacrifice, so the charm was revoked and the woman grew well.”

Divorce is extremely easy under native law. The most common rite for freeing a wife is to rub white chalk on both her hands. If a woman wishes to free herself without the consent of her husband, she usually rakes out the fire and pours water on the embers until they die out. She then cuts her hair and covers herself with white paint. After this, even if both parties wished it, she could never return to her husband. Such a case occurred on December 3rd, 1908, when Awaw Otu stated on oath:

> “Machott was my wife. One day she pulled out the kitchen fire onto the floor and poured water on it until it died out. Then she cut her hair and covered herself with white. This is against our rule; so now she cannot come back to me as my wife.”

In cases of divorce, public sympathy is usually on the side of the wife, as will be seen from the following story:—

### WHY WIVES SOMETIMES LEAVE THEIR HUSBANDS.

Once an animal named Mbaw and his wife Ma Ndikange were eating young coco-yams. He said to her, “I will go and set a trap.” So he went into the bush for that purpose. Next morning an <term>Etuk</term> (<term>duiker</term>) was found inside. He gave it to his wife and said, “Boil this, but it is taboo for you, as it is the first animal caught in the trap.”

Next day and the next, he said the same, and ate everything he killed. On the excuse that each animal was caught in a new trap, he gave none to Ndikange, even though she had cooked it.

On the third day he caught a pig. This he took home and said to his wife, “Boil it well. I think you will eat some of this pig.” After the meat was cooked, however, he made the same excuse as before and ate it all himself.

Then the woman thought to herself, “What can I do? All this time I am eating only young coco-yams. My husband gives me none of the beasts he traps.” She made a plan.

She got her basket and went out; then she collected magic leaves, mixed them together, and made “medicine.” Next, she went down to the river-side and poured the medicine into the water. Soon the river dried up because of the magic medicine. So she walked along its bed and caught four baskets full of fish of a very good kind, called <term>Noi-oshi</term>. She then went home, cooked these, and ate her fill of them, for they were

At daybreak, the husband said he felt very sick, so the woman left him to rest in the house and went alone to the farm. No sooner had she gone than he sprang up and tasted the fat left in the pot from the fish his wife had caught. At once he said to himself, “Oh, what a sweet taste! This is what my wife ate yesterday.”

Now the fish was inside a native pot, and before the woman left her house, she had put a <term>Juju</term> upon the fish to protect them.

The husband was so greedy that he stuck his head right inside the pot so that he might more quickly eat up the good fish.

When he was finished, he would have pulled his head out again, but the <term>Juju</term> caught him and held him fast.

He knocked his head up and down and tried to break the pot, but the <term>Juju</term> still held, and he could not free himself.

All of a sudden, he heard his stepson, the lame boy, greet <term>Ndikange</term> as she came back from the farm. The lame boy was her son.

<term>Mbaw</term> did not want to face his wife in that state, so he ran out, his head still covered with the pot, and stuck it in the deep gutter in front of the house. He thought that all of him was hidden, but alas! his feet stuck out.

The woman said to her son, “Where is my husband?”

The boy answered, “He has eaten your fish. When he heard you returning, he ran outside to hide. Here he is, with his head in the gutter and his feet sticking out.”

The woman went and caught her husband by the feet. She pulled him out and said to him:

> “You killed three animals. You ate all of these without giving me any. Look at your head covered with the pot! <term>Obassi</term> sees everything. That is his judgment on you. You have stolen my fish.”

The husband went out with the pot on his head and called together his “<term>age class</term>.” When they were all gathered before the house, he said to them:

> “I have stolen my wife’s fish. When she went away, she...”

His companions took his side and said that the matter went against the woman, and that she must take off the pot.

She said, “Why should I do so? If the pot is taken off his head, I will not be his wife again forever.”

Then she threw some medicine onto the pot, and it fell away. The man’s neck and head swelled up. The woman ran from them all and said, “I will be his wife no longer, but will marry another man.”

The husband remained full of sorrow. Then he disguised himself and followed her. He went around by another way and lay down in the road where she must pass by. When the woman came up to him, he said:

She said to him, “You are too like my former husband. I will not marry you, but someone else.” She then went on her way.

Again the husband disguised himself and ran on. He caught her up and accosted her as before. She said to him:

“Very well, I will marry you temporarily, to see how you will be. If you behave badly, like my first husband, I shall divorce myself again and leave you.”

This is the reason why women divorce themselves and marry other men. Whenever they marry a husband and find that he is good, they stay with him. <term>Ndikange</term> remained with this husband and had six children by him. She often said to herself, “If I had stayed with my first husband, I would not have done as well as this.”

During all this time the husband took such good care of her and her children that she became very rich.

The reason why people sometimes say “Women roam too much” is because these women have not found good husbands. When they find a good husband they stay with him and do not want to leave him to go to another.

Divorced wives may marry again, but a widow must not listen to the proposals of any man until the mourning period for her late husband is over.

WOMAN—POSITION, ETC.

On July 17th, 1909, a case came before the Court, in which Asot Ankpe confessed, “During the mourning for my husband, I accepted a certain man as a ‘friend.’” According to native custom in such a case, a woman must be handed over to her children, and the latter will have no right to their late father’s property.

During another trial on August 3rd, 1909, Ekpri Nwan Ndifon stated on oath:

“Okon Ene Okpo said to me, ‘What about the widow of your late master?’ I said, ‘She is still mourning. You must not talk about courtship yet. After the mourning is over, you can speak to her, but not now.’

“Later I said to him, ‘Our custom is that when a widow is released from mourning for her husband, you can approach her regarding a new marriage, but not now.’ Another day I said further, ‘After the mourning is quite over, you may bring a gift of one bottle of palm wine to the widow, but even then you must not talk of courtship at once.’”

The respective duties of husband and wife are clearly laid down by native law, and will be found fully treated on pp. 269 *et seq.*

Custom also insists that no favoritism may be shown to one wife over another, except for the privileges enjoyed by the first wife. An elderly woman has no cause to complain of neglect because of her advancing years, for what she loses in youthful attraction is made up for by the reverence given to age.

Custom regulates even the smallest matters. In spite of the growing liking for European finery, no Ekoi woman could be persuaded to wear a hat. For them, such a thing is “taboo,” and as a reason the following legend is given:

### Why Women Do Not Wear Hats.

Obassi Osaw had five wives. Among them was one named Ekwaw, whom he loved above all the rest. She did no work, but stayed at home all day, while the other wives were made to wait upon her.

One day Obassi brought a little slave, and said to his

> “In seven days you may perform the play called <term>Nsibidi</term>. I will find out what is happening in my house.”

Women always have bad consciences. After they have married, they should not be unfaithful at all. Up to that time, if you loved your wife, you used to exchange hats with her, but since Ekwaw deceived her husband, women must not wear hats anymore.

# CHAPTER XI

## BIRTH CUSTOMS

Like most primitive peoples, the Ekoi have the vaguest ideas regarding the causes of their existence. Those who have come under white influence during the last few years do, it is true, pretend to be amused by the foolish stories of the “bush people”; but in the interior, the old vague myths still hold their ground.

There are many interesting beliefs regarding the arrival and death of babies. One charming superstition forbids all quarreling in a house where there are little children. The children, it is said, love sweet words, kind looks, and gentle voices, and if these are not found in the family into which they have been reincarnated, they will close their eyes and leave the earth until a chance offers to return among less quarrelsome surroundings.

As an example of how closely primitive thought sometimes reaches the most cultured minds of our own time, perhaps it may be of interest to mention the Ekoi equivalent for the "Song of the Mothers" who come forth to welcome the newborn in M. Maeterlinck’s play, “The Blue Bird.” Once, upon arriving at a small town among the hills in the interior after a long, hot march over difficult terrain, we stopped for the night at the Egbo house in the center of the town, as one always does where no rest-house has been built. From a nearby compound came the sound of singing, accompanied by drums and <term>okankan</term>. Since Bimba had developed a bad headache on the march and found the noise very trying, the inhabitants were requested to postpone their rejoicing or carry it out in a quieter manner. Upon hearing this, a small delegation was sent by the head woman of the compound to say that twin sons had just been born to her, and that if the family stopped singing and playing to show their joy, the newborns would think themselves unwelcome and go back to where they came from.

# BIRTH CUSTOMS

In Nigeria, twin births are a cause for great rejoicing. The accompanying photograph shows a dance held to celebrate such an event. The father and mother were rubbed with native red dye, and the mother was further decorated with white chalk spots. The babies were carried by the two oldest of the town's prominent women, who hold a position similar to godmothers to the newborns and are called "mother" by them in later life. Parents and "sponsors" wear ornaments made of young palm leaves around their necks. On this occasion, they danced to the accompaniment of the following song:

> "Ofung okupba, ojokk okupba.
> Buffaloes come, elephants come.
> ->Aya aya pong ki pong.<-
> Egimamfuk, ka osaw are aje, ka nsi are ayingi.
> Cork tree, in the air are leaves, in the ground are roots."

The refrain "Pong ki pong" is added to provide an onomatopoeic sound of the heavy tread of the approaching buffalo and elephant, and it may perhaps be compared with the "*Iliad*," Book XXIII, line 116,

> "πολλὰ δ'ἄναντα κάταντα πάραντά τε δόχμιά τ'ἦλθον";

and the "*Aeneid*," Book VIII, line 596,

> "Quadrupedante putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum."

Two very old songs in honor of the birth of twins are as follows:

The third line from the end is somewhat reminiscent of the hint given by the dish placed on Polish tables to signal that a guest has outstayed his welcome.
   If a woman remains childless for several years after marriage, it is thought that there must be some specific reason for the baby's absence. The cause is usually attributed to the “ill-wish” of some witch in the town—often a jealous fellow-wife or relative—who, like the mother-in-law in “Willie’s Lady” or the abandoned mistress mentioned in the “Metamorphoses of Apuleius,” has used magic to prevent the birth of the child.

The principal <term>Juju</term> used to protect women about to become mothers, or those suffering from infertility induced by witchcraft, is named "<term>Isse Obassi Nsi</term>." It consists of two different parts. First, a double string of knotted palm-leaf strips hung up over the door of the woman's room, and secondly, a little shrine within. On the latter, a small lamp is to be found, unlit by day, but burning all through the night. “Not long after, the great <term>Juju</term> Akpambe arrived at Okuri. When Aya heard this, she sent for her daughter and told her to go before Akpambe. <margin>When a woman is childless for several years after marriage, it is thought that the baby has lain for all that time in the womb, waiting until the right moment should come for it to be born. Such a case is told in the following story:</margin>

### SEVEN YEARS IN THE WOMB.

Once, long ago, God made a man and a woman and placed them in a little hut which he had built for that purpose.

In a few months, the woman began to think that she ought to have a child. Nevertheless, she remained childless for seven years.

One day, when that time had passed by, the husband went off to hunt. He went very far from their hut and was gone for many nights and days. When he came back, he saw a boy sitting in the house.

Now while he was away, his wife went into the bush to gather firewood. On the road, she felt that her time had come. She laid her hands upon a tree and held it firmly. Then, instead of a tender baby, behold! there appeared a boy whose size was

...nearly equal to her own. At once the latter took her by the hand and led her home, for she was very faint from giving birth to such a person.
When the husband came back and saw the boy, he asked the child where he had come from. “I am your son, <term>Tata</term>,”* answered the child.
“How can that be?” asked the man.
“I was born of my mother, who is your true wife,” answered the child; “but as I knew that you needed a helper, I would not come to you for seven years. I finished my time of helplessness in her womb and am now ready and able to help you both.”
The man could hardly believe the boy’s story and was very much afraid. He thought he was going to die after seeing such a wonderful sight. “Perhaps,” thought the father, “he is sent by the spirits to fetch me.”
So his thoughts wandered, although the wife also told him that the child was really his son.
For four days the boy stayed at home and looked after his mother. On the fifth day, he begged his father to give him a machete, with which he could go into the “bush.”
In one hand he carried the machete, and in the other he held a double-edged knife called <term>Isawm</term>. The latter was a magic knife and pointed out the direction of any place where its owner wished to go. For instance, should he want to reach a town which lies to the south, the knife bent of its own accord if pointed toward the east, north, or west, yet kept quite straight if held to the south.
The boy set snares as he went along. He went on and on, making traps, until at last he thought the time had come for him to return. On the way back, he found many birds caught in the snares he had set. These he took home to his parents, and they thanked him heartily.
The next day he went out again to set more traps, and just as he was turning to come back as before, he heard distant music playing as if for a wrestling match.
Now the lad was very fond of wrestling, so he hurried back home and told his parents that he had heard the sound of

...wrestlers’ music, and he decided to set out the next day to find where it came from. His parents advised him not to go, but he would not be deterred and set out with <term>Isawm</term> in his hand.

When he reached the part of the forest where he had previously heard the playing, he stopped and listened, but the woods were completely silent. The magic knife had led him directly to the place where it originated.

At the sound, he rushed forward as if he had wings and found himself at the foot of a very steep mountain, from the top of which the long-sought, longed-for music sounded clear and certain.

The face of the mountain was so steep and slippery that no human could have climbed it without help. The boy set to work, however, using <term>Isawm</term> to carve two holes for his feet; then, standing in these, he carved two more higher up, and continued in this way until at last he reached the top of the mountain. The moment he reached the summit, he saw—and was seen by—the people who lived on the plateau above the cliff he had climbed. He immediately joined in the wrestling.

Now, the best wrestlers among these people were seven in number, but the newcomer defeated them all.

<term>Obassi</term> heard the noise of the struggle and came at once to see what was happening, for the town belonged to him. He saw the boy, recognized him as the one he had sent to help the poor couple, and motioned for him to come closer.

Even though it was only the seventh day since his birth, the boy had already grown into a man. <term>Obassi</term> said, “You have defeated all the others; therefore, I will adopt you as my own son.”

The youth was so handsome that when <term>Obassi’s</term> head wife saw him, she immediately fell in love with him. At first, the boy rejected her, but it was not long before he gave in to temptation and foolishly accepted her advances. <term>Obassi</term> knew everything, for nothing can be hidden from him. He asked the woman if she would admit what she had done, but she denied it. He then asked his adopted son, who admitted his mistake; consequently, <term>Obassi</term> immediately forgave him.

After staying for a week, the boy told Obassi that he would like to go and see his other parents, but that he would come back.

To this Obassi agreed, and gave him a rich present to take to his poor parents; and the boy started off, well content.

When he had reached the halfway point on the homeward road, he heard a sound in the bush at the side of the path. The branches were pushed back, and out stepped the woman whom he had left in the mountain town. She had heard the conversation between her lover and his adopted father, and had quickly followed.

The boy, who had by now learned the benefit of having a mate, was glad to take her to his home, and never returned to Obassi again.

Obassi knew that his wife had gone away with the lad, but he was patient, thinking, “Perhaps he will come back to ask forgiveness as he did before.” When the boy did not return after a long time, however, Obassi sent out his war-men to punish him.

<margin>* Compare Genesis 3:5.</margin>
Now, upon adopting the boy, Obassi had shown him the <term>Jujus</term> of good and evil.* When the war-men appeared, therefore, this wicked youth put forth a strong magic and commanded them to fight among themselves. So each man’s hand was turned against his neighbor, and they fought together until all died, except for a very few. These went back to their Lord and told him how they had fared. When Obassi heard what the boy had done, he was very angry and shut the gates of mercy to mankind. Were it not for the fault of this couple, we might at any time have run to Obassi and pleaded for forgiveness for whatever evil we had done, and he would have pardoned us at once and spared our lives. Since the sin of this pair, however, the road to mercy is blocked forever.

# CHAPTER XII
## BIRTH CUSTOMS—*continued*

From the moment a woman knows she is about to become a mother, she must take many precautions to ward off evil. For instance, she must be careful when passing along a road, or through the bush, never to go near the Njo Uru tree, the bark of which is used in fishing; otherwise, the child will die.

Neither she nor her husband may eat elephant meat, and she must also abstain from porcupine, water chevrotain, and the leaves of gourd or pumpkin. It seems probable, from certain indications, that these plants were once regarded as totems. She must sacrifice to her household Juju—the most common of which is Osam (Spear). For this rite, a calabash, or native pot of lightly-baked earthenware, is filled with food, and the spear is driven through it.

Just before the birth is expected, the leading women of the town gather and administer soothing drinks to the mother. From the moment of their entry until after the washing of the baby, no man may approach the house, though the father and his male relatives may be present for the anointing with palm oil.

After the birth, the mother is secluded for one or two months. If the grandmother is still alive and in a position to afford the expense, the mother generally goes to the fatting-house for a period varying from four to six months, during which time the husband does not visit her. On returning to ordinary life, the young mother must sacrifice to her Juju, while the husband makes an offering to his.

When a baby is first carried outside the birth-room, the mother herself, or her mother, must carry it to the threshold between her two palms. One of the female relatives, either the grandmother, sister, or aunt, then throws water onto the

roof so that it drips upon the child. If this is not done, the child will develop a fever. A week later, it is rubbed with white chalk to bring good luck and is then carried around to the houses of friends. On this occasion, gifts are presented to the mother.

The first curl on the head of a baby is carefully cut by the grandmother, wrapped in a cloth, and hidden in a box.

If a woman is unable to nurse her baby, she may give it to her sister to nurse; however, this practice is generally viewed with disfavor, and the mother must be treated with medicine so she can tend to her own child as soon as possible. After two or three months, crushed plantains are given as additional food. When the infant is considered old enough, its wrist is cut and magic medicines are rubbed inside. The medicine generally used to give strength is made from the index finger of the Nyokk (Chimpanzee, *Anthropopithecus troglodytes*), and for quickness and activity, crushed Nsoii—the large, fierce black ants (*Paltothyreus tarsatus fabricius*)—are used.

A child is usually given its first name based on the day, time, or place of its birth. For instance, if it is born on a native Sunday, it would be called “Edet” if a boy, and “Ared” if a girl. If it were born during the night, it would be called “Okun” or “Akun” (night). If born at a farm, it would be called “Etim” or “Atim” (bush). The name is given immediately after birth. In many cases, Efik names are chosen, as they are often shorter than their Ekoi equivalents.

If the child remains healthy for a full year, the name first given becomes permanent; however, if the child falls sick, the parents take it to the “Mboni” (Diviner). The Diviner tells them to prepare a sacrifice consisting of meat, plantains, and coco-yams. On the appointed day, the family assembles and calls a meeting of the townspeople. The head of the house then slowly recites the names of the ancestors on both sides of the family. As each name is called, the Diviner answers “No,” until finally one is mentioned that he accepts. This name is given to the baby, in the belief that the soul of that particular ancestor has been reincarnated in the child. The illness is thought to be a sign sent to show that the spirit wishes the Diviner to be consulted so that the right name may be given.

<header>IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH</header>

The name of the father or the father’s brother is added as a surname, though it is not often used in everyday life.

After the ceremony described above, if a child becomes sick, the illness is usually attributed to the influence of witchcraft. All possible precautions are taken and charms are used to safeguard the child from being "overlooked" by the evil eye. If the child dies through no fault of its parents—such as quarreling, etc.—but merely through the ill will of an enemy, it may return again and again to the same family. It is, therefore, not unusual for parents who have lost several children in succession to say of the first one they have succeeded in raising, "He has been born three times," or "seven," as the case may be. Subsequent children are usually given a protective name, such as Ajomm (Juju spirits) or Obassi (God), in much the same way as many Israelite names were formed from Yahweh, Baal, Bel, or El. All children born as a result of special prayer to the Juju are called Njomm or Ajomm. Before the birth of a baby, the mother generally makes a pilgrimage to the most famous shrines in her region.

In the old days, if a husband and wife were childless, or if an old woman was lonely and longed for a son or daughter, legends claim there were many ways to obtain babies. Fruits, flowers, vegetables, and even fungi might, upon the prayer of the childless, open and provide them with a son or daughter. Indeed, in many cases, prayer was unnecessary; the mere intensity of the wish was enough to bring about its fulfillment.

Perhaps, in the belief in flower and fruit births, some faint, distant echo may be traced of those vague myths, the most beautiful of which grew into the story of the birth of Adonis.

To quote *The Golden Bough* (p. 281):
> "His (Adonis') connection with vegetation comes out at once in the common story of his birth. He was said to have been born from a myrrh tree, the bark of which, bursting . . . allowed the lovely infant to come forth."

And again (p. 298):
> "His origin is further attested by the story that he was born of a virgin, who conceived by putting in her bosom a ripe almond or pomegranate."

The stories given next are typical of the Ekoi version of such legends.

# THE FLOWER CHILD.

### BY EFFA MBOP, WOMAN OF NIAJI.

There was once a woman who was very sad because she had never had a child. She said to herself, “What can I do so that a baby may come to me?” She went into the bush and searched around, then came back and planted what she had found. Every day she looked after it well, and it sprouted; she always said, “Other women have many children, but none come to me.” One day she went to her plant, and look! It bore great flowers, while at its root sat a beautiful boy. She carried him home and kept him hidden in her room. All day she talked to him and was very happy. The child said, “Let no one know where I came from.”

One day someone said to her, “With whom are you always talking in your room?” She answered, “I talk to myself.”

Later she had to go to the farm with the other women, but after they had started, one of them ran back to the compound, opened the door of the childless woman's room, and saw who was inside.

When they came back, the two women had a quarrel, for one accused the other of having stolen the baby she had found. While they quarreled, a third woman came up. “It is no proper child at all,” she said, “but only the son of the flowers of the tree.”

The childless woman went into her room and took the little baby in her arms. “If you are born of a flower,” she said, “you are just the same as my own to me.”

The boy began to cry bitterly and said: “I told you that no one must know you had found me. Now that everyone knows I am a flower-child, I must go back to where I came from.”

The next day, very early in the morning, the boy said, “Now, I am going.” He ran from the room and into the bush. The childless woman followed, but though she searched, she could not find him. At length, when the day had grown very hot, she came to a place where a great plant bloomed full of the flowers beneath which she had first found the baby. There, at the foot of the plant, he lay dead.

<vocab>Effa Mbop, Niaji, Flower Child, folklore, West African mythology, birth customs</vocab>

<summary>A childless woman miraculously finds a beautiful boy at the root of a flowering plant she grew, but the child dies and returns to the plant after his secret origin is revealed during a quarrel.</summary>
<keywords>Effa Mbop, Niaji, Flower Child, folklore, West African mythology, birth customs, supernatural birth, Ekoi culture</keywords>

--- Page 186 ---
<meta>This page concludes the story of "The Flower Child," explaining the origin of the "bitter leaf" plant, and begins a new folktale titled "The Fruit Child," shared by Ikpuma of Ndebbiji.</meta>

Until then, if a woman had no child, she could get one from a fruit or a flower, but since the boy ran away from this woman, no one can get a child from a plant anymore. If this one had stayed with his foster mother, it would still have been possible to obtain children in that way.

White people call the plant “bitter leaf,” because its leaves have grown bitter from the tears of the woman as she buried her little dead child at its root.

## THE FRUIT CHILD.

->By IKPUMA OF NDEBBIJI.<-

Two young men were great friends. The name of the one was Okun and the other Eret.

One day both went into the bush to hunt. On the way, they saw an Mbum fruit which was quite ripe. This they gathered and carried with them.

When they came to the hunter’s hut where they were to spend the night, they laid the fruit down on the bank of a stream which flowed close by. This was in the evening. The next day both went out to hunt, and when they returned, a calabash of food stood ready, and all was prepared for the meal. Both wondered who could have cooked for them, but one said, “Anyway, let us eat. We are hungry.” So they ate, and the food was very good.

The next day again they went out to hunt, and once more, on their return, the meal stood ready. They ate it and said, “Tomorrow we will go out, but will come back early and watch.”

Okun reached the hut before his friend and hid in a hollow tree. After he had waited a while, he saw the fruit open and a beautiful girl step forth. She began setting everything in order, and then cooked <term>chop</term> for the evening meal. Okun came from his hiding place and would have spoken to her, but when she saw him she tried to run away. He, however, said, “Do not leave us. We have something to say to you.” He then called his friend, “Eret, Eret. Come, I have found out who it is who has worked for us.”

They persuaded the girl to stay with them, but when many moons had gone by she said to Okun, “I must go back to my

One day, when her child was a few weeks old, she left it in the house and went to work at the farm. While she was away the child cried. The husband's sister said to it, "Hush! You son of a fruit!"

Though the mother was far away, the wind carried the sound to her, and she ran home crying, "All of you promised that none would ever say that I came out of a fruit."

She took the child in her arms and ran to the great Mbum tree which was growing nearby. This opened, and she stepped within, and it closed over her and her child.

In those days if a woman had no child she could go into the bush and ask Mbum to open and give her a baby, but since they said to this little one, "You are the young child of a fruit," no one can get children in this way anymore.

### THE FUNGUS DAUGHTER.

->BY BAI EFFIONG, A GIRL OF NSAN.<-

There once lived an old couple who had never had any child at all. One day the old man went out into the bush and searched and searched to find a child. He found nothing but a great Ebbuya ball, which the Ekoi people use to grate up finely and then put into the soup to thicken it. This he took and put into his bag, for he said to himself, "I have heard that when a lucky person finds a thing like this, he can carry it home and it becomes a child to him." When he reached his hut, he heard a voice from the bag, which said, "Take me out of the bag, my father, for it is very hard for me to breathe here."

The old man put his hand into the bag and, instead of the Ebbuya ball, drew forth a beautiful young girl. You may think how pleased he was to have found a child so easily! His wife also was delighted when she heard the good news and did everything she could to make the new daughter happy. After a while the girl grew old enough to be sent to the fatting-

When the foster daughter spoke to this maid, however, and asked her to cook or perform any other service, she answered, "I do not recognize you at all as my mistress, for I well know that you are not the true daughter of those whom you call your parents. You are nothing but an <term>Ebbuya</term> ball!"

On hearing this unkind speech, the foster daughter went sadly back to the bush and once more became a fungus.

When the old couple returned, they found their foster child missing. Now, in the same house there lived a lame boy who had overheard the whole matter and told them everything. Then the old people knew that their child had gone back where she came from and would never come to them anymore.

Again the old man set forth to look for <term>Ebbuya</term> balls, but though he found many, none ever turned into a child again.

Had the little slave not taunted the <term>Ebbuya</term> maiden for not being the true daughter of the family, she might have remained with them; from that time on, it would have been the custom for a man or woman to get a child this way, if they were lucky enough to find the right <term>Ebbuya</term> ball.

## THE HERB DAUGHTERS.

->BY AKON EKPO, A WOMAN OF NSAN.<-

There was once a woman who was very, very old and had never had a child. Around her hut grew many edible herbs which she had planted. Among them were <term>Etigi</term>, <term>Etinyung Ikaw</term>, and <term>Etidut</term> roots.

Day by day, the woman left her home and went into the bush to search for nuts and wild fruit. Each day when she had gone, four beautiful girls crept out from the herbs. They went into the house, cooked food on the hearth, ate, and then went back to their herbs once more.

One day, a neighbor passed the hut, and as she went by, she heard voices within. She knew that the old woman had no children and wondered who could be talking so gaily. So she went to the hut and looked inside. To her surprise, she saw

The old woman did not need to be told twice, but did exactly as her neighbor had said. She pretended to go out as usual, but hid herself near the hut, and soon came back and peeped stealthily inside. The secret of the girl’s birth was shared with him; he was willing to do all that was asked and went home to gather suitable marriage presents.

> Etidut sister, come to me; we must go.
> Ikaw eyene ka ‘mi di inyawng-o.
> Ikaw sister, come to me; we must go."

As she sang this, calling her sisters Etigi, Etidut, and Ikaw—who had also been married in the meantime—they all rushed from their husbands’ houses back to the hut of their foster mother. There they told what had happened to them and once more became the herbs they had been before.

If Ekpenyong’s other wife had not been so cruel as to give Etinyung the forbidden herb to eat, it would still be possible for a woman of any nation—who had grown too old to have a child in the ordinary way—to be lucky enough to obtain one or more in the same manner as this old woman.

When the herb-daughters had left, the foster mother had to be content with the servants given to her by her son-in-law, but Ekpenyong’s grief at the loss of his sweet wife was greater than words can tell.

# CHAPTER XIII

## BEYOND NIAJI

AFTER leaving Niaji, the first village reached is Ikpai, which has a great reputation as one of the homes of “Mfam.” Behind the Egbo house is a tiny shed, built over this <term>Juju</term>, and close by stands the <term>Mfam</term> tree, the scientific name of which is *Croton amabilis*. It has small leaves and insignificant, almost invisible flowers; as far as could be learned, it possesses no medicinal properties. Its importance in the mystical herbal lore of the people is therefore difficult to understand.

When a rich or influential man is sick, he sends for the priest of Mfam to bring him some of the branches of the sacred tree. Unless the Fates are spinning the last strands of life, the mere touch of the leaves is said to restore health.

The branches are brought to both the rich and the poor when they are at the point of death. The priest stands by the side of the dying man and draws them gently over his face so that his spirit may pass painlessly to the realm of <term>Obassi Nsi</term>.

On August 19, 1907, I was present at the revocation of the <term>Juju</term>.

Obu of Ikpai had sworn “Mfam” against anyone who might try to take a young girl named Nkoiyu from him, as he wished to keep her in his family.

When all the members of the <term>Juju</term> had gathered before the shrine, naked to the waist, Itagbun, the head priest, opened the <term>Juju</term> shed and took from it six horns containing “medicine.” He laid these on the ground and, after drinking a little palm wine, sprinkled some over the horns.

Next, he took up two of these, one in each hand, and calling on the names of <term>Obassi Nsi</term>, <term>Obassi Osaw</term>, and the ghosts, he prayed:

> “Look! Obu has come to remove the Juju that he swore,

<summary>This chapter describes the sacred Mfam tree in the village of Ikpai and its role in healing rituals and easing the passage of the dying. The author also recounts witnessing a priest perform a ritual to revoke a Juju curse sworn by a man named Obu.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the religious rituals associated with the Mfam Juju in the village of Ikpai, specifically detailing the ceremony to revoke an oath sworn by a man named Obu.</meta>

when he asked that if anyone should take the girl from his house, <term>Mfam</term> might kill them. He has now come to pray to the <term>Juju</term> to lift the curse so that the whole matter may end."

While Itagbun spoke to the <term>Juju</term>, the people knelt or stood with their eyes reverently lowered. He then drank a little more palm wine and tested the leaves to see if the <term>Juju</term> agreed. The answer was favorable.

Obu himself next stepped forward and said, "Look! I have come to remove the <term>Juju</term> from the girl. Let the <term>Juju</term> oath be canceled. Let her go to her former mistress, Idan Awaw. May the <term>Juju</term> no longer interfere with this matter. I leave her now to Idan Awaw. May the <term>Juju</term>'s curse not fall upon Idan!"

Itagbun continued, "O <term>Juju</term>, hear what I say. Obu has come to tell you he has nothing more to do with Nkoiyu. Make it so that nothing can hurt her. Should anyone try to harm Nkoiyu or Idan, may you stop them!"

He then sat down, poured palm wine into a small <term>calabash</term>, drank some, and poured the rest on the ground before the <term>Juju</term>. Then he stood up and placed two leaves beneath it. Next, he poured palm wine on the six horns and prayed:

> "This is the palm wine that Obu gave. Accept it and let all be well for the people who have come before you today."

After this, he laid the two leaves on the back of his left hand and struck them with his right hand, saying, "If you accept the palm wine and everything is finished, tell me now."

The leaves agreed, and the people shouted "<term>Ohe</term>!" (It is good!).

All the chiefs drank a little palm wine. Then the meat brought by Obu was cut into small pieces. Some pieces were placed on each of the horns, and the rest were distributed.

Itagbun then stood before the <term>Juju</term> and said, "This is the beef which Obu has given you." He then took a cloth and waved it over the horns, saying, "Look, O <term>Juju</term>, at the cloth Obu has given. Set Nkoiyu free from the curse which was sworn against her in your name."

A third time he picked up the leaves and asked, "Everything is finished. Do you agree?" To this, the leaves again gave a favorable answer.

# BEYOND NIAJI

Itagbun then called Nkoiyu. As she stepped forward, she dropped the long cloth that she wore and stood before the <term>Juju</term>, clothed only in a small loincloth.

Itagbun said, "Come, hold out your hands." She held them together, palm to palm, as if to receive a gift. Then he spat solemnly into them and said, "Everything is finished. Go in peace."

Last of all, Idan was called, and the same rite was performed for her.

After this, the priest replaced the horns in the little shed, and the people went back to their homes.

Itagbun, priest of Mfam, has amassed great wealth from the offerings of pilgrims who come from many miles around to invoke the <term>Juju</term>. His "treasure house" is elaborately decorated, as can be seen from the ornamentation of one of its seats. The most valued possessions of the wealthy <term>Ekoi</term> consist of collections of glass, pottery, and china.

Among the latter, beautiful old specimens, collected during the slave-trading days, are often to be found.

The <term>Etai Ngbe</term>, or <term>Egbo stone</term>, in the local club house has a particularly clear, sharp edge.

At Ndebbiji, the next town of interest, another fine example of these stones can be seen. It stands before the base of the <term>Egbo pillar</term>, on which there are some curious drawings.

The animal represents an antelope, the upright rods are meant for native money, and the figure in <term>Egbo dress</term> is holding out its hand in the traditional posture to indicate the sharing of news.

IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

### HUNTING CUSTOMS.

The Ekoi are a race of hunters, but the northern towns, such as Niaji and Ndebbiji, are the most celebrated in the District for their skill in the chase. As long as gunpowder was available, they never failed to arrange a good drive on each visit, and some of their hunting customs are of great interest.

Usually, before the hunt, each man sacrifices to his own <term>Juju</term>. If a leopard has been killed recently, <term>Juju</term> leaves are rubbed over its skull and prayers are offered to its spirit, asking it to go to the left and drive the gentler game toward the hunters who stay to the right. It is also asked to help in the killing of other leopards or any dangerous beast, should any be encountered.

On one occasion we started at seven o'clock with about sixty guns and a large number of beaters, and marched to a little glade about three miles away. Here we separated to take up our various stations.

Usually, nets about 6 feet high and, when joined, half a mile long, are stretched across the angle formed by the junction of two rivers. Here the principal gunmen are posted, while the rest, when they have reached a sufficient distance, form a huge semicircle and, on a given signal, bear down toward the apex, driving everything before them.

The wait is more exciting than might be imagined by those unaccustomed to this method, as there is an interesting uncertainty as to what game may first appear. On one occasion a leopard flashed past within a few feet of me and cleared the net before it could be dropped.

It is not often that an <term>Ekoi</term> hunter misses, even in the thick undergrowth and with primitive flint-lock guns. Among the animals killed in this hunt were seven fine antelopes, one of which—a harnessed antelope—was given to the carriers.

A few minutes after the distribution had taken place, the interpreter came up and asked if he might be allowed to mention that the carriers did not like the skin of the animal. When I suggested, with some astonishment, that they were not expected to eat the skin, he showed obvious embarrassment, and at length explained that none would dare to eat the flesh of a

This taboo, like many others, probably originated from totemic causes.<note>For a list of taboos, see Appendix A.</note> Others were imposed for sanitary reasons, and many from the desire of the elders to obtain a share of what was killed by their juniors, as in the following story:

### WHY A HUNTER MAY NOT EAT APES KILLED IN THE BUSH, BUT MUST FIRST BRING THEM BEFORE HIS FATHER OR THE HEAD OF HIS HOUSE.

Once, long ago, a man named Atai Ikot (Ikot the hunter) went out into the bush. He saw many Nyori nuts, so he collected them into a heap. Then he made a fire and sat down to crack the nuts between two stones.

Some Oiyokk (chimpanzees) came down and watched. After a while, when the hunter had gathered many kernels, he went a short distance away. When he looked back, he saw that the monkeys had descended. They took the Nyori in their hands and tried to crush them with stones as he had done, but only injured their hands. The hunter laughed at them, and when his friend Okun joined him, Okun laughed as well. They went to spend the night in a hunter’s hut, and while there, Ikot said:

“Let us go back to where the monkeys are and pretend to fight each other, then we will leave our machetes behind. It is very likely they will take them and kill one another.”

The two friends did this, and when they had left again, the Oiyokk returned and picked up the machetes. One struck at his friend, and the latter cried:

“How is this? Blood is coming out of my skin.” He

The hunters saw that the apes wanted to kill them, so they made a great fire and began roasting nuts. They ate the kernels and threw away the shells, and then hid themselves to watch.

The Oiyokk also wished to roast nuts and eat them but did not know how to do it properly, so they burned their fingers and threw away the nuts, kernels and all.

Okun said to his friend, “You see, they do not know how to eat such things! But if they catch us with all this Oiyokk meat, they will kill us, for they are too many for us. Let us run and get help.” So they ran to their town and called all the people to come out and bring in the kill.

When the townsfolk learned what had happened, they said, “You have done well, because you brought all this meat to the town instead of eating it yourselves in the bush.”

After this, a law was made that whoever should kill an ape in the bush must not eat any of it there, but must bring it before his father or the head of his house.

Elephant was angry because he himself could shoot nothing, so he took Crab’s gun away from him.

Crab went back and entered the compound where all the women were cooking. He said, “I am a messenger from Lord Elephant. He bids each woman to put much pepper in the food today, and also to throw away all water. There must be none left in the town when my Lord comes home.”

After a while, Crab went again and said, “I have come to see that you have obeyed the order, lest Elephant should blame me.” He inspected the houses and saw that not a drop of water remained, so he said, “I will tell Elephant that all has been done according to his command.” After this, he went away and hid in his own hole.

When Elephant came back from the hunt, he said to his wife, “I am thirsty. Give me some water.” She answered, “There is none.” He said, “Why is this?” and she replied, “Crab said that you had ordered all the water to be thrown away.”

Elephant was very angry, but all the people said, “We know Crab. He is a sensible man. Eat your food, and when he comes back, he will explain about the water.”

All began to eat, but the pepper burned their mouths and made them more thirsty than before, so they cried out. Ise was sent to call Crab, but could not find him. Then Etuk was sent, but he was faint with thirst and lay down on the road.

In the meantime, three of the animals had died for lack of water, so they called Pig and said to him, “Find Crab, or we must all perish.”

Pig went around in the bush and dug up all the ground with his snout. At length, he came to Crab’s hole and dug him out. He said, “You are wanted by the Chief;” but Crab answered, “I will not go. I am also a chief.”

On this, Pig said, “Please follow my orders and let us go.” Crab replied, “First, get back my meat and my gun.”

Pig went to his house, took his own gun and some meat that he had, and brought them to Crab, who accepted the offering. The latter said:
“You are my friend and have behaved justly. For your sake, I will give back the water.”

So these two went before Elephant, and Crab said:
“Before I give back that which you desire, you must proclaim one thing throughout your town. That is, that whenever we go hunting, the townsfolk may have one leg of each animal killed, but the rest shall belong to the actual slayer, to be divided by him according to hunter’s law.”

All the people agreed to what Crab proposed and confirmed it, for they said, “Many people have died of thirst already, and we must have water.”

Crab then announced to Elephant, “Though you are bigger than I, yet the water is mine and I have control over it.” He took his <term>Juju</term> and poured it into the streams, whereupon the water flowed once more.

This is the reason why, when Ekoi men go hunting, one leg of all their kill is the right of the townsfolk, but the rest belongs to the hunter or the owner of the gun, to be divided by him among all those to whom a part of his kill is due, such as the head of his household, his parents, wife, etc.

Sometimes, also, in seldom-visited areas, one encounters a deep pit dug by the wayside and hidden by green branches to ensnare the feet of unsuspecting buffalo.

It is probably due to their highly developed musical sense that Ekoi hunters possess their marvelous ability to imitate the cry of any beast for which they wait in ambush. The imitation is so perfect that the animal nearly always follows the sound to its own destruction.

The common West African form of trap is frequently used for catching leopards, genets, and wild cats, and there are many bird traps, mostly operating on the lever principle.

Although there are no Ekoi words to express the points of the compass, their sense of direction is very keen, as is common among forest peoples. It is rare for men to get lost in the bush, no matter how far they may follow their prey. They are quick to read woodland signs and are wonderful trackers—in this, the hunting dogs are of great help. Certain rites are performed over the dogs before they are allowed to roam the bush, as is mentioned in the following:

### CONCERNING HUNTING DOGS.

One day the Ennying (francolin) was sitting on her eggs. She became very hungry and went out to find some food. While she was away, Njaw (the dog) ate her eggs. Then he went off, stole some feathers, and covered himself with them so that he would not be discovered. When an inquiry was made about the egg thief, Porcupine said, “It is Njaw who is guilty.” The dog therefore thought, “From today, Porcupine is my enemy.” He ran after her, but she reached her home and hid inside it. Njaw obtained nets and hung them around the hole. Then he waited, and after a while, she tried to come out and was caught.

That is the reason why, when a hunting dog goes into the bush, he always seeks out the place where Porcupine lives. They have been enemies for many years. Whenever he can, Njaw goes down the hole, kills Porcupine, and then returns.
