...to his master, wagging his tail. The master follows the dog to the hole and gets the porcupine.

Often a man buys a young dog and consecrates him for hunting through Juju. Until the proper rites have been carried out, the dog is not of much use to his master. Afterward, when he grows large, he can go out alone and hunt.

Some dogs go with their masters, but many go alone. When they have killed anything, they return and wag their tails. Often the master sees blood on their mouths.

<margin>(</margin>Before starting out after an elephant, the hunter almost always sacrifices to the special fetish which is to be found in most villages. This act is supposed to be of the first importance, as it is universally asserted that no hunters have been killed unless the sacrifice has been neglected. The rites are also effective in another way, for a man so protected is in no danger of shooting a were-elephant <note>A human being who has transformed into an elephant through magic.</note> by mistake for an ordinary animal. The beast always gives some sign by which it can be recognized. Usually, this is said to be done by lifting the right forefoot and at the same time bending down its head.

An unsuccessful hunter almost always attributes his failure to witchcraft. In order to break such evil spells, he takes an offering of dried meat and plantains to a place on the road outside the village. There he spreads out the sacrifice and pours a libation of spirits upon the ground, praying at the same time to Obassi and the ghosts that they will set him free from the spells which hold him.

If the ill luck continues, the hunter next consults a Diviner, who, after questioning the charm, tells him that the witchcraft is very strong and can only be broken by resorting to a powerful Juju. On such an occasion, the prayer is always offered: "This hunter begs you to protect his gun and himself, so that no evil spells may have power over them."

At the conclusion of the ceremony, when all the members of the Juju have feasted at the hunter’s expense, the Diviner returns the gun to its owner with the words:

“Go into the bush, and may good fortune attend you.”

It indicates a certain side of the Ekoi character that they deem it necessary to explain the right by which a hunter may kill the beasts of the bush. The reason for this is given in many tales, of which the following is perhaps the best known:

### HOW ALL THE BEASTS CAME UPON EARTH.

->By NDUM OF NSAN.<-

Obassi Osaw and Obassi Nsi were, as we know, great friends. Once upon a time, the former told the latter that he was going to set a day to invite him, with all his people, to a great feast at his home in the sky.

Obassi Nsi answered that he would be very pleased and, when the day arrived, went with a large following to the feast given by Obassi Osaw.

Until this time, all the beasts had lived in the sky, and only we human beings, then as now, lived on earth with Obassi Nsi.

The guests ate their fill and were afterward entertained with dances and games. When the time came to say “farewell,” Obassi Nsi thanked his host but said that he thought he himself could give an even more splendid feast if his friend would come with his people to visit him on earth. The day was set, and all promised to attend, but Obassi Nsi warned them that they would not be able to eat in a year half of what he would spread before them at this single day’s feast.

Obassi Osaw said that this was well, and no sooner had his guests gone back to earth than he sent word to announce to the sky people—for the heavens were then inhabited by every kind of animal—that on the appointed day, all the beasts must go with him to earth to visit his friend Obassi Nsi. No excuse would be accepted from anyone who failed to come.

When the time for the feast arrived, all the animals, from the smallest ant to the largest elephant, followed their Lord Obassi Osaw earthward to the land of his friend.

Now, the day before, Obassi Nsi had gone around the whole

The story details how all animals originally lived in the sky and were summoned to earth for a great celebration.</summary>

earth and commanded every tree and bush to bring forth an abundance of fruit. This they did, and yielded to the utmost of their power, so that the whole land was beautiful with ripe fruits, which hung down temptingly from every stem and bough. Besides all this, Nsi ordered great calabashes of cooked food to be prepared, and many drinks readied to receive his guests.

All the beasts came down from the sky and saw an infinite number of trees laden with fruits of the most enticing ripeness. They broke away from their master and spread themselves over the land, feeding eagerly. The monkeys were busy with bananas, the pigs rooted for cassava, while the birds hardly knew what to choose from all the feast provided for them.

Obassi Osaw was asked by his friend why his people did not attend to him, and he answered, very sadly, that they were coming along behind. He saw at a glance that he was surely outdone by Obassi Nsi, just as the latter had said. However, he sat down at the table and enjoyed all the good things. It began to grow dark, but still none of his people returned to him. Again Nsi asked him where his people could be, since they did not come to attend to him. Osaw answered nothing, but, sadly and alone, went back to his home on high.

Afterward, he sent word to Nsi that he and his people might hunt the beasts and kill them, for they should no longer be sky people, but only food for the earth men, as they had disgraced him, their Lord, and refused to return to their own land.

This, then, is the only basis by right of which we may kill the beasts and eat their flesh, and this is truly the way in which the animals came to this world. Some of them were free, from this time, to prey upon others, such as leopards, bush cats, crocodiles, etc., but they have long since forgotten the way back to their old home in the sky, and must now stay here, whether they like it or not.

# CHAPTER XIV

## THE SOUTH CAMEROONS

After Ndebbiji, the road leads up sheer precipices to the towns of Ojokk and Obepp. These were once great centers of the slave trade, but now they lie—veritable gardens of palms, sunny and peaceful—at the foot of their crescent-shaped mountain background.

About three miles further stands Nkami, the last British town; its inhabitants are among the simplest and most charming of their race. Here, as well as at Ekoneman in the German Cameroons, some traces of cat worship still remain. At night, when a performance of this nature is given, the people spring upon the roofs just as cats do. Ntui Esame of Ekoneman is especially famous for the cat dance.

A few miles beyond Nkami flows the Awa River, which is generally taken as the boundary between Southern Nigeria and the South Cameroons. At the time of writing, the actual frontier line has not been ratified by the governments concerned.

Over this river, the courteous German Commissioner, Dr. Mansfeld, had a new suspension bridge built and had told the chief of the nearest town to set up a <term>Juju</term> so that no one would use it before our party arrived.

Nfunum is located just on the other side of the water, and here our complimentary escort—a Black sergeant-major with a couple of privates—was awaiting us. In one of the houses was a small “treasure chamber,” the wall design of which seemed worth copying (see p. 152).

Dr. Mansfeld had suggested meeting us at Lake Ijagham, the sacred lake of the Ekoi, which he discovered about three years ago.

Here and there along the roadside, amid the lush growth, a fallen <term>Juju</term> post or <term>Egbo</term> drum showed the site of some abandoned settlement. Vegetation grows so rapidly to cover the rain-leveled walls that, except for signs such as these, one would pass by without noticing sites where thriving towns had stood only a few years before.

<page-num>153</page-num>
<header>THE SOUTH CAMEROONS</header>

It was through noticing the recurrence of the word “Ijagham” in the phonograph records of folk songs he was collecting, and the fact that no translation could be obtained from the people, that Dr. Mansfeld’s suspicions were aroused. After a long time and through significant bribes, one man was persuaded to explain that it meant a great body of water that existed in the neighborhood. It was still difficult to discover its actual location, but in time, this was also accomplished.

The word “Ijagham” bears a strong similarity to “Ejagham,” the name the Ekoi people use for themselves; but so far, it has been impossible to persuade them to explain the similarity. The word Ekoi itself is Efik, but it is the only name by which the people are generally known and is therefore a more convenient designation for them.

Like the smaller Lake of the Dead near Nsan, <note>See page 23.</note> Ijagham—or *Toten See*, as the Germans have named it—is supposed to be haunted by the ghosts of the departed Ekoi.

According to legend, the center of the lake is of immense depth and contains a whirlpool into which all who venture to bathe in its waters or attempt to cross them in a canoe are sucked. No such evil fate, however, overtook the little *Berthon* boat in which we crossed. Perhaps the *Genius* of the lake was too chivalrous to harm the first white women to visit its shores.

As in the Nsan Lake of the Dead, a great snake dwells beneath the waters, and this at least is fact, not legend alone; Dr. Mansfeld informed us that a skin was found less than 100 yards from the huts he had built on the shore. It had only just been shed and measured 18 feet. Wild ducks cling in flocks to the branches of dead trees that raise their bare limbs above the surface, while hawks and eagles circle continually in the clear air above.

The lake is shaped like an oval cup, ringed by tall trees that reach right down to the water’s edge. There is no encircling belt of reed or fern, and notably little undergrowth. The bed is made of clean white sand, which seems to

stretches from rim to rim. Through the clear green water, hundreds of fish dart here and there; they are of different sizes, but only one variety. They look and taste much like trout but require no salt for cooking. The locals say, "They have salt in their bodies," and experience would seem to prove them right. Possibly the fact that the lake lies in the center of a circle of thirteen salt springs may have something to do with this peculiarity, though the water of Ijagham itself is beautifully clear and sweet.

Surprisingly, the temperature of the water at the bottom of the lake is much higher than that of the surface, even on the hottest day. On September 24, at 8 a.m., a temperature of 81° was obtained on the surface and 84° at a depth of 72 feet. No river enters the lake and only one flows from it, which eventually empties into a tributary of the Cross River.

Before the sun set, it caught the tops of the trees which ringed the far side, turning their fresh green into a magnificent display of russet and gold. As the glow faded, and we sat watching the shadows darkening around the quiet surface, a ring suddenly appeared near the center of the lake, slightly to the right. This spread in our direction—a thin circle of mist—until it enclosed about one-eighth of the total area. From that point it faded, always spreading outward and growing fainter and fainter until it was quite swallowed up in the darkness. It had the appearance of steam rising from some giant cauldron.

After a while, a splendid moon rose over Ijagham, turning its surface into a mirror of silver.

I am indebted to Dr. Mansfeld for much of the information contained in the preceding account; he also most kindly raised no objection to our visiting all that we wished to see of the Ekoi country under German rule.

We marched back to Ekoneman by the way we had come, and from there over the 2,000-foot-high hills by Naretim to Mbabong.

### THE FOLLY OF THE MBABONG.

#### BY NDUM AGURIMON OF NSAN.

### I.

There was once a very handsome young man of Mbabong who had an old mother. He was quite poor, but he promised that when she died, he would get a cow and slaughter it so that the people might eat and honor her memory.

At the beginning of the year in which her death occurred, he established his farm close to a cave where a buffalo lived. One day, he went into the nearby bush to cut sticks to support his yam vines. In the cave, he saw the buffalo lying asleep and went back quietly so as not to disturb it. He warned his wife not to make any noise when she went to the farm, lest she should frighten away the cow which <term>Obassi</term> had sent.

The wife was a good woman, so she carefully followed this warning.

Not long after, the old mother died. As soon as she had ceased to breathe, the son sent his wife to announce the death to the town.

When the people began gathering together for the mourning, the man took a rope and went toward his farm, saying that he was going to bring the cow for his mother’s funeral feast. He tied the rope properly around his waist, made a slipknot in the other end wide enough for the head of the cow to pass through, and laid the snare across the entrance of the cave. He then hid himself and let out a great shout. On hearing the noise, the buffalo dashed out. She ran over hill and dale, through bush and river, dragging the poor man of Mbabong to a terrible death.

A wise man would have asked some strong men to go with him to help hold the rope, or else would have made it fast to the trunk of a great tree. In either case, he would have won the cow with cheers! Because of this folly, whenever we wish to express contempt for anyone, he or she is simply called a "Mbabong."

<summary>This page recounts a folk tale from Nsan about a man from Mbabong who foolishly tried to capture a wild buffalo alone, leading to his death and the naming of his town as a term for a fool. It explains the origin of a local insult through the story of an ill-fated funeral sacrifice.</summary>

### II.

This second story is about another Mbabong man, who was also very ridiculously foolish.

One day, he stood watching a friend of his climb a palm tree by using an “nded” loop. This is a rope used to climb trees with smooth, straight trunks. First, it is tied around the trunk of the tree, but so loosely that while one side of the circle touches the trunk, there is a space of about three feet between it and the other side. The climber slips the loop over his head and lets it fall to his waist. He then presses his feet against the tree and his back against the rope. Next, he makes a short leap, raising the rope at the same time with both hands. A good “nded” climber will go up two feet with each leap.

The Mbabong man saw his friend climb the palm tree to the very top and then take another long leap. At this point, the rope slipped, and the man fell dead to the ground below.

The second Mbabong man could not understand what had happened and went to try it for himself. Being a good climber, he went leaping up proudly, but he made the same unnecessary leap at the end and also fell down dead.

Because of this, it has become a proverb in the country—

> “Mbabong agyut obi, echi ekin.
> Mbabong climbs a palm, head half.
> Akin mfong ngu, nkipp.
> Dries a cowhide, flayed side downward.”

During our visit, my interpreter caused roars of laughter from his own countrymen and embarrassment for the inhabitants of the town by asking, with a seemingly innocent air, to be shown the famous palm tree.

### III.

A third Mbabong man went hunting in the “bush.” Almost as soon as he had left his town, he saw an antelope. He fired, and the animal fell dead after running a short distance. Although it lay motionless on the ground, the man kept firing at it until a hunter from another town approached, guided by the

sound of the shots. The newcomer asked, “What are you shooting at?” To which Mbabong answered, “I am shooting at the antelope that fell over there, and I will keep shooting until I have made it come over here to me.”

The other man explained that this was impossible because the animal was dead, and that if it were alive, it would run further away instead of coming near him. “If you ever happen to shoot another beast,” he said, “I would advise you to run toward it, rather than wasting shots trying to force it to come to you.”

Were they not a foolish people in those days? We may hope that they have grown wiser now.

---

Since the majority of the Mbabong, like many other Ekoi people, have left their old homes in the Cameroons and migrated to the Oban district to avoid the poll tax imposed across the border, I venture to echo the narrator's sincere hope.

The people seemed simple and friendly; after a few suffering people were given the various medicines they came to ask for, the residents came out in crowds to request treatments.

The town stands on the top of a hill, offering a splendid view of the mountains to the south and southwest. From Babi, our next stopping place, the path—which is merely a hunter’s track—led through the beautiful pass below Okuri Peak. During this march, we crossed two hills, each over 2,000 feet high. At the summit of the last hill was a small cleared space called “Anwan Nsibidi”—the place of cunning words. This name was given during the old days of the slave trade, when chiefs from the main towns on each side met here to arrange a treaty. By this agreement, they bound themselves not to raid one another’s territory to capture people to sell to the slave traders at Calabar.

At the next town, Mbinda, we bought the Eja fetish <note>A ritual object or power symbol associated with the Eja cult</note> described on page 76.

The town is surrounded by an amphitheater of mountains, shrouded in mist and tinted purple in the soft light of a late rain’s sunset. Looking back, the pass we had traveled through was clearly visible, appearing as a cleft in the surrounding mountain wall.

It had been a town of considerable importance and the home of many powerful <term>Jujus</term>. It was from there, for instance, that Akpambe crossed the border to invade the Oban district. Dr. Mansfield has described the elaborate decoration of the <term>Egbo house</term>, which was the largest in the whole countryside. Now only low mounds remain to show its original dimensions. Within these, a smaller building is under construction, but there was no sign of ornamentation.

On the road, not far from Okuri, is a sad reminder of the <term>Ekoi</term> struggle for independence. As we passed along, we noticed a group of carriers who had laid down their loads and were gathered in the shade of a great tree. They looked unusually sad, and large tears were rolling down the cheeks of some. As we approached, one of them bent down and pulled back the creepers from the base of the tree. Low on its trunk, a round hole was visible, made by the bullet which killed the chief of a neighboring town. The latter was a close relative of some of our men and, according to their story, had been shot because he first protested against his yams being taken without permission by the soldiers, and then tried to escape after being arrested. He was recaptured, forced to stand before the great tree, and shot by the officer in charge.

Traveling at night is not popular among the Ekoi, but this road is especially avoided after sunset because of fear of the restless ghost which is thought to wander there.

We had already passed another sad reminder of the struggle. Near Ekoneman stands the tree from behind which Lieutenant Queisz was shot in the chest in November 1899. An echo of this tragedy was heard a few months ago when the man who had fired the shot was caught and hanged. After the uprising was suppressed, he had fled, but, drawn by a yearning for home, had crept back later to his own town. For ten years he had dragged out a miserable existence, hidden in a hole in the ground behind some boulders in the nearby bush. His secret was faithfully kept until an accident revealed it to a native official, who, as duty required, reported it to the “white man.” One would think that it would be almost a relief when the long agony of such an existence was over, and he paid with his own life for the life which he had taken.

As we passed along, we noticed a group of carriers who had laid down their loads and were gathered in the shade of a great tree. They looked unusually sad, and large tears were rolling down the cheeks of some. As we approached, one of them bent down and pulled back the vines from the base of the tree. Low on its trunk, a round hole was visible, made by the bullet which killed the chief of a neighboring town. The latter was a close relative of some of our men and, according to their story, had been shot because he first protested against his yams being taken without permission by the soldiers, and then tried to escape after being arrested. He was recaptured, forced to stand before the great tree, and shot by the officer in charge.

Traveling at night is not popular among the Ekoi, but this road is especially avoided after sunset because of fear of the restless ghost which is thought to wander there.

We had already passed another sad reminder of the struggle. Near Ekoneman stands the tree from behind which Lieutenant Queisz was shot in the chest in November 1899. An echo of this tragedy was heard a few months ago...

# THE SOUTH CAMEROONS

The period of the Ekoi struggle for independence was inevitably a time of great suffering. How intense this must have been is demonstrated by a fact recorded by Dr. Mansfeld in his book <term>“Urwald Dokumente”</term> (Forest Documents), page 21:

> “From several sources,” he says, “I have received definite reports that the mothers killed almost all the infants during the uprising. The reason given to me was that the babies’ crying, especially at night, constantly betrayed their hiding places in the forest to the soldier patrols.”

The Ekoi are such devoted parents that the idea of a mother killing the baby at her breast to ensure safety is almost inconceivable. Perhaps the lack of proper nourishment, combined with the necessity of constant traveling and hiding in the bush, caused such hardships for the little ones that the mothers killed them out of pity for their suffering, and in the firm belief that their spirits would return to earth as soon as all was peaceful once more.

The description given by Dr. Mansfeld of the state of the country at the end of the war is sad indeed:

> “The sight the country presented in the autumn of 1904 was desolate: burned-down huts were everywhere; the empty walls, where they had not collapsed from the rain, were overgrown with all sorts of grasses, violet and yellow flowers, and numerous climbing plants. The paths were almost impassable, as they had not been cleared for a year. The farms were all empty, and no bananas could be bought for miles around; not a single person, goat, or chicken was to be seen. If one left the camp to search for people along the bush paths, one would come across isolated dwellings consisting of a hearth covered with a mat roof but otherwise entirely open, from which men and women with their small children fled in wild panic.”

<summary>This page describes the extreme hardships faced by the Ekoi people during their 1904 uprising, including reports of mothers killing their infants to avoid detection by patrols and the total desolation of the countryside after the conflict.</summary>

# CHAPTER XV

## ALONG THE BORDER

The last of the German Ekoi are found at Ndebbiji Itaokui, a nearly deserted village inhabited by only two men.
Shortly after re-entering British territory, as we were crossing a small river, a dark object was noticed swimming rapidly downstream. The carriers shouted that it was a large fish and begged me to shoot it. It was below the surface, but from the ripple, I felt sure that it was not a fish, but probably a monitor lizard. A shot seemed likely to settle the question, and so it did, but in a way that astonished everyone. The supposed fish leaped to the bank and disappeared in a series of graceful bounds—revealed to be a water chevrotain.
This beautiful little antelope is so rare in most parts of the world that travelers are advised to send the skin and skull of every specimen obtained to the Natural History Museum; however, it is so common here that a hunt is almost never organized without catching at least two. It is strange that such a small and graceful creature should be, in some respects, a link between deer on one hand and camels and boars on the other.
I believe that we were the first Europeans fortunate enough to see a water chevrotain actually swimming beneath the surface, although Major Powell Cotton once saw one enter the water.
Along these roads, as everywhere in Ekoi territory, stones about the size of a palm are seen tightly wedged into the forks of small trees. If a casual visitor happened to ask a native the reason for this, the latter would probably answer vaguely that someone has put them there to mark the place where he has hidden his kill, or where rubber vines are located, or perhaps where he should return later to gather ripening fruits or nuts. When one has gained their confidence, however, through living among them for a long time, quite a different story is told.

Sometimes, instead of stones, bare corn cobs may be seen, similarly held in the fork of a tree. For a long time when questioned as to the cause of this, the men answered with a shrug, “For no reason, Sir.” At length one day someone, whose store of tobacco had run short, came up on the road, and, in the hope of thus earning a fresh supply, explained that the corn spirit gets very angry should even the bare core be left to rot on the ground. As this decays, the body of the man who had discarded it would waste away also. In dread of such a fate, the core is placed where, after rain has fallen, sun and air may dry it again, so that it may be preserved for as long as possible. Subsequent inquiries proved the truth of this explanation.

The first town in British territory is Ako, which has already been described, but leaving this on the right, one can pass on to Okarara, where on our last visit the inhabitants were even more clamorous than most on the subject of the bush-cow and elephant which were devouring their farms. On one occasion during our stay in the neighborhood, news was brought of the presence of a herd of six, which had grown so troublesome that the children feared to go down to fetch water or cut plantains.

The bush in this area is honeycombed by elephant roads, which are often much broader and more distinct than the little-used native paths. They are so clear at times that, on his way to visit us, Dr. Mansfeld followed one for several miles, under the impression that he was walking along the regular road. Indeed, the entire stretch of land along the frontier, by the Awa and Akwa Yafe rivers, forms a natural forest reserve, for it is almost uninhabited and teems with animal life.

Near the falls of the Akwa Yafe, we were fortunate enough to come across an interesting discovery.

Less than a mile from the bank, on the British shore, a bush path leads down into a bowl-like depression. At the bottom, in the wall-like side, looms a great cave. From the blackness within, countless bats shriek ceaselessly above the dull rush and boom of water, for just beyond the opening, two underground rivers join. Except for the heavy odor of swarms of bats disturbed by our approach, the air was clear and pure, indicating the presence of many openings. This system of vast underground halls and vaulted tunnels extends for miles, in many cases with roofs smoothly curved as though they had been carved by human hands.

The caves are said to extend as far as the first falls, but time did not permit anything like a thorough exploration. They are the property of the Ododop people and are highly valued because of the bats that inhabit them in vast numbers, which are considered a delicacy.

The method of capture is as follows:—

At each known entrance stand men armed with long sticks to strike down the escaping bats. The primary hunters then enter the caves, accompanied by lantern bearers and carrying triangular nets fastened to the ends of long poles.

Great clouds of them flew toward the exits, only to fall, row after row, under the blows of the beaters waiting outside. Many others also carried young perched on their backs.

The Ododop (or, to use their own name, Korawp) are an interesting people. To quote Professor Keith’s remarks on measurements I took,<note>* See Appendix C.</note> they represent “what Sir Harry Johnston has named the Forest-negro type. Their height is short, their arms are long, and their faces, heads, and noses are massive; however, the head is proportionally long, as it is in most of the Northern negro tribes.” They appear particularly gentle in character, and even the most careful inquiries failed to find any trace of cruel rites or customs.

On my second visit to their town, I was astonished to find that they had, on their own initiative, built a small three-room rest house. This was especially generous of them, as they were new arrivals from the Cameroons, and their own plantations were too young to provide palm leaves for the roof mats; consequently, they had been forced to buy every single mat from the next town, Mfamosing.

Because the rest house had been built as a surprise for me, it was not possible for me to have a say in choosing the site. It was placed right in the middle of the town instead of at a sufficient distance to ensure quiet, as was the case with those I had selected myself.

As bad luck would have it, during our visit, my sister-in-law had developed malaria on the march, which caused a very severe headache.

At first I thought that her neck must have been broken by the fall, but after a door had been unhinged and brought, she revived, and, strapped to this, was carried over the twelve-mile march to Mfamosing, in order to get at least that much closer to a doctor, in case it should be necessary to summon one. A delegation of Korawp accompanied us the entire way and spent the night away from home in order to make inquiries the next morning. On learning that the injuries were not as serious as had been feared, the Head Chief made a charming little speech, expressing how great the grief of his people would have been had any serious mishap happened to their white visitor.

# CHAPTER XVI

## ORDEAL

Up to 1907, Mfamosing had been the scene of a true reign of terror under Chief Nenkui. The latter was a giant of a man, with a huge bull neck and the arms of a prize fighter—a good chief according to his own standards, but so obsessed by the fear of witchcraft that he forced every single person in the town, at some time or other, to undergo a trial by ordeal in order to clear themselves from the suspicion of black magic. Many died from the tests imposed, while others suffered horribly. He had killed two of his wives in this way, and forced his own children to take <term>Esere</term>. This is the most common form of ordeal among the <term>Ekoi</term>. The bean itself is found growing wild all over the District. The ordeal is practiced by giving the bean, ground up and mixed with water, to the accused person, who must then drink the potion.

The belief is that a wizard or witch will die upon drinking it, but that no ill effect will be produced on innocent persons. In fact, if the bean has been boiled before the ordeal is tried, it will result only in intense pain followed by vomiting. This, however, is a carefully guarded secret. Some natives claim that the danger varies in proportion to the quantity administered. If either too small or too large a dose is given, it will only result in vomiting. The exact amount is known only to initiates.

The ordeal by boiling palm oil is far less dreaded, not only because its results were almost never fatal, but because the physical pain involved is acknowledged to be less intense than that produced by <term>Esere</term>.

When the surviving townspeople of Mfamosing found that the “white man” was strong enough to protect them against Chief

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

Regarding Nenkui, many charges were brought against him; the following cases may be cited as typical:

### I.

Itagbo Arap of Mfamosing had reason to believe that his wife Ada was unfaithful to him. She acknowledged her fault in part, but he thought that she was still concealing something. He stated on oath:

> “Nenkui said that the charm should be consulted to see if my wife had confessed everything, so I told her to ‘practice’ the ritual with palm oil. We boiled the oil, brought coco-yam leaves, and laid them on the ground. Then we took the shell of a giant snail (*Achatina marginata*), dipped it into the pot, and poured boiling oil on the leaves. We knew that if they shriveled, it would prove that the woman had lied. The leaves were completely destroyed, but the woman would not confess.
> “Then she herself sent for some oil and demanded that it should be tried in another way. A new pot was brought, and again we boiled the oil. When it was ready, we told the palm oil all about the affair, pointing toward the woman. We put medicine in the pot. It caught fire, the flames rose, and we found that the palm oil pronounced her guilty a second time. Still, she would not fully confess.
> “Then Nenkui shouted, ‘Pour the oil on the woman’s hands!’
> “Ada stated: ‘I was not willing for them to pour the boiling oil on me; my heart trembled and I grew weak with fear. But Nenkui shouted at me again and again to do it. So at last, in terror of him, I held out my hands. The oil burned both my palms so fiercely that I could not endure the pain, and at last I confessed everything.’”

"Early in the morning I woke up and saw my mother lying by the fire in my room. She said, 'I have eaten Esere.' I sprang up to go to her, but just then a woman named Ndu Mojong came in and asked what had happened. When she understood, she said to me, 'I will tend your mother. You yourself must not go near her, because you are about to bear a child, and it is not lawful that such a person should touch a woman who has eaten Esere.' Then she called other women to my mother’s help, and they tended her until she grew well again."

### III.

Awo Mbu of Mfamosing stated under oath:
“My son Okon Itagbo was sick at Mfamosing. I gathered together all that I had to sacrifice to the <term>Juju</term>, so that he might be made well again. One day Nenkui came to my room. He stood looking at me and said:
“‘You are a witch. You are killing your son because you wish to give him as an offering to your witch company.’
“I answered, ‘I am no witch, but if I were, I would beg my witch company to take me and spare my son.’
“Nenkui still said, ‘I know that you are a witch. If you wish to prove that you are not bewitching your son, you must eat <term>Esere</term>.’ So I went to my town and did as he told me, to show that it was not I who was harming my son.”

### IV.

Ngob Anyok of Mfamosing stated:
“I had two children, both of whom died. Chief Nenkui came to me and said, ‘Your mother was a witch. She took <term>Esere</term> and died. You also are a witch and have caused the death of your children.’
“I ate the <term>Esere</term> bean so that, if I were a witch and had killed the children, I might die also; for I did not want to live if I had harmed my little ones. This happened a long time ago, before the Government came to Oban.”

### V.

These are but a few of the stories told by survivors. Regarding
the far more terrible cases, in which countless victims died,
no reliable information was available. As a result of
the trial, Nenkui was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment at
Calabar.

His family considers him dead. The part of his compound
once reserved for his use is left unrepaired. Sun, wind,
and rain have faded the bright colors of his mural paintings.
Many of his carved pillars lie rotting on the ground, while
others lean at a dangerous angle. The roof has fallen in. Only
the Juju tree still flourishes amid the ruins, like the promise of
new life springing from the wreckage of the old.

Another form of ordeal involves putting pepper into the eyes. If this causes no injury, the accused is declared innocent.

<image-desc>A line drawing depicting "Nenkui's Deserted Compound," showing a dilapidated structure with a thatched roof supported by wooden pillars. Two of the pillars feature intricate carvings. A small tree grows in the center of the compound floor, and various pottery vessels are visible in the background among the ruins.</image-desc>

->Nenkui's Deserted Compound.<-

If inflammation occurs, he is considered guilty. The pain often leads to a confession. This ordeal was used in the case of Ndifon of Ndebbiji, who was accused of shooting a fellow townsman in the bush.

After leaving Mfamosing, the road leads through the former site of Abbiati, a town that was abandoned nearly two years ago because a simple-minded woman, while quarreling with her husband, threw salt on the ground and cried, “May God do the same to you all.” To avoid this curse, the entire town fled into the bush and has never gathered together again. Vegetation grows so rapidly here and erases all signs of human life that hardly a trace remains to show that a town once stood on this spot.

In front of the site of the old Egbo house stands a six-sided stone, about six feet above the ground and, the local people claim, almost as deep below it. While searching for a site for their town, the inhabitants of Abbiati found this carved stone and took it as a sign that they should settle in that location.

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

It was then raised up before their <term>Egbo</term> house, painted with black and white circles, called the <term>stone of Nimm</term>, and sacrifices were offered before it as the guardian of the town.

Many such stones lie buried in the bush, and when discovered, they are objects of great reverence to the <term>Ekoi</term>. Even those who have been educated in government schools insist that all such stones are the work of <term>Obassi</term> alone, and that no human has carved them. Yet they are clearly cut, not split by fire, and show the presence of some ancient race to whom stone shaping was well known. No legend of such a race can be found, though this is, after all, natural, as the Ekoi themselves only arrived to take possession of the country a few hundred years ago.

Each Egbo house has one of these cut stones called “<term>Etai Ngbe</term>” or “<term>Leopard Stone</term>,” erected before the second pillar, and we ourselves have come across countless examples in the bush. From some of these, sharp angles have been cut out, seemingly for the insertion of corresponding pieces protruding from other blocks, roughly in the manner of <term>Inca masonry</term>. Many stones show merely natural fractures, which are to be expected among the <term>gneiss</term> and <term>granite</term> of the district, but a careful examination shows that they cannot all be accounted for in this manner.

The subject is fascinating, and a closer study seems to point to the possibility of a <term>Carthaginian</term> origin. When the Carthaginians circumnavigated Africa in their small coasting ships, it is unlikely that they would have passed by the <term>Calabar River</term>, one of the best natural harbors on the coast,

<image-desc>A detailed line drawing of a carved, curved stone object, appearing somewhat like a decorated sausage or thick crescent. The entire surface is covered in rows of intricate, concentric circular and spiral patterns. One end of the stone is a smooth, un-carved cylinder.</image-desc>

without stopping for shelter, repairs, or provisions. In such a case, it is easy to imagine that some of the crew might have remained behind, either as a small colony or as captives or deserters.

# CHAPTER XVII

## DIVINATION

This practice, which among the Ekoi is called "Ebu,"<note>Compare Ebo, the Bini name for minor deities.</note> or by the older title "Efa," but is more generally known to Europeans by its Efik name "Idiong," is very commonly used. Almost all questions are referred to the diviner (Mboni) and answered by him after consulting the charm, which consists of two pairs of strings, each composed of four "Osing" shells. These are laid side by side on each hand of the diviner. Those on the right are supposed to be male and those on the left female. Each pair must "confirm" the other by falling in exactly the reverse manner. If the pairs do not agree, everything must be begun again, and should the question be at all important, it is often repeated several times.

A man who wishes to qualify as a diviner (Mboni) must first learn how the charm (Ebu) makes its communications. He then goes to an old diviner and asks him to "confirm" the power. This is done by gathering leaves and bark from various Juju trees. The old man chews these and spits out small quantities into the shells. The aspirant then takes the shells and places them high up in the roof-thatch, so that they may listen to Obassi Osaw and talk with him. After a while, they are taken down and carried outside the town to a place where crossroads meet, and are buried there to talk with the ghosts and with Obassi Nsi. After a few days, the strings are dug up again, and the man starts his practice as a full-fledged "Mboni."

Osing shells are the dried covering of the seeds of the Osing tree, which in itself is sacred; but they cannot be used for purposes of divination until an elephant has taken the ripe fruit into its mouth and then ejected the seeds. These are

<image-desc>In the right margin, a vertical line drawing depicts a string of four small, round objects, likely shells or nuts, connected by a cord with a knot at the bottom.</image-desc>

Other objects, always spread out before the magician, are—First, the egg of a bush fowl. It is believed that this bird calls up the dawn each morning,* so the Diviner holds up its egg, pointing toward the sun, and prays:
> “As the bush fowl cries for the light, so may light be shed on what we wish to know.”

Secondly, a quill and tail of a porcupine are held up, because in all legends Porcupine is the great diviner. White chalk is laid out to bring good luck, and a boar’s tooth is used, like Neapolitan coral, to ward off evil influences from the questioner. After being held out toward the questioner, the shells are touched with the tooth, one after another.

The small horns usually to be seen are those of Ise, the blue duikerbok, because it is regarded as the ally of magicians and is thought, like the dog, to have “four eyes”—that is, to be able to see by night as well as day, and to recognize ghosts, witches, and all such strange beings when they pass invisible to human eyes.

The shells composing the four strings are naturally capable

<image-desc>A horizontal arrangement of three drawings: on the left is a curved animal horn; in the center, a thin stick rests on two rounded shells; on the right is a single bird feather.</image-desc>

of falling in almost countless combinations, and, as a consequence, an expert Mboni has an extensive system on which to work.

As an example of the vocabulary used—

| | |
|---|---|
| One shell turned upward and all the rest downward | means a young man. |
| Two shells turned upward and all the rest downward | mean water. |
| Three shells turned upward and all the rest downward | mean food. |
| Four shells turned upward and all the rest downward | mean sickness. |

An instance of consulting the charm was observed at Ndingane in 1907, when a sick woman went to inquire about the cause of her illness. After the preliminaries described above, the <term>Mboni</term> called to <term>Ebu</term>:

"Wake up."
A. "We are awake."
Q. "Why does the woman call you?"
A. "Because she is sick."
Q. "What is the matter with her?"
A. "Something bad has caught her."
Q. "What has caught her? Ghosts, <term>Juju</term>, or witchcraft?"
A. "A noise has caught her."

<note>If ghosts quarrel near a person, some sickness "catches" them unless sacrifices are made.</note>

This answer was contradicted by the <term>second hand</term> <note>referring to one of the four strings of divination shells</note>; so the query had to be repeated. The next answer was a laugh of ridicule, and the questions had to be started again from the beginning.

Q. "Is it witchcraft?"
A. "No."
Q. "Is it <term>Juju</term>?"
A. "No."
Q. "Is it ghosts?"
A. "Yes."
Q. "Is it the mother's ancestors or the father's ancestors?"
A. "The mother's family."
Q. "A man?"
A. "No."
Q. "A woman?"
A. "Yes."

All the names of female ancestors on the mother's side were then called, until the charm signified which of them had caused the sickness.

Q. "What does the ghost want?"
A. "Libations."
Q. "Anything else?"
A. "Yes. Food sacrifices."

The inquirer then proceeded to make a round basket of palm leaves. In this she put some palm wine, together with a small quantity of rum. She then went before the town and put the

The spirit of <term>Osing</term>, which inhabits all <term>Osing</term> trees, gives the power of divination to the shells “*<term>Akparhe Osing</term>*.” In the beginning, the tree itself had the power of talking to human beings, but it lost it in the way related below:—

### WHY THE OSING TREE CAN NO LONGER SPEAK TO MEN EXCEPT THROUGH THE CHARM.

In the beginning of all things, both <term>Ojje</term> (Witchcraft) and <term>Osing</term> (the Spirit of the Osing tree) used to live with <term>Obassi Osaw</term> and accompany him wherever he went.

One day <term>Obassi</term> disguised himself as a man and journeyed through the length and breadth of the earth to see how people were faring. In the course of time, he came, with his two companions, to the place where a peasant was clearing the bush for his farm.

<term>Obassi</term> asked what he was doing and how many people there were in that place. The man answered that there was only one other beside himself, that he was making a farm, and that next year he was going to clear a larger space adjoining the one on which he was now working.

<term>Obassi</term> said “goodbye” to him and went on to a second man, of whom he asked the same questions. This latter man answered that there were two of them and that, God willing, he hoped to continue his work next year.

Now <term>Osing</term> stood near and heard both replies. Afterwards, he went back to the first man and told him how foolishly he had spoken, and how wise the second man was for saying “If God wills” before anything he intended to do; for the questioner was <term>Obassi</term> himself, who greatly disliked overly free and presumptuous speech.

<summary>A woman completes her ritual sacrifice to the spirits to cure her illness, and a folktale begins explaining how the spirit of the Osing tree once lived with the deity Obassi Osaw.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the folktale from page 177, explaining how the spirit Osing’s attempts to help humanity by teaching them how to please God led to his loss of speech.</meta>

The first man took the lesson to heart, and the next time <term>Obassi</term> came in disguise to question him, he answered, modestly enough, that he hoped to extend his farm if God were willing.

Now <term>Obassi</term> saw at once that this change of speech was due to <term>Osing</term>, who had thus taught the man how to draw down a blessing upon his future projects.

If <term>Osing</term> had continued to tell such secrets, men would have learned all those things which are able to bring trouble or danger upon them, and at last be freed even from death itself. So <term>Obassi</term> ordained that <term>Osing</term> should no longer be able to talk unrestrainedly. Yet he allowed him to communicate with men when the hard shells of his seeds had been made into a ritual charm. Now the fruits of this tree are edible and something like mangoes. Diviners collect the seed shells, and through them <term>Osing</term> can still speak, and give answers as to whether accused persons are innocent or guilty, and on many other subjects. When the charm is proclaimed in this way it is given the name of "<term>Efa</term>," or "<term>Idiong</term>."

Thus <term>Osing</term> lost his right to be the companion of <term>Obassi Osaw</term>, and also the advantage of speaking freely with whomever he chose. Had he been left to do so as before, we should by now have learned how to avoid the consequences of wrongdoing, sickness, trouble, and even death.

<term>Ojje</term>, on the contrary, told no secrets, but kept them all hidden in his breast. Therefore, he was not driven away from the fellowship of <term>Obassi Osaw</term>, and can communicate as he chooses with his evil followers, both witch and wizard.

He walked very softly, and found that seven ghosts were talking together before a small hut. He went behind this, and watched the ghosts. Each of them held in his hand a <term>calabash</term> containing a black <term>Juju</term>, which they rubbed on their faces, saying, “May this make me invisible.” Then each hung up his <term>calabash</term> on the wall of the little house, and went into the town.

When the seven were out of sight, the man crept into the house, and took down one of the <term>calabashes</term>. He poured some of the black <term>Juju</term> onto his hand, smeared his face, and said the same words which he had overheard from the ghosts. One of the richest men in the town stood up and served out much food. He then poured out rum into a glass. One of the ghosts was about to drink the essence of the spirit, but the poor man stretched out his hand and said, “Stop, do not touch it.”

The ghost stopped still, and for the rest of the feast the poor man prevented any of them from eating or drinking with the living. The ghosts said among themselves, “What can be the matter? Someone is preventing us from eating with the living as we used to do.”

His brother called a meeting of the townsfolk and said, “This woman caused the death of her husband, so I ask that she should die too.”

The latter was very pleased and announced, “I remove the law I made. All priests may practice the charm as usual.”

## II.

### How Obassi Drove Out His Unloved Wife.

Before Obassi Osaw left the earth, he married many wives. Two of these he loved, but he did not care for the others. One day, one of his favorite wives saw a woman weeping in the compound. “What is your trouble?” she asked, and the woman answered, “I weep because I am the wife of Obassi, yet I may never come near my Lord.”

The favorite wife felt pity for her and, at night, led her privately into their husband’s chamber.

Some months later, Obassi happened to pass by this woman as she sat working and saw what had happened to her. He thought she had been unfaithful and therefore ordered her to be driven away from the town.

The woman fled into the bush, and there her child was born. For several years they lived together until the boy grew tall and strong.

One day, Obassi's people set out to clear the "bush" for new farms. While doing this, they saw a boy coming and said to their master, “This youth is very much like you.” They roasted yams and offered them to the newcomer, but he said:

> “I cannot eat the food of Obassi, nor can my mother, because he drove her away without cause.”

Another day, the woman also came to visit them. Upon seeing her, the second of the favorite wives approached her husband and said, “Here is the woman whom you turned out of your compound. Her son is named Effion Obassi.”

Obassi caught his discarded wife and handed her over to the people so that they might put her to death, but Effion stood forward and said:

> “I want to know why you wish to kill my mother.”

The wife who had first befriended her also said: “Why should the woman be killed? What is the name of her son?” and they answered, “He is called Effion Obassi.”

Effion bent down and held out his hands toward him, touching the ground with his fingers. The man was Obassi. He arose, looked at the lad, and recognized him as his son, and told him to wait for one night.

He saw people coming towards him and ran into the bush to hide his treasure, for his father had said that he must tell no one of his secret; otherwise, he would be able to get nothing from it except with much trouble.

When all was finished, Effion went back to the town where his mother lived. He brought her with him, together with his brothers and sisters. Then she grew afraid because of what she had done and went to Porcupine to beg her to perform a charm.

Now, a hawk had watched the entire time, both when the girl went to consult Porcupine and again when she made the medicine and brought her parents back to life. That is the reason why you often see a hawk circling round and round over a rubbish heap; he wants to get the medicine the girl threw away so that, if his parents die, he may also be able to bring them back to life.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### OJJE OR WITCHCRAFT

It is perhaps during long "bush" tours that one comes closest of all to understanding forest people such as the Ekoi. During the night, when the voices of the tired carriers have at last died down, and one lies awake, listening to the myriad sounds of restless Africa, one is aware of a soft undercurrent: the murmur of countless streams rippling over pebbly beds, the far-off splash of little waterfalls leaping from rock to rock, the gentle rustle of surrounding leaves, or the sleepy chirp of the cricket and its even smaller relatives—"The manifold soft chimes" that fill the "haunted" vastness of the African night. Against this restful undercurrent, the harsh cries of nightjars, the howl of a leopard, or the scream of a giant cicada—as yet unnamed—sound with startling distinctness close to one's ear. This latter sound almost always makes the newcomer spring up to search the area, so similar is it to the cry of a child in pain.

The camp clearing is often as much as 100 feet by 50 feet, but the great branches still arch high above, shutting off all but the merest glimpse of the blue sky beyond.

In the whole land there are no open spaces, except those which have been cleared as sites for villages or farms. The heavenly bodies play very little part in the life of the race, for, as one of the men remarked, "Ekoi people do not trouble themselves about the stars, because the trees always hide them." Very few have distinctive names. Among these are:

Nkai Okott 'Mi: The woman of the moon's love (Venus).
Nkai Nkokk Obassi: The hen of Obassi (Aldebaran).
Aati Ikang Aiyu: The yam rack (the belt of Orion).
Nkokk Abonn: The hen's chicks (Pleiades).

Besides these, none seem to have particular significance. To those of us whose interests are to a large extent geographical

<summary>The author describes the atmospheric sounds and dense environment of the African forest at night, noting how the thick canopy limits the Ekoi people's interest in and naming of celestial bodies.</summary>
<keywords>Ekoi, forest, night sounds, astronomy, Venus, Aldebaran, Orion, Pleiades, Obassi, West Africa</keywords>

--- Page 259 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Chapter XVIII, transitioning from a discussion of the forest’s physical environment to its psychological and spiritual impact on the Ekoi people.</meta>

### OJJE OR WITCHCRAFT

...and botanical, the study of the part played by the land itself in molding the character of its people must appeal to a special degree, and it is the all-enfolding mysterious bush that, more than any other influence, has formed the Ekoi. To this they owe that *leucocholy* <note>a state of "white" or gentle melancholy</note> which lies deep down beneath the surface gaiety of their natures, and makes the dread of the unknown the dominant note of their lives.

The bush, with its soft green twilight, its dark shadows and quivering lights, is populated by many terrors, but among these, that of <term>Ojje</term> <note>witchcraft</note> reigns supreme. Some people, indeed, believe that there are good <term>Jujus</term> which are stronger, but many think that none but <term>Obassi</term> himself can provide protection against this dread, which walks by day or night and may manifest itself in the least suspected ways. Mother, sister, or sweetheart may be witches in disguise. The bird that flies in at your open door in the sunshine, the bat that circles around your house at twilight, the small bush beasts that cross your path while hunting—all may be familiars of a witch or wizard, or even the magic-users themselves, disguised to do you harm. In this world of magic, shape-shifting is an everyday occurrence, and it seems scarcely harder to believe that a man should be able to change into a leopard or crocodile than that tiny flowers, no bigger than a pinhead, should become huge fruits, hanging from tree and <term>liana</term> <note>woody climbing vines</note>, ready to fall on and stun the passerby. To those who know the depths of virgin forests—with their strange solitudes, filled by the thousand unexplainable sounds which together make up one vast silence—such beliefs seem not only natural but inevitable.

Witchcraft and all bad Jujus are thought to have been sent to earth by <term>Obassi Osaw</term> <note>the Sky God</note>, while the good ones came from <term>Obassi Nsi</term> <note>the Earth God</note>. Sometimes people pray to the latter to destroy <term>Ojje</term>, for it is well known that no witchcraft can stand against his might.

A case which came before the Native Court on January 5, 1909, shows how the smallest event is sometimes thought to have been caused by supernatural agency.

Those possessed by <term>Ojje</term> <note>witchcraft</note> have a power that warns them of the approach of others similarly possessed, just as the magic knife in the belt of the king’s daughter rang at the arrival of Weland.
Should a witch or wizard wish to kill a man, they gather together at night in front of the town and dance—not on the ground, but a few feet above it. While dancing, they often grow to a giant size. No noise can be heard, and they are invisible to all who do not have the “four eyes” <note>the spiritual sight required to see the supernatural</note>.
E. E. Offiong, one of the best-known chiefs of Calabar, claims to have the power to witness these witches’ revels. He says that he has often seen them dancing in the moonlight, and that after watching for a long time one night, he went the next day to each of the men and women he had recognized and forced them to confess that they were possessed by <term>Ojje</term>.

# OJJE OR WITCHCRAFT
S.B., O

knowledge. They can sit on the roof of a house at night and suck out the heart while the victim sleeps; without the aid of some strong <term>Juju</term>, he will never know what is killing him. A man wasting away from consumption or Beri-beri is usually thought to have been bewitched in this manner.

When the witch knows that her victim’s final hour is approaching, she sends the <term>Ekpangpang</term> in the night to the town of the dying man. This is the bat (*Hypsignathus monstrosus*), which is always regarded as the servant of a witch or wizard; its sinister reputation is well supported by its hideous, hippopotamus-shaped head and large, unwinking yellow eyes. One afternoon we watched a pair flying in blazing sunlight from one side of the Kwa River to the other. The paddlers were overjoyed when one fell to my gun and was retrieved from the water in a butterfly net.

The name <term>Ekpangpang</term> is the same as that of the brass pan used in Ekoi-land for washing hands. When not needed for this purpose, it is often held up and struck with the knuckles against the back to form a sort of gong. When used this way, it produces a sound from which its name is onomatopoeically derived. The same name has been given to the bat because its dull, monotonous cry, “*Pangpang*,” sounding out of the darkness, is mistaken for the hammering of nails into a coffin which the bat has been ordered to prepare for the burial of some victim. When such a sound is heard during the night, it is a matter of faith that by dawn there will be one fewer inhabitant in the small town.

In the old days, if a man was thought to be a wizard, he was taken into the bush to be “examined.” There he was bound, and a hole was cut in his body just above the liver. From this, the officiating “<term>Juju</term> man” usually succeeded in removing the suspected <term>familiar</term>, generally in the form of a bird, toad, or other small creature, but sometimes in the form of a tiny man. If nothing was found, the victim was cleared of all suspicion, but unfortunately, death always resulted from the procedure.

Even now, the bodies of those who have fallen under suspicion of witchcraft are examined in this way after death. Should the ceremony be omitted and the <term>familiar</term> remain unkilled, it is thought that it will emerge from the grave at night

“ ‘Take your wife home. Give her one <term>Esere</term> bean to drink. If she dies, come and take back all the goods you have paid to me; but if she does not die, you will know that I have done well in driving out the witchcraft from her, and that the goods are therefore mine.’

“When I reached home, I explained everything to the townsfolk and to my elder brother <term>Mbe</term>, who got the bean and ground it on a stone. My wife drank it and vomited as the priest said she would. When she was well again, I went out hunting. No sooner was I gone than she ran away to <term>Akot Ekpim</term> and complained to him that all the townsfolk had seen her shame, so she did not wish to live in my house any more.”

Another case was brought to my notice in which a great <term>Juju</term> man had exorcised a witch’s familiar in the form of a black butterfly. This he drove out from between her lips after laying his own hand across her mouth.

As was the case in Europe from the fourteenth century onward, there are thought to be far more witches than wizards. Although both can transform themselves at will into the shape of any animal, they more often take the form of a bat or owl than of other creatures. All witches have a special cry like that of a bird. This is believed not only by the <term>Ekoi</term>, but practically all over West Africa. The shell of the groundnut is their boat, and in this they can travel through air or by water.

There are some trees, for example, the <term>Mbaghe</term>, which, like our own rowan, have the power to keep witches at bay. The leaf of this, pressed against the nostrils, will save a man from death if he is suffering through witchcraft, and green boughs are also often burned over a fire so that the smoke may drive witches away. Should one of them be forced to drink water into which <term>Esere</term> has been scraped, she will confess all her misdeeds before dying.

In much the same way as with us, the owl is looked upon as a bird of ill omen and a familiar of both witch and wizard. The origin of this belief is explained in the following way:—

### WHY OWL IS THE WITCHES' FAMILIAR.

->BY <term>NTUI MFUM</term> OF <term>NIAJI</term>.<-

<term>Egut</term> (Parrot), <term>Nkundak</term> (Greater Plantain-eater), and <term>Ekku</term> (Owl) were all great friends. One day they consulted together and said, "Let us pretend to die, so that we may see whether our children mourn for us or not."

First they acted as if they were very sick, then all three lay down and pretended to die. When the children saw their mothers lying motionless and seemingly dead, the daughter of <term>Egut</term> began to weep bitterly, as did <term>Nkundak's</term> daughter also. The son of <term>Ekku</term>, however, did not mourn at all, but went gaily away to the place where the dried meat was kept and began to eat it greedily. When <term>Ekku</term> heard what he was doing, she called to her friends, "It is time to wake up. My son has eaten almost all the dried meat in the house." So they arose and told their children the trick that had been played on them. <term>Nkundak</term> put her daughter into the <term>fatting-house</term>, as did <term>Egut</term> also. When the right number of months had gone by, they both made ornaments for their daughters as a reward for the affection shown by them. <term>Nkundak</term> gave her child glistening feathers, and <term>Egut</term> brought red tail-feathers for hers. That is why these birds are so beautiful even today.

<term>Ekku</term>, however, said to her son, "Because you had no love for me and did not mourn my death like the others, from today, wherever your cry is heard, people will swear <term>Juju</term> against you."

This is the reason that whenever local people hear an owl hoot they say, "A bad man is near." When such a cry is heard, they go at once to the <term>Juju</term> man and ask him to make a "medicine" to protect them from witchcraft; for since the day on which <term>Ekku</term> cursed her son, he has been driven away from among the other birds and has become the familiar of witch and wizard.

### WHY CRAB'S CLAW IS SACRIFICED.

Once the Lord <term>Njokk</term> (Elephant) sent word to his people to tell them that they must come together on a certain day to hunt for him.
All the animals brought good guns, except for <term>Crab</term> alone, whose weapon was so old that it appeared quite useless. The other animals taunted him and asked, "How can you expect to kill anything for our Lord with such a miserable gun?" Nevertheless, when the hunt began they all missed everything at which they aimed, while <term>Crab</term> alone killed five great antelopes, one after the other.
Then the animals were very angry and took away from him all his kill. They took the gun away also, and wrecked it utterly. <term>Crab</term> said nothing, but left them in the bush, and went back to the town. He entered the compound where Elephant's wives were, and said to them:
"Your husband has sent me to tell you to get ready his <term>chop</term> <note>food</note>. You are to put in it much pepper and plenty of local salt. When you have done this, you are to throw away every drop of water that is in the compound, and none is to be fetched until after his return, for he wishes that all should be brought to him fresh from the spring."
Next, <term>Crab</term> went off to his home by the riverside, and drank up all the water, so that the stream ran dry.
When the hunters returned they began hungrily to eat up the food that had been prepared for them. Soon they grew very thirsty because of the pepper and salt. They went to the water pot, but found nothing there. All had been thrown away by Elephant's wives.
At once they sent to the river to get water, but found that all had dried up.
Elephant called <term>Ise</term>, the little grey duiker, and ordered him to fetch water. On his way, <term>Ise</term> saw <term>Crab</term> run to his hole, and knew that it was he who had brought the trouble upon them. He therefore went back and told Lord Elephant.

...this, there was no more sickness in Oban. Almost exactly the same thing happened at Aking a little later.

Some hold the belief that a witch or wizard, upon death, passes out of the human form to take up residence in that of an animal.

There are supposed to be seven different kinds of witchcraft, as will be seen from the following:

### THE SEVEN WITCHCRAFTS.

Once, long ago, seven different kinds of witchcraft lived together in a little town. Four were wizards and three were witches. They lived all alone because everyone feared them.

At that time, people did not know about making offerings against witchcraft. They only knew how to hang up charms to keep these evil creatures out of their houses. One day, the seven witchcrafts gathered together and said, "We are all hungry, yet we cannot enter into men’s houses to take food from them. Let us devise some way by which they may be forced to bring us offerings."

The first said, "I will choose a man and put a bad Juju in the path to his farm, so that he shall become cold and sick when he steps across it. In a few days he will die, and I will let the people know that if they do not set offerings for us on the farm paths, they also will perish in this way."

The others said, "Good." Next morning, all seven went out to the farm road and buried medicine in the ground.

Not long after, the owner of the farm came along. He crossed the spot where the magic was buried. Afterwards, he began to feel cold.

As he went back home, he crossed the place again and saw the seven kinds of witchcraft standing there: the four wizards on one side and the three witches on the other.

They said to him, "Go home and tell all your people. If no offerings are made against witchcraft on the path, all the town will die as they go to their farms. You yourself will die, so that all men may know what we tell you is true."

The man went home and gathered his friends around him.

He told them what had happened to him, then lay down and died. All the townsfolk were very afraid, so they made offerings in front of their farms as the evil beings commanded.

After this, the second wizard called all seven together and said: "It is not enough. Let us go to the place in the road where the large rocks stand. There we will perform magic and wait until a man comes by. When he comes, we will fasten him inside the rock." The others said, "Very well. We will put him within the rock, except for one hand, which shall remain outside so that all who pass by may see and fear our power and offer sacrifice."

The next morning, very early, they did as they had said. Then they waited, but no one came.

About noon, they heard a man coming. He came very gaily. Behind his ear he wore a red flower, *Akpane Besin*, as a sign that he had defeated the wrestlers in his town and was now going to another to challenge all newcomers.

The wizards seized him and shut him up within the rock; they left only one hand free, so that all passers-by might see it and take warning.

During the afternoon, six of the townsfolk came by. They were taking their farm produce to sell at a village some distance away. As they passed the rock, one of them stopped and said: "I see a man's hand." The second said, "I do not see it." The third said, "I see it, and it is holding the red flower that *'Ne Ikomm* (Strong Man) wore behind his ear." The fourth said, "It is surely a man's hand. Some wizard must have killed him and put him inside."

Since then, everyone knows that a person may be imprisoned in rocks and large stones.

All the other magicians killed a person in some way, each after his own kind. So people learned to make offerings and hang up charms in many places, so that wizards and witches might be powerless to harm them.

<header>OJJE OR WITCHCRAFT 201</header>
<meta>Pencil marks/lines in right margin next to first, second, and third paragraphs.</meta>

together on a certain day. When all were present, he ordered that the Juju "Njomm Aiyung" (the Blood Juju) should be practiced. A cut was made in the body of each person, and a few drops of blood were allowed to flow into a calabash half full of dry corn, which had been brought for the purpose. None were exempt; even the babies born that day gave one drop of blood, and when all had been collected, each man, woman, and child was made to partake of the corn. This was done so that witchcraft might no longer be practiced against any of the townsfolk; for after mingling blood and then partaking of it, should one of the parties attempt to harm another, Njomm Aiyung would catch them, and the evil they had tried to inflict would fall on themselves.

Much the same ceremony is used, though more rarely, to bind friends in a blood bond. In this case, after cuts have mutually been made, the blood is allowed to flow into a small clay basin in which some strong Juju "medicine" has already been placed. This is then drunk by the participants. Should one of them afterward act in an unfriendly way toward the other, the Juju will catch him and he will die.

Sometimes the terror of witchcraft will scatter a whole town. Such was the case with Oberekkai ("Obet Ekkai," Crab mud), which stands on a little tributary of the Kwa river. This was, in the old slave-dealing days, a large and prosperous town, and its Chief, Nataba, was the wealthiest man in the district. As more labor was needed to develop his great cocoa and other plantations, he sent to buy workers from the German Cameroons.

In the course of time, the messengers returned with a group of about thirty captives, whose large limbs and strong appearance gave promise of excellent labor material.

The newcomers kept apart from the people of Oberekkai and refused to take any share in the social life of the town. When "plays" were performed, they stayed together at the edge of the crowd, looking on somberly, but more often they gathered secretly in the night at a farm hut belonging to one of them. After a while, strange stories began to spread of midnight rites practiced before unknown Jujus brought by the newcomers from their own land. Then the townsfolk fell ill. One after another they died, and the survivors whispered that the

Terror took the people, many fled, and in a comparatively short time the inhabitants were reduced to a mere remnant. Nataba, and those of his family who still survived, decided on desperate measures. One after another the slaves disappeared. Their magic was powerless to protect them from the vengeance of the infuriated survivors, and Oberekkai remains, with its untended plantations, over which the bush is rapidly creeping, a shrunken survival of its former prosperity.

---

One of the real causes of the decrease in population became painfully evident during our stay, and proved to be nothing more mysterious or romantic than the unsanitary conditions prevailing. When this was pointed out to Chief Nataba, he answered in a bewildered kind of way that native people did not notice bad smells like white men, but he professed himself willing to obey orders about cleaning up the town, and ended by saying, “I almost believe what the White Man says, that this is the cause of the deaths of my people.” A great improvement in the sanitary conditions has now been made.

# CHAPTER XIX

## OBEREKKAI TO ETARA

A few hours after leaving Oberekkai, we reached Obutong once more. That evening, as we sat working in the rest-house after dinner, there was a timid tap at the door. Outside, we found the interpreter and a tall, slim girl dressed in the graceful native style, which is now rapidly disappearing. She wore a piece of cloth passed under her right arm and knotted over her left shoulder; beneath this, her only garment was a ribbon-like strip around the waist, with ends falling down on the left side where the upper cloth swung slightly open. Around her slender ankles and wrists were strings of dark blue beads, and the entire length of her left arm, from almost the shoulder to the wrist, was decorated with carefully made round scars about the size of a wafer. She told us that it was her people’s custom to make these on their arms because, after death, a ghost could remove them one by one and sell them to the spirits in exchange for food. This is a widespread belief among the Ekoi, though not all scars seen on their arms should be attributed to this superstition. Many are due to a simple desire for decoration, while others are the marks of native inoculation described on page 10.

The girl had come down from a town about sixty miles away to ask for protection from her father, who was trying to force her into marriage against her will. When asked the reason for her unwillingness, she answered modestly enough that she was too young for wifehood and did not wish to be married until she had learned to know herself better and also more thoroughly understood the meaning of marriage.

On the following morning, we set off for a climb along the riverside to the uppermost of the Kwa falls.

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

the place has a quiet charm all its own. On both sides, the high banks are covered with tall trees, which cast a cool green light on the dark, swift-flowing water. Hardly a ray of sunlight filters through, and no flowers, except for a few heavily scented white <term>landolphias</term>, break the restful green of the gorge.

The rocks here are made of <term>foliated gneiss</term>, mixed with a considerable amount of manganese. The centuries-old lapping and washing of the water has worn the stone into great dark folds, which in places enclose little stretches of golden sand and shining pebbles. The rocks in many parts of the District are highly <term>garnetiferous</term>, and gold dust and sapphires are reported in many streams, though in our case, careful washings only resulted in the slightest trace of "color."

In the middle of the river, immediately above the falls, is a large <term>pot-hole</term>, more than seven feet across and very deep.

On the farther shore, the ground slopes down to a little bay over which the trees arch from side to side, until it looks like a dim, cool arbor. As we sat watching the lace-like mist rise from the edge of the falls, a fawn and kid came down to drink at the water's edge. The golden brown of their coats stood out with startling clarity against the twilight of the alcove; but, though we were so near, we sat motionless and went unnoticed for a time. Suddenly, the fawn looked across and seemed to give a warning signal. Both stood for a while frozen with amazement at the sight of the strange white creatures on the other side, but they seemed more curious than afraid, and after watching us for some time, they turned and trotted off in a leisurely manner.

It would have taken a harder heart than any there to spoil the beauty of the picture or break the silence of the place with the crack of a rifle; so the fawn and kid escaped safely for the time being.

The way from the falls leads past several leopard lairs and over tree trunks covered with orchids and flowering creepers, down to <term>Obutong beach</term>. Here, a dugout canoe is stationed to ferry traders across, supplementing the somewhat dangerous <term>tie-tie bridge</term> which spans the river immediately over one of the highest falls.
