...to the top of the bank. It seemed to me that this climb was too steep and dangerous for traders, especially the women traders who come down in great numbers with heavy loads on their way to Calabar; so a broad flight of steps has now been constructed, similar to the one on the other side of the river.

The path from Obutong to Mbarakpa is a bush road, but it is clear and wide, and bordered almost continuously by an endless variety of <term>cauliflorous</term> trees and bushes. These strangely flowering growths are so rare in most parts of the world that, as we learned from the authorities at Kew Gardens, they had remained almost unstudied because no significant collection of them had been made. Here, however, they occur in vast numbers and almost countless varieties, several hundred of which have now been sent to England. The strangeness of their appearance is matched in many cases by their beauty; for, with the *Napoleonas* and many of the more showy species, one suddenly comes across a great trunk in the deep green of the bush, covered from its roots to its branches with myriads of flowers. At first sight, the trees look as if they are wreathed in garlands, like those offered at some festival in *Arcadia*, or brought as gifts to the fairies by little old-world children, like those of *Domremy* in the time of *Joan of Arc*.

Above the town of Mbarakpa stands the rest-house, in a clearing at the top of a small hill. On their own initiative, the inhabitants had made a broad road leading up to it. This was particularly kind of them, as the town is a small one, and the task of keeping even narrow roads in good repair is not at all popular.

On one occasion, soon after our arrival, a boy arrived with a bird he had snared and brought in as a gift. This was placed in a makeshift cage on the veranda. During the night, it seemed to flutter and beat its wings; then there was a noise like something falling. I was about to go out to investigate, but the march had been a long one that day, and laziness suggested waiting to see if anything else would happen. I must have fallen asleep again, for suddenly the voice of the "small boy" <note>A term for a junior servant or house-help.</note> woke us all with a start.

"Sir, Sir," he yelled, "a leopard caught a fowl; he seized it and ran for the bush!"

## IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

It did not take long to pick up my rifle and follow. The trail led to the edge of the clearing, but the light of the few hastily brought lanterns failed to show anything further. Next morning, unmistakable signs were found that the beast had devoured its prey in the shadow of a bush, the outermost branches of which must have brushed my rifle. Before seizing the chicken, it had paid a visit to our veranda, and the noise we had heard had been caused by the fall of the cage, which the animal had knocked over in trying to get at the bird. The latter had escaped, flown through the ventilation space at the top of the mud wall, and taken refuge on Bimba’s mosquito net, where it was found and released the next day.

At Mbarakpa, the children have a club, in close imitation of the <term>Egbo Society</term> of their parents. They usually came up to give a "play" before the rest-house during our visit, at the end of which we often threw handfuls of "tenths" among them, for the children dearly love a "scramble." These coins are, as their name denotes, of the value of one-tenth of a penny. It struck me that the little <term>Okum</term> or "image" was heavily handicapped by the cloth which concealed its face, so, as it passed by, I thoughtlessly pulled off the covering.

A cry went up from the children, all of whom stopped the scramble as if at a word of command. The little <term>Okum</term> covered its face with its hands, and the elders hastened up to rearrange the veils about it, volubly explaining that the face of the "image" must never be seen by its companions.

---

The whole country is honeycombed with waterways, which meander in every direction through the green of the bush, like the veins in some giant leaf. Across many of the smaller streams stepping-stones are placed, while, over larger ones, tree trunks have been felled to serve as bridges.

On one tour, when nearing the river before Nsan, terrified screams were heard, and, on hurrying up, some women were found huddled together on the near bank, while, from a branch overhanging the far end of the rough bridge, a great snake dangled. The water was too deep for fording, and the reptile hung, darting its wicked head threateningly here and there.

as if fully conscious of the terror it caused. A shot cleared the way and gave me a fine skin about 14 feet long.

The name Nsan (Thunder Town) is common in Ekoi folklore. One of the dangers to which Obassi Osaw, Obassi Nsi, or indeed any unjust father doomed his unloved son was a visit to a town of this name, usually in the underworld, on a mission planned for the youth’s destruction. Such a story can be found quoted in the Creation stories (“How the Two Brightest Stars Came into the Sky”), but there are many others, among which the following are perhaps the best known:—

### ABOUT OBASSI OSAW AND HIS UNLOVED SON.

Obassi Osaw married a woman who bore him two sons, one named Oru and the other Agbo. The first work given to them was making native traps. Before they set about this, both went and asked their father to give them each a machete. He gave one to Oru but refused Agbo. The latter, therefore, went and complained to his mother, “Our father refuses to give me a machete.” His mother gave him an old one, which was the best she had.

Both sons went into the bush. Agbo caught many birds in his traps, while Oru caught none. Agbo gave twenty of his birds to his brother, and they took them all to their father. The father rejected Agbo's birds and drove him away, but accepted those from Oru. Agbo therefore took the birds to his mother and said, “My father refuses them.” The mother took them and ate them.

When the boys were old enough to use a gun, both went to their father to ask for one. As before, Obassi gave one to Oru but refused Agbo, saying, “I do not like you at all.” Both asked for gunpowder, but this was again refused to the unloved son. The mother, however, provided him with a very old gun and a little powder.

Both lads went into the bush. Agbo killed many antelopes, then called his brother, who had killed none, and said, “Let us divide them, half for me and half for you.”

They then went into the town, and Agbo said: “Take the meat home; it is for yourself and your wife.”

When Agbo got back to the compound, he took his kill to their father, who refused it and drove him away. Then he took it to his mother, who accepted and ate it.

In the evening, Obassi sent for Agbo. He pointed to a silk-cotton tree and said, “Tomorrow, go and cut it down.”

When Agbo saw the huge girth of the tree, how tall it was, and how strong, he wept and went as usual to his mother, who told him to be comforted. When night had come, she went with a witch to the place, and together they sucked out the inside of the tree.<note>Witches are believed to be able to “suck out” the inside of things, such as trees, rocks, and even human hearts. See p. 192.</note> At dawn, the boy went with his machete, and after two or three blows, the tree fell down.

Next, Obassi pointed to a very high rock and said, “Tomorrow, go and break it into pieces.”

Again the lad complained to his mother, and once more she went with her witch friend in the night, and together they ate up all the inside of the stone. At dawn, the boy went, and after a few blows, the rock split just as the tree had done. People went to see the wonderful feats Agbo had performed and said to Obassi, “What is the matter with this son? He does the most difficult tasks easily.”

Next, Obassi showed him a very large lake and said, “Tomorrow, dive into it and pick up a heavy stone which lies at the bottom.”

Again the boy complained to his mother about this new task. When night came, the woman went and slipped into the water. She found the stone, carried it to the edge, and laid it down by the bank. At daybreak, the lad went and brought it back to his father.

Also, Obassi said, “Tomorrow, go to Nsann, the Thunder Town, and ask for my elephant tusk which is there. Do not come into my presence again unless you bring it.”

At dawn, his mother cooked plantains and gave them to him, saying, “Go with good courage. I will make the way safe before you.”

Agbo did so and told her to lean on him as she came up from the spring. He showed her a place to sit down and gave her some of his plantains to eat. A bird flew by; he turned for a moment to watch it, and when he looked back, the woman was gone.

The youth walked on until he came to the side of a river. There he saw the same woman, who again asked him to help her wash her body. He did as before and again gave her some plantains. She said to him, “Do you know where you are standing?” He answered, “Yes, in the middle of the bush.” She said to him, “No, this is not the bush at all.” Again she asked, “Do you know who has played a trick on you?” He answered, “No.” So she said, “I will tell you something. I know that your father does not like you at all and has sent you on this journey so that you may die.”

She struck her belly,<note>* Striking the belly in Ekoi legends produces the same effect as the stroke of a magic wand in European fairy tales.</note> and at the stroke, the bush became a town; also, her sores disappeared, and she became very beautiful. She said to him, “I wish to help you.” So she washed him all over in the river and turned him this way and that. Then she said, “I will tell you where the tusks are that your father sent you for. There is the road to the ghost town, and here is a piece of chalk.<note>† The word used means chalk, but from the explanation given, probably a kind of edible clay or “<term>steinbutter</term>” is meant here. Chalk is a great <term>Juju</term>, and marks are made with it on the bodies of men, women, and children to bring them good luck.</note> When you reach the town and they cook <term>chop</term> for you, touch none of it, but throw it on the ground and see what will happen. Eat only your plantains and this piece of chalk. When night comes and they ask you where you will sleep, say you will sleep among the goats; but, when all the people are asleep, leave the place quietly and just choose a manger. You will see what the ghost people will try to do.”

When Agbo reached the town, they brought him <term>chop</term>, but he said:

“I never eat out of a calabash.”* So they brought a plate, and put the <term>chop</term> upon it.

He took this around to the back yard, threw it on the ground, and saw that the grass withered where the <term>chop</term> was thrown.

When night came, they asked, “Where will you sleep?” He said, “I will sleep among the goats.”

When they had all entered their houses and closed the doors, he went quietly out, and slept in the manger with the cows. In the middle of the night, they sent a thunderbolt to kill him. It fell among the goats and struck many of them. In the morning, very early, he went back and lay among the dead goats.

When the people came to see what had happened, they saw the mark in the ground which the thunderbolt had made, and the dead goats and other damage, but Agbo sat there unharmed.

During the entire time of his stay in the town, he did not eat their <term>chop</term>, but only what he had with him.

At last, the townspeople grew tired and said, “We will try now to send the boy back with his father’s tusk.”

They brought all the tusks from the <term>Egbo</term> shed and laid them down before him, saying, “Choose.”

Agbo stood there with <term>Mfut</term> his guide, and the fly settled on one of them. He caught hold of this and lifted it up. All the people clapped their hands, because he had chosen rightly.

The new town is one of the best in the District—large and clean, with broad, well-kept streets and plenty of space between the compounds.

Many years ago, the jar containing the <term>Eja</term> medicine, which belonged to the town, was accidentally broken. In terror of the consequences, the inhabitants scattered into the bush, hoping that if they stayed apart and well-hidden, they might escape the vengeance of the <term>Juju</term>. It seemed to them that it might not take the trouble to search out and strike down each family individually, though it certainly would have avenged itself if it could have done so in one single stroke. Now that so much time had passed, the people of <term>Obung</term> thought the danger might have subsided, and they had gathered together once more to form a town. They had bought a new pot of <term>Eja</term> medicine and seemed to be in a very flourishing condition.

During one visit, the rain fell in torrents; it poured through the roof of the little <term>Egbo</term> shed, and as it had no walls, the floor soon became like a pond. The head chief invited us into his compound, where there was a picturesquely arranged <term>Juju</term>. While my wife was sketching this and I was busy hearing a complaint brought by some of the townspeople, my rifle suddenly went off with a tremendous report within about a yard of us. The <term>gunboy</term> had been too interested in the proceedings to pay attention to his duties, and the curiosity of one of the spectators regarding the new type of weapon proved too strong for discretion. While he was examining it, the little safety catch became displaced, and, considering the crowded state of the room, it was almost a miracle that no one was harmed.

Beyond <term>Nsan</term>, the next place of importance is <term>Netim</term>, a town about 4 miles away which had at first been reluctant to submit to European rule, but like all others, soon decided to accept the inevitable with good grace. It is the largest town in the District, and the only pure <term>Ekoi</term> one; its inhabitants live on their bush farms during the majority of the year and only return to their town houses in the dry season and on special occasions. # OBEREKKAI TO ETARA

I decided to pay a visit to this place while staying at Nsan, in order to inquire into the complaint of a man who was too ill to come over to plead his own cause. Soon after starting, the rain began to come down in sheets. It continued in a steady downpour during our visit and on the way back. When we were about two miles from Nsan, a rushing, roaring sound made itself heard, growing momentarily louder and louder, much like an approaching express train. We had crossed no river on our way to Netim, only some small streams; but one of these, which had been a mere trickle flowing between steep, wide banks, had now become a torrent, more than 60 feet wide at our crossing place, and over 100 feet a little further down. A foot or so from the bank, the water was up to my shoulders, and the current tearing down like a mill race made swimming out of the question.

While we were trying to make a bridge of some sort, the Netim children, on their way back home from Nsan school, appeared on the opposite bank. Ropes of <term>tie-tie</term> were thrown over to them and they were shown how to fasten these to some of the trees, but this device broke under the strain of the mass of water, tearing against the body of the man who tried to cross by its means. A way had to be cut through the bush by the water-side to search for some place where a crossing would be possible. After some time, the trunk of a tree was found which had fallen half across from the opposite bank. Another was cut down so that it almost joined the first, and by this means we managed to reach the other side and were able to get the children over in the same way.

From Netim to Ibum, the march leads through the midst of the Forest Reserve, a stretch of land nearly 400 square miles in extent, which has been set aside by the wish of the Government as a sanctuary for all wild bush things. Here one evening we came upon a great herd of elephants, which melted silently into the shadows on our approach. One cow, however, bolder or more friendly than the rest, paused a moment to wag its tail before disappearing in the wake of its companions.

Once, too, on pitching camp, the arrival of the carriers disturbed a leopard, which was busily eating an antelope. The

The meal had hardly begun, however, and the men were delighted by this welcome addition to their larder.

The inhabitants of Ibum itself are far more enterprising and hardworking than their relatives in the lowlands. Farms stretch for miles in every direction, and one of these shows a truly remarkable amount of energy; for, to create it, the entire surface of a small hill had to be cleared. From the top, a panoramic view can be seen reaching to the base of a great circle of mountains, which encloses the landscape on all sides. Standing in the middle of this natural amphitheater, the place looks very much like a huge crater.

Ibianshi Peak, near Ibum, divides the headwaters of the Calabar and Kwa rivers. From its summit, which can only be reached by a difficult climb up the bare face of the rock, a magnificent view can be obtained of the cluster of hills in the middle of the Forest Reserve. These hills, with their sharply defined outlines of every imaginable shape, seem so closely huddled together that it looks almost as if they had been suddenly dropped in a heap by some Titan who had grown weary of carrying them further. It was on this peak that a beautiful specimen of *Napoleona* was found, which is not only a new variety of this interesting group but also displays a cluster of flowers <note>inflorescence</note> previously unknown. I have ventured to name it *Egertoni*, after the former Governor of Southern Nigeria, who managed somehow, amid all his work, to keep track of and encourage every effort of his subordinates, even in a matter as small as a botanical collection. Another has been named after the Provincial Commissioner, Mr. Widenham Fosbery, C.M.G. It is impossible to adequately express my thanks to both for the help and encouragement they so generously extended. A third has been called *Alexandri*, after my friend and former leader, Boyd Alexander. The whole family bears the name of his hero, Napoleon, so it seems fitting that one of them should also bear his own name.

From Ibum, the path is steep and difficult, almost untouched by human hands, and very beautiful. However, as my companions had to be lowered down huge boulders or occasionally thrown upward to be caught and pulled to safety by someone stationed above, it was natural that they expressed a preference for the humbler beauties of easier paths.

# OBEREKKAI TO ETARA

The road often leads down the faces of small cataracts that dash from the steep hillsides to the rivers below, one of the most important of which is the River Ukpon. As we wished to explore this, we waded on one occasion for a considerable distance up its shallow bed. After a while, the water deepened; a great tree trunk jutted out of the bank at a convenient angle, and my companions chose to rest there while I went on. I was just turning to leave them when the orderly—after saluting with great formality—very slowly and respectfully begged leave to inform us that beneath that particular tree was the home of a crocodile, whose eggs the carriers <note>laborers hired to carry supplies and equipment</note> had just discovered and were taking home for supper.

In less time than it takes to write, my companions had left their seat and reached shallow water nearly a quarter of a mile downstream!

Some of the people of Ibum have now migrated to the town of Etara, twelve miles away; for, as the chief explained sadly, bachelors were growing scarce in his town, and the young and beautiful women did not find a sufficient choice of suitors, so they wished to go down to the larger town below.

In many of the houses of Etara, elaborate graves can be seen. These usually take the form of a low divan <note>a long backless sofa or raised platform</note> made of mud, eight to ten feet long, three feet wide, and about one and a half feet high. All along the edge, plates and dishes have been pressed into the mud while it was still soft. These were first broken—as is always done with the property of the dead—but the hardening mud acts as cement to hold them together. In the case of a rich man, a fresh coating of mud is plastered over the wall behind the grave, and in this, more plates and dishes are fixed in a rough design.

# CHAPTER XX

## EKOI OF THE CROSS RIVER

The first town beyond the Oban-Ikom boundary is Abijang. Here the Ekoi have intermarried significantly with their neighbors in the twin town of Akam, which moved over from Obubra and settled so close to Abijang that, at first sight, the two towns seem to form only one.

->Egbo House.<-

The decoration of some of the compounds, and of the Egbo house, is different from that in most Ekoi towns, though a little later we came upon a particularly beautiful example of this style made by an Oban man. Instead of the pattern being molded in relief on the surface of the wall after it has been roughly plastered with mud to form a background, the design here is first marked on the surface, which is then dug out between the

The figures shown in the drawing were explained in various ways as Obassi Osaw, his wife, and Nimm (the Snake); Obassi Osaw and Nimm in her three forms (woman, snake, and crocodile); or Obassi Osaw and Obassi Nsi with Nimm.

The clay near this part of the Cross River is especially suitable for pottery, and particularly beautiful examples are therefore found in the neighborhood.

The head chief of Abijang has literally dozens of skulls embedded in the mud before the entrance to his room, as well as in the ends and sides of the mud couches along the walls. The atmosphere of this apartment is exceptionally foul-smelling, even for this part of the world, due to a small pool of fermenting palm wine in front of the entrance.

In one corner of the room was a very old, roughly carved wooden figure holding its pointed beard with its right hand. The style of the head is strangely similar to some ancient Egyptian burial masks discovered by my late brother-in-law, Dr. Hugh Baker, in the sands of the Egyptian oasis of Kharga.

At Nchofan, the next important place on the river, where the people are almost entirely Ekoi, a wonderful variety of designs was found.

Here the children came to perform a very charming “play.” The performers consisted of about fifty boys and girls dressed in brightly colored cloth and bead chains, wearing belts <note>Original: ceintures</note> with little bunches of brass bells or tiny rattles attached. These rattles were made from the seeds of the “Agara” tree, with three large pods brightly painted in red and white, tied together by strings and fastened just below each knee. In their right hands, they carried thin toy swords made of white wood, decorated with Nsibidi writing and long fringes of red-dyed palm fiber.

The drum belonging to the club was a magnificent example of its kind. It was carved from a single solid piece of wood, shaped like a trough, with a roll of soft cloth fastened to its edge. This was held in place by nails, which also served to separate the rough slabs of corkwood laid across it, much like a xylophone. At either end sat a carved

...figure, a male to the right and a female to the left; and to the right hand of the latter, raised on a post, was Tortoise. These again were explained to us in two ways. First, as the three principal characters in the well-known story, “How Obassi Osaw Proved the Wisdom of Tortoise”; and secondly, as Obassi Osaw, Obassi Nsi, and Tortoise, representing certain attributes of the latter, much in the same way as in the worship of Aphrodite Hestia.

Two performers sat facing each other at opposite ends of the instrument, beating out the songs of the club—true “Songs without Words”—for this society, unlike most others, has no song which can be put into words and sung. The subject of drum songs is treated more fully in Chapter XXVII.

On this occasion, the songs beaten upon the drum were:

> “Makara araw ba, kun abonn akam asum.
> (If) the white man had not come, then the children would have become slaves.”

The second referred to the arrival of the first white women in Insofan:

> “Nkanang oiyenn ntuk nji, njum nji ’me nyenn A.
> (I) never saw anything like this; a thing such as this I have not seen.”

The head chief of Insofan possessed a particularly elaborate example of a “chief’s dish,” which he unfortunately declined to sell at any price, though he was delighted with the <term>dash</term> <note>a gift or tip</note> of tobacco leaves given to him for allowing it to be drawn. These dishes are carved, lid and all, from solid blocks of wood, and are suspended by a string passing through the base and lid from the roofs of the houses of head chiefs until a neighboring chief of equal or superior position comes on a visit. The dish is then taken down, and the visitor’s food is served in it.

Another object of interest in the same room was a drum-shaped box made of antelope and leopard skin, in which were kept the caps worn by the principal chiefs of Insofan for many generations.

Before the entrance was a little pool for ghost libations, like the one already described at Abijang, but surrounded by a crowd of objects: old bronze bracelets and anklets, and Nimm stones of

On first entering one of the compounds with the idea of purchasing typical examples of pottery, etc., the women rushed away in a state of panic to hide their treasures. However, no sooner did they understand that we wished to take away nothing that they did not want to sell, and at a price for which they were willing to exchange, than we were almost mobbed by would-be sellers.

<image-desc>An illustration of a cylindrical hat box with a lid, covered in a material featuring a leopard-spot pattern.</image-desc>
->Hat Box.<-

A march of thirteen miles took us once more across the Oban border to the ruined town of Mkpott. On the way there, we passed a deserted farm close to the overgrown road of Itaka. Here, before the abandoned Juju tree <note>a tree associated with local spiritual or magical practices</note>, we found one of the pointed stones, roughly sugar-loaf in shape. It might have been a fragment of the larger piece later discovered before the Egbo house <note>a communal building for the Egbo secret society</note> at Mkpott. Within the latter building, just in front of the mud base in which the great end pillar is embedded, a splendid example of the <term>Etai Ngbe</term> was to be found, the sides of which were absolutely clear-cut and four-square (see p. 172).

In the lowest circle of this base was a Nimm stone, which served to close up a small hole in which "medicine" was concealed to ensure the birth of many children to the townspeople.

The former inhabitants of this once large and flourishing town have now divided and formed several smaller ones, each under the leadership of its particular chief or group of chiefs.

In one of the deserted houses, the “treasure chamber” remains intact and is a truly beautiful example of native ornamentation. No color is used; the entire structure is made of clay, with a surface as smooth as that of pottery. The pattern, consisting of conventionalized leaves, is left in relief by depressing the background, similar to those already described at Abijang.

At the next stopping place, Ewaw-Offong, we noticed a curious little custom. As was usual upon arriving in a town, a stand was built for the cases of botanical specimens. As soon as this was finished, the carriers brought logs and lit a fire beneath it. The spot chosen was under the sheltering eaves of a house. We had found it better to have these small structures built outside rather than inside the compounds, and quite near our own quarters, for it was easier to see that the fires were not allowed to die out.

In the center of the open space before the Egbo house <note>a communal building for the Egbo secret society</note>, a Juju tree <note>a tree associated with local spiritual or magical practices</note> is to be seen, growing from a heap of small stones brought as offerings. Around this, a circle of larger stones is laid to serve as seats for headmen when special rites are being performed.

After dark had fallen, a bright light suddenly flared up from the edge of the heap of stones. It was so brilliant that every leaf and flower on the Juju tree stood out against the night. The fire rose into a great flare, which flickered and wavered over a semicircle of men who had silently gathered in the background, then settled down to a clear, steady flame. Investigation showed this was caused by a resin which drips from the Njaii Asung cactus.

The reason for the ceremony proved to be that, in this town—as in all those which possess the Juju Ngbe Abum Obbaw—it is unlawful for a fire to be lit outside the compound walls. Should this rule be violated, according to old tradition, the Juju which protects the town from leopards will no longer be effective. On the very night after the offending fire has been lit, one of these beasts will break through and carry off some of the goats or sheep. Only by means of the rite described above can the power of the offended Juju be restored.

<summary>The author describes an ornate clay "treasure chamber" in a deserted house and observes a ritual fire ceremony in Ewaw-Offong involving a resinous cactus. The ritual is necessary to appease a Juju that protects the village's livestock from leopards after a fire is lit outside the compound.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXI

## FUNERAL CEREMONIES

In December 1907, the head chief of Oban, named Itorok, died. The funeral was typical of those for the more important members of his people, so an account of it may be of interest.

First, water was heated and the body was washed. It was then dressed in the best robes the dead man had owned and wrapped in a wide native mat made of braided reed. Pieces of new cloth were wound around this, and then three more mats were added, fastened with tie-tie <note>strong vines or local rope used for binding</note>.

The body was then carried into the bush, about 100 yards from the town, and laid on the ground while a grave six feet by six feet was dug in the presence of all the chiefs.

When the grave was ready, Agbashan, the dead man’s chief representative, approached with two bottles: one containing rum and the other Juju <note>spiritual or magical</note> “medicine.” He had smeared red and yellow powder over his face and poured out the spirits as a libation, while he took some of the “medicine” into his mouth and spat it out near the head of the corpse. Next, he placed two dishes in the grave where the feet would lie, and a cup and spoon by the head.

A net was then brought and divided into three pieces, which were placed under the body. By means of these, six of the dead man’s “members” <note>family or society associates</note> lowered the corpse into the grave. While this was being done, Chief Itaban took a Juju spear and struck it twenty-five times against the heart, counting each stroke. Each time he touched the body, all those present called out, “Owe.” Throughout this time, three young men were beating drums very softly, and a sound was heard whose origin was difficult to locate. This was said to be the voice of the invisible Egbo <note>the spiritual representation of the secret society</note>, mourning over the dead chief. It was

It was unfortunately impossible to determine the actual cause of the sound, but it was produced by something quite different from the bull-roarer <note>a ritual musical instrument made of a slat of wood tied to a cord</note>.

The nets were next drawn up, another cloth was spread over the body, and three calabashes filled with earth were placed upon it. Then the grave was filled in.

After this, a brass pan was brought, holes were made in it, and it was set at the head of the mound. A sapling was taken from one of the Juju <note>spiritual or magical</note> trees and planted close by.

The burial took place in the bush instead of within the house, as is usual for people of distinction, because the deceased had died of dysentery and a cough, which are considered very infectious.

All this time the women, who are never allowed to attend the funeral of a chief, sat in the house of the dead man, naked except for loincloths, and weeping by an empty coffin. When the real burial was over, this coffin was let down into a hole in a small inner room. After this, the house was cleared of all inhabitants, and young palm leaves were tied against the lintels as a sign that no one might enter, as well as to keep out evil ghosts and spirits.

On the eighth day, the door was opened, and a goat and a cow were sacrificed. The former was placed with an offering of plantains under the Juju Obassi Nsi <note>the Earth God or a representation of him</note>, in the courtyard. The latter was killed, as is always the case under such circumstances, by suffocation, through having its mouth and nostrils tightly bound. Then the various Clubs to which the dead man had belonged came and performed plays, during which all the performers had yellow powder rubbed over their faces. At all funeral dances, free men carry a spear in both hands, while those who are not free are only allowed to hold one in the right hand.

A wake was held more or less continuously for several months, especially when groups of kinsfolk arrived from long distances. If the Government had not already taken over the District, the six members who lowered the coffin would probably have been murdered and buried in their master’s grave. By ancient custom this was always done, so that a chief might not arrive servantless in the spirit world.

Two years after the funeral described above, the headmen of Oban came up to the station to invite us to be present at a great play which was to be held in honor of the same chief, and act as a *finale* to the long burial rites.

In the principal compounds, stands had been decorated, much like the stalls of a country fair. These were spread with blankets or other bright cloths and hung around with colorful handkerchiefs and gaudy prints. On them was set out an array of china, from beautiful old Dutch pieces—brought by early traders—and groups of "cottage" figures, down to the crudest and coarsest examples of present-day earthenware.

The Ekoi happened to be very pleased with me, as my efforts to procure gunpowder with which to protect their farms from the ravages of buffalo and elephant, and their cattle from those of leopard and wildcat, had just been successful. They well knew my interest in all their old customs, and I attributed it to a childlike wish to show gratitude for my efforts on their behalf that two figures, which here, at any rate, had never before shown themselves to a white man, suddenly appeared before us.

The first, a dark mask covered with skin and with a ridiculous snake-like nose, was called Igumi, the name of a tree with tiny, inconspicuous flowers and a leaf much like that of Virginia Creeper. This tree has a bad reputation among the natives, partly because its hollow stems harbor innumerable ants and partly for supposed occult properties. The Club had originally been formed to wage war on the neighboring town of Aking, and the curious head was adopted as its standard or emblem.

Roars of laughter greeted the image and were redoubled as the other figure sprang forward and came bobbing and dancing in our direction. This one, named Ojjen, was a sight which, for actual grisly horror, would be hard to beat. On its head, it bore a human skull, or rather a dried head, the mouth of which was fixed open in a ghastly grin. The parched skin was wrinkled around the eye-holes in a way that produced the effect of ghoulish merriment. Words can give but a feeble

<margin>x</margin>
The skull is a great Juju. It was brought by the Ekoi when they traveled down from their old home near Mkpott, and now forms the chief treasure of the "company" "Etim Ngbe" or "Ojjen." Its present-day use is interesting enough. Upon the marriage of a member of the club, or of any man wealthy enough to pay for the privilege, it is carried to the door of the bride’s chamber. There it remains, a grim sentinel on the threshold, until the company comes to fetch it again at dawn. It is thought that this will ensure faithfulness on the part of the wife, for, should she attempt to leave her husband, the horrible head would follow her through the night, and, if necessary, summon to its aid countless hordes of dim, grimacing shapes from the ghost towns, which would crowd around and block the way to the house of another lover.

The "customs" now to be described are typical of those performed at the funeral of every woman of importance.

<margin>curved pencil mark</margin>
Upon the death of Adet Awaw, one of the leading women of Oban, the friends and relatives, who had gathered around her bed, remained for a short time mourning their loss. Then water was heated, and the women washed the body. New clothes were placed upon it, and the hair was elaborately arranged in tufts. By ancient custom no coffin was provided, but in this case one was brought. It was lined with new cloths, and on these four pillows were laid: one for the feet, one for the head, and one under each elbow. The hands were folded across the chest, and, after the coffin had been nailed shut, a new cloth was spread over it. The women now accompanied it outside the house, and a goat and cow were sacrificed while the men dug a grave, 6 feet deep, in one of the rooms. When all was ready the coffin was carried back, and gently lowered. Then the earth was filled in again, and smoothed over.

This is the same as the one called “Oóm” at Big Kwa town, and its rites are always held on the death of a member. Around January, when the bush is cleared for farms, and in the new yam season from September to October, Ekkpa performances are also given. By some people, this society is thought to be so powerful that it takes the place of the men’s Egbo for women. The Juju is strong enough to kill a man and can ward off sickness—especially smallpox—from the family or town.

On the occasion of the death of Adet Awaw, the members of Ekkpa ran through the town in a frenzied state, nearly naked; many brandished guns and swords, and all looked fierce and wild. The men stayed carefully out of sight, though their presence is not absolutely forbidden in daylight; however, after dark, no man must show his face. The women dance completely naked the whole night through, and should any man attempt even a glance at these mysteries, his strength will ebb away, and all his vital powers will shrivel up forever.

Men may join the cult by paying four “wires” <note>A form of copper currency used in the region.</note> and three pence worth of spirits, but they can only be regarded as outside members and have no part in the ceremonies.

While the “plays” <note>Traditional ritual performances or dances.</note> were being given in honor of Adet, the animals offered for sacrifice were divided. When this had been done, the Head of the House arose and took four small pieces of goat’s flesh and some boiled plantains. He called on the names of his principal ancestors and said:

> “Listen, my family! Here is the goat we have killed for our sister who has just died. Here is your portion.” On this, he threw the meat into the middle of the court, crying, “It is time for us to eat.”

The men and women gathered together in separate groups and sat down, and the meat was divided between them. Next, the sister of Adet Awaw stood up and gave a small quantity of spirits to everyone. Then the Head of the House poured out upon the ground what was left so that the ghosts might also drink, calling, “Here is rum for you.” After this, the people left the compound, but a wake lasting several weeks was held in the dead woman’s honor.

<margin>(</margin>
A goat is always sacrificed at funerals, and in explanation of this custom the following story is told:

### WHY A GOAT IS SACRIFICED AT EVERY FUNERAL.

One day, the ghost of a woman returned to earth. She brought a magic cloth with her, which she laid down by the side of the road near a town before entering.

A boy saw the cloth by the roadside and picked it up. He ran away, and when the ghost returned for it, behold! It was gone.

She went back into the town, crying, “Who has taken my property?” The cloth itself answered and said, “A living person took me. Here I am, tied around this boy’s waist.” The boy was terrified. He ran away and said to himself, “How is it that a cloth can talk like a human being?” He took it off and threw it over a male goat. The goat tied it around his middle. The Ghost Woman still cried out, and the cloth answered her. Then the male goat also said, “Strange! I never before saw a lifeless thing that could talk!” He ran and buried himself in the earth, but left one hoof above ground.

When the ghost passed by, this foot trembled. She chopped at it with a machete <note>A heavy knife used as a tool and weapon, referred to in the text as a "matchet."</note> and saw blood running out. Then she took hold and pulled until the goat came out with the cloth still tied around him. She cried aloud, and at her call, other ghosts came. They spat upon the goat and threw foul things upon his body because he had taken the cloth. That is the reason why male goats smell. They also said, “From today, whenever anyone dies, they may sacrifice you.” That is the reason why the native people always kill a goat at funeral ceremonies.

When a stranger dies, he is not buried in the bush, but on the road by which he entered the town, so that his spirit may easily find the path back to his own place, or at least see the way to his home, and listen and watch for the coming of friends.

Certain burial customs are illustrated by the following story:

### WHY CHIEFS ARE BURIED IN THEIR HOUSES.

Once a woman had a son. He prepared his goods to carry them to market in a far-off town. The mother said, "Do not leave me, because I am old now, and near to my death." The son answered, "I go, but will soon come back." He went to the trading place and began to sell his wares. Then he thought of his mother and looked within himself, and saw that she could only live for two more days; so he started back home. When he was only about 11 miles away, he again looked within himself, and saw, and said, "My old mother, only one day left for her!" When he reached home the woman cried, "O my son, you have come!" She looked at him with great gladness, and that same day, before the sun sank, she died.

At midnight, the townspeople chose a few of their number to go and dig a grave, but the son thought to himself, "I will bury my old mother without the knowledge of anyone." He went alone to the small inner room of his house and there dug a grave. He made the coffin with his own hands, and at midnight buried his mother alone.

Afterward, he made another coffin and placed it outside, so that all who entered the compound should see it. In the morning, he called together his "age class" and that of his mother. He feasted them, and at eight o'clock they started to carry the coffin into the bush where the grave had been dug. There they laid it down and opened it, but lo! there was nothing inside except some stones. So they buried it, full of wonder, and went away.

Now among them was one old woman. She said to herself,

Three days later, the father sent for his son and said, "Prepare to go to market once more." The boy answered, "There is an old woman named Anyin, who gave me clear orders to bury her as I buried my mother. She might die any day. How can I bury her if I am away at the market when she dies?"

The father said, "Regardless, you must go." He would listen to no further excuse. The boy thought, "There is only one way to keep my promise." He therefore went to the old woman and said, "My father wants me to go to market. Will you die today so that I may bury you before I set out?"

The woman answered, "If I had known there would be such a hurry about it, I would not have given you the order. I did this because I saw that you were a dutiful son, and I have no child to bury me."

The boy still told her that she had better die at once. She refused, but he entered the small room of her compound and dug the grave. When all was ready, he called a meeting of the townspeople. He related all that had happened between himself and Anyin, and asked what should be done.

The Head Chief stood up and said: "The woman gave a specific order. Agreements never change, except with the consent of both parties. She is old and may as well die today, so that the boy can bury her."

Anyin still refused. Therefore, the boy killed her and buried her at midnight as he had promised.

Afterward, he went to market.

# FUNERAL CEREMONIES

...buried in the bush, but from the day that the boy buried his mother in the house, the custom arose to bury all important people in their homes, except when they died of something very evil.

According to Ekoi belief, in the beginning of the world when men died, they were carried in a sort of dream to the home of Obassi Osaw. If Obassi thought it would be a good thing, he would command the dead man to wake and stand up before him. Then he would make him alive again and send him back to earth, but such men, upon their return, could never tell what had happened to them.

One day Obassi thought, “Men fear to die. They do not know that perhaps they may come to life again. I will tell them that sometimes such a thing may happen; then they will have less dread of death.” So he stood up in his house in the sky and called a frog and a duck before him. To the first he said, “Go to earth and say to the people: 'When a man dies, it is the end of all things; he shall never live again.'” To the second he said, “Go tell the people of earth that if a man dies, he may come to life again.” He led them a little way and showed them the road, saying, “Take my message. Duck, you may go to the left. Frog, stay to the right.”

Frog continued until he came to earth. He told the first people who met him the message which Obassi had sent. In the course of time, the duck also reached earth. She came to the place where they had been making palm oil and began to gobble it up. She was so eager that she forgot all about the message, and thus men never heard the good news which Obassi had sent.

That is the reason why, when a man dies, we cannot see him again; it is because Duck lost the message, and we must live according to the one which Frog brought us.

# CHAPTER XXII

## GHOSTS

<term>Ntuanto</term>, the word sometimes used for a ghost, actually refers to the soul or spirit of a person. It is in some way connected with the breath and leaves the body with the last exhale. While inside the form of a living person, it is a small thing and lives in the chest; however, once set free, it expands and thins out until it reaches the size and shape of the body it used to inhabit. It is intangible like air, though to those who have "four eyes" and can see spirits, it looks just like a person. This gift of "second sight," or <term>Eénna</term>, is not limited to human beings. Dogs have it, as does the little <term>Ise</term> <note>The Ise is a species of mongoose often mentioned in Ekoi folklore.</note>, as has been mentioned previously. They use two eyes during the day and two others at night. According to all <term>Ekoi</term>, these latter eyes can be seen when the animal is killed; they are located behind the first two, beneath the eyebrows.

The word commonly used for a ghost is <term>Akaba-Nsi</term>—meaning "One-who-cannot-come-back-to-earth." There are evil and good ghosts, but it is very rare for evil ones to be allowed to roam alone. Usually, a good spirit accompanies an evil one to prevent it from harming the living. If a person without "four eyes" meets an evil spirit alone on the path, the ghost will not step aside; it waits until the person reaches it, then stretches out an invisible hand and strikes a blow to the face. This causes lockjaw, which always leads to death.

Regarding this belief, it is quite striking that the <term>Buduma</term> people assured me that the <term>Djinns</term> of Lake Chad cause death in exactly the same way for any of their race who are unlucky enough to meet them at night. The <term>Djinn</term> strikes the person across the face with its long, thin hand, and it is well

...is known that death must come before the moon and stars have climbed to the same place in the sky the next night. The <term>Genii</term> of the great <term>Baobab</term> trees of <term>Bornu</term>, too, kill anyone against whom they have a grudge by a blow across the face.

To return to <term>Ekoi</term> beliefs. Ghosts can be kept from entering a room or compound during the night by burning spices or tobacco, by keeping lamps lit, or by wearing amulets. Some magicians can make a preparation—which ghosts dread—for washing the face and body; evil spirits will never appear to anyone protected in this way. Should a person meet a ghost without such a safeguard, they will probably fall sick and must go to the <term>Diviner</term> to find out why they were visited in this way.

The soul is the real person and can never be destroyed, while the body is something inferior and temporary, which rots away when no longer needed. The shadow cast by a living person is actually the shape of the soul within them, though compressed, for the time being, into a small space.

Sometimes the soul leaves the body and then returns. Living beings, more often women, can enter a kind of trance in which their souls fly away. While absent, they can see what is taking place in other worlds, much as some people do in dreams.

Once during my absence from <term>Oban</term>, a <term>Nimm</term> woman was thought to have died and was therefore buried with the usual rites. Some weeks afterward, her spirit is said to have appeared to one of the initiates and complained of a premature burial: “It was a great pity that my kin were in such a hurry to lay me in the grave,” the ghost is reported to have said, “for my soul had only gone away for a time, and I only died after its return, because I could no longer breathe in the earth.”

A person has two minds, a good one and a bad one, but these are only connected with the body and die with it. He has only one soul.

With regard to dreams, the <term>Ekoi</term> may be divided into two classes—those whose dreams come true, like the visions which in the *Odyssey* pass earthward through the portals of shining horn; and those whose dreams mean the opposite. Should the latter dream of a wedding, it is the sign of a

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

funeral; while dreaming of a newborn baby means a death in the house.

Everything that exists has its own soul, from trees and rocks down to weapons and the most common household goods; it is their astral forms that are visible in dreams.

Wraiths of dead friends often appear in night visions to give warnings of danger or to ask for offerings. If a man unknowingly eats food that has been laid out for ghosts, no harm will come to him; but if he does so intentionally, some misfortune is sure to happen to him. Food is always placed on graves, and though it seems to undergo no change, the spirits can feed on it by sucking out the essence and leaving only the shell of the offering.

Many beliefs held by the <term>Ekoi</term> are shared with <term>Brahmins</term> and <term>Shintoists</term>, which seems to point to the probable eastern origin of these people. After death, spirits who have lived a full life on earth, or who have no special reason for staying, are supposed to go directly to another world and only return in exceptional cases. Others, who have died a violent death or are held back by some special cause, wander about this world and trouble people until the time comes when they are set free to join those who have gone before. Such unhappy wanderers usually stay near their graves and only enter the towns between midnight and 3:00 a.m. Therefore, if anyone passes through a burial ground at this time, they will suffer no harm, because all the ghosts are away in the town.

If a wraith is called up by a <term>Diviner</term>, he is always in a great hurry and cannot be persuaded to answer many questions. He never says that he is dead; if a man with <term>"four eyes"</term> meets such a person, there is nothing to show that it is not an ordinary man whom he has met.

The reason why living men no longer visit the ghost town is given as follows:—

## WHY LIVING MEN CAN NO LONGER SEE THE ROAD TO THE GHOST TOWN.

### BY NDUM OF NSAN.

There was once a man with two wives. One day they went down to the stream to bathe and fill their water pots. While they were standing in the water, the younger one cried out. The other looked at her and saw that a child was about to be born. At once, this cruel woman picked up her pot and ran back home, leaving her poor companion alone and helpless.

The young wife still cried for help, and a witch named Ngbe Eing (Leopard-tooth) heard her and ran toward her. No sooner was the child born than the monster said to the mother, “We will cut the baby into equal shares and devour him, you and I.”

The poor woman did not know what to do, for she was too weak to defend her child, but fortunately at that moment Ise, the little gray <term>duiker</term>, ran up and said:

“It is quite right that Eing should claim half the child, only first she must go down the stream until she comes to the deep part and search for a large flat stone which lies there. This she must bring back, for it is only on such a stone that the child may be laid to be killed.”

Eing was so pleased that Ise had said she was right in her demand that she never saw the trick, but went dancing gaily downstream in full confidence that she would find the stone. The way she had to go was about three times as far as the house of the terrified woman, and no sooner was she out of sight than Ise told the mother to make all haste to her home.

When Eing came back with the stone and found that her prey had escaped, along with Ise, she was very angry. She

When a person dies, they can see the road to the ghost town, but while alive, they can find it no more.

Not only eggplants, but native tomatoes, are also thought to have come from the ghost town, as related in the following story:

### HOW THE FIRST TOMATOES CAME TO EARTH.

There once lived a man named <term>Effa</term> and his wife named <term>Akat</term>. The spirit of the dead woman went to a ghost town, which was as far from where her son lived as <term>Niaji</term> is from <term>Nkami</term>. One of the ghosts, named <term>Echi</term>, who in life had lived near them, thought that he would like to attend the ceremony for the old woman's death, so he set out to go to <term>Effa's</term> town.

# CHAPTER XXIII

## BEYOND NETIM

Three miles beyond Netim flows the Calabar River, which is the boundary between the land of the Ekoi and that of the Ojo and Uyanga tribes.

A few yards from the bank lies a great oval-shaped stone, half embedded in the ground. Behind it a Juju tree has been planted, and in front a heap of leaves is piled, similar to that near the River of Good Fortune. The stone is one of the altars of Nimm, and it is well to seek her protection before entering the water, for the river has a sinister reputation, and is here over 300 feet wide and very rapid. The Ekoi have a little song about it, which, in all except the name, is the counterpart of our:

->“River of Dart, River of Dart<-
->Every year you claim a heart.”<-

To ensure safety in crossing, leaves should be plucked and rubbed on the forehead, over the pineal gland, with the following prayer:

->“Me <gloss>May I</gloss> eyange, <gloss>be free from danger,</gloss> eyange, <gloss>from danger,</gloss> nkiji ka njimm <gloss>I go to the other side</gloss> aiya ‘ ni <gloss>in the water,</gloss><-
->kpe <gloss>may I</gloss> njum ebi <gloss>evil thing</gloss> nkaien ! <gloss>not see!”</gloss><-

The leaves are then thrown upon the heap, with this invocation:

->“Nkupba <gloss>I am coming</gloss> aiya oiyange, <gloss>across the river,</gloss> kpe nyipp <gloss>may the crocodile</gloss> aserre <gloss>lay down</gloss> echi ! <gloss>his head!”</gloss><-

At the time of the new yams no prayer is made, as everyone knows that it would be unheard; for just as the Kwa is the dwelling place of Nimm, so the Calabar is the special home of the Efumi of crocodiles and elephants, many of whom have their homes in its deep places.

# CHAPTER XXIII

## BEYOND NETIM

Three miles beyond Netim flows the Calabar River, which is the boundary between the land of the Ekoi and that of the Ojo and Uyanga tribes.

A few yards from the bank lies a large oval-shaped stone, half embedded in the ground. Behind it a Juju tree has been planted, and in front a heap of leaves is piled, similar to the one near the River of Good Fortune. The stone is one of the altars of Nimm, and it is wise to seek her protection before entering the water, for the river has a sinister reputation and is over 300 feet wide and very rapid here. The Ekoi have a little song about it which, in everything except the name, is the counterpart of our own:

->“River of Dart, River of Dart<-
->Every year you claim a heart.”<-

To ensure safety in crossing, leaves should be plucked and rubbed on the forehead, over the pineal gland, with the following prayer:

->“Me <gloss>May I</gloss> eyange, <gloss>be free from danger,</gloss> eyange, <gloss>from danger,</gloss> nkiji ka njimm <gloss>I go to the other side</gloss> aiya ‘ ni <gloss>in the water,</gloss><-
->kpe <gloss>may I</gloss> njum ebi <gloss>evil thing</gloss> nkaien ! <gloss>not see!”</gloss><-

The leaves are then thrown upon the heap with this invocation:

->“Nkupba <gloss>I am coming</gloss> aiya oiyange, <gloss>across the river,</gloss> kpe nyipp <gloss>may the crocodile</gloss> aserre <gloss>lay down</gloss> echi ! <gloss>his head!”</gloss><-

# BEYOND NETIM

->R 2<-

At one Ekoi town, a little further down, where all the inhabitants are believed to be “Efumi” of crocodiles, they give notice that for seven days during the new yam festival all traffic should be stopped; for if any man enters the water during that time, he would never reach the further bank. The Efumi are holding their great festival to the Juju “Animm” (the plural of Nimm), and anyone rash enough to enter the water, or unfortunate enough to be caught and dragged down from the bank, must be sacrificed. Nimm will hear no prayer, as she longs for offerings; in return for these, she makes the farms of her worshippers productive. At this time also, each crocodile soul leaves the body which it has inhabited during the past year and chooses another in which to live during the next twelve moons.

Early in 1911, the towns of Nsan, Obung, and Netim begged me to send a hunter to drive away the herds of wild animals which were devastating their farms. This same request had come in from so many towns, however, that it was not until late in the year that I could send my hunter to that part of the District. He seemed reluctant to go, but this might have been due to the fact that he had no friends there, so I did not give the matter further thought. The reason for his unwillingness was explained, however, when a little later, circumstances made it necessary for me to visit the neighborhood.

One morning, a boy of about fifteen ran into my office in the final stages of terror and exhaustion. According to his story, two men named Tambe and Wanchi hired him in Calabar to go with them to the interior. They did not allow him to enter towns on the way but sent him through the bush, giving the excuse that there was something in his load which they did not wish to be seen; in reality, they feared that questions might be asked upon their return without the boy. Just before reaching Ojo Nkonmba, food ran short, so they stopped at one of the towns to buy more. At Ojo, Ongwaw, the son of one of the chiefs, asked the boy what country he came from; afterward, he was taken by his masters to the house of Chief Ikum, where they arranged to sell him for £20. The next day he was left with Ikum, while Tambe and Wanchi went back to Calabar. Soon after they had left,

A cage formed of iron rods was brought out, 4 feet by 4 feet by 2 feet, the kind used only for human sacrifice to the Jujus. The Chief wanted to make the boy drink rum, but he would not do so, because one of the women cried out that they were going to kill him. Ikum himself ate and drank, then tied his hunting knife around his waist. One of his wives, named Ekungbe, called out and said, "Do not kill the boy." Ikum was very angry and struck her. The chief stood by the door. 

The boy stated, "It was nighttime, and I was on the other side of the compound with the head wife. She said to me, 'I am sorry for you, because you are a good boy. You brought firewood and helped with other work in my house. If you could get away, perhaps you might reach the "white man."' I slipped behind her and ran into the bush. People came out with lanterns to search for me, but I hid from them. I dared not follow the road for fear that men from other towns might be warned of my escape, catch me, and hand me over again to the people of Ojo. On the third day, I saw Forest-guard Okore, so I ran to him and begged him to help me get to the white man."

Under these circumstances, it was necessary to visit the town concerned, both to inquire into the story and to ensure the safety of the friendly woman.

After crossing the Calabar River, the road leads through beautiful and relatively easy country, over streams, many of which are, during the dry season, mere strings of tiny waterfalls dashing down between fern-fringed banks; however, in the rains, they swell into torrents which tear down from the mountains, sweeping away everything in their path.

Just before Ojo Nkonmba, we came upon a little river. On its banks, by the ford, grew a great clump of ground orchids, related to *Horsmanii*, but with some points of difference. The flowers, shading from the palest mauve to the deepest purple, were carried on stems 4 to 5 feet high. The whole clump stood out from its dark background with the luster of dew-drenched amethysts, and was mirrored again, narcissus-like, in the clear stream below.

<meta>This page continues the account of the Ojo people and their leader, Chief Ikum, following the visual documentation of the chief provided on the previous page.</meta>

# BEYOND NETIM

They are generally known by their Efik name—"Ojo." They belong to the same race as the people of Ekuri, whom we shall mention later on, but they separated from them many years ago. Even in a comparatively short space of time, and although a certain amount of communication has been kept up, the language has considerably altered. Like all other tribes in this neighborhood, they have gradually come down from the North.

The old chief is an object of great reverence to his people. On a former visit, when he came up to welcome us, he was wearing a gorgeous cap of scarlet cloth, cut somewhat after the Phrygian style, and decorated around the base with two double rows of leopards' claws. By old custom, he is never supposed to be seen bareheaded and is the subject of several interesting taboos.

In a country like this, where the black population outnumbers the white by about 4,000 to 1, it is a matter of absolute necessity that certain signs of respect should be shown to the ruling race. Had the chief been allowed to continue covered, it would not only have meant that white rule would have fallen into discredit in his town and for many miles around, but that he himself would have had no respect for those who did not exact this token of it from him. He was therefore told that the hat must be removed while addressing the white man, and after some little trouble, he consented. His submission had one curious result. An elderly woman, with hair once bright red but now tinged with gray, came up, positively capering with joy, which she made no effort to hide. She brought us a present of the largest yam we had ever seen and explained that she was the head wife of the chief who had just had a lesson in manners. Her evident delight at her husband's discomfiture puzzled us until we found out that he had been annoying her for years with airs and graces—invented to enhance his importance among his people—besides those taboos imposed on him by reason of his position as head priest of Akillinga, such as the rule of eating alone.

When we reached the town to inquire into the boy's story, we found it divided against itself. The townsfolk had decided to move to another site, and the women, the young men, and "members" were strongly opposed to that which the head

## IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

The men had chosen a location. The first group argued that they did not want to leave the main road to go deep into the "bush," and also that there was no good water near the new site. When I visited this site the next morning, the reason for both the people's objection and the chiefs' choice became perfectly clear. The chiefs had chosen a spot where they hoped to be visited less often by government officials or anyone likely to report their activities to the white man. It was a long distance from the main road, along a difficult path, and, as the opposition had stated, the only water nearby was a stream that dried up during the dry season. However, the new town would have been close to the place where the head chief had built his compound, which contained the shrine of the great <term>Juju</term> Akillinga.

It is no wonder that the women, the young men, and the "members" feared leaving the main road. On the main road, there was always a chance that a passerby might hear cries for help or appear in time to make the chiefs afraid to sacrifice them to the <term>Juju</term>, for fear that news of their actions would be carried to those who would demand swift vengeance.

Akillinga has a reputation, even in this land, for being a particularly cruel <term>Juju</term>. Before it, until quite recently, enemies were admittedly sacrificed and cannibalistic rites were carried out, though such practices are now energetically denied. The relief of the community members—from whom sacrificial victims would naturally be chosen—was so obvious when I ruled against the site favored by the chiefs that the reason for their objection was clear to even the most unobservant person.

The people of Ojo Nkonmba and their neighbors in Ojo Akangba, who have all now agreed to join together to form one town, believe that their souls are the <term>Efumi</term> of elephants. Their farms are untouched, and not a single uprooted palm tree was seen, even though only a few miles away in Ekuri territory, the people were complaining of starvation due to the destruction caused by vast herds of elephants.

### ADA THE FOREST DEMON.

->By NDUM OF NSAN.<-

Awsang Atikawt was a great hunter. He was so skilled that he never gave up the chase of any animal once he had started to follow its trail. One day, he was sitting with some friends when they began complaining about how their farms were being destroyed by elephants. Atikawt asked why they did not immediately follow the tracks of the beasts and kill them. They answered that they were afraid to do this, for fear that they themselves might be killed by the elephants. Atikawt called them cowards and said that he himself would not rest until he had destroyed every elephant that might dare to leave its mark upon his farm.

Now among those present were two men who were <term>Efumi</term> of elephants. One of these <term>Efumi</term> stood up and said to Atikawt, “Ka kpe awkame. Ojjokk kun oyi ebin eja awsem” (“Boast no more. Elephants may eat your farm and go free”).

But Atikawt answered steadily, “Ofu ojjokk awgae, tik oyen ngam” (“The day elephants try, they will see me”).

When they heard this, the two <term>Efumi</term> men looked sharply at one another. Then they arranged to go and destroy the farm to see what would happen.

Not long after, Atikawt’s wives brought him news that their farm had been ruined by elephants. At once he began to gather provisions, and having filled his hunting bag, he set out well-armed for the chase. He soon found the trail of the beasts and followed them until dark. All night he rested, leaning against a tree, and started again as soon as dawn broke. On and on he went until it was dark once more. Then he climbed

> "Monn-I-Mbuni" (Child of Lameness), she called to the little maid. The latter came to her slowly, pretending that she had been sleeping. In her forest language the Giantess said, pointing to her guest, "Tomorrow we shall have good meat for dinner."

> "Anaw" ("Just so"), answered the girl.

When the evening meal was ready, the monster dropped "medicine" into Atikawt's share. He, however, told her that in his country it was only lawful for a man like him to eat in the goat pen, so he was allowed to carry his food there.

When he reached the place where the goats were, he spilled the food on the ground so that the beasts might eat it. At the moment when it touched the ground, a flame sprang forth, but he sat, quietly watching, until the fire had gone out, and the goats ate everything. Then he went back to the Forest Woman, and, after a short talk together, they went to bed.

Just before he had reached the other side, however, he heard a sound like thunder from the palace. “The Forest Woman is coming,” he thought.

Once on shore, he felt quite safe. He threw the “medicine” over his shoulder without looking around, and then turned to see what would happen. Meanwhile, about midnight, the Giantess awoke. She went to the fire and drew from it the sharp-pointed iron, which was now glowing red. She forced this through the pillows that Atikawt had arranged. They immediately caught fire. Imagine if the monster was angry or not! The fire raged all around, and the man on whom she had intended to feast the next day had fled homeward!

She turned to follow in hot pursuit, but in her haste, she forgot to take the magic herbs with her which would cause the water to divide. Therefore, when she came to the torrent, she could not cross; so she stood on her side of the river and called to him on the other side:

Before this, the Giantess had put a sharply pointed iron instrument into the fire to heat. She intended to thrust this through Atikawt when he fell asleep. After a while, she began to snore like a tornado, just as the little lame girl had said. He lay very quiet, and in a short time, the snores grew so loud that the whole palace trembled.

Then the hunter crept out, took some pillows, and put them in the place where he had been lying. Next, he drew a cover over them, and when everything was arranged smoothly, he went in search of his little lame friend, who gave him the promised "medicines."

When the first drops squeezed from the magic herb fell upon the gate, it flew open before him; and upon crushing the leaves so that their juice fell into the river, this also held back the flow of its waters and allowed him to cross. Just before he had reached the other side, however, he heard a sound like thunder from the palace. "The Forest Woman is coming," he thought.

Once on shore, he felt quite safe. He threw the "medicine" over his shoulder without looking back, and then turned to see what would happen. Immediately the river began to rise, and soon the whole pass was blocked by the swirling water, so that Atikawt could go on his way without fear of pursuit.

Meanwhile, about midnight, the Giantess awoke. She went to the fire and drew from it the sharp-pointed iron, which was now glowing red. She thrust this through the pillows that Atikawt had arranged. They immediately caught fire. Imagine whether the monster was angry or not! The fire raged all around, and the man she had intended to feast on the next day had fled homeward!

She turned to follow in hot pursuit, but in her haste, she forgot to take the magic herbs with her which...

Filled with fury at this, the Giantess went back to her palace, but Atikawt went on his way and was received with the utmost joy.

A few days later, a beautiful woman was seen coming toward the town. On her head, she carried a calabash full of food (“chop”), and her robes were richer than any others there. She stopped to ask which was the house of Atikawt and was at once led toward it. When the hunter came forward to welcome his guest and ask what she desired of him, she said that she came from a neighboring town through which he had passed some time ago. She had seen him and immediately fallen in love, but, though she had asked everyone about his name and where he lived, it was only that very day that she had finally found out. Awsang Atikawt listened to her flattering words and never doubted that everything was as she said.

Now, one of Atikawt's wives was a witch, and by her magic, she discovered that the visitor was none other than Ada Etim Agbo Etum (Ada the Forest Ruler). So she called to her husband and warned him, saying as plainly as possible that the beautiful stranger was the very monster from whom he had lately escaped—the fiend-woman with the drums, bugles, guns, and all manner of terrors in her belly.

Atikawt only laughed and said that if his wife could see the Giantess, she would know at once how different the monster was from their visitor.

When evening came, the witch-wife went to him again and begged that now, at least, he would send the stranger away, for indeed she was the very monster whose cruel deeds he had been so ready to talk about a few days before. He, however, instead of consenting, only laughed all the more and told his wife that she was far too jealous.

At night, when he was going to rest by the side of the beautiful stranger, his wife again called him aside and begged even more earnestly that at least he would not sleep with their guest, lest she should kill him; for she was indeed none other than the forest woman Ada Etim Agbo Etum. When he remained stubborn, the woman saw that warnings were useless, but she determined to do what she could to save him, for she was

Atikawt awoke at once, and Ada, full of vexation, struck her belly once more, whereupon the red-hot iron sprang back inside and was hidden. She then pretended that she also had been disturbed by the dogs and said that she could not sleep if they stayed in the room. He therefore got up, took a stick, and soundly beat the poor dogs who had saved his life. Afterward, he chained them up on the veranda and went back to his guest once more.

As soon as he had entered and closed the door, the witch-wife crept out of her room, unchained the dogs, and whispered to them to stay as wide awake as before.

When Ada saw the hunter sleeping once more, she got up again and hit her belly, whereupon the red-hot iron reappeared. The dogs sprang in through the window and attacked her, barking as loudly as before, so that Atikawt was awakened again. Just at that moment, the cock crowed.

Ada sprang up at the sound and told Atikawt that she must set out for home at once. She begged him to chain up his dogs and lead her on her way himself.

On the way, the stranger told Atikawt to walk in front of her, but he refused her request and said that he would rather she go before him. This was the first and quite necessary opposition Atikawt offered to his guest. His refusal, however, warned her that he might be growing aware of her true nature. She waited for her chance and often turned around to look at him, but she could do nothing since she was in front of him, and he could see everything she tried to do.

In a short time, she hit upon a plan by which she thought she could rid herself of him for a while. Near the road grew a tree, which was covered by a climbing plant. On this hung ripe fruits of a kind called <term>Nsebbe</term> by the Ekoi, though the Efik people call it <term>Eting Keni</term>. She asked the hunter to climb this tree and gather fruits for her. No sooner had he obeyed than, by her magic, she caused it to grow until it was taller than any tree in the whole world. Then, when she saw that Atikawt was safely held so far above her that he could not get back to prevent anything she might do, she struck her belly once more. About twenty men sprang out fully armed. They surrounded the tree and called up tauntingly to the hunter, “Now fly.” Ada also began to boast and to speak like this:

> “ ‘We oyen, okkpe oyen se oyen njum ebi.
> If you look, (and) again look, you can say you see a bad thing.”

When Atikawt heard this, he thought of all his wife’s warnings and burst into tears. Also, he understood the true reason why his dogs had barked in the night. From the top of the tree where he clung, he could see his native town. He thought of the dogs whom he had chained up and began to call for them, weeping for his own folly.

Ada meanwhile ordered her men to cut down the tree with the axes which they carried. They began to do this, and while the blows fell, a parrot flew by. He saw what had happened and bore news of the wretched plight of its master to Atikawt’s house. He told them to loose the dogs at once, or the one who had gone forth that morning would never come home. The keys could not be found, and the other people

The people at home would have given up in despair, but the witch wife saw through her vision that the tree was near falling, and that only if the dogs were set free at once could they reach their master in time. These had not gone halfway, however, before the tree fell; but, happily for Atikawt, it was caught by another tree, and so could not fall to the ground. Then Ada gave orders that the second tree should be cut through, so that Atikawt might at length fall into her power.

At the moment when this tree also came crashing down, the dogs reached the spot. Now one of them was called Oro Njaw. He was the fiercest of them all, and at once lunged at the Forest Woman, while the others attacked her men and put them to flight. Many of these were killed, but some escaped. Ada herself was torn to pieces.

Thus ends the story of Awsang Atikawt, the famous hunter, and Ada Etim Agbo Etum, the terrible Forest Woman, who had within her belly all the music of all the world, and also all weapons which have ever been made.

So we see that the plot made by the two Efumi of elephants to destroy this hunter's farm brought about a great advantage to us: namely, the death of Ada Etim Agbo Etum, the Forest Woman. Atikawt must indeed have been a famous hunter to have freed the bush from such a cruel monster!
