# CHAPTER XXIV

## UYANGA AND EKURI

To the north of the Ojo people live a small tribe called the Uyanga, who have settled at Ifunkpa, Owai Ifunkpa, and the three Iko towns. They are renowned all over this part of the country for their knowledge of medicine and magic. According to an article written by the Rev. J. K. MacGregor, in the *Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute*, June 1909, they are supposed to have learned the greater part of their magic lore, and also their knowledge of Nsibidi—the secret primitive writing already mentioned—from monkeys who came and sat around their campfires. Unfortunately, it has not been possible to find a trace of this interesting legend among the people themselves. Perhaps it is permissible to mention here that the Ekoi claim to have originated this script, of which several hundred characters and a considerable number of complete stories were collected during our stay.<note>See Nsibidi, Chapter XXVIII.</note>

Up to fifty years ago, the whole Uyanga tribe lived together by the River Tegott, north of Owai Ifunkpa, but separated about that time and founded the different towns in which they now dwell. Early in 1909, the tribe was in a state of great excitement. They had heard that a force was marching against them to arrest the persons concerned in the maltreatment of a Court Messenger. A Native Court Clerk had sent in a highly picturesque account of their habits. Among other pleasing details, he wrote that the houses were all “occupied with skulls.” <margin>//</margin> Up to this time, the people had been dwelling on more or less debatable land, as the country was not yet mapped, so it was not certain to which District they belonged.

The people had a sinister reputation, but when Owai Ifunkpa was reached, white rags were seen fluttering from bamboo poles to serve as flags of truce. The Juju trees and stones had been freshly smeared with blood, or in some cases red and yellow paint, in order to appease the spirits and ensure protection from any danger that their white visitors might be bringing to them.

Iko Akperem is only about eight miles from Owai Ifunkpa. No white man had traveled through this part of the country before, and Juju offerings were to be seen everywhere in the bush—overhead, underfoot, and at each side of the road. Here, as at all non-Ekoi towns in the District, the people were away at their bush farms. They only come into the towns during the rainy season or on special occasions, for, unlike the Ekoi, they have not yet reached the sociable "town" stage. The difference is very clearly marked in their manners, which are not nearly as polite or friendly as those of the Ekoi. Some of the Iko chiefs were in the town, but from their behavior, it was evident that their feelings were far from friendly. This was fully explained when we heard, on our return, that not many miles away, vigorous hostilities were taking place between two tribes, one of which was allied to the people of Iko. A Government force was at the moment employed in restoring order, which was attended with considerable difficulty, as the warring tribes had provided themselves with rifle pits and similar "luxuries."

About twenty miles from Owai Ifunkpa lies Ekuri Owai. The road leads through difficult, hilly country and is crossed by innumerable streams and rivers. It is in this part of the district that the rare and beautiful tree, the *Baikiea Insignis*, is to be found, with its creamy white petals over half a foot long and velvety buds of dark golden brown.

On first visiting the place, nothing but a bush track was to be found, and men with machetes had to go on ahead to clear a path for the carriers, who could not march at a rate of more than a mile an hour. The inhabitants are called Ekuri by the Efik and Ekoi, but "Nkokolle" is the name they give themselves.

They gave as a reason that it was impossible for them to live in their current town because of the destruction caused by elephants in outlying farms, which the villagers were not numerous enough to protect. They described the bush around them as full of elephants, but, although I had come across a herd on a previous visit, the statement on this occasion seemed so exaggerated that I thought it possible the chiefs were letting their imaginations run wild, in the hope that, by doing so, a few extra kegs of gunpowder might be obtained.

However, these statements were completely confirmed during the march the next day. We had barely left the outlying farms behind us before we saw the traces of great herds of elephants, and we had traveled only a few miles when a delighted exclamation broke from one of my companions. “Oh,” she cried, “we have nearly reached camp! I can hear them cutting and hammering.”

At almost the same moment the chair-carrier, who was a little ahead, came rushing back, his face a picture of terror.

There was only time to ask my companions to take cover behind some big trees and grab my rifle. The sounds came nearer, and a great herd of dark forms could be seen crashing through the bush in our direction. A few loud blows on one of the tree trunks by the path were enough to turn them, however, and they headed away from us. They had hardly disappeared when something must have startled them from another direction—possibly the voices of carriers descending the hill to the rear. Anyway, they turned again, and this time seemed to be making a blind rush down upon us. A shot from my .470 <note>A .470 Nitro Express, a large-caliber rifle used for hunting big game.</note> turned them once more, and they made off determinedly through the bush to our right.

One huge bull was hit in the forehead and left a great trail of blood, which was easy enough to follow. About an hour’s stalking led past a mud bath, which they had made for themselves, to a little clearing, where the wounded bull was found in the company of four others, all fully grown and with splendid tusks. They described the bush around them as being full of elephants; but, although I had come across a herd on a previous visit, the claim on this occasion seemed so exaggerated that I thought it possible the chiefs were letting their imaginations run wild, in the hope that, by doing so, they might obtain a few extra kegs of gunpowder.

However, these statements were completely confirmed during the march the next day. We had barely left the outlying farms behind us before we saw the traces of great herds of elephants, and we had traveled only a few miles when a delighted exclamation broke from one of my companions. “Oh,” she cried, “we have nearly reached camp! I can hear them cutting and hammering.”

At almost the same moment the chair-carrier, who was a little ahead, came rushing back, his face a picture of terror.

There was only time to ask my companions to take cover behind some big trees and grab my rifle. The sounds came nearer, and a great herd of dark forms could be seen crashing through the bush in our direction. A few loud blows on one of the tree trunks by the path were enough to turn them, however, and they headed away from us. They had hardly disappeared when something must have startled them from another direction—possibly the voices of carriers descending the hill to the rear. Anyway, they turned again, and this time seemed to be making a blind rush down upon us. A shot from my .470 <note>A .470 Nitro Express, a large-caliber rifle used for big game hunting.</note>

That night there was great rejoicing. Fires were lit to keep off unwelcome visitors, while, with the same object, lamps were hung from poles outside the tents.

A beautiful spot had been chosen for the camp, within the loop of a river, which encircled it on three sides. During the night, several times, strange boomings and trumpetings were heard, and next morning, not 100 yards from the farther bank, great five-toed indentations, only a few hours old, were found, to prove how near to us the herd had passed. I followed them up, and for hours they kept tantalizingly just ahead, but time did not allow for tracking them down. No matter how often one has been out after elephants, it still remains a somewhat curious experience to follow, hour after hour, in the footsteps of these strange survivals from another world. The very irresistibility of their onward march, crushing down, by sheer weight, all but the very greatest of obstacles, appeals curiously to the imagination. As if in contempt of danger, or indeed as a kind of challenge thrown down to possible pursuers, they leave records, often strangely intimate, of themselves and their doings, for him who cares to read. One huge bull had stayed to sharpen his tusks upon a tree, which was scored again and again at least 14 feet from the ground. Countless palm trees were uprooted to enjoy the soft “cabbage,” while in places regular slides had been made in the clay banks down which the great beasts might glide, as on an inclined plane, to gambol in the baths below.

On one occasion, an old war dance was performed in our honor. Today, thankfully, only skin-covered wooden masks are used instead of the freshly severed heads of enemies formerly carried by the victors.

# CHAPTER XXV
## CONDITIONS OF LIFE IN PEACE AND WAR

<insert>Pencil bracket in left margin</insert>By ancient custom, land can never be sold, but belongs to the heirs of the first settler, even if it has been abandoned for hundreds of years. It is doubtful whether any part of the Ekoi country remains unowned at present, though there are great spaces—for instance, the Game and Forest Reserve, nearly 400 square miles in size—which have been uninhabited for many years. A town, therefore, that wishes to move to a fresh site must purchase the right of settlement, not ownership, from another. This is usually a matter of little difficulty, and the founding of Oban town on its present site, some fifty years ago, may be taken as typical.

The land belonged to the Ojuk people, who charged the newcomers:
One machete, 1 sheep, 1 piece of iron, 1 hoe, and 7 iron hooks for the right to settle.
Forty pieces of dried meat for the hunting rights.
Fifteen baskets of fish for water rights; while, for forestry rights, 1 goat, 5 pieces of dried meat, and 500 pieces of ebony were required.
In addition, 3 pots of palm oil, 500 yams, 500 sleeping mats, and 10 bundles of corn were demanded in final settlement.

<insert>Pencil bracket in left margin</insert>On starting a new town, a meeting is called, and after the site for the <term>Egbo house</term> has been agreed upon, each family is assigned its share of the new bush. As a rule, the first newcomer to explore a particular part has the primary claim to it. The bush beyond the immediate vicinity is considered to belong to the men who found it.

As already mentioned, the first ceremony of all is the choosing of the new site for the <term>Egbo house</term>. On this, a little hut is erected, called "<term>Ekpa Ntan</term>" (the house without walls), and

Here, too, as in old Rome, the head of each house is the priest of its particular <term>Lares and Penates</term> <note>Household gods of Roman tradition.</note>, though each <term>Juju</term> has in addition a head priest for the whole town.

One of these would be that of the husband, and each of the others would belong to one of his wives with her family, or to a married son. At night, the animals were always driven into the central compound—as they still are in most towns—to ensure safety from leopards and other wild beasts. Should an enemy break into a compound, he would find it no easy matter to capture or kill the occupants, for the number of small secret chambers crammed into an Ekoi house is hardly believable.

As soon as the private dwellings are finished, the inhabitants begin building an Egbo house, nearly always according to the plan given on the previous page.

This style of architecture is exceptionally well adapted to the conditions of the country. The open front and many loopholes, sheltered by overhanging eaves, provide the maximum amount of air with the minimum amount of glare—while complete protection is provided against tornadoes.

Perhaps the most important part of the whole structure is the <term>Etai Ngbe</term>, the long, cut stone usually found standing before the second pillar. When this stone is first erected in a new town, every chief must bring food in a <term>calabash</term> <note>A container made from the dried shell of a gourd.</note> and palm wine in an earthenware pot. A portion is offered in sacrifice, and the rest is eaten.

<image-desc>A line drawing of a "Typical Pillar in Egbo House". The stone is often transformed by crude painting into the rough appearance of a human being. A cap is made to fit the upper end, and iron in some form is always present, either in bars twisted around the stone or laid beneath it.

Women plaster the walls with mud, which they decorate after smoothing, but afterward they are never allowed to enter, except for cleaning purposes.

A village is usually composed of two rows of houses bordering the main road, which opens out into a broad space where dances are held in front of the Egbo house. The road then divides into two semi-circular arms which surround the latter and join together again behind it. Sometimes several streets run parallel to the main one.

To a certain extent, the Ekoi may be described as an industrious people; with the exception of some restless individuals, both sexes have now become keen traders, though the greater share of this occupation naturally falls to the men. They have almost secured a monopoly of trade with the South-Western Cameroons, where they find a ready market for the salt, tobacco, cloth, and hardware from Calabar, which they themselves have purchased in exchange for chickens, dried meat, sleeping mats, rubber, and palm kernels. ...the last four years. To take mats alone—where about fifty were sent daily in 1907, over 500 are carried now.

In another direction, commerce is also greatly increasing, as the Hausas have begun to come directly down from Northern Nigeria. If the railway from Calabar to Ibi on the Benue—and from there through Bornu to Lake Chad—is ever built, it could hardly fail to become one of Africa's greatest trade arteries, given such a harbor as its base and such a vast country to open up. There is little doubt that such a line would attract all the trade of the Central Sudan, and I have received assurances from French sources that the project would be warmly welcomed.

It is rather curious that among a people with such a well-developed instinct for trade, there are no market squares across the entire land. These are, however, constantly mentioned in folklore, which shows that before dividing into small forest communities, the Ekoi were used to such institutions. I have twice established markets at Oban. These were opened with solemn ritual and seemed to promise great success for a week or two. Gradually, however, the inhabitants of other towns stopped bringing their farm produce, as elephant raids left them with barely enough for their own needs; meanwhile, the three traders established at Oban met the demand for European goods.

Naturally, there are some unruly members of the community who refuse to take up any money-earning work and regret the old way of life, when town and tribal wars offered a faster way for the strong to enrich themselves than is possible today. Descriptions can be found in folklore—often quite simple—of the lawless state indicated by the <term>Nsibidi</term> sign shown in the right-hand corner of the Nsibidi story No. 9, Appendix G. This sign represents the condition of the country before the arrival of "white" rule: "When there was no justice if a man hit you on the head." The following story is typical:

## WHY NTABE NO LONGER WENT TO WAR.

There once lived a man named Ntabe, who went about with his gun and—unlike the hero of Aristophanes' "The Acharnians"—made war only for himself. He had a wife named Asim Eji. One day, she went to visit a female friend who gave her the meat of a newly roasted duiker to eat and asked, "Where is your husband?" "He is always at war," said Asim Eji. "It is his only business. He never brings me meat from the bush like the husbands of other women do."

When the unhappy wife reached home, she thought to herself, "What can I do? I must try to stop my husband from such an occupation." She therefore cooked fufu and placed it in a calabash. In the middle she set a human skull, but she piled the fufu high so that nothing else could be seen. Then she cooked soup and poured it over everything.

When the husband came in from his fighting, he asked, "Where is my food?" She answered, "Before I bring it, call all the townspeople to come and dine with you, for I have prepared a great feast."

When the neighbors were gathered together, the woman set the table before them and placed the food upon it. Next, she put a knife into her husband's hand and said, "Will you cut the fufu?"

The man took the knife and tried to divide the food, but no matter which way he turned the blade, he found it struck against something hard. So he dug down and discovered what lay beneath.

The people all wondered and said to the woman, "Why did you do such a thing?" She answered, "I married him when I was a very young girl, and since our marriage he has never hunted for me as other women's husbands do; instead, his only business is to kill men."

On hearing this, Ntabe got up and said, "I am not angry with what you have done today." He stood before the table and called to the townspeople, "What my wife, Asim Eji, has done is simply to advise me to give up the killing of men and take up another occupation, just as the rest of the townspeople do."

Then he went into a small inner room and took down a large

calabash from the wall. In this, he laid ten parcels of salt and spread two pieces of native cloth over everything. This he brought and set down before Asim Eji, and said to all the people, "Here is a present for my wife. Will you kindly plead with her for me? I promise that I will war no more from this day forward."

Then the woman also stood forward and said, "Should my husband not take to some other way of life, according to this promise, I will divorce him and marry another man." To Ntabe she said, "Will you promise solemnly in the presence of all these people?"

He answered, "How can I promise more than I have already?"

She said, "Unless you get two kola nuts and bite a piece from one and give it to me to eat, and also take from me a piece which I have bitten off from the other, I will not believe you. Also, you must take some of my blood and some of yours, so that we may mix it together. Then I will believe that you will give up, and never war any more. Otherwise, I will never believe you."

This the man did, and from that day he warred no more, but kept the faith which he had sworn on the kola nut.

The division of work between the sexes has been clearly laid down from time immemorial, and neither would dream of encroaching on that of the other. Indeed, there would seem to be something indelicate and even impious in the mere thought of such a thing.

The chief occupations are hunting for men and farm work for the women, but it is the task of the men to cut the bush in December and January for the new farms. This should be begun at the time of the new moon. The big trees, especially the cotton trees, are left standing, but all undergrowth is cleared away. The men help the women to plant yams and plantains, but coco-yams and corn are planted later by women alone. All weeding is done by the women, with the help of their "members." <note>This likely refers to members of their family or cooperative work groups.</note>

The yams may be harvested in October, but, as has already been mentioned, are not eaten in towns where the rites of Eja or Mfuor are practiced until these have been performed. They can be stored for a whole year in racks built on the farms for the purpose.

Coco-yams ripen in September and can be kept in heaps for nearly a year. They are considered women’s food. Corn ripens in July and can be kept until January, though it is usually eaten at once. Farms are left to lie fallow after one crop, except for plantain farms, which can be used for two years.

It is interesting to note that Sir Walter Egerton pointed out in a recent speech that, despite all our science, the Forestry Officers have as yet discovered no better way of farming the land.

Fishing is also looked on as almost exclusively women’s work. For this purpose, they generally use one of the many varieties of vegetable poison. They throw this into the water. The fish rise stupefied and float on the surface, becoming easy prey.

Each woman is expected to give her husband one big fish from her haul, generally the “Monn Aiya” (Child of the Big Water), and some to her father and mother. Before starting, she usually rubs “lucky” leaves over her hand-net.

Except during June and July, when fish is in high demand to eat with the new corn, most fishing is carried on during the dry season, which the Ekoi consider to begin from the flowering of the grass *Setaria Mauritana* (Sprengel), usually about October. This lasts until June, when the heavy rains begin.

The division of work is strictly maintained in building a house. The husband cuts down the necessary timber, and, with the help of his male friends, fixes all the posts into the earth and binds them with wattle. This forms the framework of the compound. The men also make the roof, usually by crossing the stems of large palm leaves over each other. They also make and fix the palm-leaf mats in place, which form a kind of thatch. There should be four thicknesses of these in a properly made roof.

It is the business of the women to spread mud over the walls and floors. They smooth these with wooden tools made for the purpose and leave them to be baked hard by the heat of the sun. When dry, the cracks are filled in, and the whole surface is smoothed over once more.

Men do all the fine plaited-work bags of colored palm fiber, while the women make the coarser mats of plaited reed for the floor and sleeping mats of screw-pine, dyed and worked in various colors.

# LIFE IN PEACE AND WAR

As has been mentioned, before the arrival of "white" rule, fighting was one of the primary occupations of Ekoi men. The flintlock gun, currently in use, replaced the spear, club, and crossbow; the latter is still used to shoot birds and serves as a child's toy. As flintlocks increased in number, the old shields of woven palm strips were abandoned, though many men still alive today have carried them into battle.

<image-desc>A line drawing of an Ekoi shield and an arrow. The shield is rectangular with rounded corners, made of a woven material that appears to be plaited palm strips. An arrow with a barbed tip and feathered fletching is depicted diagonally behind the shield.</image-desc>

->Ekoi Shield of Split Palm Stem.<-

Before setting out to attack an enemy, solemn sacrifices were made to the local war Juju. In Oban, this was Oke Ewara. Every warrior drank from a vessel of "sacred" water and poured some over his body. Strips of palm leaf were tied around the neck of each man.

Small groups were then organized to set out for the farms and watering holes of the enemy to lie in wait there.

A slave who fell into such an ambush would either be shot on sight or kept as a sacrifice to the war Juju of his captors, while a free-born man would probably be spared for the sake of ransom. Old women were sometimes killed, but young women and children were carried off as slaves.

Sometimes all the warriors of a town, with the exception of a small group left as guards, would set out in the nighttime and surround the enemy’s village. Everyone who left the

<summary>This page describes the shift in Ekoi weaponry from spears and crossbows to flintlock guns and details the ritual preparations and ambush tactics used in tribal warfare.</summary>
<keywords>Ekoi, warfare, flintlock, Juju, Oban, Oke Ewara, sacrifices, military tactics, slavery</keywords>

--- Page 372 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of Ekoi warfare, shifting from ambush tactics and the capture of prisoners to the triumphal rituals, the preservation of trophies, and the process of negotiating peace.</meta>

houses would be seized or killed, but apparently towns were never rushed, nor were compounds broken into.

The victorious party carried off the heads of all slain enemies in triumph to their town, where they laid the trophies before the Egbo house or the war Juju.

The “Egyuk” drum was beaten, and a great dance, in which only warriors could take part, was held to celebrate the return of the victors. Each danced with his gun and machete, or in older times, with a shield, spears, and crossbow. The same dance is now performed after the killing of an elephant. The chiefs and elders distributed the Nkundak’s (Greater Plantain-eater) feathers. To those who had killed an enemy, a long tail feather was given; to the rest, only the smaller wing feathers.

The heads were first smoked, then plastered thickly with mud and dried again. In this state, they could be kept for many years. A large number still exist and are used for Juju purposes. Some of these, strangely pitiful in expression, as if still suffering behind their masks of clay, can be seen raised on little altars in towns of the interior. By some strange mental process, the spirit of the slain foe, represented by the head, has become the guardian of the slayers’ hearths and homes, just as the slain leopard was invoked to aid the hunter (p. 142).

After a war dance, the oldest man and woman present took palm oil, plantains, and dried Nsun meat and offered them at the edge of the town to their own ancestors, praying that they would not allow the ghosts of the dead enemies to enter the town to do harm. They also made a sacrifice to <term>Obassi Osaw</term>, and, at the same time, poured a libation of palm wine on the ground. Then they took gunpowder in the palms of their hands and scattered it in the air, so that the eyes of the ghosts, and those of their living enemies, might be filled with dust and thus blinded.

Any slave caught alive would then be taken to the altar, his throat cut, and the blood poured over the Juju. The body would be thrown away, but the head was kept by the Juju and mummified as described above.

If either side wanted peace, a man from a neutral town, or one belonging by birth to both, would be sent, holding a palm leaf in his hand. Negotiations then took place, and terms were settled.

### WHY NKUNDAKS FEATHERS MAY ONLY BE WORN BY A WARRIOR WHO HAS SLAIN A FOE.

->By NDUM OF NSAN.<-

Ekandem Obassi was the daughter of Obassi Nsi. She was as beautiful as the sun, and when the time came for her to enter the <term>fatting-house</term>, all the richest and noblest young men in the land asked for her hand in marriage. She said that since no one was her equal in beauty, she would not marry any of her suitors; therefore, her father no longer troubled her by asking her to look favorably upon them.

Soon, however, the princess grew tired of living without suitors, so she sent out her maid—a girl three years younger than herself—to the marketplace with orders to try to find her a husband.

For two days the girl searched, but she returned each evening and said that she had failed to find anyone worthy to be her mistress’s husband. Ekandem was sorry but asked her to try a third time. To this the maid agreed, for although she was a servant, she was also a faithful friend.

On the third morning, soon after arriving at the marketplace, she saw a handsome young man coming toward her. He was so handsome that everyone forgot their wares and sought neither to buy nor sell, but only gazed at him. Except for Princess Ekandem Obassi herself, no one had ever been seen who could compare with him in beauty or attractiveness.

The little maid ran at once to her mistress and told her that she had finally seen exactly the kind of suitor she had been waiting for.

Ekandem ordered her to go back to the market at once and stand where the man was sure to pass; then, when he drew near, she was to tell him that her mistress was calling for him and bring him back with her immediately.

The girl did this and led the willing youth to the <term>fatting-room</term>. What a merry party they were! The meat of a duckling was made into a stew for them to eat with <term>fu-fu</term>. For

They went on and on, and one after another, the hands, feet, and other limbs departed from <term>Ita 'Ne Echi</term> and went back to those from whom he had borrowed them in order to become such a captivating beauty. <term>Ekandem</term> noticed the strange sight and began to wish to go back. Then, alas! she discovered the truth of his words, for a skull is indeed not worth looking at, much less living with.

Poor Ekandem! What could she do? When she tried to turn back, she found that the road closed up and was dark behind her, though in front it was still bright and clear. So, against her will, she had to continue. It was terrifying to see, instead of her beloved, a skull bouncing and rolling by her side.

When they arrived at Mfam Ane Achi, both she and the little maid were terrified by the way they were greeted. From every corner of the town, skulls rolled out. They bounced up into the air and then fell back onto the ground with a terrible crash. Some knocked against others so hard that it seemed to the onlookers as though they must break. In the whole town, there was not a single inhabitant except for these bouncing skulls. It was indeed a terrifying sight!

It seemed even worse to the two girls when the skulls began to thank Ita 'Ne Echi for bringing them such a feast of fresh meat! Poor Ekandem and her maid stood trembling for fear that they might be killed and eaten on the spot, while all the skulls shouted through the spaces where their noses should be, some calling out one thing and some another.

Suddenly, one of the skulls asked the rest to stop making such a noise. He said that the girls were far too beautiful to be killed and eaten, but should instead be given in marriage to Abia-Nkpaw, the king of the skull-people. To this, they all agreed and thanked him for having such a good idea.

Now, Abia-Nkpaw is a giant. His bed is 70 feet long and his house is 120 feet high. Terrible as he was, however, Ekandem preferred him to Ita 'Ne Echi; she was therefore willing and even glad to become his wife, and she went to his house.

That night she sang as follows:

> "Obassi, obod owo onnaw isŏng,
> Ekandem Obassi, angwan Abia-Nkpaw.
> Obassi, obod owo onnaw isŏng."*
> "Obassi, when he created a person, gave him land,
> Ekandem Obassi is now the wife of Abia-Nkpaw.
> Obassi, when he created a person, gave him land."

This song seemed to excite the skulls. It gave them a tune to chatter about, and they started to dance. When dancing, a skull will often leap to a distance of a mile and back again. Isn't this curious?

When Ekandem's parents returned from their farm in the evening, they could find neither their daughter nor her maid. Therefore, they immediately began to search for them and promised great rewards to anyone who could provide information about their whereabouts. However, it was all in vain.

As the wife of King Abia-Nkpaw, Ekandem was now less afraid; she was allowed to go wherever she pleased in the town, because the skulls were quite sure that she could not find her way home.

One day, she went with her little maid to fetch some water from the spring. As she drew near, she heard a bird called Nkundak—whom she knew well to be a friend of her father's—crying, "Kawkaw kawkawk kru kru kru kru kru kru kru." She called out, "Nkundak, Nkundak, where are you?"

"Who is it that calls?" asked the bird. "I am Ekandem Obassi, the daughter of your friend Obassi Nsi," she answered eagerly.

The bird darted down, spread his wings over the two girls, and told them each to grab a wing and hold on tightly.

It flew off with them to its own house, where it left them and went to tell the good news to Obassi Nsi.

Obassi was completely overcome with joy when he found his two lost children in Nkundak's house. He thanked the bird again and again and told him to choose anything he liked from the whole world, and it would be his as a reward for what he had done.

Nkundak begged that he should be given a splendor of plumage beyond that of all other birds.

So Obassi painted his tail feathers with a bar of black on pale yellow. He dyed the breast and wings a glorious blue and placed a beautiful crest on his head. He also gave him a very strong voice, which might cause his enemies to fear when they heard it: "Kawkawk Kawkawk kru kru."

The monotony of life in the bush is described by most white men as being among its greatest drawbacks. Curiously enough, it seemed to us to be almost overcrowded with incident. At the most unexpected times and places, the silence would suddenly be broken by a cry for help, or a few steps would lead us straight from the drowsy peace of the forest into the heart of a tragedy.

Once, for instance, we reached a town just as the Juju image was busy "smelling out" <note>A ritual practice to identify a person suspected of witchcraft</note> a case of "witchcraft," and, in defiance of all proper etiquette, we attended the ceremony. Had the proceedings been forbidden, they would only have been delayed until our departure; and, besides an inherent interest in such matters, it was possible, by staying alert, to ensure that no ill effects resulted. Not long after the supposed "magic" was unearthed, the unmistakable sounds of a commotion brought us hurrying to the scene. We found a wretched woman struggling in the grasp of her husband, who, eager to show his zeal, was forcing her down on the ground—which was extremely rocky just there—before the accusing "image."

At the sight of us, she wrenched herself free and, throwing herself through the crowd, lay clutching my boots, every muscle twitching with terror. The onlookers drew back, their expressions of hatred changing to shamefaced submission, but none would approach the suspected witch. At last, one woman plucked up courage, and, kneeling down, folded the poor woman in her arms and tried to soothe the sobs that were tearing her. It was the usual story. Several well-known men had died in the town, and the woman accused of bewitching them—a childless wife who had come from a foreign land with no relatives except one sister—was chosen as the most suitable victim. Both women followed us through the long trek and are now happily settled under the white man's supervision.

# CHAPTER XXVI
# LIFE IN PEACE AND WAR—continued

### MEDICAL

According to Ekoi beliefs, illness is usually sent by ancestors as a reminder that offerings have been neglected, by some offended <term>Juju</term>, or by the malice of a witch or wizard. Therefore, when a man or woman falls sick, they go to the <term>Diviner</term> to discover the cause of the affliction, except in the case of a few illnesses, such as a cough or dysentery, which are recognized as being due to natural causes. For these, native doctors are consulted. These doctors possess considerable knowledge regarding the curative properties of barks, leaves, and roots, which are often gathered—just as they were by the <term>Leeches</term> <note>Physicians or medical practitioners</note> of the Middle Ages—at the time of the new moon. That celestial body, now as then, is supposed to have great influence on disease. A sick man’s malady increases as the moon waxes and lessens as she wanes, while a madman has been observed to grow more violent after she has passed her first quarter. Snake fat also holds an important place in the Ekoi <term>pharmacopoeia</term>.

Most Jujus are supposed to inflict a specific disease. For instance, <term>Mfam</term> and <term>Onnuri</term> cause dropsy <note>Edema; swelling caused by excess fluid</note>.

<term>Ebangi</term>—a split palm leaf set up as a protection against farm thieves—causes pleurisy or pneumonia.

<term>Emenn</term>, a large pod used for the same purpose as the last, produces sciatica or lumbago.

<term>Etokk</term>, a large round fruit, causes rheumatism and a pain in the ankle.

A simple sort of surgery is practiced. For instance, a man gored in the abdomen by an elephant replaced his own bowels, which had been partially torn out; he inserted a small calabash to keep them in place, then drew the skin over everything and sewed it

The most common diseases are malaria, dysentery, yaws, craw-craw, pneumonia, consumption, elephantiasis, and beri-beri. Leprosy is rare, and to explain its origin, the following story is told:

### HOW LEPROSY CAME.

There was once a man of Nsan named Nsonn Agbe, who was a great wizard. All the people feared him for miles around, for it was well known that he had the power to kill men by his magic arts. One day the townsfolk gathered together and said, “What can we do to rid ourselves of Nsonn?” The wizard heard this and was very angry. He killed a man, drained his blood into a great calabash, and then went among all the people, sprinkling the blood to the right and left. Wherever a drop fell, whether on man or woman, a leprous spot appeared. That was the first time that leprosy was seen in our country.

In the old days, a man could force a woman to marry him as payment for having nursed her through an illness, but this was forbidden many years ago. Doctors’ fees, for cases requiring long attendance, were also fixed, as is related in the following tale:

### HOW DOCTORS' FEES WERE REGULATED.

Once there lived a doctor named Abia Ankokk. A woman named Adet was cutting firewood when a small splinter flew into her eye, so she went to Abia to be treated. For about two weeks he looked after her, and then the woman recovered. She offered twenty pieces in payment for his services, but the man refused them, saying:

> “I wish to take you yourself either as a wife or slave, and will accept nothing else.”

Then the townsfolk held a meeting and asked, “Why do you refuse the twenty pieces?” Abia answered:

> “Because I want the woman herself.”

Then the people said:

That rational ideas exist regarding some causes of disease is shown by the next story:

### WHY DISEASE OFTEN COMES.

Once a husband had two wives. Both went with him to plant yams on the farm. When they came home, one woman had no water with which to cook, so she went and borrowed some from the other.

The next day, the first woman sent her daughter to fetch water so that she might repay what she had taken. It was very hot, and when the daughter reached the stream, she found that it had all dried up. She went on and on, seeking water, but could find none; so, after a while, when she came to a market-place, she sat down quietly, thinking, “Perhaps I may buy some water.”

A ghost-man noticed the girl sitting among the stalls. He saw that she was very beautiful and wished to have her as his wife, so he said, “Will you come home with me?” To this she agreed.

When they reached the man’s house, his people asked the girl, “Where do you come from?” She answered, “My mother sent me to fetch water.” Her lover said, “We will ask no questions at present. Let us at once prepare the marriage feast.”

No sooner was the wedding over than the girl heard a voice calling her, “Strange maiden, come here to me.” She looked up and saw the Lame Boy standing at the door of his house. She went to him at once, and he said:

“If your husband offers you food, you must not eat it. Put it on one side, and eat only what I give you.” With that, he

One day at dawn, she was sweeping the house, which she always kept clean and sweet. She saw a piece of stale meat lying on the floor and swept it up with the ashes, then threw everything into the backyard where dead leaves lay among the other rubbish.

Another ghost came and said, “Let me,” but she refused again. After this, she went for the last time down to the spring. When she came back, the ghost people all said, “Are you ready to go home now?” She answered, “Yes,” and went into the house to fetch a small box. They asked, “Is it yours?” She said, “It is mine,” so they bade her farewell.

The husband accompanied her on the road toward her mother’s town. When they had reached the halfway point, he said:
“Of these two things, breeze and wind, which do you like best?” And she answered:
“I like ‘breeze’ best.”

When she prepared to go home, she went inside the house and took a very large box. This she filled with all the goods she could lay her hands on. The husband did not accompany her as he had done in the first case, but asked, “Of these two things, wind and breeze, which do you like best?” She answered, “I like wind.”

Then a strong wind arose and blew the girl up and down and threw her against the trees, one after another. When she reached her home, no one knew her, for her face and body were so changed by disease and blows. Soon she died and went back to the ghosts forever.

### AMUSEMENTS

Life in an <term>Ekoi</term> village is fuller of amusement and variety than might appear at first sight. There is a strong local feeling in every town, and the inhabitants are very protective of its reputation, whether for wealth, size, or the power of its <term>Jujus</term>. Social qualities are very highly developed—nothing is more prized than popularity, and nothing is more dreaded than ridicule.

On almost every day of the year some wedding or birth is celebrated, some girl leaves the <term>fatting-house</term>, some <term>Juju</term> gives a “play,” or one of the many clubs or age-classes holds a feast. As has already been mentioned, these last-named associations, for which the <term>Ekoi</term> name is “<term>Ekan</term>” (plural “<term>Nkan</term>”), consist of everyone of one sex born within the same three-year period. The <term>age-class</term> forms a kind of self-governing community, with the power to oversee the conduct of its members, much like the experimental “<term>Children’s Republics</term>” of the United States. Not long ago, a case came to my attention of a small girl of seven who was fined by her <term>age-class</term> for having allowed a boy friend to behave too freely. When the members have reached the age of about fifteen years, they usually send a delegation to some influential man in the town and ask him to become their president. If he accepts, he gives them a name—usually that of some former age-class which has now died out—and also the authority to play the club drums and “<term>Okankan</term>.” In return for all this, they clear farmland for him and perform other services. The <term>age-class</term> is then launched on its career, and its reputation depends on the energy and capabilities of its members.

Should a boy be from a wealthy family, his admission fees to the <term>Egbo</term> and other clubs are paid while he is still quite young. In such a case, he is considered an honorary member, but is not...

Theoretically, all <term>postulants</term> are beaten before the mysteries of any club are unveiled to them. The more important the club, the more painful the initiatory rites, but these may be exchanged for a fine in the case of some clubs. In others, such as <term>Ekkpo Njawhaw</term>, no bribe can help.

Most clubs hold their initiatory ceremonies and secret rites at some place in the bush, not far from the entrance to the town. This is approached by a winding path, cut through the thick bush, which provides almost the privacy of a yew hedge. Over this path, at intervals of about 10 to 20 feet, hang split palm leaves, held up at each end by thin posts. These arches are usually seven in number, and members are stationed before each, armed with whips or rods, to flog the <term>postulants</term> as they run through at top speed.

Before this ceremony, the youth must have undergone <term>circumcision</term>, though this is usually performed a few weeks after birth by some old woman of the town. Should the boy be sickly, the ceremony may be deferred until the age of eight or nine years, or even later, in which case he is afterwards confined in the <term>fatting-house</term> for three or four months.

In some clubs, the “<term>Enyara Akum</term>,” the “dark things of the clubs,” *that is*, <term>bull-roarers</term>, are used. These were formerly only played in secret; no woman was allowed to see them or know the cause of the sound. My wife and her sister were the first women in this part of the world to whom this highly-valued secret was disclosed.

Another carefully guarded mystery was the art of walking on stilts (<term>Ekoi</term> “*<term>Abia-Nkpaw</term>*” or “*<term>Abum-bum</term>*”), which no woman was allowed to see.

The origin of the custom was obligingly written down for me in the following words:

> “In the very ancient town of <term>Oban</term>, there was once an old man named <term>Awo Ntui Ane</term> (<term>Awo</term> the Chief of Men). He was working on his farm, where he had planted yams. One day, he found the earth very hot from the sun, especially in the dry season. He cut pieces of wood and put them in...”

By these first stilts the feet were only raised a few inches from the ground, but the height was gradually increased, until now a good performer can walk level with the heads of the spectators.

On New Year's Day, 1910, a particularly interesting "stilt play" was performed. There were four principal performers, each thickly veiled; among them was one with only one stilt, very short and bound to his right leg in such a way as to make him limp like a cripple. In him we recognized the "Lame Boy," the "Good Fairy" of Ekoi tales.<note>See pages 58, 370 etc.</note> The heads of several of the minor characters were bound with wreaths, from which hung—covering the ears—leaves of the *Piper* plant, which is sacred to the ghosts. It is curious that the name for stilts, *Abia-Nkpaw*, is the same as that of the giant King of the Skulls, mentioned on page 275. We gathered that the play was in honor of the ghosts, and that the other principal characters were Obassi Osaw and Obassi Nsi.

Next to their dances, the exercise which gives most delight to the people in general is undoubtedly wrestling. The style is Greco-Roman and interesting enough to watch, for not only are the men surprisingly light on their feet, but they show a distinct sense of sportsmanship. It is rare for even the greatest strain to overcome the good humor of the combatants, but at the slightest sign of anger or foul play, the bystanders rush in and stop the contest. Before and throughout a wrestling match, the drums are beaten in the manner used only on such occasions. Before beginning each bout, both wrestlers bend before the drum and touch the earth with their hands. The monotonous drumming seems to affect the heads of performers and spectators alike and produces intense excitement.

Among ball games, the most popular is perhaps *Ukpe Ewaw*, in which any number of men can join. Two unequal sides are chosen. The smaller party divides into two and stands about 50 yards apart. In between stand their opponents. The outside

# CHAPTER XXVII

## ART

The belief has gradually grown upon me that among the Ekoi there exists the seed of a love of beauty almost Greek in character, though warped, and indeed almost overwhelmed by the introduction of blatantly hideous European goods with which the country has been flooded.

That pure beauty does appeal to the people is shown by their surprising knowledge of flowers, and their delight in their form and color, and even in the texture of leaves. On first coming among them, it seemed that they cared little for the wealth of blossoms strewn on every side, for one rarely finds flowers used for personal decoration, and never to decorate their homes. Closer study, however, has made it doubtful whether this is not due to other causes than a lack of appreciation. For the Ekoi, not only great trees but even the smallest plants possess a soul and can feel pain when plucked. Very occasionally, one sees a young girl with a single vivid flower twisted into her hair for decoration, but more usually, among both men and women, leaves or blossoms are only worn as signs to express a specific message. For example, the scarlet Akpanebesin is worn as a challenge behind the ear of a wrestler, or the little Ishut flower or leaf of the Ekuri fern, when worn in the hair or cap, announces a death in the house of the person addressed by anyone so decorated.

Wherever suitable clay is to be found, infinite pains are taken to mold even the water-pots into beautiful shapes. None of these are used for house decoration, as would be the case with us, so the time spent in molding the many-handled, strangely graceful jars must be driven by that indwelling love of beauty which, prevented from expression on almost every side, finds an outlet in this one primitive art. no market for the pottery, it is made solely for domestic use. Obviously a jar with a slender neck from which spring three or four thin, outstanding handles is far more liable to break than the plainer pottery in general use among more civilized peoples—such indeed as the comparatively cultured inhabitants of Northern Nigeria.

In many cases both form and decorative pattern strike a curiously modern note, indeed that of "**L'Art nouveau**" itself. An example of this came to my notice among an even more primitive people, namely, the Banana of the Logone, the decorative lines on whose weapons might have been designed by Liberty.

In seeming contradiction to this feeling for beauty is the undeniable crudeness of the wall paintings. The most elaborate of these are naturally to be found in the Egbo houses, and typical examples are shown on the next page. Yet the designs painted on their foreheads, or clipped on their heads, show a sureness of drawing which few white people could equal. When the head chief of Ibum was questioned as to whether any of the younger people were taught to paint by their elders, or if some members of the community practiced the art more than others, he answered that the women alone made the walls beautiful in this manner, and that they needed no teacher, except for the good sense which Obassi had given them.<note>Compare the custom in Bohemia and Moravia, where the house walls are decorated each spring by the peasant women.</note> Although only capable of such rude expression, all Ekoi are quick to understand the meaning of drawing or painting. If, for instance, my wife wished for specimens of a flower which we had reason to believe grew in the neighborhood, she had only to show what was wanted by a few rapid pencil strokes, or a brushful of color, and delighted exclamations proclaimed its recognition. Search parties scattered in every direction, and not long afterward some triumphant individual usually returned with the specimen, to be exchanged for leaves of another plant in great favor with the Ekoi, namely, tobacco.

...an incident which occurred after we had returned from a long tour. The chief men of Oban came up to congratulate us on our safe return from what seemed to them an almost incredibly long and dangerous journey. We had collected many interesting objects on the way, especially specimens of pottery made by a distant branch of the Ekoi, and some musical instruments of a pattern unknown in these parts. The interpreter asked, on behalf of the chiefs, if they might be allowed to see the collection of “fine things” in my house. After examining these, they showed the most lively interest and admiration for the simple furniture and the few pictures and ornaments scattered around. I had just had a couple of gaudy pictures of the King and Queen in their Coronation robes framed for the office. These were shown to the visitors, and they expressed respectful interest, but no admiration. Suddenly we heard an exclamation of delight, and a moment later all our visitors were crowding around one of their number—who happened to be a member of the highest grade of Egbo—who had picked up a black and white reproduction of Long’s “India.”

The man’s face was alight with joy, and his hands kept moving up and down, following the folds of the drapery and the lines of the figure, in the same manner as one has seen employed over and over again by artists—whether Chinese, Japanese, or European—when explaining the beauty of some wonderful old painting. Several of the others caught fire from his enthusiasm, and his voice was positively unsteady with excitement as he said:

> “I never knew that white people could be so beautiful in shape, nor that they ever wore such long, graceful robes. I thought white people always wore clothes like those they bring out here. Why are they so unkind as not to let us see things like this?”

If, too, as many people contend regarding the Greeks, color terminology is any test of color perception, the Ekoi are by no means backward in this respect.

Thus roughly doubling the color terms of Homer’s days.

It is certain that white influence is to blame in many ways for corrupting the taste of the people. Even now, except at trading centers, one practically never sees any color chosen for loincloths or shoulder robes except dark blue, sometimes with a white or paler blue pattern. This tint is, above all others, suited to bring out the warm brown skin tones and satisfy one’s sense of color.

The lines of the piece of cloth which, until a few years ago, was the ordinary women’s wear, and which is still always worn for farm work, could hardly be improved. The garment passes under the right arm and falls from a knot on the left shoulder in free, graceful folds which reach well below the knee. It is our influence, alas, which is changing the deep, quiet tones of the old blue native dyes for the hideous reds, yellows, and greens which have dazzled the untrained eyes and are ruining the once-true color sense of the people. To the same cause is also due the hideous shape of the pinafore gowns, short in front and trailing behind, often further disfigured with common lace, or strips and yokes of cotton-backed velvet and satin, and sleeves which do their utmost to disguise the shape of the usually well-molded arms. It is true that one garment can be bought which is perhaps as little ugly as any of European make for the use of primitive peoples is likely to be. This is a simple little gown, cut somewhat in the style of those made familiar by the drawings of Kate Greenaway, and with sleeves which only cover the arm two or three inches below the shoulder.*

<page-num>293</page-num>
### ART

Many Ekoi men owe their magnificent physique largely to being free from the distorting influence of clothes. Very young girls, too, are often beautifully shaped, but constant walking over stony ground roughens their bare feet, just as farm work coarsens their hands. One undeniable charm is possessed by almost every member of the race—men and women alike have noticeably long, exquisitely curved eyelashes.

<margin>|</margin>
The <term>fatting-house</term> was not originally established with the idea that mountains of flesh were beautiful, but because the treatment was supposed to strengthen the girl before and after any special physical strain. Fat in a daughter or wife came to be desired as a sign of strength and well-being, and eventually—though not universally—as attractive in its own right.

Two other major factors have helped the physique of the Ekoi. First is the habit, common to most primitive peoples, of carrying large water jars and other loads requiring careful balance on their heads. Second, and perhaps most important of all, is their love of dancing, to which <margin>|</margin> reference has <margin>2)</margin> already been made.

All other pastimes pale in comparison to the attractions of the dance, which, for the Ekoi, is one of the main occupations of life,

> nothing can be said in its favor. West Africans look better in African dress, such as the robes of Muslims and many pagan Africans. It is much healthier for them. It preserves their racial identity, and that is perhaps the most important of all arguments that can be put forward for its retention. With very slight modifications—such as those seen among the native staff and personal servants in many parts of Northern Nigeria—it can be made suitable for any form of labor, clerical or otherwise. Clad in national dress, Africans have a dignity which in most cases they lose almost entirely when they dress themselves in a costume totally unsuitable for the country, and hideous at best. To my mind, nothing is more pitiful than to visit school after school in West Africa filled with boys and girls in foreign clothing, seeing the process of stripping them of their national identity continue day after day with nothing being done to stop it. In the case of women, it is not only dignity and national identity which are concerned, but decency as well. The national dress of women in West Africa is classical and graceful, and although it leaves more of the body exposed than is usual at home (except in a ballroom), it is not suggestive. It does not accentuate the figure. It emphasizes that racial difference—not inequality, but *difference*—which it is so essential to emphasize. By substituting European dress, especially the current fashions, the West African woman loses much that she should never lose, and gains something that is of no benefit to her. These things cannot be changed in a day, nor would it be possible in some cases for the current generation of adults to return to African costume. However, it would be possible in many cases, and the reform could begin immediately as far as the children are concerned."

<page-num>294</page-num>
<header>IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH</header>

and, as with the Greeks of old, provides an outlet for the dramatic instinct and religious fervor of the race. It affords the one means of expressing, as perfectly as possible, their otherwise wordless sense of the mystery of existence, the power of the supernatural influences which surround them, and the ecstasy of joy in life—of youth and strength and love—all the deeper and more poignant feelings so far beyond expression by mere words.

Every event, either in the life of the family or that of the community, is celebrated in this way. Occasions of rejoicing or grief, such as births, a girl's reappearance from the <term>fatting-house</term>, marriages, successful hunts, the entertainment of visitors, deaths, funeral rites, and the thousand and one religious observances—all have their special dances. No noonday sun is too hot, no rain too heavy, to cause their enthusiasm to flag, or to dampen the passion of the people. For hour after hour the performance continues, monotonous indeed to European eyes and ears, but capable of causing frenzied excitement in the dancers, and showing a feeling for true rhythmic motion which is little short of marvelous. Every atom of the body dances, but the point which distinguishes an accomplished dancer from others is the never-ceasing, wave-like ripple which runs down the muscles of the back, and along the arms to the fingertips.

Though dancing is carried on during every hour of the day, and in all seasons of the year, it is by the light of the full moon that the Ekoi most love to indulge in this pastime. On such occasions, when the people of some town in the interior have gathered together to give a series of dances, the scene possesses a weird beauty impossible to define or express, but which, like the monotonous chant and drumming of its accompaniment, vibrates on chords of being which more strictly beautiful performances fail to touch.

This is one point of view. That there is another is shown by the description sent home by my wife and sister-in-law soon after their arrival:—

> "The dance was a maddening performance," they wrote, "and made all the more unbearable to us by P. A.'s attempts to draw our attention to the 'rhythmic harmony of the monotone' or some such appreciative expression. To our

unmusical ears, it sounded far more as if all the fiends had been let loose around us. When, after hours of dancing, the performers broke into a new song—the refrain of which sounded exactly like ‘hustling and bustling away,’ but proved to be the prelude to a yet longer and more energetic series—it really seemed as if insult had been added to injury to an almost unendurable degree.

It was not until months after their arrival that I discovered what terror these dances had at first caused my companions. During any such performance, they sat smiling and apparently interested, and it never occurred to me that the sight of the brown figures painted with patterns in white, red, and yellow—dancing in and out of the flickering torchlight—could conjure up Fenimore-Cooper-like visions of frenzied savages working themselves up, through uncouth dance and song, to a sudden, treacherous attack. Only when a more intimate knowledge had banished fear was the secret of this initial terror confided to me.

Whatever may be the difference of opinion regarding the merit of <term>Ekoi</term> dances from an aesthetic standpoint, there can be none as to their interest from an anthropological one. Some of the oldest hold enshrined within them traces of beliefs and fancies which have faded from every other record.

<margin>[</margin>
Such is “<term>Ejame</term>,” a solemn dance, never given except during the funeral rites of very great chiefs.

Seven men dance in the center of an immense circle formed by the other performers a long way off. Each of the seven must take care to leave a great space between himself and his neighbor on either hand; for should the <term>aura</term> of one of the seven—which on this occasion is thought to extend beyond its usual limits around his body—overlap that of any other present, both will die. It is forbidden for any of the principal performers to raise their eyes. From beginning to end of the dance, each must keep them fixed upon the earth at his feet. Three at least must wear rattles around the neck and carry spears. The songs sung during this dance are declared to be so old that their meaning has long since been forgotten.

The secret of <term>Okpata</term> has been handed down from father to son for many generations in the family of <term>Obassi Unaw</term> of <term>Oban</term>.

The musical talent of these people is certainly wonderful, though developed along distinctive lines. They have a considerable number of musical instruments, but among these the <term>drum</term> reigns supreme. There are many varieties of these, from the small boy’s <term>tom-tom</term>, about 6 inches high, to the long drums almost the height of a man, and the great drum of the town. This latter is an object of reverence to the inhabitants, and in honor of

<image-desc>An illustration of a traditional tall drum. The drum has a cylindrical body that tapers slightly and is wrapped with several horizontal bands or cords. It is mounted on a decorative stand consisting of a curved, horn-like support structure resting on a small circular base.</image-desc>

Mbi (sworn), "When Itoga went to Itayin's house, he began to beat the drums. The owners asked from whom he had authority. He answered that I myself had given it to him. At night the club members gathered together and summoned Itoga before them. They found him guilty of beating their drums. He told them that I was responsible, but I said, 'I am not a member of this club. How then could I give Itoga authority over the drums of others?'"

For this unauthorized performance the Club claimed goods to the value of 30 shillings.

The study of the drum is well worth the attention of officials, as it is possible in this way not only to know what is going on in native towns around one—for every event has its different tune by which to summon the inhabitants, such as <term>Egbo</term> and <term>Juju</term> performances, wrestling matches, etc.—but one is able to learn the drum language, and so interpret almost every secret message sent in warning to counteract one's orders or plans.

Two drums are generally beaten, of which the first leads while the second responds. In the transcription attempted here, the top line represents the notes of the first drum and the bottom one that of the second, usually lower in pitch. A dot represents the value of half a dash. When only one performer is available, he beats the two drums.

The combinations are so limitless that any attempt to do more than indicate the method employed would only weary my readers.

> “Ekut ekui nyaw ebuk eriti.

At dawn, after the death of a great man in the old days, the <term>Egbo drum</term> could always be heard insistently beaten in a series of five equal strokes—

> “Kran, kran, kran, kran, kran,
> Kran, kran, kran, kran, kran.”

While this sound boomed through the town, the people sought a victim to seize and offer as a sacrifice, to be laid in the grave beneath the wrapped body of the deceased chief. As soon as the strokes stopped, strangers approaching from a distance knew that they could enter the town safely—the victim had already been found. In such cases, the person was usually put to death near the <term>Juju stone</term> by means of brass rods twisted around the throat. The body was then thrown down before the great drum, which was solemnly beaten once more.

Besides the drum, the principal musical instruments are the harp, <term>okankan</term>,* and rattle, but there are countless others, such as one made from a palm mid-rib three to four feet long, shown here:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### RECORDS

RECORDS are usually kept by using various kinds of tallies—by dropping small stones or corn grains into a calabash, and by making marks on walls.

The system of counting was to count first on the fingers and then on the toes. If the number exceeded twenty, a person would lay down a small piece of grass, a stick, or a palm leaf for every five extra, or for every twenty if large numbers were involved. It was customary to begin with the little finger on the left hand.

To express numbers up to twenty, the following signs are used:

1, 2, 3, and 4: the corresponding number of fingers is held out on one hand.

5: a closed fist is shown.

6: three fingers are held out on each hand.

7: two fingers of the right hand are struck twice onto the palm of the left hand; alternatively, four fingers of the left hand and three fingers of the right are held out.

8: four fingers of each hand are held out.

9: the left hand is held out with the fingers loosely closed, and the right hand, with the thumb against the palm, is drawn from the left hand across the chest—clearly imitating the old custom of shooting with a bow.

10: two closed fists are held out.

15: the tips of the fingers of the right hand are bent over to touch the right shoulder.

20: the right hand is raised before the face and then swung downward with the index finger extended.

### NSIBIDI.

In 1905, Mr. T. D. Maxwell, District Commissioner of Calabar, discovered a secret, primitive writing system used by the Efik people. Twenty-four signs, the meanings of which he had successfully learned, were published in the Government Civil List of July 1905. Later, an article by the Reverend J. K. MacGregor appeared in the *Anthropological Journal* in 1909. In this paper, the author states first that Nsibidi originated among the Ibo people, or alternatively among the Uyanga, who supposedly learned it from the monkeys that gathered around their campfires. He says that he has been unable to find any trace of such a script in the Cameroons, and in his opinion, it was unlikely that such a script would exist among peoples of Bantu descent. However, he adds a note that a work by Dr. Mansfeld—*Urwald Dokumente*—has since come to his attention, in which some signs are provided.

<margin>A vertical pencil bracket in the right margin covers the following two paragraphs.</margin>

Regarding the Ibo people, everyone of this nationality whom I questioned denied the existence of any writing system except the one adopted from missionary sources, which has been modified for their own convenience.

Among the Uyanga, it has also unfortunately been impossible to find any trace of the interesting legend mentioned above. Furthermore, far from a Bantu connection being a barrier to knowledge of the script, the Ekoi—who certainly have a strong Bantu heritage—claim, and with seemingly good reason, to have <insert>underlined in pencil</insert> **originated the entire system**. Today, a greater variety of signs seems to exist among the Ekoi of the interior than among any other tribe.

The script is certainly quite old and is largely pictographic, though it has become highly conventionalized over the years. The Ekoi explanation for the name Nsibidi (or more accurately, Nchibbidy) is that it is derived from the verb “Nchibbi,” meaning “to turn.” This has come to mean mental agility, and therefore cunning or a double meaning.

One of the oldest clubs, which apparently existed before the start of the Egbo society, carries the same name. This was a

Both went into the bush. When the false friend had climbed the tree, Obassi called to it, “If this is the man who deceived my son, and gave him up to be killed by the people, O tree! grow up very high, and throw him down to the ground, so that he dies. If he is innocent, you shall not grow.”

Then the tree shot up into the sky, carrying the man with it. It shook its top and flung him down to the ground, so that he died.

Obassi went home for a time, but another day when he was hunting in the bush, he saw a porcupine run into its hole. He said to himself, “If my son were here, he would kill that animal for me. I will try to kill all those people who put my son to death.”

# CHAPTER XXIX

## GOVERNMENT, ETC.

In the old days, each town was ruled by its council of elders—the Homeric “<term>γερουσια</term>”—and in most ways, this still holds true. Anyone, from the greatest chief to the smallest child, has the right to summon such a meeting and lay complaints before it. Most of the townspeople attend, but only the elders have the right to speak; others do so only by permission. A powerful chief naturally would have more influence than a poor man on such occasions, but should the case be clear against the chief, the meeting would never decide in his favor.

In most ways, the Ekoi are still ruled according to old custom, but an appeal can always be made from the decision of the elders to that of the Native Court, and from the latter directly to the District Commissioner. The old “<term>γερουσια</term>” no longer has the power to enforce punishments.

The Native Court is composed of representatives from different towns of the District, who sit in turns, usually under the presidency of the Commissioner. If the Commissioner is unavoidably absent, his place is taken by the principal chief present, but all decisions are inspected by the Commissioner upon his return.

In this manner, the people may be said to have almost complete self-government. Indeed, among people of a high type like the Ekoi, who have comparatively few customs repugnant to the English sense of justice, self-government is more truly a fact since the arrival of the “white man” than before, when the rights of the poor and those not born free were too often set aside.

The only serious crime prevalent among the Ekoi is poisoning, and this is more often directed against suspected magicians than private enemies. That it is all too common,

<summary>This page describes the Ekoi governance system, explaining how traditional councils of elders have been integrated into a colonial legal framework featuring Native Courts and District Commissioners. The author notes that this system preserves self-government while providing more protections for the poor than existed previously.</summary>
<keywords>Ekoi government, council of elders, gerousia, Native Court, District Commissioner, self-government, colonial justice, poisoning, magicians</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the prevalence of poisoning and details the legal customs of the Ekoi regarding murder, accidental death, and theft.</meta>

<header>GOVERNMENT, ETC.</header>

however, is proved by the fact that antidotes are kept close at hand, usually in the form of dried herbs hung from the roof. These are sometimes used as a lotion and sometimes given as a drink.

It is usual to take an antidote before going to a meal if there is any reason to suspect one’s host of evil intentions. After this precaution, if poison is administered, the guest vomits at once and suffers no further ill effects.

The only cases of violent deaths known to me in the District were both committed by former "members" of an alien race.

The Ekoi custom regarding the murder of a free man was to summon the head chiefs of the neighboring towns to inquire into the case. Judgment was given after seven days, and, if found guilty, the murderer was immediately put to death. No compensation was permitted, and the wealth or position of the guilty man was not allowed to carry any weight at all.

If the death was proved to be due to an accident, the killer could ransom himself by the payment of one slave, or equivalent value, for his own life, and one for each full brother, and two for each full sister he possessed, so that the blood guilt would not fall upon them as well.

The punishment for serious theft in the old days was to cut off an ear, toe, or finger. For some time now, however, the procedure has been as follows:

For the first offense, the culprit was fined by the <term>Egbo Club</term>; for the second, his "company" <note>An age-grade or social group</note> fined him more heavily; while for the third, he was fined very heavily indeed. A cow was usually shot, and he was forced to refund the value to the owners. Next, a bell was hung around his waist, he was painted over with black and white, and driven around the town. The owner of the stolen property was not allowed to inflict any punishment himself.

Most other offenses were punished by fines. Someone who broke the marriage laws would have to pay damages to the injured party. As far as possible, punishment was made to fit the crime, and, in the old days at least, a murderer was put to death in the same way as his victim.

### WHY A MURDERER SHOULD DIE IN THE SAME WAY AS HIS VICTIM.

There was once a man who had two wives. The name of the one was Nka Menge Njum (Know nothing) and of the other Menge Marri (Know all). After seven months the first woman bore a daughter, but the second wife remained barren.

The child grew up very quickly, and after five months could walk alone. One day she went to the house of Menge Marri, but the latter drove her away and said, "I want no children in my room." A second day the same thing happened.

Once the father went out hunting. Menge Njum said to herself, "I want to go to my farm and get food; firewood also is needed, but there is no one to take care of the child. If I could see anyone with whom to leave her, I would go at once."

On hearing this the daughter herself said, "If you do not fetch food, we shall die of hunger, so you must go. If Menge Marri were your friend, you could leave me with her; but she does not like you, so I am better alone."

The mother set out and collected all that was needed. On her return she found her daughter safe in the house. Nothing had happened to her. Next day, therefore, the woman went forth again to her farm.

This day, however, Menge Marri came to the house of her rival and said to the child, "Your mother is away. Let us go together to the bush. We will catch fish in the river."

To this the girl agreed, and, when they had gone some way, they came to a river in which there were many fish. Menge Marri took her little companion and flung her into the water, so as to form a dam. A high tree was growing by the side of the river, and on this sat a blue bird. He cried:—

> "I never before saw any woman take the daughter of another and lay her across the water like this. If you want to dam the water, why do you not cut sticks?"

When the wicked wife heard this she picked up many stones and threw them at the bird, but it flew away safely. She caught plenty of fish, and, after she had finished, drew the body of the drowned girl up from the water, and laid it across her

She did this until she reached home. When she arrived, she put the dead body of the little one in the mother's room, then went to her own house and began to clean the fish.

When Menge Njum came back from the farm, she called to her daughter, "Come, help me lower my load, for it is very heavy." The child did not answer, so the mother let her load fall, and ran and caught hold of her. Then she began to weep bitterly.

A little time after, the father returned from hunting and asked: "What is the matter? When I started, I left my daughter healthy. How is it possible that she could have died in two days?"

The blue bird flew down and perched on the roof.

"I never saw a woman take another woman's daughter and use her to dam a river instead of sticks," he sang.

The father stopped his wife from weeping and said, "Let us listen to the bird;" and the bird sang further:

"There is the woman who took your daughter and used her to dam a river." At that moment, Menge Marri went by, but the man could not believe what the bird sang.

Next morning the wife said, "Our child is dead. Let us go and bury her." The man answered, "We will do as you say, but, as long as I live, I will find out who has killed her."

While they were burying their little one, the bird flew down once more and sang, "It was Menge Marri who took the child to the river to drown her, and afterwards carried the body back to the house. She is the one who killed your daughter."

Then the parents called a meeting of the townspeople and accused Menge Marri of what she had done.

Menge Marri stated, "The reason I killed their daughter is because I had none of my own."

On this, the meeting gave judgment that she must die in the same way as she had killed the girl.

From that day, a man who kills another must be put to death in the same way as his victim.
