Upon death, all property goes by right to the eldest brother of the deceased. If the heir is a good man, he would share with the dead man’s children, but he cannot be forced to do so.

Any property given to a wife remains hers upon the death of her husband if she has children, but if she is childless, it all goes to the elder brother.

A strict account of property is kept between husband and wife. A rather amusing instance of this came before the Court soon after my arrival:

A man had lent his wife goods worth fourteen pieces of cloth. She acknowledged the debt and was anxious to repay it. Since she could think of no other way to do so, she set out in true Amazonian style and seized another woman, whom she brought back captive and presented to her husband to fully settle her own debts.

The practice of seizing free persons and converting them into slaves has naturally been forbidden throughout the land since the arrival of white rule. Consequently, a complaint was filed, with the result that the whole affair was brought into Court.

That this strict attention to “ <term>Meum</term> ” <note>Mine</note> and “ <term>Tuum</term> ” <note>Thine</note> extends also to children was proven on one occasion by an eight-year-old child who claimed damages against her father because he had used, without her permission, a cooking pot which he had given her some time before. Under native law, she won her case. The father was ordered to return the pot and pay compensation to his daughter for having made unauthorized use of her property.

Before entering into the next section of my subject, I should like to state that I myself do not consume intoxicants of any kind and hold the cause of temperance close to my heart, while I yield to no member of the Native Races Committee in my interest in the people among whom my life is spent.

At all hours, without a moment’s warning of our arrival, native houses of every class of Ekoi have been open to us, as hundreds of sketches of interiors, character studies, etc., can testify. In the course of my life here, and the thousands of miles traveled, only two cases of natives being the worse for drink have come to my attention. Neither was more than slightly intoxicated, and

both lapses from virtue were due, not to imported liquor, but to palm wine, though in the last case about a teaspoonful of gin had been added.

The Ekoi are a thoroughly sober people, and, although a considerable amount of European spirits is brought to the district, a great part of this is used for libations or sacrificial purposes. The only native intoxicant is palm wine, of which there are two kinds. First, there is the kind obtained by climbing up the tree, making an incision at the top, and fixing a gourd or demijohn to catch the flow of sap. This is a troublesome process, owing to the height of the tree and its spiked leaves.

The wine thus obtained will keep for some time, but after the first few days it begins to grow heady. “Medicine” is then mixed with it, and it is used almost exclusively for Juju purposes.

The second kind of palm wine is obtained by felling the tree, cutting out the greater part of the “cabbage,” and affixing some receptacle in much the way described above. The sap thus obtained must be drunk within thirty-six hours and is no more intoxicating than cider. This method is discouraged by the government because, if allowed, it would cause the destruction of many oil palms. The vast number of these trees now makes Southern Nigeria the wealthiest of our Crown Colonies, and, if properly preserved, they will form an inexhaustible source of trade with Great Britain and a means of building up an ever-increasing market for her goods.

As has already been mentioned, an enormous amount of imported liquor is used for libations at funeral ceremonies and at “plays” in honor of deceased chiefs. At practically all sacrifices and religious ceremonies, libations play an important part. Until we can educate the natives—not through book learning, but by a gradual raising to a higher plane of thought—it is useless to attempt to keep them, through forced legislation, from what they deem necessary to bring good fortune to themselves and happiness to their dead kinsfolk. They will have spirits, if only for the reasons mentioned, and if importation is forbidden, not only will the palm trees be sacrificed to this end, but illicit distilleries will spring up everywhere, as has been repeatedly pointed out by the press. <page-num>316</page-num>
<header>IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH</header>

For the greater part of the Protectorate, a whole army of officials would be unable to control this danger, and the resulting degradation of a people, who are currently law-abiding and sober, would be the responsibility of those who, in mistaken zeal, are anxious to bring about immediately what must require years of patient teaching.

If those who have the real good of the native races at heart could cast aside prejudice and come to study the workings of the present administrative system, I venture to believe that they would return to their own country and redirect their zeal for temperance into channels that so badly need it. Centuries of education, backed by the full strength of our police force, have not succeeded in making wife-murder caused by drink uncommon among us; yet, among the Ekoi, the murder of a woman is utterly unknown, with the exception of those offered in sacrifice or killed in time of war.

Surely, for shame’s sake, we should wait until at least such a hideous crime is stamped out in our own land before attempting to force our own unsuccessful experiments in temperance on a people who—to our utter disgrace be it said—are incomparably more sober than ourselves. When we can point to the self-conquest whose unmistakable outward sign will be a sober England, there will be no need for temperance legislation in Southern Nigeria. Its people, most of whom are law-abiding and loyal to the core, would follow us in stopping the use of harmful spirits just as surely as they are already doing by discarding their old customs of ordeal and torture—provided they are not forced into other paths by legislation which, in their present state of evolution, they could only regard as a tyrannical abuse of power. These changes must be made gradually, as the evil of such things can be explained to them, and in this, no amount of legislation can have the force of example.

Is it too much to plead for a little patience—for a few years in which to bring about such vast changes—and, above all, for the charity of judgment, which we all need, to be extended to those at the head of the Administration who have striven so nobly for the good of the people entrusted to their care?

# GOVERNMENT, ETC.

### ORIGIN AND CHARACTERISTICS.

That the Ekoi are mainly of Bantu stock is shown both by their language and the shape of their heads. The latter point has been determined by Professor Keith from skulls which he was kind enough to analyze for me. <note>See Appendix C.</note> Distinctly Himyaritic types are, however, still to be found.

The original Bantu stock is now generally acknowledged to have arisen from a mixture of Hamitic and negro blood. The Ekoi were probably among the first of the races formed this way to split off from the parent stem, and they seem to have come straight from the lower end of the Nile valley. There are many points about <term>Nsibidi</term> writing <note>See Appendix G.</note> which recall traces of the earliest Egyptian hieroglyphics. It is perhaps worth remarking that, with hardly any exceptions, buildings are represented in this script as circular, <note>See Story 4, Nsibidi Signs, Appendix G.</note> a form generally considered peculiar to parkland peoples and quite different from the rectangular houses of forest-dwellers.

That the Ekoi are descendants of a people living in large communities and governed by powerful rulers is shown by the fact that ancestor worship—practically unknown to tribes consisting of small settlements—is still so strong. To the reasons already cited for believing that they have come down from the northeast, and probably from a land not so densely forested as Southern Nigeria, may be added the fact that, with hardly an exception, the former sites of all their towns are north of their present ones, and that the great <term>Nkí</term> (lion) figures very largely in their early folklore. It is not impossible that this animal should occasionally leave its home in the grass country to the north and cross the Cross River. There is more or less trustworthy evidence for believing that it has actually penetrated as far south as Aking, but such incursions are certainly rare.

The salt springs which occur around the sacred Lake Ijagham and in other parts of Ekoi land—some indeed quite near to Oban station—were possibly a determining factor in the final

...choice of settlement, as the need for salt is strong among all tribes.

With the exception of a few towns near Obokum, all Ekoi now seem to have settled south of the Cross River. There are, roughly speaking, 20,000 in British territory, mostly in or bordering the Oban district. Across the border in the Cameroons, according to Dr. Mansfield, they number fewer than 6,000; however, if one includes the tribes he calls the Keaka and Obang—with whom the Ekoi claim kinship and who speak an almost identical language—the number would be raised to over 12,000. To the east of these are the Banjangs, a related tribe about 5,000 strong, whose language is also very similar. If the current rate of immigration into British territory continues, however, the number of Ekoi in the Cameroons will soon show a great decrease.

The inhabitants of Big Kwa Town, near Calabar, claim to be the first Ekoi to have come down from the north and were certainly there before the arrival of the Efiks, as the latter people obtained permission from them to mark out a site for their new settlement. The land within the bend of the Cross River was apparently uninhabited upon the arrival of these pioneers, but other branches of the tribe soon followed until practically the whole territory was settled.

The average height of the men is about two inches less than that of Englishmen, while the women are even shorter in comparison with those of Teutonic races. My own experience of black peoples is far from coinciding with that expressed by Mr. Northcote Thomas (p. 6 of *Report on Edo-speaking Peoples*, Part I.):

> "Although the Negro is able to carry loads for long distances, he must go at his own pace; even without a load, his endurance is small when he is called upon to move faster than usual,"

I have found that the Negro shows great powers of endurance over the whole extent of country I have covered in West and Central Africa since 1902. Leaving aside such splendid examples as the Mende, Hausa, the inhabitants of the Tuburi marshes, etc.—to take the Ekoi alone—it is quite common for them, when carrying for themselves, to bear a 100-pound load over the fifteen-mile hilly road from Oban to Obutong and return the same day. Like most hill tribes, the men prefer to carry heavy loads on their shoulders, kept in place by a strap around the forehead. Women and girls, however, carry everything on their heads, and their loads of firewood, etc., must often weigh over 60 pounds. Like those of most tropical tribes, the women age quickly, though some keep their good looks until they are over forty. It is impossible to obtain accurate ages, as these are never known by the people themselves, but those over seventy seem rare, and I do not think it would

Contrary to the custom of many West African tribes, artificial disfigurement of the face or body is extremely rare among these people. Until a few years ago, the two front incisors were filed so as to form an inverted **V**, but this custom is now dying out. In earlier times, three small circles of concentric rings were cut into the side of the face from the temple downward. Some claim that they had made the alteration beforehand and the Efiks adopted it from them. This custom is also dying out, and since my arrival in the District, no child has been so marked.

In the interior, children and young girls still have their bodies painted with designs made by black vegetable dyes. The most usual of these is extracted from the rhizome of the little flower “Ibiri Nsi,” which is much like a wild hyacinth. A small amount of tattooing is practiced, as well as the ghost marks described on p. 203. As regards <term>coiffures</term>, the variety of designs to be found among young girls and children is astonishing. Usually they first shave the head; then, when the hair has grown to a uniform length of about a quarter of an inch, they trace out an elaborate pattern with chalk, which is left standing against a clean-shaved background.

Young women and children are also fond of ornamenting their faces, especially their foreheads, with designs in various colors. The absolute mastery of outline shown by these, as well as by those mentioned in the last paragraph, is far beyond the average to be expected from Europeans. The variety of such patterns is extraordinary. Several hundred sketches were made by my wife and her sister—indeed, the supply seemed inexhaustible. The outlines are often filled in with <term>Nsibidi</term> writing, and sometimes a girl’s whole life history is proclaimed in this manner. Such patterns are always traced by a female relative, usually the aunt of the person decorated.

The <term>Ekoi</term> are mentally an intelligent race, and though they do not have the concentration of mind possessed by white people, they can undeniably fix their attention for hours at a time on any subject that interests them. Their memories are incomparably better, and their senses—at least those of sight, hearing, and smell—are, as is to be expected, far keener than those of Europeans.

They are an eloquent people, and there are very few who cannot, at a moment’s notice, speak fluently on any topic with which they are familiar, or defend themselves ably enough on every occasion. Their points, though sometimes long and drawn out, are well made in the end, and their words are accompanied by expressive tones and gestures. They have a keen sense of humor,

# GOVERNMENT, ETC.

These traits are often disguised by a child-like guilelessness, cropping up in the most unlikely times and places. Once a prisoner was brought before the Court on the charge of having broken the prison rules by speaking to his wife without permission. When brought up by the Corporal, he pleaded "not guilty" despite the many witnesses against him.

He stated: 
> "Among those who brought rations to the prison gate, I saw my wife with a basket of plantains. I would have liked to speak to her, but could not get permission, as the Corporal was busy. I thought to myself, 'Our Father the <term>D. C.</term> <note>District Commissioner</note> has forbidden us to speak with the townsfolk who come to sell us food, but never has he forbidden us to speak with the plantains.' Therefore I looked sadly upon those which lay in the basket and asked, 'O plantains! why are you so few? If more of you do not come quickly, I shall surely die of hunger!' I swear to Your Worship that that was all. I said no word to anyone, except the plantains, and against conversing with them there is no law."

The simplest statements, too, often show a touch of unconscious poetry. Not long ago at Nsan, we were visited by a very old woman who had come to present us with a small mat made by her own hands.

She stood in the vivid sunshine leaning on her stick, shrunken and feeble—an image of extreme old age, but with eyes still bright and a clear, kind voice.

> "Each time the <term>D. C.</term> came to our town," she said, "I thought, 'This time at least he will come to my compound, so that I shall learn to know him, for I am the oldest woman of Nsan.' Yet he never came to see me, so I have come to him that I may at last see the face of my Father."

We were very sorry that she had been unvisited for so long, but found that her house lay by itself in a little side street at the back of the main road. She took great pride in her age and told how she had come from the old town of Nsan when she was already old enough to bear a small load for herself. We asked if any others of her "<term>age class</term>" <note>A social group consisting of people of similar age who transition through life stages together</note> were still alive, but she answered, "Of all those who were with me, dancing up and down in the moonlight or the sunshine, I alone remain. The others long since lie sleeping."

S.B.

<header>IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH</header>

The two most noticeable qualities of the Ekoi are their reverence for age and their love of children. The oldest man of the town is always its head chief, unless he has been so poor all his life that he was excluded from joining any of the clubs. Only one case of harshness toward a child has come to my notice during the entire time spent among them, and the spirit of indulgence with which children are everywhere treated shows its results in the independence and utter fearlessness of even the smallest.

One day at Nsan, while my wife and her sister were alone in the Guest-house, a small child of three entered their room. He announced that he had come to see the "white man" and lay a complaint before him. They at once sent to request my return from the school playground, where a football match was in progress, and when I got back to interview the complainant, his story was told without delay. The small visitor declared that his father had not given him enough to eat; therefore, he came to lay his "case" before the "white man." His well-nourished little body looked as if any dietary error had been in the opposite direction. Biscuits of various kinds proved inadequate for his needs, but at length he was made happy with a corn-cob nearly as big as himself, and with this he toddled away.

On another occasion, while standing at the <term>theodolite</term>, I felt a touch at about the height of my shooting boot. Looking down, I saw a little child who could only just have learned to walk. In his raised hands were some limes about the size of acorns.

He had come all alone, and quite on his own initiative, to "<term>dash</term>" the "white man," and had selected these tiny limes as a suitable offering.

Everywhere the small children seem fond of playing at <term>Juju</term> processions, in imitation of their elders. A typical one was seen at Mfamosing.

The tiny "<term>Okum</term>" wore a long ragged garment of blue fabric, which had once formed part of his mother's gown. This trailed behind, but was held up in front by both small hands. He glided, curtsied, and turned in a carefully studied imitation of "<term>Akpambe</term>." Before him marched a tiny gnome-like child, solemnly drumming on one of our discarded coffee

### PROVERBS AND OMENS.

The language has an extensive vocabulary, and many phrases show unexpectedly poetical turns of thought. It is also rich in proverbs, some of which are apt enough, though many have little meaning for European ears.
The following are perhaps typical:—

" Eeti ejim ka mkpe aiya, mbuta anak amobikk
<gloss>A big tree stood on the bank of a great water; the rain fell (but) could not</gloss>
etim.
<gloss>cover (it)."</gloss>

" Nse oa, nkpe oa, na akpawoi, odikk amitt amobikk
<gloss>Your father, your mother, if they die, crying (but) eyes cannot</gloss>
etannum.
<gloss>break."</gloss>

*i.e.*, A high tree grew by the side of a great water; the rain fell and fell, and the water rose, yet could not overflow the top of the tree.

If your father or mother should die, you weep and weep, yet grief cannot quite overwhelm you. Your eyes will brighten again some day.

" Ofung otue okett, ojokk otue okett, njinni ba ntue.
<gloss>Buffaloes grow tired of pulling, elephants grow tired of pulling, small birds come to pull."</gloss>

*i.e.*, What great folk failed to do, may sometimes be done by the small and weak.

" Ikuni igbaw mfepp. Chong obinn eye okaka eyuk.
<gloss>Firewood falls in the wind. Go break it today, don't sleep cold."</gloss>

The firewood has been blown down by the wind. Go and break it up and carry it home today, so that you should not have to sleep cold tonight; *i.e.*, Don't miss an opportunity.

Great attention is paid to any signs supposed to foretell the future, whether from outside or inside influences. Among the

<page-num>324</page-num>
<header>IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH</header>

Regarding the former, the cries and flights of birds hold an important place. There are five principal kinds with the gift of prophecy:
&emsp;&emsp;The <term>Nkundak</term>, or Greater Plantain-eater.
&emsp;&emsp;The <term>Osaiiri</term>, or Kingfisher.
&emsp;&emsp;The <term>Aru</term>,
and two varieties of <term>Itott</term>.
   In making a journey, it is a good omen if either of the first three of these birds cries on your left hand, but it foretells ill-luck should they be heard on the right. The <term>Itott</term>, on the other hand, brings good fortune if it crosses your path from right to left, but bad luck if in the contrary direction.
   Of divination by feelings in different parts of the body:—
   A twitching in the upper eyelid of the left eye denotes that one is about to see a bad thing, such as an ordeal by burning oil.
   A twitching in the upper eyelid of the right eye, on the contrary, foretells a fine sight, such as a dance.
   The same sensation in either of the bottom eyelids predicts a coming cause for tears.
   Should the twitching be felt in the top of the left arm before starting on a journey, it means that evil awaits you, and that the friendly powers are trying to hold you back. If this warning be disregarded, misfortune is sure to follow. Should the twitching be felt, however, in the top part of the right arm it is a good sign, and foretells that a friend’s arm will soon lie within one’s own.
   If this sensation comes in the hollow of the elbow of the right arm, or the palm of the right hand, it means that you will be called on to pay a debt or give a gift; if in the left hand, that you are about to receive one, as in our own “Right hand take, left hand pay.”
   A twitching above the heart means danger, trouble, or punishment, as also a tingling on the forehead or left thigh. On the right breast or thigh it means good luck. The same sensation below the elbow on either arm denotes that news of a death will soon reach you. On the sole of the right foot, it means that a strange man is coming to see you; on the left foot, that you will be visited by a strange woman.
   When a meteor falls to the ground, it is a sign of a coming death in the neighborhood; while a comet or a dark ring round the moon betokens the death of a chief.

# CHAPTER XXX

## Treatment of "Members"

In the past, Calabar and Bonny were rivals for dominance among the slave ports of Africa, and few places in the world could have seen more misery. In this infamous trade, the Ekoi acted as "middlemen" for the greater part of the land to the north and northeast. Most of the victims were brought down from the "slave towns," as they are still called—that is, those lying between the Cross River and the Benue, and more especially near the line of the then-present Anglo-German border. The Ekoi did not usually travel far into the interior themselves; instead, the slaves were brought down and delivered into the hands of those living furthest north, and from there passed from town to town until they reached the Calabar traders.

The abolition of slavery by England put a stop to all such export trade, but it still continued among the natives in remote areas, such as the Ekoi country, which had not yet been fully taken over by the Government. For the first year after my arrival in 1907, one of my principal duties was to stamp it out.

The administration of Southern Nigeria is carried on to a large extent through the so-called "Heads of Houses." The word "House" includes not only the immediate family, but also its retainers, freed slaves, and their descendants—all, in fact, who recognize the authority of the Chief of the <term>sept</term>. All, except for blood relations, would perhaps be best described by the old Latin word <term>Clientes</term>, and the mutual duties of the Roman noble and his retainers are closely paralleled by those of the present-day Ekoi. The Head of the House now, as then, supports his "members" during infancy and sickness, sees to their general well-being, and in return receives their services and requires submission to his authority in all lawful ways.

<summary>This chapter discusses the historical role of the Ekoi as middlemen in the African slave trade and explains the traditional "House" system of social and administrative organization in Southern Nigeria.</summary>
<keywords>slave trade, Ekoi, Calabar, Bonny, Southern Nigeria, Heads of Houses, sept, Clientes, social structure, colonial administration</keywords>

--- Page 448 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the social structure of the Ekoi, specifically the "House" system and the transition from traditional slavery to colonial legal recognition.</meta>

IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

This state of affairs has been recognized by the Government of Southern Nigeria, and if either party does not fulfill their part of the agreement, there is a legal remedy. The one objection from a practical point of view is that, in the minds of the people, a distinction still exists between free-born “members” of such a house or clan and those who are not free. They are beginning to understand, however, that no such distinction exists before the law, and the difference will undoubtedly gradually die out. According to the unanimous opinion of those who have experience governing the local people, it would be most unwise to suddenly deprive chiefs and heads of families of their hereditary authority. Such a course would reduce the coastal parts of the Central and Eastern Provinces of Southern Nigeria to anarchy, unless the number of officials was multiplied tenfold—and even then, the people would be less happy and contented than under the current state of affairs. The necessity for slowness and caution in all changes is brought home daily with greater force to all who have to do with ruling West African people. To change, with a stroke of a pen, the system of government developed by the local people over thousands of years would have far-reaching negative results. Under the current state of affairs, at least no one is left uncared for, and beggars are unknown throughout the entire Ekoi country.

Pledging free-born persons for debt was common among the Ekoi, but this was a mild form of slavery. “Members” pledged in this way were treated particularly well and returned to freedom upon payment of the debt. At death, they were also buried like free-born men—not, as in the case of slaves, tied to bamboo poles to be carried to a distant part of the bush and left unburied.

Today, a good “member” gives up one-third to one-half of his time to serve the Head of his House, mostly through farm work or hunting. Sometimes he trades, usually with capital supplied by the “Head,” to whom the profits go, though a portion is almost always returned to the “member.” In the past, a lazy slave was flogged, but if the punishment was excessive, he could complain to the principal chief of the town. # TREATMENT OF "MEMBERS"

complaints were too often ignored, in which case the slave usually ran away. If he was caught, he was sometimes cruelly punished, but more often sold at Calabar.

To guard against escape attempts, upon first arriving at the house of a new master, the latter usually cut off a lock of hair and some nail parings, and then took a piece of old cloth that the slave had worn. These were carried before the <term>Juju</term>, and a prayer was offered that death or recapture might follow any attempt to escape. After the ceremony, the pieces were carefully kept in a secret place, and the slave believed that, should he run away, the <term>Juju</term> would definitely "catch" him.

Not long ago, one of the wives of Chief Nataba of Oberekkai ran away, and he brought a legal action in court for her return. She was his "<term>member</term>" and accused him of practicing witchcraft against her because, seven years earlier, he had cut a strip from the hem of her gown and hung it up before the <term>Juju</term>. She is a light-skinned woman with some claim to beauty, and during the eighteen years they had been married, she had no other act of unkindness to cite against her husband, nor any other reason for wishing to leave him. The old man pleaded pathetically that she should not be allowed to desert him, because all his other wives had quarreled with him for loving her so much more than any of them, and for giving her an unfair share of ornaments and presents of every kind. "Just recently," the old Chief said, "the Oberekkai women were dancing, so I adorned my wife with many traditional ornaments so that she could go and dance with them. When the dance was over, she came and piled up all the property of her dead mother—who had been my '<term>member</term>'—outside my door, saying that by doing so, she would free herself from me forever."

Until twenty years ago, the ordinary price of a slave was:

IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

At the time of my arrival, the price had risen to thirty pieces of cloth or one cow—that is, £7 10s. to £10.

As a general rule, slaves were treated kindly, as "members" are at the present time, but cases of cruelty were not unknown and are still occasionally brought before the Native Court.

Once at Nsan, a man came forward to beg that he might be allowed to settle in the Oban District instead of having to stay with the master whose slave he had formerly been, and in whose house he still lived as a "member." He said that this man had recently returned from the funeral of a neighboring chief and had been overheard saying to his son, "Formerly, when such a great chief died, slaves were sacrificed around the grave so that they might serve him in the spirit world. Now it is the day of the white man's rule, and we are no longer allowed to do this. Nevertheless, I have thought of what to do. One by one, I will kill my 'members' as if by accident. Half I will leave alive for you. Some we will hold down while crossing a river; to others, we will give poison and say they died of snake bites or other causes. Then, when I come to die, they will all be waiting to serve me, so that I will not be poor and unattended among the ghosts."

On another occasion, while I was at Niaji, a large Juju dance was held. The head priest, a man named Erim—who was feared for his magic by the entire countryside—attended dressed in his full robes. Around his ankles, he wore deep bands covered with little bells. In one hand, he carried green boughs, which he kept waving before my eyes, and in the other, his Juju staff, which he pointed almost continuously in my direction. Both actions were performed with such peculiar intentness that it would have been impossible not to suspect some serious motive. He was obviously trying to work magic on the "white man," whose presence appeared to have a disturbing effect on him. Inquiries led to the following case coming before the Native Court:

Ekpiri Otu, who had once been a slave-wife of Erim's, after taking an oath on the Juju "Mfam," said:

> "Before I make my statement, I beg that the <term>D. C.</term> <note>District Commissioner</note> will protect me so that no man shall be able to hurt me because of what I may say."

# TREATMENT OF "MEMBERS"

“Erim was my first husband; I know him well. His belly contains poison, and his body all over is poisonous. He is a great Juju man and has a medicine which protects him, so that if anything like this happens, he can gain favor for himself by magic, ensuring the Court shall decide for him.

“One of his wives reproached him for having married me, because she said that he should not have wedded a slave. He therefore divorced me in the name of his wife. In the month of February, at night, the woman came and told me that a tree had fallen down in the farm. The next day Erim found me working there and said I was to give up work and go away. The next morning, when the day broke, they went and cut off part of my farm and gave it to a young boy. The big tree had fallen in the corner, and the owner of the next farm complained that it had spoiled her crops. She said, ‘You are just like a younger sister of Talbot’s,’ because whenever she called me a ‘wild animal’ or anything like that, I said, ‘I will go and complain to Talbot.’ I answered her, ‘If I were his younger sister, this very day I would go and live near him; then you could harm me no more.’ 

Then the woman, named Ode, told her husband that I was going to take them to Court before Talbot. I was in the farm. They came and asked my daughter, ‘Where is your mother?’ She said, ‘She has gone to the farm.’ Erim said in front of my three children that he would meet me on the road and kill me, so that I might not take them down to Oban. He also said, ‘I should like to die with my slaves. When Otu died, no one killed slaves to bury with him, as was formerly the custom with chiefs.’ 

When I came back, I found him in my house. He called, ‘Come here.’ Then he caught hold of me, pushed me down on the floor, and began to kick and beat me. Our custom is that whenever a master beats a slave, the slave cannot touch the master. My children all cried out. He said, ‘You cry because of your mother.’ My daughter Omin was in the fatting-house, but he beat me so badly that she came out. He caught her and pushed her away. Once a small boy of nine, a mere bag of skin and bone, ran into the office. He stated that he was bought from his parents only two years ago, but that his master dared not bring him into the town, because "Makara" (the white man) has his eyes everywhere; he walks always up and down, and would say at once, "Who is this 'man'? It is a new face. I do not know him." So he kept me in the bush at a farm that he has. There he beat me often for no cause. Then I heard the other "members" say, "The white man fears no one, not even great chiefs. If the smallest slave goes to him he will see that justice is done." Then the others asked, "Shall we bring a complaint of our master's cruelty before him?" But each one answered, "No, lest he kill us, when the white man does not know." But I know that the "white man" will not let him hurt me, so I come to bring my complaint."

Such, given in their own words, are the darkest cases brought by "members" against the Heads of their Houses. Now, the cases brought by the latter against "members" far outweigh in number those against themselves, and there is little doubt but that, at the present time, the pendulum is beginning to swing too far in the other direction. This is only natural, however, after the centuries of repression imposed by the free-born. That, even in the old days, these modern <term>helots</term> occasionally turn on their masters is shown by many legends,

### HOW SLAVES USED TO LIE IN WAIT TO KILL THE FREE-BORN.

#### BY ETA NDOM OF NIAJI.

A woman named Ome once left her town to visit a friend who lived some distance away. She took her daughter, Ara, and a female slave called Ngonne with her. When they came to a shallow stream, Ome said, “Let us bathe here;” but Ngonne answered, “The water is not good. Let us go further.”

After a while, they came to the banks of a river where the water was deep in some places but shallow in others. Here the slave woman said, “The water is good; let us bathe.”

While they washed, Ngonne said to her mistress, “Let me rub your back.” No sooner had the other turned around than the slave pushed her into a deep hole where a crocodile was living. The beast rose and caught the woman, and Ngonne took the child and went back to the town where they had come from.

When they arrived, the slave carried her mistress’s child to her own sweetheart's house. As they entered the compound, the people greeted her and said, “Welcome, Ngonne. Where is Ome?” To this, she only answered through her nose, “Hong, Hong, Hong.” <note>This is the noise made by the Ngonne, a Hornbill—a bird with a very long beak.</note> Her sweetheart cooked and brought food for her to eat. Ara wanted to eat also, but the slave woman drove her away and would give her no food except for two pieces of plantain. For a long time, Ngonne acted this way toward her mistress’s daughter, eating all the good food herself and giving very little of what was left over to the child.

One day, birds were spoiling the beans in the field, so the slave woman called Ara and ordered her to go there and drive them away. All day the little girl wept in the field, and a man who was cutting palm kernels came down from the tree to find out who was crying so bitterly. He found no one, for she had wandered away from the farm, and came at

To this they agreed, took their nets, and went.

The next time the slave cooked <term>chop</term> and began to eat without giving any to Ara, the girl called out in a loud voice, "Why do you eat before me? Do you not know that you are my mother's slave?"

Ngonne replied, "You have not said such a thing as this for a very long time. I think that something must have happened."

At that moment, Ome came out from her hiding place. In her hand was a sharp knife. She caught the slave and killed her.

At that time, slaves were always seeking to kill their masters and hide the bodies. Since Ngonne tried to destroy her mistress, however, people have watched their slaves closely, lest they should do harm.

# CHAPTER XXXI

## FOLKLORE

UNLIKE most primitive peoples, whose legends deal mostly with the terrifying, there are many tender and gracious touches in Ekoi stories, while several show a distinct sense of humor. In many, too, traces may be found—half-understood or wholly misapplied—of beliefs that have come down from ages so remote that they are forgotten except for such faint echoes. Some refer to times when snakes still possessed hands and feet *; and one, Oporopóotop, appears to be a relic of times when farms were actually subject to the destruction of dinosaurs and similar monsters.

Much of the charm of these tales was undoubtedly due to the manner of their telling; for the Ekoi are wonderful storytellers, and many, especially the young boys, recount their legends in a sort of dramatic performance, chanting and crooning at times until the words almost turn into song.

Most of the tales recorded were taken from sources that had never before come into contact with white influence. Some, despite modern touches, show a close resemblance to well-known stories from the *Arabian Nights*, for instance, "The Treasure House in the Bush." In some, again, I have imagined that echoes of Herodotus may still be traced. All have been recorded exactly as they were told, except for the one on page 337, "How all Stories and all History came on Earth." The introduction to this was told by one man, and the main part of the story by another, but the *conclusion* so obviously belongs to the same story—of which the first otherwise disconnected fragment forms the beginning—that it seemed better, in this one case, to combine the two.

One of the most persistent characters in these tales is the

<margin>1)</margin>
A woman covered with sores, who meets all travelers to the underworld and helps them to success or dooms them to failure, depending on whether their goodness of heart is sufficient to pass her tests. In only one case (p. 62) is this figure male.

<margin>2)</margin>
Another interesting and persistent character in Ekoi mythology is the "Lame Boy," already mentioned in the "Stilt Dances"* who plays the role of "Good Fairy" wherever he appears. As will be seen from the story "How Fire first came on Earth," he holds much the same position for the Ekoi as Prometheus held among the Greeks. In one tale, "Ada, the Forest Demon," the character is female.

<margin>|</margin>
My knowledge of such things is unfortunately too limited for my opinion to carry weight in the matter; yet I venture to think that the importance of the "Lame Boy"—not only among the Ekoi, but in West African ritual generally—has not yet been appreciated by Europeans. Otherwise, the significance of the lame man dragged around Benin would surely have been clear to Mr. Northcote Thomas; yet he passes it by with only the remark, "Another custom commanded that once a year a lame man should be dragged around the city, and then as far as a place on the Enyai road called Adaneha. This was probably a ceremony of purification."†

Another point that may perhaps be worth mentioning is that, as in the case of Persephone, no visitor to the underworld may eat food offered by the ghosts, otherwise they will never return to the sunlight. Usually, the necessary food is provided by the Lame Boy or the Woman with Sores. In one case, tomatoes were given by the ghost of a dead sister,‡ and those not eaten were brought back to be planted in the world above. In another case,§ eggplants were given by the Chieftainess of the Ghosts to the last visitor she allowed to return from her kingdom, on the condition that they should be distributed among the living.

## HOW ALL STORIES AND ALL HISTORY CAME AMONG MEN.

->BY AGRA OF MBEBAN.<-

Mouse goes everywhere. Through rich men’s houses she creeps, and she visits even the poorest. At night, with her little bright eyes, she watches the doing of secret things, and no treasure-chamber is so safe that she cannot tunnel through and see what is hidden there.

In the old days, she wove a story-child from everything she saw, and to each of these she gave a gown of different colors—white, red, blue, or black. The stories became her children; they lived in her house and served her because she had no children of her own.

---

Now, in olden days, a sheep and a leopard lived in the same town. In the course of time, the Leopard became pregnant, and the Sheep did too. The Sheep bore a daughter and the Leopard a son.

There was a famine in all the land, so the Leopard went to the Sheep and said, “Let us kill our children and eat them.” The Sheep thought, “If I do not agree, she may kill my child in spite of me,” so she answered, “Very well.”

Then the Sheep went and hid her own baby. She took everything she owned and sold it for a little dried meat. This she cooked and set before the Leopard, and they both ate together. The Leopard killed her own child and ate that also.

In another year, they both became pregnant once more. This

Once again the townsfolk were hungry. Leopard came as before and said, "Let us kill these children also." She cooked these and set them before Leopard as she had done before, instead of her baby. Leopard ate and said nothing.

Some years later, Leopard sent for Sheep and said, "Come; today you shall feast with me."

Sheep went and found a great calabash on the table. She opened it and found it full of food, with three spoons laid ready.

She was astonished and questioned Leopard. "Previously we used two spoons, you and I. Why should there be three today?"

Leopard laughed, opened the door of the inner room, and called, "Come, daughter, let us eat." Her daughter came, and they all ate together. Then the mother said, "When my first child came, I killed and ate him because we were very hungry; but when I learned how you had saved your child, I thought, 'Next time I also will play such a trick on Sheep.' Therefore, I saved my daughter alive."

After that, Sheep went home and tended to her two children. Years passed, and all the daughters began to grow up. Leopard put her child into the <term>fatting-house</term> <note>A traditional place of seclusion where young women are fed and prepared for marriage.</note>. Then she went to Sheep and said, "Give me one of your daughters to stay with mine in the fatting-house. She is alone and cannot eat."

Now Sheep and both her daughters were quite black, but there were some young goats in the house which served them as slaves. These were white, so before Sheep sent her daughter to Leopard's house, she rubbed her all over with white chalk, then dyed one of the young goats black, and sent them together.

When they both arrived at the house, Leopard thought that the goat was Sheep's daughter. All three of the young ones were placed in the <term>fatting-house</term>. During the night, Leopard entered the room, took the goat and killed her, then cooked the meal and gave it to her own daughter to eat, thinking it was the daughter of Sheep whom she had slain.

The door was old and it broke, and all the stories on earth, and all the histories ran out. After that they never went back to live with Mouse anymore, but remained running up and down over all the earth.

### HOW THE FIRST RAIN CAME.
->BY OKUN ASERE OF MFAMOSING.<-

Once, long ago, a daughter was born to Obassi Osaw, and a son to Obassi Nsi. When both had reached marriageable age, Nsi sent a message to say “Let us exchange children. I will send my son so that he may marry one of your maidens. Send your daughter down to my town, so that she may become my wife.”

To this Obassi Osaw agreed. So the son of Nsi went up to the heavens carrying many fine gifts, and Ara, the sky maiden, came down to live on earth. With her came seven male slaves and seven female slaves, whom her father sent so that they might work for her, so that she should not be called upon to do anything herself.

One day, very early in the morning, Obassi Nsi said to his new wife, “Go, work in my farm!” She answered, “My Father gave me the slaves so that they should work instead of me. Therefore send them.” Obassi Nsi was very angry and

“Go at once to the river and bring water for the household.”

She answered, “I am weary from working on the farm; may my slaves not at least do this while I rest?”

Again Nsi refused and drove her out, so she went back and forth many times, carrying the heavy jars. Night had fallen long before she had brought enough.

Next morning Nsi ordered her to do the most menial tasks, and all day long he kept her at work cooking, fetching water, and making fire. That night again she was very weary before she could lie down to rest. At dawn on the third morning he said, “Go and bring in a lot of firewood.” Now the girl was young and unused to work, so as she went she wept, and the tears were still falling when she came back carrying her heavy burden.

As soon as Nsi saw her enter, he called to her, “Come here and lie down before me. . . . I wish to shame you in the presence of all my people. . . .” At that, the girl wept even more bitterly.

No food was given to her until midday the next day, and even then, it was not enough. When she had finished eating all there was, Nsi said to her:

“Go out and bring in a great bundle of <term>fish poison</term>.”

The girl went into the bush to look for the plant, but as she walked through the thick undergrowth, a thorn pierced her foot. She lay down alone. All day long she lay there in pain, but as the sun set, she began to feel better. She got up and managed to limp back to the house.

When she entered, Nsi said to her, “Early this morning I ordered you to go and collect fish poison. You have stayed away all day and done nothing.” So he drove her into the goat pen and said, “Tonight you shall sleep with the goats; you shall not enter my house.”

That night she ate nothing. Early the next morning, one of the slaves opened the door of the goat pen and found the girl lying inside, with her foot all swollen and sore. She could not walk.

so for five days she was left with the goats. After that her foot began to get better.

Next she lifted it onto a tree trunk that lay by the side of the river, and, kneeling beneath it, tried to pull it onto her head in that way; but the pot fell and broke, and in falling a sharp sherd cut off one of her ears. The blood poured down from the wound, and she began to weep again, but suddenly thought:

"My Father is alive, my mother is alive, I do not know why I stay here with Obassi Nsi. I will go back to my own Father."

Then she set out to find the road by which Obassi Osaw had sent her to earth. She came to a high tree, and from it saw a long rope hanging. She said to herself:

"This is the way by which my Father sent me."

She caught the rope and began to climb. Before she reached halfway she grew very weary, and her sighs and tears mounted up to the kingdom of Obassi Osaw. When she reached the midpoint she stayed and rested a while. Afterward she climbed on again.

After a long time she reached the top of the rope, and found herself on the border of her Father's land. Here she sat down almost worn out with weariness, and still weeping.

When the Angbu Club had cut off the ears of the son of Obassi Nsi, they brought them before Obassi Osaw and drove the lad back on the road toward Earth, just as they had been ordered.

Osaw took the ears and made a great Juju, and because of this, a strong wind arose and drove the boy toward Earth. On its wings, it carried all the suffering of Ara and the tears she had shed because of the cruelty of Obassi Nsi. The boy stumbled along, half-blinded by the rain, and as he went, he thought:

> "Obassi Osaw may do to me whatever he chooses. He has never done an unkind thing before. It is only in return for my father’s cruelty that I must suffer all this."

So his tears mixed with those of Ara and fell toward Earth as rain.

Until that time, there had been no rain on the earth. It fell for the first time when Obassi Osaw created the great wind and drove out the son of his enemy.

### HOW THE MOON FIRST CAME INTO THE SKY.

->BY OKUN ASERE OF MFAMOSING.<-

In a certain town, there lived Njomm Mbui (Juju sheep). He became great friends with Etuk (antelope), whose home was in the "bush."

When the two animals grew up, they went out and cleared land for farms. Njomm planted plantains in his, while Etuk planted his with coco-yams.

When the time came for the fruit to ripen, Njomm went to his farm and cut a bunch of plantains, while Etuk dug up some of his coco-yams.

This was arranged, and Etuk said to Njomm, “Try to pound some fufu.” Njomm tried it and found it very good. He gave some to Etuk. The latter ate all he wanted, then took the bunch of plantains and hung it up in his house.

The next morning, he found that the fruit had grown soft, so he did not care to eat it. He therefore took the plantains and threw them away in the bush.

During the day, Mbui came along and smelled the plantains. He looked around until he found them, then picked up one and began to eat. They were very sweet. He ate his fill, then went on, and later met a crowd of the Nshum people (apes). He said to them, “Today I found a very sweet thing in the bush.”

In the course of time, Etuk grew hungry again, and Njomm said to him, “If you are hungry, why don’t you tell me?”

He went to his farm and got four bunches of plantains. As he came back, he met the monkey people. They begged for some of his fruit, so he gave it to them.

After they had eaten all there was, they in their turn went on and met a herd of wild boars (Ngumi). To these they said, “There is very fine food to be obtained from Njomm and Etuk.”

The Ngumi therefore came and questioned Etuk, “Where can coco be found?” and Etuk answered, “The coco belongs to me.”

The boars begged for some, so Etuk took a basket, filled it at his farm, and gave it to them.

After they were satisfied, they went on their way and the next morning met Njokk (the elephant).

Njokk at once ran and asked the two friends, “From where do you get so much food?” They said, “Wait a little.”

Elephant. After the latter had eaten all this, he thanked them and went away.

Now, not far from the two farms, there was a great river called Akarram (the One which goes around). Deep down in the middle of it lived Crocodile. One day, Mfong went down into the water to drink, and from him Crocodile learned that plenty of food was to be had nearby.

At this, Crocodile came out of the water and began walking toward the farms. He went to Njomm and Etuk and said:

“I am dying of hunger; please give me food.”

Etuk said, “I will give all I have to the animals who are my friends, but I will give you nothing, for you are no friend of mine;” but Njomm said:

“I do not like you very much, yet I will give you one bunch of plantains.”

Crocodile took them and said, “Do not close your door tonight when you lie down to sleep. I will come back and buy more food from you at a great price.”

He then went back to the water and sought out a python who lived there. To the python, he said:

“I have found two men on land who have plenty of food.” Python said, “I am hungry too. Will you give me something to eat?”

So Crocodile gave him some of the plantains he had brought. When Python had tasted them, he said, “How sweet it is! Will you go back again and bring more?” Crocodile said, “Will you give me something with which to buy it?” and Python answered, “Yes. I will give you something with which you can buy the whole farm.”

At this, he took a shining stone from inside his head and gave it to Crocodile. The latter started back toward the farm. As he went, night fell and the whole road grew dark, but he held the shining stone in his jaws, and it lit up his path so that the whole way was bright. When he neared the home of the two friends, he hid the stone and called:

“Come out, and I will show you something I have brought.”

"I am trying to gather palm kernels, but I cannot do so, for it is very dark amid these great leaves."

Njomm said to him, "It is useless to try to do such a thing in the dark. Are you blind?"

Effion answered, "I am not blind. Why do you ask?"

Then Njomm said, "Good; if you are not blind, I beg you to throw me down only one or two palm kernels, and in return I will show you a thing more bright and glorious than any you have seen before."

Effion replied, "Wait a minute, and I will try to throw a few down to you. Afterwards you shall show me the shining thing as you said."

He then threw down three palm kernels, which Njomm took, and stayed his hunger a little. The latter then called, "Please try to climb down. We will go together to my house."

Effion tried hard, and after some time he stood safely at the foot of the tree by the side of Njomm.

As soon as they got to his house, Njomm said, "Will you wait here a little while I go to question the townspeople?"

First he went to Etuk and asked, "Will you not give me a single coco to eat? See, the thing which I bought at the price of all that I had turns darkness to light for you, but for me, I die of hunger."

Etuk said, "I will give you nothing. Take back the thing for which you sold your all, and we will stay in our darkness as before."

Then Njomm begged of all the townsfolk that they would give him ever so little food in return for the light he had bought for them. Yet they all refused.

So Njomm went back to his house and took the shining stone, and gave it to Effion Obassi, saying:

"I love the earth folk, but they do not love me. Now take the shining thing for which I gave my whole possessions. Go

Then Effion took the stone and went back the way he had come. He climbed up the palm tree, and the great leaves raised themselves upward, pointing to the sky, and lifted him until, from their tips, he could climb into heaven.

When he reached his home, he sent for and called all the Lords of the Sky and said, “Today I have brought back a thing that can shine so that all the earth will be lit. From now on, everyone on earth or in heaven will be able to see at the darkest hour of the night.”

The chiefs looked at the stone and wondered. Then they consulted together and made a box. Effion said, “Make it so that the stone can shine out from only one side.”

When the box was finished, he set the globe of fire inside and said, “Behold, the stone is mine. From now on, all the people must bring me food. I will no longer go to seek any for myself.”

For some time they brought him plenty, but after a while they grew tired. Then Effion covered the side of the box so that the stone could not shine until they brought him more. That is the reason why the moon is sometimes dark, and people on earth say, “It is the end of the month. The sky people have grown weary of bringing food to Effion Obassi, and he will not let his stone shine out until they bring a fresh supply.”

Around five o'clock, Ebopp called out, "Let us go back to the old town now, for it is very far away."

At last, he went down to the place where they were making palm oil by the river. Near there lived <term>Iku</term> (the Water Chevrotain). Ebopp explained his trouble and begged for help, but Iku said, "I am very sorry for you, but I have nothing to give."

Ebopp was quite discouraged by now and turned to go away full of sorrow. When Iku saw this, he said, "Wait a minute; there is one thing I can do. You know that I have the 'four eyes.' I will give you two, and with them, you can buy all that you need."

From out of his head, he took the two eyes with which he used to see in the dark. They shone so brightly that Ebopp knew they were worth a great price. He took them home and showed them to his wife and his friend Mbaw.

The latter said, "From today, you are freed from all anxiety. With those, you can buy all that is needed."

The next morning, they gathered together all that had been collected: the plantains and the two shining eyes. Ebopp, Mbaw, and Akpan carried the loads between them. They set out for the dwelling place of <term>Obassi Osaw</term>.

When they reached the entrance of the town, Akpan Anwan began to weep bitterly. She threw down her burden and ran to the spot where her sister lay buried. Then she lay down on the grave and would not rise again.

Then Osaw said, “All that you brought has been eaten. If you can give us no more, you shall not take my daughter back with you to your country.”

Ebopp went to find his friend and told him what Obassi had said.

“Shall I sell the two eyes?” he asked. “They are worth hundreds and hundreds of plantains and many pieces of cloth, but if I sell them now, the people are so hungry that they will only give a small price.”

Mbaw said, “Do not worry. See, I will teach you how to gain more sense.”

“You hold one in your hand, and it is a large thing like a great shining stone, but if you put it in a mortar and grind it down, it will become not one, but many, and you can sell some of the small pieces.”

This Ebopp did, and he ground up the great bright stones which had been Iku’s eyes until they became like shining sand.

Then they went and got a black cap, which they filled with the fragments.

Mbaw said, “Now go and look around the town until you find someone who can sell what we need.”

Ebopp did so, and in the house of Effion Obassi, he saw great stores hidden—food and palm wine, palm oil in jars, and rum for the sacrifice.

Ebopp said to Effion, “If you will sell all this to me, I will give you in exchange something that will make all the townsfolk bow down before you.”

He brought the cap outside and opened it before them. All the shining things fell out. As they fell, a strong breeze came and caught them and blew them all over the town. They lay on the roads and on the floors of the compounds, each like a little star.

All the children came around and began picking them up. They gathered and gathered. In the daytime they could not see them, but every night they went out and sought for the shining things. Each one that they picked up they put in a box. At last, many had been gathered together and shone like a little sun in the box. At the end of about a month, nearly all had been collected. They could not shut the lid, however, because the box was too full, so when a great breeze came by, it blew all the shining things about again. That is why sometimes we have a small moon and plenty of stars shining around it, while sometimes we have a big moon and hardly any stars are to be seen. The children take a month to fill the box again.

### HOW THE TWO BIGGEST STARS CAME INTO THE SKY.

Obassi Osaw had three sons. Two of these he loved, but Ndifemm, the third, he did not love.

One day the three brothers went out to see what had been caught in the traps they had set. The two favorite sons found nothing, but Ndifemm found an animal in each of his six traps. Four of the beasts he “dashed” <note>In this context, "dashed" means to give as a gift or share.</note> between his two brothers, and the other two he took home to his father. Obassi refused them, but accepted from his other two sons those which Ndifemm had given them.

Another day, Obassi ordered his three children each to dig a hole. They did so. He went and examined the work and said, “I find the two holes well done,” but to Ndifemm he said, “Your hole is not deep enough.”

The boy began to dig deeper, but one of his brothers went to him very softly and said, “Our father is attempting to kill you. Will you go to consult the charm? That will tell you what you should do.”

Ndifemm, therefore, went to Nyopp (Porcupine) and asked him to practice the charm.

### HOW THE SUN CAME INTO THE SKY.

->BY OKUN ASERE OF MFAMOSING.<-

Once there lived a man named Agbo and his wife named Nchun. They had a daughter called Afion. When the latter was about fifteen years old, her father and mother agreed that it was time to put her in the <term>fatting-house</term>. So they sent for an old woman named Umaw, who was very wise in such matters, and told her to prepare everything. She came and made all ready, and then said, “There is nothing more to be done. I will go back to my own place.”

The parents gave her two bottles of palm oil and two pieces of dried meat. To the townsfolk, the father also gave many demijohns of palm wine. He took ten pieces of dried meat, cooked them, and called all the people to a feast, because his daughter had entered the fatting-house that day.

After about four months the mother, Nchun, said to Afion, “You have stayed long enough. You may come out tomorrow.”

Then the father gathered several demijohns of palm wine—the kind that is drawn from the tops of the palm trees—and five pieces of dried meat. The mother also took the same amount of meat and drink. The father announced to the townsfolk:

“My daughter is going to clean her face tomorrow. Let all men stay in the town.” Next morning the parents cooked ten calabashes full of <term>chop</term> for the people, who feasted all that day.

In the evening the father took his daughter into the other

“I do not care much if you kill me. I would rather die than marry such a terrible being as you.”

As soon as Eyo heard this, he stretched out his hands and truly killed her.

During all this time, the small boy had hidden himself where he could see everything that happened. He watched the terrible visitor draw the body into the middle room. Next, he saw him go into the inner place where Nchun kept the fine mats. He took four of these and covered the <term>fatting-girl</term>. Next, he went into another place where the fine cloths were kept. Of these he again took four, along with four blankets and two small loincloths. All these he laid over the dead girl.

After this, Eyo left the house and stood in the little courtyard at the back. He began to lift his body up to the sky. He was so long that, although he tried all day, six o’clock in the evening had come and he had not quite finished. Some of him was in the sky and some still remained upon earth.

When Agbo and Nchun came back from their farm, the small boy crept out from his hiding place and said to them:
“The man who killed your daughter is a very tall man.”

<summary>In this folk tale, the Sun (Eyo) attempts to woo a girl named Afion; when she refuses him because of his frightening size, he kills her and begins his ascent into the sky. A young boy witnesses the murder and the Sun's transition from Earth to the heavens, later reporting the event to the girl's parents.</summary>

Father and mother began to weep. They took the body and called all the townsfolk together for the burial.

The people came with four guns. They wished to shoot the man who had killed the <term>fatting-girl</term>. At the back of the house, they found him. They could not see his whole body, but only his feet. With their four guns, they shot at these. Then he gave a great leap and drew his feet up after the rest of him into the sky.

A fine house was standing there ready. Eyo entered and closed the door so that he might be safe from the guns of the townsmen. In the morning, around six o’clock, he opened a window and looked out a little way, very cautiously. When no one shot at him, he felt safer and put his face all the way out. All day he looked down in case Afion was not dead and he might see her once more. The people were busy away at their farms. At six o’clock they came back, so he drew his face in again, lest they should begin to shoot once more.

That is the reason why you only see the sun in the daytime. In the evening, he draws back into his house and shuts the windows and doors.

### HOW SUN AND MOON WENT UP TO THE SKY.
->BY ITE OKONNI OF AKING.<-

Obassi Nsi had three sons, named Eyo (Sun), Ejirum (Darkness), and ‘Mi (Moon). The first two he loved, but the last he did not love. One day Nsi called to ‘Mi and said:

“Go into the bush, catch a leopard, and bring him to me.”

‘Mi went sadly away, and as he reached the outskirts of the town, he began to weep. A man named Isse saw him and called, “What is the matter?” ‘Mi answered, “My father does not love me and is sending me to catch a leopard in the bush in order to destroy me.”

The man said, “Take comfort; I will give you a ‘medicine’ which will make you successful.” He went away but soon returned with what he had promised and rubbed the “medicine” on the boy’s hands.

“Even if you yourself did not blind my son, you must still come up to me.”

"Here are forty pieces of cloth. Will you take them to Osaw and plead for me?"

Eyo started on his journey and had reached about halfway when he saw five beautiful women standing at the entrance to a town. No sooner had he seen them than he forgot all about his errand and began to sell the cloth for plantains, palm oil, and palm wine, with which he made a feast for the beautiful women. There he stayed for some weeks, then took what was left of the goods and went on a little further until he came to another town, where he found two more women as beautiful as the first. For four years he stayed at one or the other of the towns, traveling back and forth between them.

After four years, when Nsi found that Eyo did not come back or send any message, he called to his son 'Mi and said:

"The case which I have before Obassi Osaw has taken a long time to finish. Go to Nsann (Thunder town) and fetch a cow from there which you will find. When you have brought it away, take it as a gift to Obassi Osaw and settle my case for me."

'Mi answered, "Very well;" and his mother called to him and said:

"Do what you can for your father, who is innocent in the eyes of Obassi Osaw, but take care of yourself when you reach Nsann town. Let no one know the place where you sleep, lest you should perish in the night."

'Mi answered, "I will do what I can."

Next morning he set forth, and before evening he had reached Nsann. The people asked him:

"Where will you sleep tonight?" He answered, "I will sleep among the goats." When all was still, he left the goat pen in the darkness and went to the <term>Egbo house</term> <note>a communal building used by a traditional secret society</note>, where he lay down and slept.

At midnight, a thunderbolt struck the shed where the goats were herded and killed them all.

Early in the morning, the people came together and opened the door. When they saw the dead goats but could not find the boy, they were much astonished. As they stood wondering, 'Mi came forward and said:

"If I were not a clever boy, the bolt would have killed me. As it is, I have saved myself."

Everybody in the town was sorry for the lad and said, “Let us give him the cow to take to his father.” So the boy set out homeward, well content.

When ‘Mi reached his father’s house and led the cow before him, Nsi said very softly to himself, so that he thought no one could hear:

> “What can I do to kill this son of mine?”

‘Mi heard him, and the next morning he took the gun which his mother had given him and went into the bush to hunt. First he shot Ise, the little grey duiker, and next Ngumi (the wild boar). He carried these home and brought them before his father, but the latter said:

> “I will not eat of them.”

So ‘Mi took his kill away sadly and gave it to his mother. The woman cooked the meat in a delicate way and then took it to her husband, who ate gladly of what he had previously refused; but when he learned what she had done, he said:

> “From today, take your son away from here. Neither of you shall live in my town anymore.”

When ‘Mi learned of this, he also was very angry. He took his gun and his machete and went to find his friend Isse, who had given him the “leopard medicine” years before. To his grief, he heard that this good friend had died while he himself was away at Nsann. So he went sadly out into the bush to hunt, so that his mother might not starve. After a while, he saw an Ikomme (squirrel) standing between the thick branches. He raised his gun to shoot, but in a moment the whole place grew dark. A voice called from the darkness behind him, “‘Mi, ‘Mi,” and he answered, “Who calls?” The voice cried, “I am your dead friend. Tell me now, which do you choose: to die or to live?” ‘Mi answered, “I am willing to die. Why should I live when my father seeks to kill me?”

After he had spoken, a deep sleep fell upon him. When he awoke, the whole place was cleared of trees. The sun was shining brightly, and before him stood a long table on which were set dried meat, biscuits, rum, and palm wine, and all kinds of gin. Then he saw Isse walking up and down as he had in life, directing everything, while many people were busily working all around.

### WHY THE SUNSET IS SOMETIMES RED AND STORMY.

In the beginning of things, Obassi Osaw and Obassi Nsi lived in towns some distance apart. The former had no sons, but the latter had three. The first of them was a great thief, the second was the same, and when they stole anything, their Father had to pay for it.

Now Obassi had great farms and plantations outside the town. Sometimes cows ate his yams; so one day he came home and put powder in his gun but no shot, meaning to frighten the beasts away the next time they came. During his absence, the two bad sons went and put shot in the gun. So when he fired at the cows, one of them died.

Obassi Nsi cried out and went back to the town. When he reached it, he told the owner, “I shot your cow by accident;” but the man replied:

“Then I must kill you, just the same as my cow.”

A meeting was held, and the townsfolk begged the man to accept another cow in exchange for the one he had lost, but he refused to do so and still said that Obassi must die.

Next morning, therefore, Obassi said to his third son, “I have to die today;” but the latter cried:

“How can you die? The first son and second son are fully grown, but I am still small. Do not leave me until I am grown up.”

The next day, six more men came and asked the same thing, but the lad said, “Wait a minute and I will see what can be done.” Then he went to the old woman and told her what had happened. She said, “Go to Porcupine, and get him to perform the charm.”

### HOW ALL THE RIVERS FIRST CAME ON EARTH.

->BY OKUN ASERE OF MFAMOSING.<-

Now up to this time all water was kept in the kingdom of Obassi Osaw. On earth there was not a single drop.

On the third morning, very early, Obassi Osaw put the water charm in a calabash, and bound it firmly with tie-tie <note>vines used as rope</note>. Etim 'Ne thanked Lord Obassi and set out on his way Earthward. Just before he came to the place where he had begun to clear a farm, he opened the calabash and found seven stones inside, clear as water. He made a small hole and laid one of the stones within it. Soon a little stream began to well out, then more and more, until it became a broad lake, as large as the distance from here to Ako.

Etim 'Ne went on and told his wife. They both rejoiced greatly, but he thought, "How is this? Can a man be truly happy, yet have no child?"

After two days his wife came to him and said, "Obassi is sending us yet another gift. Soon we shall no longer be alone on Earth, you and I."

When the due months had passed, she bore him seven children all at once. They were all sons. Later she became *enceinte* <note>pregnant</note> again, and this time bore seven daughters. After that she was tired, and never bore any more children.

In the course of time the girls were all sent to the fatting-house <note>a traditional place where young women were secluded and well-fed to prepare for marriage</note>. While they were there, Etim 'Ne pointed out to his seven sons where he would like them to build their compounds. When these were finished, he gave a daughter to each son and said, "Do not care that she is your sister. Just marry her. There is no one else who can become your wife."

The eldest son lived by the first water which Etim 'Ne had made, but to each of the others he gave a lake or river—seven in all.

had seven children: three girls and four boys. Etim 'Ne said, "It is good." He was very happy. As the children grew up, he sent them to other places.

Now the seven sons were all hunters. Three of them were good and brought some of their kill to give to their father, but four were very bad and hid all the meat so that they might keep everything for themselves.

When Etim 'Ne saw this, he left the rivers near the farms of his three good sons but took them away from the four bad boys. The latter were very sad when they found their water gone, so they consulted together and went and got palm wine. This they carried before their father and said:

> "We are seven, your children. First you gave the water to all. Now you have taken it away from us four. What have we done?"

Etim 'Ne answered, "Of all the meat you killed in the bush, you brought none to me. Therefore, I took away your rivers. Because you have come to beg me, I will forgive you and will give you four good streams. As your children grow and multiply, I will give you many."

After another year, the sons had children again. When the latter grew up, they went to different places and built their houses.

When these were ready, Etim 'Ne sent for all the children and said, "At dawn tomorrow, let each of you go down to the stream which flows by the farm of his father. Search in its bed until you find seven smooth stones. Some must be small and some big like the palm of your hand. Let each one go in a different direction, and after walking about a mile, lay a stone upon the ground. Then walk on again and do the same, until all are finished. Where you set a big stone, a river will come, and where you set a small stone, a stream will come."

All the sons did as they were bidden, except for one alone. He took a great basket and filled it with stones. Then he went to a place in the bush near his own farm. He thought, "Our father told us, if you throw a big stone, a big river will come. If I throw down all my stones together, so great a water will come that it will surpass the waters of all my brothers." Then he emptied his basket of stones all in one place, and, behold!

<summary>Etim 'Ne punishes his selfish sons by taking away their water but later relents, instructing his grandchildren on how to create new rivers and streams using magic stones. One greedy grandson attempts to create a superior river by dumping all his stones in a single spot.</summary>

water flowed from every side, so that his entire farm and all the land around it became covered with water. When he saw that it would not stop but threatened to overflow the whole earth, he became very afraid. He saw his wife running and called to her, “Let us go to my father.” Then they both ran as hard as they could toward the house of Etim ’Ne.

Before they reached it, the other children, who had been placing the smooth stones in the bush as their father had told them, heard the sound of the approaching waters. A great fear fell upon them, and they also dropped what remained and ran back to Etim ’Ne.

He also had heard the rushing of the water and knew what the bad son had done. He took the magic calabash in his hand and ran with his wife to a hill behind their farm. Many tall palm trees grew on this hill. He stood beneath the tallest of these, while his children gathered around one after another as they returned from the bush. Etim ’Ne held high the calabash which Obassi had given him and prayed:

> “Lord Obassi, do not let the good thing you gave for our joy turn to our harm.”

As he prayed, the water began to recede. It searched around until it found places where there had been no water. In each of these places, it made a bed for itself, large or small—some for broad rivers and some for little streams. Only where the bad son had emptied his basket did the water not retreat; instead, it remained as a great lake covering his entire farm. As a result, he was very hungry and had to beg from his brothers until the time came for the fruits to ripen on the new farm he had to clear.

After many days, Etim ’Ne called all his children together and told them the names of all the rivers and of every little stream. Then he said, “Let no one forget to remember me when I have left you, for it was I who gave water to all the earth so that everyone might be happy.”

Two days later, he died. In the beginning, there were no people on the earth and no water. It was Etim ’Ne who first came down to dwell with his old wife, Ejaw, and it was he who begged water from the god Obassi Osaw.
