### HOW THE LAME BOY BROUGHT FIRE FROM HEAVEN.

->BY OKON ASERE OF MFAMOSING.<-

In the beginning of the world, Obassi Osaw made everything, but he did not give fire to the people who were on earth.

Etim ’Ne said to the Lame Boy, “What is the use of Obassi Osaw sending us here without any fire? Go, therefore, and ask him to give us some.” So the Lame Boy set out.

Obassi Osaw was very angry when he received the message, and sent the boy back quickly to earth to reprimand Etim ’Ne for what he had asked. In those days the Lame Boy had not become lame, but could walk like other people.

When Etim ’Ne heard that he had angered Obassi Osaw, he set out himself for the latter's town and said:

“Please forgive me for what I did yesterday. It was by accident.” Obassi would not pardon him, though he stayed for three days begging forgiveness. Then he went home.

When Etim reached his town the boy laughed at him. “Are you a chief,” said he, “yet could get no fire? I myself will go and bring it to you. If they will give me none, I will steal it.”

That very day the boy set out. He reached the house of Obassi at evening time and found the people preparing food. He helped with the work, and when Obassi began to eat, he knelt down humbly until the meal was ended.

The master saw that the boy was useful and did not drive him out of the house. After he had served for several days, Obassi called to him and said, “Go to the house of my wives and ask them to send me a lamp.”

The boy gladly did as he was told, for it was in the house of the wives that fire was kept. He touched nothing, but waited until the lamp was given to him, then brought it back as quickly as possible. Once, after he had stayed for many days among the servants, Obassi sent him again, and this time one of the wives said, “You can light the lamp at the fire.” She went into her house and left him alone.

The boy took a firebrand and lit the lamp, then he wrapped the firebrand in plantain leaves and tied it up in his cloth, carried

The boy went to the bush outside the town where some dry wood was lying. He laid the burning stick among it, and blew until it caught fire. Then he covered it with plantain stems and leaves to hide the smoke, and went back to the house. Obassi asked, “Why have you been gone so long?” and the lad answered, “I did not feel well.”

That night, when all the people were sleeping, the thief tied his cloth together and crept to the end of the town where the fire was hidden. He found it burning, and took a glowing brand and some firewood and set out for home.

When Earth was reached once more, the lad went to Etim and said:

“Here is the fire which I promised to bring you. Send for some wood, and I will show you what we must do.”

So the first fire was made on earth. Obassi Osaw looked down from his house in the sky and saw the smoke rising. He said to his eldest son Akpan Obassi, “Go, ask the boy if it is he who has stolen the fire.”

Akpan came down to Earth and asked as his father had commanded him. The lad confessed, “I was the one who stole the fire. The reason why I hid it was because I was afraid.”

Akpan replied, “I bring you a message. Until now you have been able to walk. From today, you will not be able to do so anymore.”

That is the reason why the Lame Boy cannot walk. He was the one who first brought fire to Earth from Obassi’s home in the sky.

Tortoise and Ram were friends. One day they went to clear their farm, but only prepared a small bit. Next day they went back to do more, but found the whole place cleared. They wondered who had done all the work for them, but started to burn the ground with fire. After this they went home to rest, and when they got back next day, behold! all the earth was ready and tilled. They began planting yams, and the next day found that this too had been finished while they slept. They wondered

They wondered very much who had done this. It was a person named Oporopóotop.

Later the wives went and planted a few coco yams, and again, on their return, found the whole place planted with these also. Next they started sowing corn, but could not cover much ground on the first day. The second day, however, a great space was found to have been planted.

When the corn grew ripe, the owners of the farm went to gather it. They took a very few cobs at first, but to their surprise, the next day all had been harvested, and so it was with the other vegetables. The two friends got a little for themselves and for their wives, but the rest disappeared mysteriously.

Tortoise said to Ram, "What can we do to find out who has stolen our fruits and vegetables?" Ram said, "Let us watch." So Tortoise went to his wife and said, "Will you go today and watch the farm?" She agreed, and after waiting a while in the little house they had built, heard something moving in the bush. It sounded like a wind among the trees, but was caused by the coming of Oporopóotop. He came to the hut and knocked at the door, shouting in a loud voice, "Who is there?"

The woman answered, "I am the wife of Tortoise," and opened the door. The visitor entered and said to her, "Go and find some fruit in the farm, so that we may eat." She answered, "Someone has stolen nearly all our fruit." She went, however, and found a few corn cobs, which she brought back and roasted over the fire.

When the meal was finished, Oporopóotop said, "Will you scratch the <term>craw-craw</term> <note>a skin disease causing itchy sores or pustules</note> on my body?" This the woman did, but he cried, "You scratch too hard!" and suddenly swallowed her up!

At daybreak, the husband came to get his wife, but found no trace of her. He said to himself, "What can have happened to my wife? I will stay here until I find out what has become of her." So he made a fire on the ground and waited.

At evening time again a sound was heard, like the blowing of a wind through the bush. It was Oporopóotop. He knocked at the door as before and said, "Who is inside?"

Tortoise answered, "It is I," and opened the door. Oporopóotop entered and said, "Go and fetch some fruits so that we may eat."

Tortoise went and collected what he could. He brought it back, cooked it, and gave it to his visitor to eat. Again Oporopóotop said, “Scratch my <term>craw-craw</term> <note>a skin disease causing itchy sores or pustules</note>,” but, while his host obeyed, the monster exclaimed, “You are scratching too hard!” and before the latter could answer, he caught him and swallowed him up!

When daylight dawned, Ram also came to the farm, but he could find neither his friend nor the wife; so he sat down to await their return. At evening, Ram heard Oporopóotop coming, just as the others had. When the visitor asked, “Who is there?” Ram replied, “Why do you ask this? Does the whole earth belong to you?” And when the monster begged for food, Ram refused, whereupon they began to fight.

Now Oporopóotop was a fearful beast, bigger than all the animals on earth in our day. He was like a great lizard but covered with a hard shell, so that he could roll himself down from a high hill and yet take no harm. His head and neck were very long, like those of some birds, so that he could reach up to eat from the high trees. In color, he was a mixture of white and black. There were claws on his wings, though he could not fly, and on his feet were terrible claws. It was with these that he usually fought.

Nevertheless, in spite of the huge size of the beast and his great strength, Ram was more cunning than he. For a long time they fought, but at length Ram struck down his enemy with his horns and broke off his feet so that he died.

Oporopóotop was a great king in the bush, and when people planted new farms, he sent his servants to help them so that he might eat the first fruits when they were ripe. If Ram had not killed him, there would soon have been no more farms, as the people would all have died. How lucky it is that the bush is now free from such a monster!

### HOW PYTHONS LOST HANDS AND FEET.

There once was a Python whose wife was about to bear him a child. One day, while coming through the bush, he saw some ripe Aju fruits and plucked them, thinking, "Perhaps my wife would like these."

The woman ate them with great delight and, from that day on, kept begging her husband to bring her more. He went out to the bush to search but could not find any. She, however, threatened that unless more were brought to her, she would lose the child.

In those days, Pythons had hands and feet like men and could walk upright. Therefore, when he found no fruit in the bush to satisfy his wife’s desire, Python went to a man's farm where an Aju tree stood, and each day he plucked some of the fruit.

Now, the owner of the tree had a son named Monn-akat-chang-obbaw-chang (Child-without-feet-and-without-hands), because he had neither hands nor feet. One day, he complained to his father that someone was stealing their Aju and begged to be carried to the foot of the tree so that he might watch for the thief. The father consented to this.

When Nkimm (Python) came the next day, he found the tree guarded by a remarkable boy without hands or feet. As soon as the boy saw the snake, he called out, "Are you the person who steals my father's Aju?" Nkimm denied his guilt and said that this was the first time he had seen the tree, but he begged the boy to give him a few of the fruits for his sick wife.

When the parents heard the singing, they ran towards their son. In his hands, the father carried a great spear. When Nkimm saw this, he rushed off for his life in the opposite direction, throwing himself along the ground in the only way possible for him.

Since then, no man has been born without hands or feet, and no python or other snake has been born with them.

### WHY SNAKE HAS NEITHER HANDS NOR FEET.

->BY ITAMBO ASONG OF OBAN.<-

Obassi Nsi once made a farm. In it, he put three animals: Mfong (the cow), Mbui (the goat), and Nyaw (the snake). Cow and Goat were the gardeners, while Snake was ordered to collect the fruits and take them to the house of Obassi.

Before leaving them to their work, Obassi said, "You may not eat any of the fruits of this farm. Even if any plantains or other fruits fall down, you must not touch them."

One day, some strangers came from a distant town to visit Obassi; whereupon the latter sent Snake to his farm to bring back a supply of food for them. At that time, Snake had hands and feet just like all other creatures. The first day he went quickly and brought back a plentiful supply, but the second day, when he went again, Cow asked, "Why does our master want so many plantains?" Snake said, "He is feeding the strangers who have come to stay with him."

Goat said, "I do not quite understand. Do you mean that our master eats none of these good things, but only gives them to strangers?" The three of them debated the matter, and it was late when Snake returned with his load. Obassi was angry and beat him because he took so long on the way.

<summary>The first story concludes by explaining that a boy's trickery led to pythons losing their limbs and humans keeping theirs. A second story begins, describing how Obassi Nsi's animal servants—Cow, Goat, and Snake—began to question why they were forbidden from eating the fruit they harvested for their master's guests.</summary>

The next time Snake was sent to the farm, he said to Cow and Goat:
"I do not see why we should starve while all the food is eaten by strangers. Why should we not enjoy the fruits of our labors ourselves?"
The others agreed to this, and Cow sent Goat to cut plantains. They were ripe, and when Cow divided them, Goat said to him:
"You are the head man on the farm. You should eat first." At this, Cow began to eat and cried out, "Oh, very sweet plantains!" Then both the others joined him in eating.
Snake went and got yams. He came back and said to the others, "Do not tell anyone what I have done, for if my master heard, he would punish me."
Upon his return, Obassi was more annoyed than before. He said, "Why did you stay away so long? You already knew that there were strangers in the house."
The next day, Obassi sent Snake again, but this time he commanded one of his daughters, named Afion Obassi, to follow him secretly so that she might learn why Snake stayed so long at the farm.
When Afion arrived, she found Cow and Goat eating. She asked, "Who told you to eat the fruits in my father's farm?" They answered, "It was Snake who told us we could eat."
After the girl returned home, she told her father what she had seen. Obassi therefore sent for the three animals. When they stood before him, he asked, "How is it that you ate the fruit on my farm, which I had forbidden you to touch?" They answered, "It was Snake who taught us to eat."
Obassi said, "Each of you must suffer for disobeying my orders." To Cow he said, "From now on, when men pick plantains, they will keep the good part for themselves and throw only the rind to you." That is the reason why we always see Cow eating plantain skins. To Goat he said, "When people prepare their yams, the peelings only shall be your portion." That is why we see Goat eating the yam parings.
Obassi seized Snake, squeezed him, and pulled off his hands and feet. That is the reason why he no longer has these, unlike other animals.

### WHY LIZARD'S HEAD IS ALWAYS MOVING UP AND DOWN.

->By Ojong Itaroga.<-

In the old days, when all the beasts could speak like men, <term>Obassi Nsi</term> married many wives. These were the daughters of nearly all the animals on earth, and each creature who gave his daughter in marriage to Obassi received a very rich gift in return.

Now Tortoise also wanted a gift like the rest, but he had only sons and no daughter. He spent a long time thinking the matter over; at length he formed a plan. He called two of his sons and told them that he was about to give them to Obassi as wives, so they must take care never to let anyone see their nakedness. After warning them in this way, he dressed them in very rich robes, like girls, and they set forth.

When Tortoise and his two seeming daughters reached the hall where Obassi was sitting, he stepped forward and said:

> "I am the best of all your friends, for the rest have each given you one wife, but I alone bring two."

Obassi thanked him, and gave him in return twice as great a wealth as he had given to the others. "My lord," said Tortoise, "there is one thing I must tell you. No one must see my daughters' nakedness, or they will die."

"What a thing to say!" answered Obassi. "It would be death to any man to see one of my wives unclothed."

"I spoke," said Tortoise, "of their fellow women."

"Have no fear," answered Obassi; "since you have told me this, there is no danger of such a thing."

With that, Tortoise went away, rejoicing in his success, while Obassi handed the two new wives over to his head wife so that she might look after them, never suspecting that they were boys.

Not long after, their mistress discovered the truth of the matter. She went secretly to Obassi and told him that the two girls whom Tortoise had given him in marriage were in fact male.

This is the reason why lizards are seen to raise and lower their heads. They are still trying to get rid of the fu-fu ball given to them by the sons of Tortoise.

That is why Tortoise's trick has never been discovered to this day, and thus it is that Lizard lost her voice and her <term>Ndipp</term>, <note>The Efik word *Ndipp* refers to Lizard's female parts, borrowed by the sons of Tortoise in the previous episode.</note> and only gained in exchange the habit of lifting her head up and down.

> "Sir, you are eating. They have sent to call me because my friend is dead. I am looking for someone who will be able

### WHY THERE ARE NO MORE LIONS IN THE BUSH.

A man named Etim married a wife. After a time, she told him that a son was about to be born. He left home and went out hunting, but Nkí (lion) sprang out from the bush and killed him.

The wife remained in the care of a brother of her late husband. When the baby was born, this man took care of both of them. One day, when the boy was nearly grown up, the uncle called to him, saying, “My son.” The lad answered, “Do not call me that. I am no son of yours. My father was killed in the bush by Nkí.”

One day, the boy went out and collected a great quantity of palm kernels. He took these to the white traders and exchanged them for guns. When he reached home, he went to the bush near the town and climbed up a tree. In this tree, he made two seats, one high up and the other lower down. ### WHY BUSH FOWL (IKPAI) ALWAYS CALLS UP THE DAWN.

->BY NDUM AGURIMON OF NSAN.<-

A man once went into the bush with his wife to collect palm nuts. He saw a palm with ripe clusters upon it and climbed up to get them. While he was trying to cut through the stems, a black fly named Njinn-I-Nyakk began to buzz around him, dashing into his eyes, against his nose, and all over his face. He raised his hand to drive it away, and as he did so, the knife fell from his grasp. “Run, run,” he called to his wife, who was just beneath the tree, for he feared that it might fall upon her. It was the woman’s seventh month of pregnancy, but she sprang aside so quickly that she was out of the way before the knife reached the ground. In her haste, she jumped over a serpent called Nkimm. This startled the snake so much that he dived down a brown rat’s hole and begged for a drink of water. Rat handed him a full calabash, and he emptied it in one gulp. Rat was so frightened by her visitor that she sprang past him out of the hole and ran up a tree, where she sat trembling. The place she had chosen was near Nkundak’s (Greater Plantain-eater) nest. No sooner did the bird see her than she raised a war cry. This startled a monkey named Nyak-I-Mbuk (Black Monkey), who rushed out ready for a fight. In his haste to meet his enemy, Nyak sprang onto a ripe fruit of the tree called Ntun. This fell from its stalk onto the back of an

<meta>This page continues the folk tale "Why Bush Fowl Always Calls Up the Dawn," detailing the chain of events that led to the darkness and the judgment of Obassi upon the Black Fly and the Bush-fowl.</meta>

elephant who was passing beneath. The latter rushed away so furiously that he tore down and carried off a flowering creeper called Mfinn, which caught around his neck.

The Mfinn in turn pulled over an ant heap, which fell onto Bush-fowl’s nest and completely destroyed her eggs.

Bush-fowl was so sad because of her loss that she sat brooding over the crushed eggs and forgot to call the dawn. For two days, therefore, the whole world was dark.

All the beasts wondered what could be the reason for this continued night, and at length Obassi summoned them before him to inquire into the matter.

When all were present, Obassi asked Bush-fowl why it was now forty-eight hours since she had called for light. Then she stood forth and answered:

> “My eggs were broken by Ekughi Nke (ant hill), which was pulled over by Mfinn, which was dragged down by Elephant, who was hit by Ntun fruit, which was plucked by Monkey, who was challenged by Nkundak, who was startled by Rat, who was frightened by Serpent, who had been jumped over by a sick woman, who had been made to run by the fall of a knife, which had been dropped by her husband, who had been pestered by a black fly. Out of vexation, therefore, at the loss of my eggs, I refused to call the day.”

Each thing and every beast was asked in turn to give the reason for the damage it had done, and each in turn gave the same long answer, until it came to the turn of Black Fly, who was the first cause of all the mischief. He, instead of answering properly as the others had done, only said, “Buzz, buzz.” So Obassi commanded him to remain speechless forevermore, and to do nothing but buzz about and be present wherever a foul thing lies. To Bush-fowl, he also gave judgment that she should call instantly for the long-delayed dawn and never again refuse to do so, whether her eggs were destroyed or not.

Were it not that Obassi had given strict orders to Bush-fowl, it might easily happen that one day or another she would again refuse to call, and then we should unwittingly enter a long night, which might perhaps last for a week or more.

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

### WHY FROG AND SNAKE NEVER PLAY TOGETHER.

Frog had a son. Snake also had a son. Both children went out to play in the bush. They said, "We feel hungry; let us go home." When they arrived at home, each of them went to his mother’s house. Mrs. Frog asked her son, "Where have you been this morning?" He said, "I was in the bush playing with Snake-child." His mother said, "Don’t you know that the Snake family are bad people? They are poisonous."

Also, when the little Snake went home, his mother asked, "Who was your playmate?" Snake-child said, "Frog was my playmate." Mrs. Snake said, "What foolishness is this to come and tell me you feel hungry! Don’t you know that it is the custom of our house to eat frogs? Next time you play with him, catch him and eat him."

Snake-child therefore went to call Frog to play with him again, but the latter refused. Snake-child then said:

"Clearly your mother has given you instructions. My mother has also given me instructions."

From that day on, Frog and Snake never played together again.

### HOW THE FIRST HIPPOPOTAMI CAME.

Once, long ago, Elephant had a beautiful daughter, whom all the beasts wished to marry. Now at that time, a very large fish named Njokk Mbonn (Elephant fish) lived in the river, and one evening he came to Elephant and said, "I should like to marry your daughter."

Next morning Leopard came as well, and said, "Do not let anyone marry the girl but me." When he heard that the King of the fishes had also asked to marry her, he was very angry and went home to call all his family together to fight. Nsun (the antelope) happened to pass by while they were arranging the matter, and he went at once and said to Fish:

"Listen to what I have heard today. Leopard and all his people are coming to fight you."

When Njokk Mbonn heard this, he said nothing, but only took a yam and roasted it. When it was ready he ate part, and put the rest to one side. Just then he heard the sound of his

## HOW BLACK AND WHITE MEN CAME ON EARTH.

->BY OJONG OF OBAN.<-

In the beginning of things, Obassi had only one wife. These two were the first of all people. Before them, neither man nor woman had ever been.

In course of time, the woman bore four children to her husband. Two were white and two black.

One day, when the children were yet young, the father called

the two boys, and sent them out hunting, while the mother told both girls to go and fish.

Now, when the white girl had been down by the river for a little while, she saw a bird catching fish and noticed that it had already thrown several on the bank. These she took and ran quickly home to give them to her mother, but the black girl still went on slowly fishing with her nets in the river.

Meanwhile, the white boy thought, "Why should I trouble myself to go hunting?" So he took his mother's goat and skinned it. Then he brought it to his father and said, "Here is an antelope which I have just killed in the bush."

When the black girl returned with the fish she had caught, her mother said, "The white girl has brought me all that I want, and to her I have given the reward which I promised to both of you."

After a time, the black boy came back with a fine antelope (<term>Nsun</term>) which he had killed, but when he laid it down before his father, the latter said:

"I have already accepted enough fresh meat from my white son, and to him I have given the hunter's reward."

In the course of time, the children grew up and thought of marriage. When this had taken place, Obassi sent the black son and daughter into the bush to live far away, but the white children he kept with him always.

When some years had gone by, the white son and daughter came to their father and said, "Where are our black brother and sister?" To which Obassi answered, "I have sent them a long way off."

Another day they came again and said, "We wish to see our brother and sister." But again they were answered, "I have made a very high fence in the road and cut down many trees so that the way is quite blocked up. You cannot go through to visit them."

Again, a third time they pleaded, but once more Obassi answered, "I have already told you, you cannot pass by and come to their town without my order."

## THE TREASURE HOUSE IN THE BUSH.
### BY OJONG AKPAN OF MFAMOSING.

Obassi Osaw had two sons. The name of the first was Oro, and the second was Agbo. When their father died, Oro took all the property, while Agbo remained in the sky as a poor washerman. One day, Agbo said to his wife, "There is no food for either you or me. I must go into the bush and hunt, so that we may not die of hunger." He traveled along a road that brought him down to earth and led him at length to a part of the bush where a house stood by itself. He wondered whose it might be and crept behind some bushes to watch unseen.

Soon, some white people came through the bush close to where the hunter was hidden. He saw them open the door, carry out a great treasure, and then lock it up again.

When his wife saw what he had brought, she said, "Where did you get all this?" He answered, "From a house in the bush where white people keep it."

Some days later the hunter went down again, and once more brought back a great load of treasure. When he had secured as much as he wanted, he went to his elder brother and said:

"Please lend me a basket; I wish to measure my money."

Oro did as he was asked, but one of his wives thought, "I should like to know how this poor man can suddenly have become rich." She followed Agbo, and, when they reached his house, offered to help him measure the money.

It took seven days to measure, and, when at last all was ended, the woman went back and told her husband how rich his brother had grown. On learning this, Oro went straight to the latter's house and said, "Open the door and let me see what you have got."

Agbo replied, "Why should I show it? I am but a very small man compared to you." His wife, however, said, "Open the door and let him see." So at length it was opened.

When Oro saw what was stored within, he asked, "Where did you get all this?" Agbo replied, "It came from the Treasure House of the white people, which I found in the bush." Then the elder brother began to beg the younger to show him the place, and the latter said, "Tomorrow I will not go; but if you will come for me the day after, we will set out." This they did, and when they reached the house, they entered and carried off a load.

Another day Oro said, "I want to go again;" but Agbo replied, "You must go alone. I will go no more." This time, therefore, the elder brother set off by himself. When he reached the Treasure House, he crept in by the way his brother had made; but instead of quickly gathering together some of the treasure, he saw rich robes lying in a heap on one side and began trying them on. One after another he tried, and each seemed to him more gorgeous than the last. While he was still

While he was robbing the house, the owners came in. They bound him, cut him into pieces, and laid the fragments on the threshold.

When night came, Agbo grew anxious because his brother did not return. All night he waited, and, when day dawned, he set out along the path which Oro had taken. On and on he went until he came to the house in the bush. There—oh, terrible sight!—he found the fragments of his brother's body lying before the door. He collected every piece and carried them sadly away. After a while, he sought out a tailor and said, "Here is the body of a man who was cut to pieces in the bush. Can you sew it together again? If you will do this for me, I will pay you richly." The tailor answered, "I will try to see what I can do."

When the owner of the treasure returned and found all the pieces gone, he was very angry. He thought, "Who can have carried away the dead man's body, and what can have been done with it?" In his turn, he also went to the tailor and asked, "Has anyone brought you pieces to repair?" The tailor replied, "Yes, a man named Agbo brought some."

The owner asked, "Who is Agbo? I do not know him." One of his servants answered, "I know who he is, and I can find out all about him."

One day, therefore, this boy sought out Agbo and said, "I want to be your friend."

Agbo was willing and cooked <term>chop</term> for his guest, but his son said, "My father, do not be friends with this boy, for he will go and tell his master all that you have done, and then they will come and kill you."

The servant went back to earth and told everything. In the night time, he came again with some white paint and painted all the posts of Agbo's house. After this, he returned and told his master, "The place where the man lives who has wronged you will be easy to find, for I have marked it with white paint. In the morning, therefore, you can go with a large following and kill him, along with all who dwell in his <term>compound</term>." Now, a bright moon had been shining while the servant worked, and the son of Agbo had seen what was done. So he also got white paint and ran hastily around and painted all the houses in the town in the same way.

## HOW HUMAN BEINGS GOT KNEE-CAPS.

Once, long ago, a woman named Nka Yenge went fishing in the river. Many other women were with her. They all went into the water, some downstream and some up. Now deep down in one of the pools, a smooth white stone was lying, something like a Nimm stone. As the women went by, several of them said, "What a beautiful stone!" but when Nka Yenge came, she stood looking at it for a long time and said, "I wish I could get that stone!" When she came back she said the same thing, and as she passed a third time she said:

> "I must have that stone."

Suddenly the stone sprang out of the water and struck against her knee. There it stayed and she could not loosen it; so she went home weeping with pain. On the way there, she met a man, who asked, "Why do you weep?"

The woman could not speak because of her tears, but the stone answered, "I was lying in the water. When the woman passed up and down, she said that she wished to have me. Her wish was so strong that it drew me up out of the water. Now I have joined myself to her, and shall never leave her again."

The man was very sorry and called to the woman, "Come here. We will go to my house, and I will try what I can do." When they reached his house, he got a strong knife and tried to chop off the stone, but it was no use. The stone had gone inside.

That is the reason why we have knee-caps. Previously we did not have any.

The man did as he was asked, and Stomach went inside.

When Hair came up, he asked the man:

"Have you seen Stomach go by?"

The man answered, "No. What is the matter?"

Hair told him all that had happened, and the man answered:

"Ah, ha! That is why Stomach was so anxious to hide. He has now gone inside my body."

Hair said, "I do not believe you." Nevertheless, he bent down his head and put his ear to the man's belly. He heard it shaking with fear, and then knew that his enemy was truly inside.

Then Hair took teeth, and set them all around the man's mouth. To these he said:

"If my enemy tries to come out this way, bite him, but do not let him escape."

He himself settled in the man's nose, and around both eyes, so that his enemy might not pass out from there, and also above the mouth in a moustache, so that he might watch over Teeth.

## HOW OBASSI OSAW PROVED THE WISDOM OF TORTOISE.

->By ANJONG NTUI ANIMBUN OF NSAN.<-

Obassi Osaw married many wives. Among these was the daughter of Tortoise. She was so proud of her father that she annoyed Obassi by exclaiming, “Oh, my father, you have more sense than any other person!” whenever the least thing happened, even if she only knocked her foot or felt surprised.

Obassi determined to find out for himself if Tortoise was really so very wise. He therefore built a room without doors or windows. Into this he secretly let down eight persons, and sent for Tortoise to come at once and tell him what was within.

Tortoise sent back a message saying that he would certainly come the next day, but in such a way that no one should see him enter; for he was surely the wisest of men, and none could know how he arrived. Obassi was even more displeased when he heard this.

Now the daughter went and told Tortoise that her husband was annoyed with her for constantly praising her father’s wisdom. “Perhaps,” she said, “it is to prove this that he has sent for you.” Tortoise answered, “It is well.”

The next morning, Obassi sent other messengers to bid his father-in-law hurry, but when the men arrived, Tortoise was nowhere to be found. His wife said that he had gone hunting, so the messengers had better not wait. They agreed to this and set out once more. The woman ran after them with a parcel and said, “Will you please take this to my daughter?”

The men promised to do this and gave the parcel to the girl, not knowing that it was Tortoise they were carrying. She carried the packet before Obassi, set it on the ground, and unfastened the <term>tie-tie</term>, when out stepped—what? Tortoise himself.

Obassi was very much surprised and told the guest to go and stay in his daughter’s house until the next morning. So they went off together.

He also ordered that the beast be positioned upright so as to look at his judge above. Obassi further decreed that whenever a person wished to make a sacrifice to him, a tortoise should be offered in this way. That is why we often see a tortoise impaled before jujus, or at crossroads.

### WHY NKI <note>Small Dormouse (*Graphiurus C. dorotheae talboti*)</note> LIVES IN THE TOPS OF PALM TREES.

A new piece of land had been cleared by the people of a certain town. The next morning, when they went there to work, they found the place fouled. They made an inquiry, but the offender could not be found. Therefore, the head chief gave a gun to Ise and set him to keep watch.

When night fell, Ejaw <note>Civet cat</note> crept out of the bushes and began to foul the place as before. Ise took aim and shot him, then ran and told the people what he had done.

At daybreak they all went out and brought in the body. They cut up the meat and asked Ise to dry it in the smoke of the fire so that they might feast upon it the next day. Ise did as he was told, and, when he had laid the pieces in order upon the drying shelf, sat down to watch by the hearth.

Now Nki loved fresh meat and thought of a way that he alone might feast upon the kill. He took a large jar of palm wine and went to visit Ise. The latter was very thirsty, so he drank a deep draft and then lay down and fell asleep. While he slept, Nki stole all the meat; then, when dawn broke, before the theft could be discovered, this treacherous animal took a drum and stood in the open space before the Egbo house playing:

Ise awoke and found all the meat gone, so he cried out:

At this the people said, “It is just,” so they killed Ise and gave his body to Etuk <note>Bay duiker</note>, so that it might be smoked before the fire.

Nki did as before, stole the meat, and at daybreak beat upon the summoning drum. So Etuk lost his life just as Ise had done, and his meat was entrusted to Nkongam <note>Yellow-backed duiker</note>.

On him Nki played the same trick, with the result that he also was killed, and his body given in charge to Ngumi <note>Boar</note>. This latter animal also fell victim to Nki in exactly the same manner as the other beasts, and this time Mbaw <note>Large dormouse (*Graphiurus hueti*)</note> was chosen to smoke the meat.

Now the latter is a very cunning animal, and as soon as he had reached his house, he laid the meat upon the drying shelf and spread great lumps of rubber over it. Next, he piled the fire high so that the rubber grew soft, and then he sat down to wait for the thief.

The thief thought that all was now safe, so he rose up softly and laid his hand upon the meat. At once, the rubber caught him and held him fast. At dawn, Mbaw went out and beat upon the summoning drum, “Day breaks now, we may know each other; drier of meat, come and give meat.”

The people came together and found the thief caught fast. They debated how he could best be punished for the deaths of all those beasts who had died through his fault.

While they talked together, each proposing a more cruel fate than the last, Nki began to wring his hands and weep. With each new suggestion he heartily agreed, adding always, “Yes, yes, kill me in any of these ways, only do not fix spears in the ground and throw me up so that I may fall upon their points.”

The people were so angry that they shouted, “Since he dreads this death above all others, it is by this that he shall die.” They got spears and fixed them firmly in the earth, points upward. Then they freed Nki from the rubber which had held him until now and placed him before the spears. Six of the strongest men advanced to seize him and fling him into the air, but to everyone's surprise, he himself gave a great leap and sprang up a palm tree which stood near.

At once, the people got axes and cut down the tree, but before it fell, Nki sprang to another. Then they said:

“If we follow this man, we shall ruin all the palm trees. It is better to leave him alone.”

<vocab>Nki, Mbaw, folk-lore, palm wine, meat, rubber, summoning drum, punishment, spears, palm tree</vocab>

<summary>Nki the thief is caught by a rubber trap and sentenced to death by being thrown onto spears, a fate he craftily suggested himself through reverse psychology. He uses the momentum of his toss to escape into the palm trees, leading the people to give up their pursuit to save their trees.</summary>

### THE LORD OF THE BUSH.

In the beginning of things, Nkimm (Python) and Njokk (Elephant) were Lords of the Bush. They argued together as to which was the strongest. One said, “The bush belongs to me.” The other answered, “No, it is mine.” Osian (the black ants) listened and said, “In seven days’ time, let us all fight; then he who beats the others shall be called Lord of the Bush.” The two great beasts laughed, because the ants are so small; but they agreed, and from that time the ants gathered together over every tree and rock. When the seventh day came, they began to fight. First, they saw Iku. They surrounded him and bit him so badly that he ran to the river and drowned. Next they sought out Nkimm, whom they found with his young ones. They came in such thousands that the great snake had to take his children and flee to the water, where they escaped. Next the ants pursued the monkeys, many of whom they killed, while the rest sprang up into very high trees, calling out, “We leave the ground to you.”

After this the Osian gathered themselves together in vast numbers and set out to fight with Njokk; but the latter only laughed. For several days they fought, but could not prevail, and at last sent a message to their king that the battle went against them, and that they would all be trampled to death beneath the great feet of their enemy if help were not sent.

Then the King of all the ants called together his people, even to the last one, and they came in such numbers that the whole earth was dark with them. Into Elephant’s mouth they poured and into his eyes, his nose, and his belly, until he could no longer stand against them, but fled to the water for refuge as the other beasts had done. When the bush creatures saw him fleeing, they knew for certain that the ants were lords of the bush. So they called a meeting and brought out a great chair. The

### WHY A MURDERER MUST DIE.

There was once a woman named Ukpong Ma, who had only one daughter. Just before it was time to put the girl into the fatting-house <note>A traditional room or house where young women are secluded and fed to prepare for marriage or womanhood.</note> the mother died.
One day the husband, whose name was Uponnsoraw, set out for market. On his way, he passed through a neighboring town, where he saw a beautiful woman and persuaded her to return with him as his wife.
When the couple reached the man's house, his daughter came out to greet them, and the new wife saw that in a little while her stepdaughter would be more beautiful than she. So she hated the girl and thought how she might destroy her.
One day, therefore, when the husband went out to hunt, the new wife called to her stepchild and said, "Take the great water-pot and go to the far river for water. Do not bring home any from the nearby streams."
As soon as the girl had set out, the new wife killed a goat, ate the best part of the meat herself, and hid what was left over.
As the girl came back from the river, it began to grow dark. Rain fell and she felt cold. When she reached home, she went to the fireside to warm herself. Some water fell down on her, and she said to the new wife, "Where does it come from?" and the latter answered, "The roof leaks."
When Uponnsoraw came back from the hunt, he could not see the goat, so he called to his daughter and asked where it was. She answered, "Your new wife sent me to the river for water. I have only just come back and do not know what has been happening at home."

# IN THE SHADOW OF THE BUSH

At this, the cruel stepmother came out of her room and said:
> "Let us perform the ritual to find who has stolen the goat."

They sent for the <term>Diviner</term>, and he came with a very long rope and said:
> "We will go down to the river where the girl filled the jar."

Now the new wife was a powerful witch, so she secretly made a strong <term>charm</term>. Then, when they came to the river and threw the rope across, she stood on the edge and called:
> "If I have stolen the goat, may the rope break and let me fall into the river. If I am innocent, may I walk over safely."

She put her foot upon the rope, but the charm held, and she crossed without mishap.

The young girl stood by the riverside and said the same words. Then she walked on the rope as far as the middle of the stream. There, the charm which the witch had made caused the rope to break, and the girl fell into the water. A large crocodile came up to the surface and caught her as she fell. Then all the people said, "She was the one who stole the goat." Only her father said:
> "My daughter never stole anything. I must find out the reason for her death."

A palm tree grew by the riverside, right by the place where the girl was lost, and one day a man climbed it to collect palm wine.

Now beneath the water was the house of a <term>were-crocodile</term>, and she was the one who had seized the girl and kept her all this time as a slave. When the man began to climb the palm tree, the crocodile was angry. So she took an axe, put it into the girl’s hand, and said:
> "Go up to the surface of the water and throw this axe at the man, so that he will leave my palm tree and go back where he came from."

The girl did as she was told, but threw the axe so as not to hit the man. As it struck the tree, the climber looked down and saw her. He therefore went back to his town in a great hurry and told her father what had happened.

The father was astonished and went before the chief and said:
> "This man says that he saw my daughter, who died two years ago in the great river."

The chief was angry because he thought that the man was lying. So he ordered that chains should be brought and put

<meta>This page serves as the book's epilogue or "L'Envoi," where the author transitions from the preceding folklore to personal reflections on their experiences in the African wilderness.</meta>

# L’ENVOI

Sitting now, in the very heart of the bush—writing, with some regret, the final words of what has been a work of pure pleasure for me, however tiring a task it may have proved to those who made fair copies of my illegible manuscripts—I cannot help but feel how powerless mere words are to express, even faintly, the charm of such a land. At best, one can only provide the bare bones of a country that can hardly be surpassed for sheer beauty. Green as if carved from the heart of an emerald, flushed by opal dawns and sunsets, watered by crystal-clear streams, and gleaming with the flash of countless waterfalls, it may be called—like the famous orchid—"Beautiful as the seven deadly sins." Yet all its loveliness cannot quite hide the deadliness lurking beneath; even on the strongest and most energetic people, the strain of the climate must take its toll after a while. The government has done wonders regarding improved drainage and so forth, but many years and enormous spending will be necessary before the country can become habitable for white men for more than short terms of service.

There are times when the beauty around you fails to soothe the sting of hordes of sandflies and mosquitoes; when you stand at the <term>theodolite</term> <note>a precision surveying instrument for measuring angles</note>, they seem determined to leave no spot on your face or hands unmarked. Nor does it relieve the torture of prickly heat as you toil painfully up some hill during the almost ceaseless journeys necessary to maintain law and order. Yet, even at the worst of times, when you are tempted to ask with Mary Kingsley, "Why did I come to Africa?", you only have to let your eyes wander over the loveliness around you to answer as she did: "Why! Who would not come to Hell’s twin brother itself for all its beauty and charm?"

<summary>The author reflects on the breathtaking beauty and inherent dangers of the African bush, acknowledging the physical hardships of colonial service while concluding their writing with a sense of wonder.</summary>
<keywords>Africa, L'Envoi, Mary Kingsley, theodolite, colonial service, natural beauty, climate, environment</keywords>

<meta>This page begins Appendix A, providing a detailed explanation of the cultural taboos and social rules that govern how game is distributed among family and community members after a hunt.</meta>

## APPENDIX A.

### Taboos.

THERE are many strict laws and taboos (*Ntubi*) which regulate the distribution of animals killed in the hunt.

After a town hunt, one front leg and one hind leg of each animal killed must be given to the townspeople. The neck becomes the property of the man who stood nearest during the kill, the tail belongs to the hunter's mother, and one leg and the back go to the father or the head of his household, while the head and the remaining front leg are left for the person who made the kill.

When a man hunts alone or with one companion, the rules vary according to the animal killed.

In the case of a boar, the tail is given to the mother, and the two legs and feet are given to the father or head of the household, though he usually returns the feet. The cheeks and jaws must be cooked for the hunter’s age group; half of the head and the stomach are given to the wife, and the other half of the head is given to the companion, leaving the two front legs for the hunter himself.

Both the water chevrotain and the bay duiker must be brought whole before the head of the household, who returns everything except the two hind legs. A similar rule applies to Ogilby’s duiker, except that this is always taken to the hunter’s father. If the father is dead, there is no obligation to offer it to the head of the household.

The rules regarding porcupine, blue duiker, and monitor lizard meat are similar, but they are not as strictly observed.

Elephant, buffalo, yellow-backed duiker, pangolin, civet cat, and genet must also be brought before the head of the household.

If these rules are violated, a Juju will afflict the hunter with a sickness from which he will not recover except through confession and sacrifice. In the case of a genet, the illness is supposed to take the form of elephantiasis.

<vocab>Taboos, Ntubi, hunting customs, animal distribution, Juju, water chevrotain, bay duiker, Ogilby’s duiker, porcupine, blue duiker, monitor lizard, yellow-backed duiker, pangolin, civet cat, genet, elephantiasis</vocab>

It also describes the spiritual punishments, such as sickness or elephantiasis caused by a Juju, for those who fail to follow these traditions.</summary>

--- Page 544 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of animal taboos, detailing the specific consequences of eating restricted species and how these laws apply differently to men, women, and social classes.</meta>

The taboo on the harnessed antelope has been described on page 142.

If a man keeps a male drill ape or chimpanzee for himself, certain death is supposed to follow; if the kill is female, an illness follows from which recovery is unlikely.

When a leopard or python is killed, the heart and gall are cut out and buried in a deep hole, and the earth is beaten down over them. Anyone eating these would die (see page 27). Only slaves eat leopards; for free men, they are taboo.

Regarding birds, the monkey-killing eagle and the greater plantain-eater must be taken to the head of the household.

Neither man nor woman may feed on any scavenger bird, such as the vulture, nor on the owl, because the owl is a witch's familiar. If killed, the owl must be offered up on two posts at the entrance to the town. The kingfisher is also forbidden as food. When killed, its skull is dried, powdered, mixed with leaves, and given as cough medicine.

Members of the Juju Mfam are forbidden from eating the bird called "Aru."

Many people may not eat the fish called Ecchan or Mbonn, the heads of which are ground up and used as "medicine."

Among the taboos for men alone, the principal ones are the fish Eddokk—which, if a hunter eats it, will cause him to be killed in the bush—and the crab, "The Father of all Jujus," the eating of which would prevent a man from participating in any ceremonies.

A woman may not eat (*a*) *nandinia binotata*, as a child born afterward would surely die;
(*b*) Wild cat, to avoid becoming barren.
(*c*) Anything killed by a leopard or wild cat; otherwise, her child would be stillborn.
(*d*) Crocodile, as her child would be born with scaly skin and die.
(*e*) The greater plantain-eater.
(*f*) The first thing caught in her husband's new trap (see the story on page 114).

The majority of these taboos probably arose from totemic causes, others from sanitary reasons, and some, obviously, from the desire of the older men to obtain a full share of what was killed by their younger members.

<header>APPENDIX A</header>

### Taboo on Fish for Men, Meat for Women.

One day Obassi Nsi called all the people on earth together. He said, "I am making a law concerning the food that is proper for you. You may eat the fruits of the earth, both men and women, but among living creatures, only women may eat fish, and only men may eat the meat of animals."

There was a woman named Aiya Ita, who had a husband named Atu Utup (<term>Efik</term> word for hunter). One day each of them went out: she to the river, and he to the bush. After she had been fishing for a little while, she caught a fine fish. She took it home and boiled it in her pot. When it was finished, she ate some of it, and some she left for the next day.

In the evening, Atu Utup came home. He had hunted all day but killed nothing, and he was very hungry. He saw the fish that his wife had left, and he took a piece and ate it.

Then a bird came out of the bush and settled on the branch of a tree that grew close to the house. Through a small hole in the wall, he saw what the man had done. At once, he flew away to Obassi Nsi and told him what he had seen.

Obassi sent for the hunter and said, "You have gone against the rule I made that no man should eat fish. Therefore, you must die."

After the man was dead, Obassi thought, "The rule that I made is too hard for my people." So he sent for them and called them before him again, and said:

> "From today, I remove the law. Men may eat fish. Women may eat meat. Only, no woman may eat the genitals of any animal killed by a hunter. Should she do so, the hunter will never be able to kill again, unless he finds out through a charm who it is that has broken my law and makes a proper sacrifice, so that the curse may be lifted from him."

<vocab>Obassi Nsi, Aiya Ita, Atu Utup, Efik, taboo, hunter, sacrifice, law, genitals, curse</vocab>

# APPENDIX B.

## CLUBS (OKUM, PL. AKUM).

The Oban Clubs may be taken as typical of those in most Ekoi towns. They may be roughly divided into (A) those only revived for special occasions, and (B) those in constant use.

### A.

The following are ancient institutions revived under special circumstances—for instance, upon the death of a member of the club, an important chief, or for the funeral customs of such people:

1.
->“ Oshum njum ka etemm. Oba eku ka nju,<-
->“ Draw thing in bush. Come die in house.<-
->Owomm okpaw.”<-
->Want die.”<-

*i.e.*, When a hunter shoots animals in the bush, he only comes to his house to die if he fails to satisfy the inhabitants. The meaning is that members of his household would want to share in his kill, and would probably poison him if he did not satisfy them.

This was originally a club for avenging the murder of its members, and was a very powerful association in old days. When a dance is performed, big rattles are worn, and should a member put on an Okum dress without the permission of the President, the superstition is that the dress would stick to him and could not be laid aside until the old men had made sacrifices in atonement.

2.
->“ Ewaw ekabomm ’ne.”<-
->“ (Name of Okum) does not cut a person.”<-

When the dance proper to this is performed, an old man must get water, mix medicine in it, and pour it over the bodies of the members while repeating the above words. The Okum carries a large cane structure on his head. The fine of a ram is levied on anyone who should cross in front of the dancers.

<summary>This page introduces the social clubs or secret societies (Akum) of the Ekoi people, specifically describing ancient clubs revived for funeral rites and their associated traditions.</summary>
<keywords>Oban, Ekoi, Okum, Akum, secret societies, funeral customs, ritual dances, Oshum njum ka etemm, Ewaw ekabomm ’ne, hunter traditions</keywords>

--- Page 547 ---
<meta>This page continues Appendix B, further detailing the various social clubs and secret societies of the Oban region, moving from ancient funeral-related associations to more active social, military, and dancing clubs.</meta>

3.
->“ Okpe etuma.”<-
->“ (The name of the Okum) jumps.”<-

This club is so named because the Okum must never stand still. He is always accompanied by two female attendants carrying mirrors. One goes before him and one follows behind.

4. 
->“ Orui. Achibbi wa njimm.”<-
->“ Go. Turn to back.”<-

“Go and come back.” These words are said to a member who, after breaking a rule, is sent to fetch the fine ordained as punishment. The name also has a secondary meaning of “backbiting” during the man’s absence.

5. “ Ikadum.” The Okum wears a skull. This club performed war dances, especially when its members returned with the heads of enemies. Meetings are never held in the town, but in the bush nearby. Guns are fired at all celebrations.

6. “ Ayunga.” Upon the death of a member, his family must pay one goat, 20 yams, and 4 bottles of palm wine to the club. The eldest son is elected in his father’s place. This society formerly used to serve as executioners for those condemned to death by the <term>γερουσια</term> <note>a Greek term used here to refer to the council of elders</note>.

7. “ Esere Ise.” No one could be found who was willing to explain the meaning of this, but the words appear to point to the practice of enforcing a trial by ordeal. Its functions were only described as those of a dancing club.

8. “ Ukwa.” This is the lodge of a Calabar club. Members dance with long swords to the accompaniment of two large drums.

9. 
->“ Adia. Akere idemm.”<-
->“ Eat. Think of yourself.”<-

A dining club. The name signifies that, while being entertained in another man’s house, you must remember that it will soon be your turn to act as host.

10. “ Erong-Isonn ” (Efik). “ Knee to the earth.” This is a dancing club. When plays are performed, rattles are worn above the knee.

11. 
->“ Ukai ke isonn obio, Oban ” (Efik).<-
->“ Life is difficult in the town of Oban.”<-

A dancing club, started by an age class whose members had gotten into trouble with the Chiefs of Oban and were heavily fined as a consequence.

<summary>This page describes various Ekoi and Efik social clubs, ranging from war-dance societies and executioners for the council of elders to dining clubs and groups formed in response to legal fines.</summary>

# APPENDIX B

12. “Nchibbi achi ebai.”
“ (Name of Okum) heads two.”

The Okum wears a large two-faced head, with one side male and the other female, decorated with the feathers of the Greater Plantain-eater. The dancers hold machetes and guns and fire the latter at intervals.

No woman can belong to any of these clubs, and none except the free-born, after passing middle age, can belong to any except the last mentioned.

->B.<-

The following are those most prominent at the present day. Any free-born man, or “member,” can join them, while women may also belong to the first one.

1. “Ikkpai,” Whip. At dances, every member carries a whip. The Okum wears two white feathers above a carved head. This association was formerly more powerful than it is now.

2. “Utap-Anam.” “Touch take from,” *i.e.*, Should you injure our club, we will fine you.

This was originally started by two age classes. Women may neither join in the dances nor see the instruments proper to the club. These are long hollow pieces of wood, which, when rubbed together, produce a loud, harsh sound. Juju worship is connected with the rites.

3. “Ekang.” When the Okum comes out, a young palm leaf and other prickly leaves are tied about him. Should he meet a non-member, he catches hold of the man so that the leaves scratch and hurt him.

4. “Ekkpo Njawhaw” (Efik). “Ghosts break,” a lodge of an Ibibio club. A common plan to increase membership of this society is to take the Okum to the house of a friend who is a non-member. Should the latter be unprepared to provide entertainment without notice for so large a number of guests, his plates and calabashes are broken by the club. The association probably owes its name to this proceeding, as the damaged property looks as if it were broken to lay on a grave for the use of the ghosts.

5. “Obbonn” (Efik and Ekoi). “Chief.” This club dances at night, and no woman may be present.

<keywords>Okum, Ikkpai, Utap-Anam, Ekang, Ekkpo Njawhaw, Obbonn, Efik, Ibibio, Ekoi, secret societies, tribal rituals, membership rules</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of secret societies and social clubs in Appendix B, specifically detailing clubs 6 through 10 and noting the distinctions between free-born and "member" associations.</meta>

# APPENDIX B

6. "Itiatt Obbonn." "Stones of the Chief." Connected with the last-named society. Only old men can become members, and a considerable amount of Juju worship is mixed with its rites. There is no dancing.

7. "Angbo." It is impossible to learn the meaning of this word. Every town has a lodge. In many, none but adults are allowed to join. Dances are always held at night, and no woman may be present.

8. "Nsikpe." A new and powerful club brought from Onun, near Calabar. The Okum wears a tall cane construction on his head, and much Juju is connected with its rites.

9. "Mfuor." This is specially devoted to the worship of the great Juju "Asunga." It is very powerful in some towns.

10. "Ekkpa." This is a powerful club in which the worship of Nimm Asam is very strong. It differs from the others because it is a women's club (see p. 225).

"Members" <note>This term likely refers to a specific social class, such as non-free-born residents or slaves, as distinguished from the "free-born."</note> have many clubs of their own. The mysteries of one of these, named "Kpifonn," may be witnessed by no free-born man nor by any woman.

All clubs have different tunes and unique ways of beating the drums, so that even at a distance it is easy to tell which of the many societies is holding a celebration.

# APPENDIX D.

## ORTHOGRAPHY.

The <term>system of orthography</term> used in this book, with the few exceptions noted below, is the one established by the Royal Geographical Society and fully explained in “Hints to Travellers.” As stated there, the broad features of the system are:—
(a) “That <term>vowels</term> are pronounced as in Italian and <term>consonants</term> as in English.
(b) Every letter is pronounced, and no extra letters are introduced.
(c) Only two <term>accents</term> are used:
1. The <term>acute</term>, to denote the syllable on which stress is placed.”
2. The sign ˘, which I have used over the short and open u, a, i, and o, when followed by ng, to avoid the more awkward nng.

To express the different sounds of the vowel u, three methods are used:—
(α) When pronounced as in “up” or “lull,” the following consonant is doubled as usual, or the sign ˘ is used;
(β) For the sound as in “pull” or “full,” no change is made;
(γ) While for the u sounded as in “flute,” a long mark is placed over the vowel, thus ū.

Before some consonants, a sound like a <term>rough breathing</term> may be heard, which, in the case of m or n, sometimes produces the effect of doubling the consonant. This sound has been marked with a rough breathing symbol, as in “‘Mi’” (moon).

At least two distinct <term>tones</term> are prevalent in the language and serve to distinguish words spelled the same way. Thus, *Nki* spoken on a high note means dormouse; on a low note, it means lion.

As with us, words spoken with a rising <term>inflection</term> denote

questions, e.g., "Akaba? Is he coming?" while without the raised tone, it merely states the fact, "He is coming."
Interrogation is often shown by the use of the word "na" at the beginning of each sentence.
As a rule, equal stress is laid on all syllables.
The letters b and p, r, d and t, sh and ch are often interchangeable, as are also, though more rarely, l and r; or it may be more accurate to say that sounds exist midway between these, which are not accurately represented by either. The same man, too, when repeating a word, will often interchange consonants.
A final vowel is elided when the following word begins with another vowel.
The detailed system of phonetics employed by some authorities does not seem applicable in the case of the tribes under consideration, since pronunciation varies considerably even within the same town.

# APPENDIX E.

## A SHORT GRAMMAR OF THE EKOI LANGUAGE.

### NOUNS.

Nouns are usually derived from verbs. The most common ways are:
1. By prefixing a vowel to the verb root, *e.g.*,
| | |
|---|---|
| Kott, love (verb). | Okott, love (noun). |
| Ji, go. | Eji, place. |
| Siri, speak. | Esiri, story. |

2. By prefixing a consonant, generally *n* or *m*, to the verb root, *e.g.*,
| | |
|---|---|
| Fonn, have. | Mfonni, possessor. |
| Chott, to speak. | Nchott, speaker. |
| Berk, cut. | Mberk, cutter. |

3. By prefixing *e* and affixing *m*, *um*, *umm*, *emm*, or *imm* to the verb root, *e.g.*—
| | |
|---|---|
| Maghe, leave. | Emaghum, abandonment. |
| Yimm, do. | Eyimmum, action. |
| Fap, go. | Efapumm, departure. |

Words formed in the latter way are verbal nouns, and may be used as infinitives.
Plurals are formed by changing the prefixes as follows:
| Singular. | Plural. |
| :---: | :---: |
| O | A |
| M | A |
| E | M |
| N | O |
| N | A |
| M | O |
| E | A |

->etc. etc. etc.<-

Examples will be found in the vocabulary.

Gender is shown in a few cases by the use of different words, *e.g.*,
->Nse, &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; father. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Nyenn, mother.<-
->Ntemm, male friend. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Nat, &nbsp; &nbsp; female friend,<-
but is usually denoted by
->Num (plural, arum), male.<-
->Nkai ( &nbsp; ,, &nbsp; akai), female,<-
placed before the word modified, *e.g.*,
->Num mfŏng, bull. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Nkai mfŏng, cow.<-
->Num njaw, &nbsp; he dog. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Nkai njaw, &nbsp; bitch,<-
except in the case of
->'Ne-num, man &nbsp; (plural, ane-arum),<-
->'Ne-nkai, woman ( &nbsp; ,, &nbsp; ane-akai).<-
No trace of declension has been found.

## ADJECTIVES.

Adjectives agree in number with the noun modified and form their plurals in the same way as the nouns, *e.g.*,

| Singular. | Plural. |
|---|---|
| Eébi, bad. | Abi. |
| Enopp, good. | Anopp. |
| Ndam, long. | Adam or Aram. |
| Iruk, small. | Nduk. |
| Ibonne, little. | Mbonne, |

with the exception of those formed—as is common today—by doubling the noun, *e.g.*,
->Ewak, quickness. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Ewak-ewak, quick.<-
->Efebbum, cleverness. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Efebbum-efebbum, clever.<-
These never change in the plural.
Degrees of comparison are expressed by the introduction of other words; the comparative by "Achinge," meaning "surpasses," *e.g.*,
> "We enopp achinge 'wa."
> "He is better than you" (literally: "He good surpasses you"),
the superlative by Mfonne, very; Etimm, oldest or last; or by repetition of the word.
*Examples:*—
->Mfonne nyenn, &nbsp; very good.<-
->Etimm eébi, &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; very bad.<-
->Ndam-ndam, &nbsp; &nbsp; very long.<-
->Ngpuk-ngpuk, &nbsp; very short.<-

# APPENDIX E 419

The rules for the position of adjectives are very complicated. Some always precede the noun, while others must follow it. A third class comprises those placed either before or after, probably according to the Ekoi ideas of euphony.

### PRONOUNS.

The personal pronouns are as follows:
->*Singular. Plural.*<-
'Me, I. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Ut or ud, we.
'We, you.* &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Un, you.
'We, he, she, it. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Abaw, they,
when used as the subject of the verb, and by themselves;
'Ngam, me. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Ut or ud, us.
'Wa, you. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Un, you.
'We, him, her, it. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Abaw, them,
when governed by a verb or preposition.

The interrogative pronouns Enne? (who?), Bagha? (which?), and Jenn? (what?) do not change. The other pronouns vary according to the category to which the word qualified belongs, as can be seen in the following list:

### CATEGORIES.†
->*Possessive Pronouns.*<-

| Meaning. | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|----------|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| My, mine (S) | Oma | Éama | Éjama | Ífima | Iima | Áwama | Áama |
| My, mine (P) | Ama or Áama | Áwama | Áama or Éama | Ífima | Ama or Áama | Ama or Áama | Ama or Áama |
| Your, yours (S) | Oa | Ea | Eja | Ifa | Ima | Oba | Ama |
| Your, yours (P) | Aba | Oba | Ama | Ima | Ama | Ama | Ama |
| His, her, hers, it, its (S) | Oe | Egye | Eje | Ife | Ime | Obe | Ame |
| His, her, hers, it, its (P) | Abe | Ebe or obe | Ame | Ime | Ame | Ame | Ame |
| Our, ours (S) | Ora | Egyira | Éjira or Éjara | Ífira or Ífara | Ímira or Ímara | Óbira or Óbara | Ámira or Ámara |

## VERBS.

All verbs are conjugated in the same way as the example given below:

I do, 'me nyimm. You do, 'we oyimm. He, she, or it does, we ayimm. We do, ut eyimm. You do, un oyimm. They do, abaw ayimm.

I do not: 'me nkayimm, 'we okai yimm, 'we akai yimm, ut ekai yimm, un okai yimm, abaw akai yimm.

I am doing: 'me nki yimm, 'we oki yimm, 'we aki yimm, ut eki yimm, un oki yimm, abaw aki yimm.

I am not doing: 'me nka yimm, 'we okai yimm, etc.

I have done: 'me ba nyimm, 'we ba oyimm, 'we ba ayimm, ut ba eyimm, un ba oyimm, abaw ba ayimm.

I have not done: 'me be nkai yimm, 'we be okai yimm, etc.

I have been doing: 'me na nyimmi, 'we na oyimmi, etc.

I have not been doing: 'me nka yimm, etc.

I had done: 'me nde nyimm, 'we ore oyimm, 'we are ayimm, ut ere eyim, un ore oyimm, abaw are ayimm.

I had not done: 'me ka ndaw nyimm, 'we ka oraw oyimm, 'we ka araw ayimm, etc.

I had been doing: 'me nde na nyimm, 'we ore na oyimm, etc.

I had not been doing: 'me are nkai yimm, 'we are okai yimm, 'we are akai yimm, etc.

I shall do: 'me tikk (or tukk) nyimm, 'we tikk oyimm, etc.

I shall not do: 'me tikk mawyimm, 'we tikk omawyimm, 'we tikk amawyimm, ut tikk emawyimm, un tikk omawyimm, abaw tikk amawyimm.

I am about to do: 'me njawe nyimm, 'we ojjawe oyimm, 'we ajawe ayimm, ut ejawe eyimm, un ojjawe oyimm, abaw ajawe ayimm.

I am not about to do: 'me mawjawe nyimm, 'we omawjawe oyimm, etc.

I shall be doing: 'me tikk njawe nyimm, 'we tikk ojjawe oyimm, etc.

I shall not be doing: 'me tikk mawjawe nyimm, 'we tikk omawjawe oyimm, etc.

I shall have done: 'me ta ba nyimm, 'we ta ba oyimm, etc.

I shall not have done: 'me kpe nkai yimm, 'we kpe okai yimm, etc.

I would do: 'me kun nyimm, 'we kun oyimm, etc.

I would not do: 'me kun mawjawe nyimm, 'we kun omawjawe oyimm, etc.

### *Imperative.*

Do: yimm; Do (plural): yimm un.

### *Infinitive and Verbal Noun.*

To do or doing: eyimmum.

No sign of a passive voice has been discovered.
"A" is added to the verb when it is followed by a plural object, for example: 'Me nyimm njum, I do a thing; 'Me nyimma mbimm, I do things.

## SYNTAX.

The construction of sentences is very simple, as can be seen from the interlined stories shortly to be published. Conjunctions are rarely used. The order of words closely resembles that of English.

## NUMERALS.

The Ekoi divide all things into seven principal categories or classes. The first nine numerals are inflected according to the category to which the word they qualify belongs:

->CATEGORIES.<-

| No. | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|-----|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | wat | yit | jutt | futt | mat | butt | mat or butt |
| 2. | abai | ebai | ebai | mbai | abai | abai | abai |
| 3. | asa | esa | esa | nsa | asa | asa | asa |
| 4. | ani | eni | eni | ni | ani | ani | ani |
| 5. | aronn | eronn | eronn | ndonn | aronn | aronn | aronn |

<meta>This page continues Appendix E, transitioning from the linguistic analysis of Ekoi numerals and syntax to the numerical system of the Ododop people, focusing on their unique grouping methods, ordinals, and numeral adverbs.</meta>

<language>English</language>
<page-type>appendix</page-type>
<page-num>423</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX E</header>

Ododop, unlike neighboring tribes, have built up their numerical system principally on groups of three and four.
There are no proper ordinals, but the following phrases are used:
The first cow, ndagha-mba (the leader on the road) mfŏng.
The second cow, mfŏng ennyere (following).
The third cow, ennyere-ennyere mfŏng.
The fourth cow, mfŏng ennyere mfŏng esa.
The fifth cow, mfŏng ennyere mfŏng eni.
Numeral adverbs are formed by the word ntimm:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Once, ntimm yit.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Twice, ntimm ebai.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thrice, ntimm esa, etc.

<vocab>Ododop, numerical system, ordinals, numeral adverbs, mfŏng, ndagha-mba, ennyere, ntimm, yit, ebai, esa, eni</vocab>

## NSIBIDI SIGNS.

<image-desc>Four Nsibidi characters are arranged in a circular configuration around a central title. 
- Top: An arched, bell-like form containing a vertical rectangular element, topped with a radiating semi-circular halo. 
- Left: A hook-shaped character with small crossbars at both the upper and lower terminals of the line. 
- Right: A complex, interlocking calligraphic symbol with several loops and strokes. 
- Bottom: A horizontal shape tapering to points at each end, with a central sun-like motif consisting of a circle with internal radiating lines.</image-desc>

<header>APPENDIX G</header>

### NSIBIDI SIGNS.

<image-desc>
Twelve numbered Nsibidi signs or pictograms.
(1) Two stylized human figures with arms outstretched toward each other, surrounded by small rectangular and circular shapes.
(2) Two vertical curved lines facing inward with a central vertical line featuring small lateral strokes (the Egbo feather).
(3) A six-pointed star within a hexagon.
(4) Two bulbous shapes joined at a central point.
(5) Two horizontal crescent shapes (canoes) with four small crosses surrounding them.
(6) A complex diagram showing a central element with multiple small humanoid figures extending from either side.
(7) Two horizontal curved lines facing each other with a small line in the middle.
(8) Two outward-curving lines back-to-back with a horizontal bar between them.
(9) A circle containing a pedestal-like shape.
(10) Two crossed lines with a textured, dotted oval at the center.
(11) A line ending in a loop with a series of short lines radiating from the bottom.

# APPENDIX H.

## BOTANY.

The Oban District has a marvelous flora. Of the 2,000 varieties we collected in 1911–12, about 150 new genera and species have already been identified by authorities at the British Museum—Dr. Rendle, F.R.S., Mr. E. G. Baker, Mr. Spencer Moore, and Mr. H. F. Wernham—to whom we owe deep gratitude for the kind interest they have shown. My wife has made 1,600 life-sized drawings, mostly in watercolor, of new and rare species.

It would be impossible to give an adequate idea of the country's flora here, but the British Museum is soon to publish a descriptive catalog of the collection. We also hope to issue a volume a little later containing full descriptions and colored plates of the new genera and species. To support this, the Royal Society has most kindly indicated its intention to provide a grant, subject to the approval of referees.

### (1) FUNGI.

*List kindly supplied by Mr. Massee of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.*

### *Galago demidoffi*, Fisch. (Monni Ebopp).

Unlike the larger forms, this small lemur enjoys a very wide geographical distribution; specimens from the Gold Coast, Nigeria, Cameroons, and the Congo all appear to be representatives of the same species.

Both of Mr. Talbot's examples of this extraordinary bat were male specimens; the unique development of the nasal region is well illustrated by these two individuals. This bat is popularly known as the hammer-headed fruit bat.

<header>APPENDIX I</header>

->*Anomalurus beecrofti argenteus*, Sch. (Ebhagi).<-

Two specimens are in complete agreement with Schwann's type, which came from Abutshi, 150 miles from the coast on the Niger River. The general pale silvery-grey tint, which is so dominant in the coloring of this flying squirrel, readily distinguishes it from all related forms.

->*Sciurus poensis*, Sm. (Isumm).<-

There appears to be no significant difference in general color between these Nigerian specimens and individuals from Fernando Po, the type locality. Probably with the help of a larger series, some racial differences might become apparent, but for the present, it is best to consider these specimens as representing the island species.

->*Sciurus stangeri*.<-
->*Heliosciurus rufobrachiatus*, Waterh. (Irun Ebange).<-

This appears to be the most common of all West African squirrels. In general coloring, this species shows a very wide range of variation, chiefly due to the bleaching of the dark-brownish tints into a rich rusty red.

->*Funisciurus auriculatus oliviæ*, Dollm., <term>sp. nov.</term> (Ebange).<-

This strikingly colored squirrel is now represented in the Museum collection by six specimens, all exhibiting the same beautiful coloring as described in the original description.

This handsome squirrel is readily distinguished from related forms by the bright, yellowish coloration of the hindquarters and lower back, the yellowish-olive neck, shoulders, and limbs, the almost pure reddish-orange color of the head without any conspicuous black speckling, and by the pale buff tint of the entire underside. *Funisciurus auriculatus*, *a. boydi*, and *a. beatus* are all much more reddish on the back, a great deal darker on the neck and shoulders, richer in color on the underside, and have the back part of the head speckled with black or yellow and black.

->*Funisciurus leucostigma talboti*, <term>sp. nov.</term> Thos. (Ikomme).<-

This squirrel was described by Mr. Thomas in a paper on "New African Squirrels" published in November 1909; since that date, further specimens of this interesting squirrel

->*Graphiurus hueti*.<-
->*Graphiurus crassicaudatus dorotheae* (Dollm.), <term>sp. nov.</term><-

The type specimen and one other are the only known representatives of this interesting dormouse. It appears closely related to the Liberian *crassicaudatus* and, at present, represents the eastern limit of that group. The cranial characteristics shown by these two forms are quite unlike those found in the “*murinus*” group; the only similarity to these conditions is found in the large *Graphiurus hueti*, which agrees with the *crassicaudatus* group regarding the broad cranial and inter-orbital regions and the narrow, parallel-sided nasal bones. These cranial characteristics, considered together with the matter of the distichous tail, appear to justify the conclusion that the *crassicaudatus* group are smaller relatives of the large West African dormice belonging to the *hueti* group.

A large collection was made, but it has not yet been analyzed. The authorities of the British Museum inform me, however, that it contains a considerable number of specimens new to science.

<header>APPENDIX I</header>

### (6) CRABS.

Crabs exist in great numbers in the District, as might be guessed from the prominent part which they play in ritual and folklore. My collection has not yet been fully studied, but according to Mr. A. T. Calman, “Some appear to come near the species known as <term>Potamon (Potamonautes) Pobeguini</term>, but the group to which they belong is still very imperfectly known, and it is difficult to speak positively as to the identification.”

### (7) MOLLUSCA.

No shells new to science have been discovered in the District, but various points in the life history of some of them have been observed which were previously unknown.

The large <term>Achatina Marginata</term>, for instance, possesses the power of screaming. This fact is well known to the natives, who were much amused at my start of surprise when one of these snails screamed upon being taken into my hand. It is supposed that the noise is produced by the creature scraping against its shell. At any rate, the sound is loud enough to prove distinctly startling on a first experience.

Another small land snail has the power of springing 3 to 4 feet.

Fine clusters of <term>Ætheria</term> are to be found in the beds of the rivers, especially in the Kwa.

# APPENDIX J.

## MINERALOGY.

->Information provided courtesy of Dr. Prior.<-

Minerals are present throughout the District in very large quantities. As an example, the compositions of panned samples from eleven rivers, which Mr. W. Campbell Smith of the British Museum (Natural History) kindly analyzed for me, are provided below:

| No. | Name of River | Number of Pans | Weight | Remarks |
|:---:|:---|:---:|:---:|:---|
| 1 | Mo, near Nkami | 2 | 389 gms. | Fine-grained. Consists mainly of <term>ilmenite</term>, with a large amount of <term>magnetite</term>. <term>Zircon</term> is abundant in microscopic, colorless crystals. Some fragments of pink <term>garnet</term> are present, along with rounded <term>quartz</term> grains. |
| 2 | Awa, near Nfunum | 2 | 68 gms. | As above (1), but very rich in pink <term>garnet</term> in small crystals and fragments. |
| 3 | Akup, near Ojokk | 1 | 32 gms. | Very fine-grained. <term>Magnetite</term> is much more plentiful than in any other sample. <term>Zircons</term> and <term>garnets</term> only occur as microscopic crystals, the latter being quite scarce. |
| 4 | Ekku, near Ako | 2 | 116 gms. | Coarser-grained. <term>Ilmenite</term> with a great deal of <term>magnetite</term>. <term>Zircons</term> are very abundant in colorless prisms with a brilliant luster, often 1 mm long. Pink <term>garnets</term> are also abundant. No <term>cassiterite</term> was found. Contains rounded grains of <term>quartz</term>. |

# APPENDIX K

The rainfall from June to December 1909 amounted to 116.83 inches, and the total for the entire year of 1910 was 144.10 inches. The latter was an exceptional year, and many streams dried up that had never been known to fail before. According to local reports, the rainfall during 1911 was below average.

<summary>This page provides supplemental rainfall statistics for 1909 and 1910, noting that 1910 was an unusually dry year that caused typically reliable streams to dry up, and records that 1911's rainfall was also considered below average.</summary>
